## Overview

The Shoshone or Shoshoni, also known by the endonym *Newe*, are an Indigenous people of the United States. Their four large cultural and linguistic divisions are Eastern Shoshone in Wyoming, Northern Shoshone in southern Idaho, Western Shoshone in California, Nevada, and northern Utah, and Goshute in western Utah and eastern Nevada. They traditionally speak Shoshoni, a Numic language in the Uto-Aztecan language family. As of 2020, 17,918 people in the USA were identified as Shoshone, including 3,638 in Nevada and 3,491 in Wyoming. Their material culture includes hunting weapons, bags, clothing, and objects represented in museum collections, while their language, regional bands, historical movements, and preservation programs are documented in the sources.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Laxskinnsväska** — A museum catalogue records a salmon-skin bag made about 1960 by Cora George at Fort Hall, Idaho, for the Tukuryka Shoshone. The bag has a decorative band around its opening and a light-skin strap attached to its short sides; the salmon skin is described as hard and stiff.

The sources used do not document additional Shoshone textile or pattern traditions, including coiled basketry, willow basketry, burden baskets, tule mats, rabbit-skin blankets, or parfleche.

### Clothing & dress

The museum records depict Shoshone men wearing tunics, leggings, moccasins, cloth shirts, hide leggings, blankets, jackets, trousers, and neck ties. A British Museum photograph shows four young Shoshone women and a Shoshone child wearing cloth tunic dresses. Another photograph shows a Shoshone woman with a baby in a baby carrier. The sources do not provide a systematic account of everyday or ceremonial dress, nor do they document named Shoshone garment terms, belts, head coverings, or distinctions between men’s and women’s clothing beyond these catalogue descriptions.

### Architecture

The sources mention traditional homes made from *sosoni*, high-growing grasses. Some neighboring tribes called the Shoshone “Grass House People” on this basis. The sources used do not describe the structure, roof, decoration, or construction of these homes, and they do not document a named Shoshone house type such as a willow wickiup.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

A catalogue records a horn bow from the United States, dated 1854, made from the horn of a bighorn sheep and covered on the inside with sinew. The record states that horn bows were less common among Plains Indians and occurred chiefly among the Shoshone, Crow, Blackfeet, and others. A Metropolitan Museum of Art record lists a 19th-century frame drum made of wood, possibly ash, and sheepskin. The sources do not document Shoshone ceramics or metalwork.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum photographs record ear-rings and a large round disc worn on the neck by Chief Washakie, a shell neck ornament worn by one Shoshone man, and a circular metal fastening on a neck tie worn by another portrait subject. The sources do not describe the meanings or ritual functions of these objects, nor do they document tattoos, henna, named jewelry types, or hair practices beyond a photograph showing hair in two bunches wrapped in decorated fabric.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not document Shoshone musical genres, named song traditions, performance contexts, or musical instruments beyond a 19th-century frame drum listed by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. The source catalogue identifies the drum as made of wood, possibly ash, and sheepskin, but does not associate it with a specific Shoshone performance tradition.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document named Shoshone dances, theatrical traditions, dramatic genres, or ceremonial and entertainment performances.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not describe an annual Shoshone festival calendar, life-cycle rites, weddings, funerals, or coming-of-age ceremonies. They do record that the Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation acquired the site of the Bear River Massacre in 2008 in order to protect the holy land and build a memorial to the massacre. The sources do not provide further details about Shoshone ritual practice.

## Foodways

The sources do not document Shoshone dishes, cooking methods, dietary rules, or ceremonial foods. They do record traditional bands whose names refer to food sources, including the Salmon Eaters, Jack Rabbit Eaters, Porcupine Grass Seed Eaters, Wild Wheat Eaters, Groundhog Eaters, Fish Eaters, Pinenut Eaters, Tule Eaters, Ricegrass Eaters, Ryegrass Seed Eaters, and Buffalo Berry Eaters. The source material does not describe how these foods were prepared or consumed.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Shoshone call themselves *Newe*, meaning “People,” and the name “Shoshone” comes from *Sosoni*, a Shoshone word for high-growing grasses. Meriwether Lewis recorded the tribe as the “Sosonees or snake Indians” in 1805. The sources used do not document Shoshone folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, or named narrative cycles. They do document contemporary language-preservation work, including Shoshoni classes, digital language archiving, dictionaries, recordings, and a Shoshone language video game released in August 2013.

## Language & religion

Shoshoni is a Uto-Aztecan language of the Numic branch, spoken primarily in Wyoming, Utah, Nevada, and Idaho. Its principal dialects are Western Shoshoni in Nevada, Gosiute in western Utah, Northern Shoshoni in southern Idaho and northern Utah, and Eastern Shoshoni in Wyoming. The language is classified as threatened, while UNESCO has classified it as severely endangered in Idaho, Utah, and Wyoming. Shoshoni has no single agreed-upon writing system; the Crum-Miller system and the Idaho State system are the two main systems in use. The sources mention holy land connected with the Bear River Massacre but do not describe a religious system, denomination, or detailed spiritual practices.

- Raymond Bial, *The Shoshone*, Benchmark Books, 2002.

## Overview

Paiute refers to three non-contiguous groups of Indigenous peoples of the Great Basin: Northern Paiute people of northeastern California, northwestern Nevada, eastern Oregon, and southern Idaho; Southern Paiute people of northern Arizona, southern Nevada, and southwestern Utah; and Mono people of east central California, divided into Owens Valley Paiute (Eastern Mono) and Western Mono (Monache). The term is a historical label rather than the name of one single, unified group. Their languages are related within the Numic group of Uto-Aztecan languages, although the three languages do not form a single subgroup. The museum records associate Paiute objects with the western United States and with people living near Pyramid Lake, in Nevada.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document named Paiute textile or pattern traditions in sufficient detail for this section.

**Basketry** — The catalogue records include baskets made of basketry and string, a water-bottle made of twigs and pitch, and a completely watertight bottle made of plant fibers. One record describes a basket as made by the Pah-utes and identifies it as a so-called Navajo Wedding basket.

**Triangular foundation** — A museum record states that the Ute and Paiute both employ a triangular foundation consisting of three rods of sumac (*Rhus*). It contrasts this with Navajo basketry, which uses a triangular foundation of two rods of sumac, with the top formed by softer yucca leaf.

**Pah-Utes basketry** — The catalogue records state that Navajos originally made a certain type of basket for themselves but later traded textiles for baskets made by the Pah-utes.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no Paiute motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The photographic records document Paiute men wearing cloth shirts, blankets, leggings, moccasins, ear ornaments, hair ornaments, necklaces, embroidered garments, and beaded decoration. One man is described as wearing a warrior shirt with beaded decoration and tassels and holding a tomahawk. A Paiute woman identified as Young Antelope (Won-si-vu) is shown wearing a fringed tunic, loin covering, and cloth headband. Another Paiute woman, Ka-ni, is described as wearing a fibre loin covering. Other records show Paiute women wearing headbands, necklaces, blankets, and moccasins. The sources also describe children wearing cloth tops, jackets, necklaces, and blankets. The sources used do not distinguish everyday from ceremonial dress beyond these catalogue descriptions.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Paiute architecture, house forms, building materials, roofs, decoration, or urban traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum records document water-bottles and baskets. One bottle is made of twigs and pitch; another is made of plant fibers and is completely watertight. The catalogue also includes a cradle or cot and a bear basket. The sources used do not document Paiute ceramics, metalwork, wooden tools, or other household forms in further detail.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The photographic records describe ear ornaments, hair ornaments, beads in the hair, beaded necklaces, and necklaces. One Paiute man has a section of his hair in a plait wrapped in cloth, while another is described with two sections of hair wrapped in cloth. The sources also document embroidered clothing, beaded decoration, and a cloth headband. The sources used do not document tattoos, ritual functions, or named Paiute adornment types.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not document Paiute instruments, song genres, musical performances, or performance contexts.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document Paiute dances, theatre, dramatic traditions, or ceremonial and entertainment performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not document an annual Paiute festival calendar, life-cycle rites, weddings, funerals, or other rituals. One museum record preserves a legend associated with Pyramid Lake: the sound of crying children is sometimes heard coming from the lake, and the sound tempts people into the water, where they drown because of strong underwater currents. The same record states that without these spirits there would be no water and that people must show the water proper respect.

## Foodways

The sources used do not document Paiute staple foods, cooking methods, dishes, ceremonial food, beverages, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The museum catalogue records one legend associated with Pyramid Lake. According to the record, crying children are sometimes heard from the lake; the sound draws people into the water, where they drown because of strong underwater currents. The record states that without these spirits there would be no water and that people must show the water proper respect. The sources used do not document Paiute folktale collections, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, storytelling contexts, or contemporary literary preservation.

## Language & religion

Paiute language may refer to any of the languages spoken by Paiute people. The sources name Northern Paiute language, also known as Numu and Paviotso; Mono language (California), specifically the Western dialect, also known as Owens Valley Paiute; and Colorado River Numic language, also known as Ute, Southern Paiute, Ute–Southern Paiute, or Ute-Chemehuevi. The Paiute languages are related within the Numic group of Uto-Aztecan languages, but the three languages do not form a single subgroup. The museum record concerning Pyramid Lake describes spirits associated with the lake and states that people must show the water proper respect. The sources used do not cover scripts or the current religious landscape.

## Overview

Paiute is a historical label for three non-contiguous Indigenous groups of the Great Basin. These are Northern Paiute, Southern Paiute, and Mono. Their languages are related but do not form one single subgroup. Museum records connect Paiute objects with the western United States and people near Pyramid Lake, Nevada.

## Material culture

The records focus on basketry, water-bottles, clothing, blankets, moccasins, beads, and hair ornaments.

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources give little detail about named textile or pattern traditions, but they describe distinctive basketry and basket foundations.

- **Pah-Utes basketry** (*Pah-utes*) — Catalogue records say Navajos later traded textiles for baskets made by the Pah-utes.
- **Triangular basket foundation** (*Rhus*) — Ute and Paiute basket makers use a triangular foundation of three sumac rods, unlike the Navajo two-rod foundation.
- **Navajo Wedding basket** (*Pah-utes*) — One basket made by the Pah-utes is identified in a record as a so-called Navajo Wedding basket.
- **Watertight plant-fiber bottle** — The records include a completely watertight bottle made of plant fibers.
- **Twigs-and-pitch water-bottle** — Another recorded water-bottle is made of twigs and pitch.

### Clothing & dress

Paiute clothing records show cloth garments, blankets, leggings, moccasins, fringed tunics, loin coverings, and beadwork.

- **Warrior shirt** — One Paiute man wears a warrior shirt with beaded decoration and tassels.
- **Fringed tunic** (*Won-si-vu*) — Young Antelope, or Won-si-vu, is shown wearing a fringed tunic with a loin covering and cloth headband.

### Architecture

The sources do not describe Paiute houses, buildings, materials, roofs, decoration, or towns.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The records describe containers, baskets, a cradle or cot, and a bear basket, but give little detail about other everyday objects.

- **Twigs-and-pitch water-bottle** — This bottle is made of twigs and pitch.
- **Watertight fiber bottle** — This bottle is made of plant fibers and is completely watertight.
- **Cradle or cot** — The museum catalogue includes a cradle or cot.
- **Bear basket** — The museum catalogue includes a bear basket.
- **String basket** — The catalogue records include baskets made of basketry and string.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Adornment records emphasize ear and hair ornaments, necklaces, beads, embroidered clothing, and wrapped hair.

- **Ear ornaments** — Paiute photographic records show men wearing ear ornaments.
- **Hair ornaments** — The records describe hair ornaments and beads worn in the hair.
- **Beaded necklace** — Paiute people are shown wearing beaded necklaces and other necklaces.

## Music & performance

The sources do not document Paiute instruments, songs, musical performances, or performance settings.

## Dance & theatre

The sources do not document Paiute dances, theatre, dramatic traditions, or ceremonial performances.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not describe a festival calendar or named rites, but one Pyramid Lake legend teaches respect for the water.

- **Pyramid Lake water-respect tradition** — A record says lake spirits provide water and that people must show the water proper respect.
- **Crying children of Pyramid Lake** — The sound of crying children is said to tempt people into the lake, where strong underwater currents cause them to drown.

## Foodways

The sources do not document Paiute foods, cooking, dishes, drinks, ceremonial meals, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The catalogue preserves one Pyramid Lake legend about crying children, lake spirits, drowning, and respect for water.

- **Pyramid Lake crying-children legend** — The legend says crying children are heard from the lake and draw people into dangerous underwater currents.
- **Pyramid Lake spirits** — The record says that without the spirits there would be no water and that people must respect the water.

## Language & religion

Paiute languages belong to the Numic group of Uto-Aztecan languages, while the sources describe lake spirits and respect for Pyramid Lake water.

- **Northern Paiute language** (*Numu*) — Northern Paiute language is also called Numu and Paviotso.
- **Paviotso** — Paviotso is another name for Northern Paiute language.
- **Mono language** (*Western dialect*) — Mono language in California includes a Western dialect also known as Owens Valley Paiute.
- **Owens Valley Paiute** — Owens Valley Paiute is another name for the Western dialect of Mono language.
- **Colorado River Numic language** (*Ute-Chemehuevi*) — Colorado River Numic language is also known as Ute, Southern Paiute, Ute–Southern Paiute, or Ute-Chemehuevi.

title: "Kiowa"
subtitle: "United States"
region: "North America"

## Overview

The Kiowa, also called *Ǥáuigú*, are a Native American tribe and Indigenous people of the Great Plains of the United States. They migrated southward from western Montana into the Rocky Mountains in Colorado during the 17th and 18th centuries and reached the Southern Plains by the early 19th century. Their homeland included areas adjacent to the Arkansas River in southeastern Colorado and western Kansas, together with the Red River drainage of the Texas Panhandle and western Oklahoma. In 1867, they were forced onto a reservation in Southwestern Oklahoma. Today the federally recognized Kiowa Tribe is headquartered in Carnegie, Oklahoma; there were 12,000 Kiowa tribal citizens as of 2011. Kiowa belongs to the Tanoan language family and is severely endangered. Kiowa culture is documented through seasonal mobility, horse culture, tipi life, warrior societies, Sun Dance practices, calendars, music, clothing, foodways, and ceremonial objects.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Parfleche** — Kiowa women painted geometric designs on parfleche. The sources identify parfleche as rawhide containing camping goods, but do not describe particular construction methods or named designs.

**Hide painting** — Hide paintings adorned the outside and inside of tipis, with special meanings attached to certain designs. Kiowa women also painted geometric designs on hides.

**Beadwork** — Museum records describe multi-coloured beadwork on skin moccasins, glass-bead decoration on black ceremonial moccasins, a black beaded sash, and a black beaded belt. The catalogue records do not identify a named Kiowa stitch or compare the work with neighboring traditions.

**Quillwork** — The sources state that Kiowa women later beaded and quilled hides, but provide no further technical description.

**Black Leggings regalia** — A museum catalogue records a replica of Gus Palmer Sr.’s ceremonial Black Leggings regalia, including an eagle feather headdress, a Warrior costume, a black beaded sash, fringed leggings, black beaded moccasins, and a black beaded belt.

**Blankets** — A museum record describes a rectangular red cotton blanket with fringing and repeated geometric patterns sewn in black, red, and white, connected by white cotton triangles.

**Garlands and wreaths** — Kiowa use *Plantago virginica* to make garlands or wreaths for old men to wear around their heads during ceremonial dances as a symbol of health.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name geometric designs and geometric patterns; they do not provide a fuller motif vocabulary.

### Clothing & dress

The sources describe clothing in both Kiowa life and museum records. Kiowa women tanned and skin-sewed hides, painted geometric designs on parfleche, and later beaded and quilled hides. Kiowa horses could be decorated with beaded masks, sometimes with bison horns attached to the sides, and feathers in their manes. During ceremonial dances, old men wore *Plantago virginica* garlands or wreaths around their heads.

The museum records include skin moccasins with multi-coloured beadwork, skin moccasin-boots with glass beads and brass buttons, and replicas of black beaded moccasins made from black leather or hide, glass beads, and metal tinkling cones. The Black Leggings regalia replica includes two fringed black textile leggings, a black beaded sash, a black beaded belt with metal buckle, and a Kiowa eagle feather headdress made from imitation eagle feathers, imitation otter fur, felt, and beadwork. A replica Kiowa Warrior costume includes a backdrop dragger made from fake black otter fur on red textile and decorated with medal buttons. The photographic records show chiefs and women wearing shirts, vests, blankets, shawls, bracelets, rings, scarves, peace medals, and woven hats.

### Architecture

The principal Kiowa dwelling was the *tipi*, also called a skin lodge. Tipis were conical structures made from bison hides shaped and sewn together. Wooden lodge poles, generally 12–25 feet (3.7–7.6 m) long, supported the structure; these poles were harvested from red juniper and lodgepole pine. Tipis had at least one entrance flap and smoke flaps at the top, allowing smoke to escape from the fire pit. Animal pelts and skins lined the floor for warmth and comfort.

The tipi was designed to remain warm during cold winter months and cool during warm summer months. It could be collapsed easily and raised in minutes, making it suitable for nomadic life. The poles could also be used to construct a travois. Hide paintings decorated the outside and inside of some tipis, and the sources state that particular designs had special meanings. Before horses were introduced, domestic dogs pulled travois carrying tipis, belongings, and small children; horses later performed this work.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources do not describe Kiowa ceramics. They document wooden bows, lodge poles, long lances, bows and arrows, tomahawks, knives, war clubs, rifles, shotguns, revolvers, and cavalry swords. Shields were made from tough bison hide stretched over a wooden frame or from bison skulls. Weapons and shields could be decorated with feathers, furs, and animal parts such as eagle claws for ceremonial purposes.

Museum records include a dark-wood bow with a thin sinew cord and two lines of green paint on the shaft. They also record a commercially tanned leather belt decorated with connected pressed chromed-steel medallions bearing engraved and repoussé floral and geometric designs. A woman’s *skärppåse med nålhus* is listed in the Museum of World Culture catalogue, but the sources do not explain its use beyond identifying it as a woman’s belt bag with needle case.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources do not document named Kiowa jewelry types, tattoos, or henna traditions. They do record hair and bodily adornment. The ancient Kiowa hairstyle was cut horizontally from the lower outside edge of the eyes to the back of the ears; the corresponding sign for Kiowa in Plains Indian Sign Language refers to this hairstyle. The cut helped prevent hair from becoming tangled while shooting an arrow from a bowstring.

Museum photographs show Kiowa chiefs and women wearing ear ornaments, bracelets, rings, pocket watches suspended from chains, peace medals, scarves, cloth ties, and woven shawls. Kiowa horses were decorated with body paint applied by a medicine man for ritual and spiritual purposes, including good fortune and protection during battle.

## Music & performance

Kiowa music is the music of the Kiowa Tribe of Oklahoma and forms part of the larger Southern Plains Indian music genre. Historically, it was strongly focused on dancing, including the gourd dance. The modern gourd dance follows Kiowa protocol and social mores, and most songs were composed or handed down by Kiowa song makers.

The sources name several song traditions: Brush Dance songs and Buffalo Dance songs, which commemorate the outlawed Kiowa Sun Dance; flag songs honoring warriors of the past, the present, and the people; memorial songs; Peyote songs; War Journey songs, also called 49 songs; war mother songs; victory or scalp dance songs; handgame songs; and hymns. Kiowa music is closely connected with warrior societies, including the Black Leggings Society, the Oh-Ho-Mah Lodge, and the Kiowa Gourd Clan.

Ceremonial elements of the four-day *k'aw-tow* included mock sham battles, purifying sweat baths, erecting the center cottonwood pole, building the arbor, bringing in brush, spreading sand, building the sacred Taimé altar, unveiling the Taimé by the Taimé keeper, distributing shields, ritual body painting, prayers, speeches, dancing, eagle-whistle blowing, visions, and feasting by pledge makers’ and dancers’ families.

The Smithsonian Institution made recordings during the 1930s, 1940s, and 1950s. Early 20th-century Kiowa recordings are held by the Library of Congress’s Archive of Folk Culture, Indiana University American Indian Studies Research Institute, the Oklahoma Historical Society’s Oklahoma History Center, and the Kiowa Tribal Museum. Named singers and musicians include Spencer Asah, Jack Hokeah, Stephen Mopope, Cornel Pewewardy, Tom Mauchahty-Ware, Terry Tsotigh, and the Cozad Singers, Bad Medicine Singers, Zotigh Singers, and Thunder Hill Singers.

## Dance & theatre

The sources describe dances and ceremonial performance but do not document a Kiowa theatrical tradition. The gourd dance is a major named performance tradition, and the four-day *k'aw-tow* included dancing, ceremonial preparation, ritual body painting, prayers, speeches, eagle-whistle blowing, visions, and feasting. Modern Brush Dance songs and Buffalo Dance songs commemorate the Kiowa Sun Dance, which the source describes as outlawed.

During the annual Sun Dance, bands had distinct responsibilities. The Kogui conducted war ceremonies; the Kaigwu guarded the Sacred or Medicine bundle and the holy lance; the Kinep or Khe-ate performed police duties and ensured security; and the Kâtá supplied bison meat and other foods. The Semat participated equally but had no specific duties. The sources do not describe masks, dramatic characters, or staged theatre.

## Festivals & rituals

The Kiowa held a yearly Sun Dance gathering. The Kiowa name given for the Sun Dance is *K’áu:d̶ó*. The ceremony involved a tipi ring, band obligations, war ceremonies, the Sacred or Medicine bundle called *Tai-mé* or *Taimay*, a holy lance, shields, ritual body painting, prayers, speeches, dancing, eagle-whistle blowing, visions, and feasting. The Kâtá supplied bison meat and other foods; the Kogui conducted war ceremonies; the Kaigwu guarded the Sacred or Medicine bundle and holy lance; the Kinep or Khe-ate ensured security; and the Semat had no specific duties.

The sources also describe funeral practices. Death was associated with dark spirits and negative forces, and spirits were believed to remain around corpses, burial places, former living spaces, and possessions. Families demonstrated grief through wailing, ripping off clothes, shaving the head, and, in some accounts, body lacerations and cutting finger joints. Women and the widowed spouse were expected to express mourning more openly.

Before burial, the body was washed; historically, a woman combed the hair and painted the face. Burial occurred promptly, preferably on the same day, or the following morning if death occurred at night. After burial, most belongings were burned with the tipi. If the tipi or house was shared, surviving relatives moved into a new house. The sources do not provide information about Kiowa birth, marriage, or coming-of-age rites.

## Foodways

The Kiowa historically had a nomadic hunter-gatherer society. The American bison or buffalo was their most important food source. Before horses, bison were hunted on foot with arrows and long lances; after horses were acquired, bison were hunted on horseback with bows, arrows, and lances. Women prepared bison meat roasted, boiled, and dried.

Dried meat was made into *pemmican* by grinding lean meat into powder and mixing it with a near-equal weight of melted fat or tallow, sometimes with berries. The mixture was shaped into bars and kept in pouches for use while travelling. The Kiowa also sometimes ate parts of the bison raw. Other hunted animals included deer, elk, pronghorn, wild mustang, wild turkey, bears, lizards, waterfowl, skunks, snakes, and armadillos. During difficult times, they raided ranches for Longhorn cattle and horses.

Women gathered berries, tubers, seeds, nuts, vegetables, and wild fruit. Plants important to Kiowa cuisine included pecans, prickly pear, mulberries, persimmons, acorns, plums, and wild onions. Squash, maize, and pumpkin were acquired through trade and raids. Before metal pots were obtained from Europeans, meat and vegetables were boiled in an earth-lined pit filled with water and heated with fire-heated rocks.

## Oral tradition & literature

One Kiowa origin story says that the people came into the world through a hollow log, but a pregnant woman became stuck, preventing further people from emerging. Ancient names, including *Kútd̶àu* or Kwu-da, meaning “emerging” or “coming out rapidly,” and *Tépdàu* or Tep-da, relate to this origin narrative.

Kiowa calendars recorded two events each year, creating twice as many entries for a given period as the systems of other Plains tribes that kept pictorial “winter counts.” Little Bluff, or Tohausan, was identified as the first Kiowa calendar keeper; Settan, or Little Bear, and Ankopaaingyadete, commonly called Anko, were later calendar keepers. Silver Horn, or Haungooah, kept a calendar and was a respected religious leader.

The sources do not describe a Kiowa epic, proverb, riddle tradition, or contemporary literary revival. Kiowa language preservation includes teaching grammars, children’s stories, language classes, and a Kiowa Language Department.

## Language & religion

Kiowa is a member of the Kiowa-Tanoan, or Tanoan, language family. The language is spoken primarily in Caddo, Kiowa, and Comanche counties, Oklahoma, and the Kiowa tribal center is located in Carnegie. UNESCO classifies Kiowa as severely endangered; the source states that it had 20 mother-tongue speakers and 80 second-language speakers in 2007. As of 2024, the Kiowa Tribe had a Kiowa Language Department.

Kiowa has been written in several Latin-alphabet systems. Parker McKenzie developed one Kiowa alphabet and worked with John P. Harrington and other linguists. The current alphabet uses barred letters including B̶, D̶, G̶, and n̶, although Unicode support has been problematic. The sources describe Kiowa spiritual beliefs concerning dark spirits, ghosts, the afterlife, the Sacred or Medicine bundle, medicine men, ritual horse painting, Sun Dance practices, Peyote songs, and hymns. They do not identify a formal religious denomination or sect.

- Parker McKenzie and John P. Harrington, *Popular Account of the Kiowa Indian Language*, Santa Fe, University of New Mexico Press, 1948.
- Laurel J. Watkins and Parker McKenzie, *A Grammar of Kiowa*, Studies in the Anthropology of North American Indians, Lincoln, University of Nebraska Press, 1984.
- William C. Meadows and Parker P. McKenzie, “The Parker P. McKenzie Kiowa Orthography: How Written Kiowa Came into Being,” *Plains Anthropologist*, 2001.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiowa
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiowa_language

## Overview

The Kiowa moved south from western Montana to the Southern Plains. Their life centered on seasonal mobility, horses, bison hunting, tipis, warrior societies, music, and ceremony. They were forced onto a reservation in southwestern Oklahoma in 1867. Today the Kiowa Tribe is headquartered in Carnegie, Oklahoma, and works to preserve its endangered language.

## Material culture

Kiowa material culture centers on painted hides, beadwork, quillwork, tipis, weapons, ceremonial clothing, and objects linked to horses and ritual life.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Kiowa women painted hides and made decorated rawhide, beadwork, quillwork, blankets, and ceremonial garlands.

- **Rawhide containers** (*Parfleche*) — Kiowa women painted geometric designs on rawhide containers used for camping goods.
- **Hide painting** — Geometric hide paintings decorated some tipis and carried special meanings.
- **Beadwork** — Beadwork decorated moccasins, sashes, belts, and other ceremonial items.
- **Quillwork** — Kiowa women later decorated hides with beads and quills.
- **Ceremonial garlands** — Garlands and wreaths made from Plantago virginica were worn by old men during ceremonial dances as symbols of health.

### Clothing & dress

Kiowa dress used painted and decorated hides, beaded moccasins, leggings, belts, feathers, fur, and metal ornaments.

- **Black Leggings regalia** — This ceremonial outfit included black fringed leggings, a beaded sash and belt, black beaded moccasins, and an eagle feather headdress.
- **Eagle feather headdress** — The Kiowa headdress used imitation eagle feathers, imitation otter fur, felt, and beadwork.
- **Warrior costume** — A replica Warrior costume included a red textile backdrop dragger made with fake black otter fur and medal buttons.
- **Beaded moccasins** — Moccasins included multi-coloured beadwork, glass beads, brass buttons, leather, hide, and metal tinkling cones.
- **Horse adornment** — Kiowa horses could wear beaded masks, bison horns, and feathers in their manes.

### Architecture

The tipi was a portable, climate-friendly home made from bison hides and wooden poles.

- **Tipi** — The conical tipi used sewn bison hides, wooden poles, smoke flaps, an entrance flap, and animal skins on the floor.
- **Skin lodge** — Skin lodge was another name for the tipi.
- **Travois** — Tipi poles could form a travois for carrying belongings and children.
- **Painted tipi** — Some tipis had hide paintings inside and outside, with special meanings attached to certain designs.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources describe weapons, shields, belts, and a belt bag, but no Kiowa ceramics.

- **Wooden bow** — A museum record shows a dark-wood bow with a thin sinew cord and two green lines painted on its shaft.
- **Bison-hide shield** — Shields were made from tough bison hide stretched over a wooden frame or from bison skulls.
- **Decorated weapons** — Bows, arrows, lances, tomahawks, knives, war clubs, firearms, and swords could carry feathers, fur, and animal parts for ceremony.
- **Steel-medallion belt** — A leather belt was decorated with connected pressed steel medallions bearing floral and geometric designs.
- **Woman’s belt bag** (*skärppåse med nålhus*) — The catalogue lists this as a woman’s belt bag with a needle case.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Kiowa adornment included a distinctive hairstyle, jewelry, clothing ornaments, and ritual horse painting.

- **Horizontal haircut** — The ancient Kiowa hairstyle was cut from the lower outer edge of the eyes to the back of the ears to keep hair from tangling with a bowstring.
- **Ear ornaments** — Photographs show Kiowa people wearing ear ornaments.
- **Peace medals** — Photographs show chiefs and women wearing peace medals.
- **Pocket watches** — Some people wore pocket watches suspended from chains.
- **Ritual horse painting** — A medicine man painted horses for good fortune and protection in battle.

## Music & performance

Kiowa music is closely tied to dancing, warrior societies, ceremony, and songs passed down by Kiowa song makers.

- **Gourd dance songs** — The gourd dance follows Kiowa protocol and social rules.
- **Brush Dance songs** — Brush Dance songs commemorate the outlawed Kiowa Sun Dance.
- **Buffalo Dance songs** — Buffalo Dance songs also commemorate the outlawed Kiowa Sun Dance.
- **War Journey songs** (*49 songs*) — War Journey songs are also called 49 songs.
- **Flag songs** — Flag songs honor warriors of the past, the present, and the people.

## Dance & theatre

Kiowa performance centers on dances and ceremony; the sources do not describe a Kiowa theatre tradition.

- **Gourd dance** — The gourd dance is a major Kiowa performance tradition.
- **Sun Dance performance** (*K’áu:d̶ó*) — The Sun Dance included war ceremonies, dancing, prayers, speeches, body painting, eagle-whistle blowing, visions, and feasting.
- **K’aw-tow ceremony** (*k'aw-tow*) — The four-day k'aw-tow included dancing, speeches, ritual painting, eagle-whistle blowing, visions, and feasting.
- **War ceremonies** — The Kogui conducted war ceremonies during the annual Sun Dance.

## Festivals & rituals

The yearly Sun Dance was the central Kiowa gathering, with strict band duties, sacred objects, ceremony, and feasting.

- **Sun Dance** (*K’áu:d̶ó*) — The Sun Dance used a tipi ring, a sacred bundle, a holy lance, shields, prayers, ritual painting, dancing, visions, and feasting.
- **Sacred bundle** (*Tai-mé; Taimay*) — The Sacred or Medicine bundle was guarded during the Sun Dance and unveiled by its keeper.
- **Funeral mourning** — Families mourned through wailing, tearing clothes, shaving the head, and sometimes cutting the body or finger joints.
- **Prompt burial** — Bodies were washed and buried the same day when possible, or the next morning if death came at night.
- **Burning belongings** — After burial, most belongings were burned with the tipi, and surviving relatives moved if the home was shared.

## Foodways

The Kiowa relied mainly on bison hunting, gathered plants, and food prepared for travel.

- **Bison hunting** — Bison were hunted on foot before horses and on horseback later, using bows, arrows, and lances.
- **Pemmican** — Pemmican was made by grinding lean meat, mixing it with melted fat and sometimes berries, shaping it into bars, and storing it in pouches.
- **Gathered foods** — Women gathered berries, tubers, seeds, nuts, vegetables, and wild fruit.
- **Important plants** — Kiowa cuisine included pecans, prickly pear, mulberries, persimmons, acorns, plums, and wild onions.
- **Earth-pit cooking** — Before European metal pots, meat and vegetables were boiled in an earth-lined pit heated with fire-hot rocks.

## Oral tradition & literature

Kiowa oral history includes an origin story, named calendars, and language teaching materials.

- **Hollow-log origin story** — One origin story says the Kiowa came through a hollow log, but a pregnant woman became stuck and stopped more people from emerging.
- **Emerging name** (*Kútd̶àu; Kwu-da*) — Kútd̶àu or Kwu-da means “emerging” or “coming out rapidly” and relates to the origin story.
- **Coming-out name** (*Tépdàu; Tep-da*) — Tépdàu or Tep-da is another ancient name linked to the origin narrative.
- **Kiowa calendars** — Kiowa calendars recorded two events each year, creating twice as many entries for a period as other Plains winter counts.
- **Calendar keeping** — Little Bluff, Settan, Anko, and Silver Horn were named Kiowa calendar keepers.

## Language & religion

Kiowa is a severely endangered Kiowa-Tanoan language with active preservation work and spiritual traditions tied to ceremony, spirits, and sacred objects.

- **Kiowa language** — Kiowa is spoken mainly in Caddo, Kiowa, and Comanche counties in Oklahoma.
- **Kiowa alphabet** — Parker McKenzie developed a Kiowa alphabet, and the current alphabet uses barred letters such as B̶, D̶, G̶, and n̶.
- **Language preservation** — Preservation includes teaching grammars, children’s stories, language classes, and a Kiowa Language Department.
- **Medicine men** — Medicine men carried out spiritual work such as ritual horse painting.
- **Peyote songs and hymns** — Peyote songs and hymns are part of Kiowa spiritual and musical life.

## Overview

The Arapaho (*Hinono'eino* or *Inun-ina*, “our people” or “people of our own kind”) are a Native American people historically associated with the plains of Colorado and Wyoming. Their traditional territory extended across southern Montana, most of Wyoming, the Nebraska Panhandle, central and eastern Colorado, western Oklahoma, and extreme western Kansas. Since 1878, the Northern Arapaho have lived with the Eastern Shoshone on the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming, while the Southern Arapaho live with the Southern Cheyenne in Oklahoma. The Arapaho language belongs to the Algonquian family. The sources describe a culture shaped by horse-based mobility, bison hunting, trade, warrior societies, sacred ceremonies, distinctive songs, and a continuing effort to maintain the language.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The supplied sources do not document named Arapaho textile or pattern traditions such as buckskin dresses, porcupine-quill embroidery, Arapaho beadwork, painted buffalo robes, parfleche, sinew sewing, rawhide containers, or tipi furnishings.

**Arapaho ceremonial regalia** — The museum records document clothing and adornment visible in portraits of Arapaho chiefs, including eagle-feather headdresses, embroidered moccasins, cloth shirts, vests, wool blankets, necklaces, hoop earrings, and decorated bags.

**Buffalo robes** — A museum record describes four Arapaho men, including Chief Friday, wearing buffalo robes, cloth shirts, and moccasins while seated before a covered wagon.

**Embroidered moccasins** — A portrait record identifies Bird Chief as wearing a pair of embroidered moccasins.

**Wool blankets** — Portrait records describe wool blankets wrapped around the shoulders, waists, or bodies of Arapaho men.

**Decorated bag** — A portrait record describes Heap of Bears holding a decorated bag.

The sources do not name Arapaho motifs or provide a motif vocabulary.

### Clothing & dress

The museum records describe Arapaho men wearing cloth shirts, vests, jackets, wool blankets, buffalo robes, necklaces, hoop earrings, and moccasins. One record identifies Yellow Calf, an Arapaho chief aged 67, wearing an eagle-feather headdress with bead embroidery, a white tunic with tassels, and a necklace. Other portraits show braided or cloth-wrapped hair, sometimes arranged in two bunches. Left Hand is described wearing a cloth scarf, cloth shirt, vest, and wool blanket, and holding a tomahawk with fur tails on the handle. Bird Chief appears in several records wearing hoop earrings, a cloth shirt or vest, and a wool blanket. The sources do not describe women’s everyday clothing, named Arapaho garment terms, belts, hip-length leggings, or a separate women’s ceremonial dress.

### Architecture

The sources do not provide a detailed description of Arapaho houses, tipis, roof forms, building materials, settlement layouts, or named architectural traditions. They state that the Beesowuunenno’ used temporary brush shelters similar to the dome-shaped shade or sweat lodge of the Great Lakes Algonquian peoples. The sources also mention that Arapaho war parties organized themselves before campaigns, but do not describe their camps architecturally.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records a *sadelväska*, or saddlebag, identified as an Arapaho object from the prairie region of the western United States. Another record describes a handled hide scraper with an elk-horn handle from the Cheyenne and Arapaho Reservation in Oklahoma. The records state that the saddlebag was brought home by Gustaf Nordenskiöld and that the hide scraper was exchanged with the Field Museum of Natural History of Chicago. The written sources also name war-clubs, lances, knives, tomahawks, bows, shotguns, rifles, and pistols as weapons used by Arapaho warriors. No Arapaho ceramic tradition or metalworking tradition is documented.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources describe Arapaho men wearing hoop earrings, necklaces, pocket-watch chains, ear ornaments, and decorated clothing. The museum records describe braided hair wrapped in cloth, hair worn in two bunches wrapped in cloth, and eagle-feather headdresses. Yellow Calf’s headdress is described as having bead embroidery. The Arapaho article states that Arapaho people traditionally tattooed small circles on their bodies. The source material does not explain the ritual function of the tattoos or name specific jewelry forms.

## Music & performance

Traditional Arapaho music includes sacred and secular songs. The music is described as using terraced-descent melodic motion, with songs consisting of two sections, each with a range of more than an octave and scales of four to six tones.

The Arapaho Sun Dance is performed in summer, when Arapaho bands come together. It is a ceremony intended to guide warriors toward a vision and the receiving of a guardian spirit; the vision is associated with intense self-torture. The sources also describe folk songs taught by guardian spirits that are supposed to be sung only when the recipient is near death.

Secular songs include round dances in triple meter, the snake dance, the rabbit dance, and the turtle dance, as well as lullabies, children’s songs, war songs, historical songs, and courtship songs. The rabbit dance is described as a partner dance introduced after European contact.

The Ghost Dance was introduced among the Arapaho from tribes farther west in the 1880s. Music was integral to the movement, and folk songs continued to be retained after it ended. Peyote songs accompany peyote ceremonies. They are characterized by rapid rhythm, two note values, vocables, and cadential and closing formulas. The sources do not name Arapaho musical instruments.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name several Arapaho dance forms: round dances, the snake dance, the rabbit dance, and the turtle dance. Round dances are described as secular songs and dances in triple meter. The rabbit dance is a partner dance introduced after European contact. The sources also connect music and performance with the Sun Dance, the Ghost Dance, and peyote ceremonies. They do not describe Arapaho theatre, mask traditions, shadow puppetry, or dramatic genres.

## Festivals & rituals

The Arapaho Sun Dance takes place in summer, when Arapaho bands come together. Its stated purpose is to guide warriors toward a vision and a guardian spirit. The sources associate the ceremony with intense self-torture and with sacred and guardian-spirit songs.

The Ghost Dance reached the Arapaho in the 1880s through tribes farther west. In 1891, the United States outlawed the religion, which led to rebellion among adherents and culminated in the Wounded Knee Massacre. The sources state that music was an integral part of the Ghost Dance.

Peyote ceremonies are accompanied by peyote songs. The sources state that peyote is a cactus native to Mexico and that its buttons, when chewed, act as a hallucinogen. They do not provide a calendar date for Arapaho peyote ceremonies.

The supplied sources do not cover Arapaho birth rites, coming-of-age ceremonies, weddings, funerals, or an annual festival calendar beyond the seasonal timing of the Sun Dance.

## Foodways

The sources describe the Arapaho as agricultural people in the western Great Lakes region, where they grew crops including maize. After moving onto the Great Plains and acquiring horses, they became nomadic and relied extensively on hunting. Their trade with the Arikara, Mandan, and Hidatsa involved exchanging meat and hides for corn, squash, and beans. The sources identify bison hides and beaver furs as important trade goods and state that Arapaho hunters pursued bison.

The sources do not name Arapaho dishes, cooking methods, food taboos, tea or coffee traditions, or ceremonial foods. They also do not document a named food associated with the Sun Dance, Ghost Dance, or peyote ceremonies.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do not provide a named Arapaho epic, folktale cycle, proverb tradition, riddle tradition, or literary genre. They do mention Arapaho historical traditions in the title of the work *Arapaho Historical Traditions: Hinono'einoo3itoono*. The Arapaho language article also identifies “The Arapaho Project” as an effort by Arapaho people to promote and restore their traditional language and culture.

The sources describe songs as including historical, war, courtship, children’s, lullaby, sacred, and secular forms. The Arapaho language article contains an Arapaho translation of Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and states that portions of the Bible were translated into Arapaho in 1903.

## Language & religion

Arapaho, whose endonym is *Hinónoʼeitíít*, is an Algonquian language of the Algic family. It is closely related to Gros Ventre and other Arapahoan languages and is spoken by Arapaho people in Wyoming and Oklahoma. The language has Northern and Southern varieties, while Besawunena is described as a dialect attested from a wordlist collected by Alfred Kroeber.

The number of speakers is described in the sources as uncertain. One account estimates between 250 and 1,000 active users; another states that slightly over 250 fluent speakers were estimated in 2008. Northern Arapaho language preservation includes the Language and Culture Commission, language instruction, language camps, bilingual education efforts, and the Arapaho Language Lodge. A 1995 immersion preschool program was established by Dr. S. N. Greymorning.

The sources document the Sun Dance, guardian spirits, the Ghost Dance, and peyote ceremonies. They do not describe a general Arapaho religious system, denomination, historical script, or contemporary religious landscape beyond these practices.

## At a glance

| Who | The Arapaho are a Native American people. |

## Overview

The Arapaho traditionally lived across parts of the northern and central Great Plains. Horse travel, bison hunting, trade, and warrior societies shaped their life. Sacred ceremonies included the Sun Dance, Ghost Dance, and peyote ceremonies. Arapaho people continue efforts to preserve and teach their language.

## Material culture

Arapaho material culture includes robes, moccasins, blankets, decorated bags, saddlebags, weapons, jewelry, and ceremonial clothing.

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources do not name Arapaho textile patterns, but they describe decorated clothing, robes, blankets, moccasins, and bags.

- **Ceremonial regalia** — Portraits show eagle-feather headdresses, embroidered moccasins, cloth shirts, vests, wool blankets, necklaces, hoop earrings, and decorated bags.
- **Buffalo robes** — A museum record shows four Arapaho men wearing buffalo robes, cloth shirts, and moccasins.
- **Embroidered moccasins** — Bird Chief is recorded as wearing embroidered moccasins.
- **Wool blankets** — Portraits show Arapaho men wearing wool blankets around their shoulders, waists, or bodies.
- **Decorated bag** — Heap of Bears is recorded holding a decorated bag.

### Clothing & dress

Arapaho men wore cloth shirts, vests, jackets, blankets, robes, moccasins, and jewelry, with special clothing for chiefs and ceremonies.

- **Eagle-feather headdress** — Yellow Calf wore an eagle-feather headdress with bead embroidery.
- **White tunic** — Yellow Calf wore a white tunic with tassels.
- **Cloth scarf and vest** — Left Hand wore a cloth scarf, cloth shirt, vest, and wool blanket.
- **Hoop earrings** — Bird Chief appears in portraits wearing hoop earrings, a cloth shirt or vest, and a wool blanket.
- **Braided or cloth-wrapped hair** — Portraits show hair braided or wrapped in cloth, sometimes in two bunches.

### Architecture

The sources give little detail about Arapaho buildings, but they mention temporary brush shelters.

- **Temporary brush shelter** — The Beesowuunenno’ used temporary brush shelters similar to dome-shaped shade or sweat lodges of Great Lakes Algonquian peoples.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources document hide objects, a saddlebag, and many weapons, but no Arapaho ceramic or metalworking tradition.

- **Saddlebag** (*sadelväska*) — A museum catalogue identifies a sadelväska, or saddlebag, as an Arapaho object from the western United States prairie region.
- **Handled hide scraper** — A hide scraper with an elk-horn handle came from the Cheyenne and Arapaho Reservation in Oklahoma.
- **War-club** — War-clubs were among the weapons used by Arapaho warriors.
- **Tomahawk** — Tomahawks were used by Arapaho warriors, and Left Hand is shown holding one with fur tails on its handle.
- **Bow** — Bows were among the weapons used by Arapaho warriors.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Arapaho adornment included earrings, necklaces, hair wrapping, feather headdresses, decorated clothing, and body tattoos.

- **Necklace** — Arapaho men are recorded wearing necklaces.
- **Pocket-watch chain** — Portraits show men wearing pocket-watch chains.
- **Ear ornament** — The sources mention ear ornaments as part of Arapaho adornment.
- **Bead embroidery** — Yellow Calf’s eagle-feather headdress had bead embroidery.
- **Tattooed circles** — Arapaho people traditionally tattooed small circles on their bodies.

## Music & performance

Arapaho music includes sacred and secular songs with distinctive melodies, rhythms, and ceremonial uses.

- **Sacred songs** — Sacred songs are part of Arapaho music and include songs connected with the Sun Dance.
- **Guardian-spirit songs** — Songs taught by guardian spirits were supposed to be sung only when the recipient was near death.
- **Round-dance songs** — Round-dance songs use triple meter.
- **Peyote songs** — Peyote songs accompany peyote ceremonies and use rapid rhythm, vocables, and closing formulas.
- **Historical songs** — Historical songs are one of the named secular and traditional Arapaho song forms.

## Dance & theatre

Named Arapaho dances include round dances, the snake dance, the rabbit dance, and the turtle dance.

- **Round dance** — Round dances are secular dances and songs in triple meter.
- **Snake dance** — The snake dance is a named Arapaho dance form.
- **Rabbit dance** — The rabbit dance is a partner dance introduced after European contact.
- **Turtle dance** — The turtle dance is a named Arapaho dance form.

## Festivals & rituals

The main documented ceremonies are the summer Sun Dance, the Ghost Dance, and peyote ceremonies.

- **Sun Dance** — The Sun Dance brings Arapaho bands together in summer and guides warriors toward a vision and guardian spirit.
- **Ghost Dance** — The Ghost Dance reached the Arapaho in the 1880s through tribes farther west and used music as an integral part of the movement.
- **Peyote ceremony** — Peyote ceremonies use peyote songs, and chewed peyote buttons act as a hallucinogen.

## Foodways

Arapaho foodways changed from farming in the western Great Lakes to horse-based hunting on the Great Plains.

- **Maize** — In the western Great Lakes region, Arapaho people grew crops including maize.
- **Bison hunting** — After moving to the Great Plains and acquiring horses, Arapaho hunters pursued bison.
- **Trade meat and hides** — Arapaho people traded meat and hides with the Arikara, Mandan, and Hidatsa.
- **Corn, squash, and beans** — In trade, Arapaho people received corn, squash, and beans.
- **Beaver furs** — Beaver furs were important trade goods.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources name historical traditions and many song types, but no epic, folktale cycle, or proverb tradition.

- **Arapaho Historical Traditions** (*Hinono'einoo3itoono*) — Arapaho Historical Traditions: Hinono'einoo3itoono is a named work about Arapaho historical traditions.
- **The Arapaho Project** — The Arapaho Project promotes and restores the traditional language and culture.
- **Lullabies** — Lullabies are among the named Arapaho song forms.
- **Children’s songs** — Children’s songs are among the named Arapaho song forms.
- **Courtship songs** — Courtship songs are among the named Arapaho song forms.

## Language & religion

Arapaho is an endangered Algonquian language supported by language programs, while religious life includes the Sun Dance, guardian spirits, Ghost Dance, and peyote ceremonies.

## Overview

The Comanche, or *Nʉmʉnʉʉ*, are a Native American tribe from the Southern Plains of the present-day United States. Their historic domain, called Comanchería by Spanish and later Mexican colonists, included present-day northwestern Texas and adjacent areas of eastern New Mexico, southeastern Colorado, southwestern Kansas, and western Oklahoma. The Comanche Nation is headquartered in Lawton, Oklahoma, and its jurisdictional area includes Caddo, Comanche, Cotton, Greer, Jackson, Kiowa, Tillman, and Harmon Counties. Approximately 17,000 people are enrolled in the Comanche Nation, around 7,000 of whom reside in tribal jurisdictional areas around Lawton, Fort Sill, and the surrounding areas of southwestern Oklahoma. The Comanche language is a Numic language of the Uto-Aztecan family. Comanche culture was shaped by nomadic horse use, bison hunting, trade, warfare, and social organization through families, bands, and divisions.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document named Comanche textile or pattern traditions in sufficient detail for this section.

The museum catalogue records do document woven and manufactured clothing, including a woven cape, woven wrap, woven shawl, manufactured poncho, and patterned dress. These records describe objects shown in studio portraits rather than explaining their techniques, regional distinctions, or pattern systems.

### Clothing & dress

The museum records show Comanche men and women wearing a variety of cloth, woven, manufactured, and European-style garments. A Comanche boy identified as Buffalo Hump’s son is described wearing a cloth shirt, a bone and shell breast plate, and a blanket wrapped around his waist. Milky Way, identified as a Comanche chief, wears a cloth shirt, neck tie, dentalium ear ornaments, and fur sash, and holds a bow and quiver of arrows. Ten Bears is shown in a cloth shirt, waistcoat, blanket around his waist, glasses, and peace medal. Gray Leggings is recorded both in a cloth shirt, waistcoat, hat, ear ornaments, and peace medal, and in a three-piece suit with neck tie, ear ornaments, and peace medal.

The catalogue records describe Comanche women wearing a cloth shirt, woven cape secured with metal fastenings, printed waistband, metal bracelets, woven wrap, and woven shawl. Other portraits show women wearing a patterned dress with a blanket around the waist, or a manufactured poncho and skirt with an abstract motif. The sources do not describe everyday and ceremonial distinctions, named Comanche garments, footwear, belts, or specific head coverings.

### Architecture

The sources used do not document Comanche house forms, architectural materials, roofs, decoration, or named building types. They state that Comanche campaign tents were made from bison hide and that, as late as 1725, large dogs were used rather than horses to carry them.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The catalogue records do not describe ceramics or a distinct Comanche ceramic tradition. They do document everyday and personal objects appearing in portraits: bows, quivers of arrows, canes, hats, glasses, peace medals, metal bracelets, metal fastenings, bone and shell breast plates, dentalium ear ornaments, and fur sashes. Timber Bluff is shown holding a cane, while Gray Leggings is shown holding a hat. The sources do not explain how these objects were manufactured or used beyond their appearance in the portrait records.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum catalogue records document dentalium ear ornaments, other ear ornaments, metal bracelets, a bone and shell breast plate, and a peace medal. Milky Way is shown with dentalium ear ornaments, while Gray Leggings is shown with ear ornaments and a peace medal. The sources also describe some of the men’s hair as plaited in the portrait of Timber Bluff. The sources used do not describe tattoos, ritual adornment, or the religious functions of jewelry and hair practices.

## Music & performance

The Comanche Homecoming Annual Dance takes place in mid-July in Walters, Oklahoma. Each July, Comanches gather from across the United States in Walters for the annual Comanche Homecoming powwow. The Comanche Little Ponies host two annual dances, one over New Year’s Eve and one in May. The sources do not name instruments, song genres, musical forms, or performance techniques.

The Comanche language had a prominent wartime use during World War II. A group of 17 young men known as the Comanche Code Talkers was trained by the U.S. Army to send messages conveying sensitive information in Comanche so that the messages could not be deciphered by the enemy. The sources do not provide lyrics, musical repertories, or information about the relationship between Code Talker practices and other Comanche performance traditions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name the Comanche Homecoming Annual Dance, the annual Comanche Homecoming powwow, and two annual dances hosted by the Comanche Little Ponies. The Homecoming events take place in Walters, Oklahoma; the annual dance is held in mid-July, while the Little Ponies dances occur over New Year’s Eve and in May. The sources do not describe choreography, regalia, named dance forms, theatrical traditions, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment performances.

## Festivals & rituals

The Comanche Homecoming Annual Dance takes place in mid-July in Walters, Oklahoma. The annual Comanche Homecoming powwow is held each July, when Comanches gather from across the United States to celebrate their heritage and culture. The Comanche Nation Fair takes place every September. The Comanche Little Ponies host annual dances over New Year’s Eve and in May.

The Annual General Council is held every year on the third Saturday in April. At this gathering, the annual budget is approved, new leadership is nominated for election, and tribal members may present resolutions for a vote. The Comanche Nation’s cultural institutions include the Comanche National Museum and Cultural Center in Lawton, which opened to the public in 2007 and has permanent and changing exhibitions on Comanche history and culture.

The sources used do not describe birth rites, coming-of-age ceremonies, weddings, funerals, initiation practices, or other life-cycle rituals.

## Foodways

The Comanche practiced a nomadic horse culture and hunted, particularly bison. Comanche group names include *Kʉhtsʉtʉhka* or Kotsoteka, “Buffalo Eaters”; *Penatʉka Nʉʉ* or Penateka, “Honey Eaters”; *Kwaarʉ Nʉʉ* or Kwahadi, “Antelope Eaters”; and *Yaparʉhka* or Yamparika, “Root Eaters.” Other recorded names include *Tanimʉʉ* or Tanima, “Liver Eaters,” *Sʉhmʉhtʉhka*, “Eat Everything,” and *Pekwi Tʉhka*, “Fish Eaters.” These names are presented in the source as group names or descriptions and do not constitute recipes or a complete account of Comanche foodways.

The sources state that Comanches traded horses and mules, hunted bison, and supplied horses to Anglo-American traders and other Native American middlemen. They also mention surplus meat in the explanation of the nickname *Itehtah'o*, “Burnt Meat,” because the meat was thrown out in spring, where it dried and became black. The sources do not document named dishes, cooking methods, staple grains, beverages, dietary rules, or ceremonial foods.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do not provide a body of Comanche folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, or named oral-literary cycles. They do record traditional explanations of several group names and nicknames, including *Nʉmʉnʉʉ*, “the people” or “the human beings”; *Nokoninʉʉ* or Nokoni, “Movers, Returners”; and *Kwaarʉ Nʉʉ*, “Antelope Eaters.”

The Comanche Language and Cultural Preservation Committee offers dictionaries and language-learning materials. The Comanche Nation Language Department has published learning materials on Memrise, and the former Comanche Nation College conducted a language-recording project. The Comanche language is described as “mostly oral,” and the preservation work emphasizes instruction and recording. The sources do not identify a named literary revival, author, epic, or storytelling performance context.

## Language & religion

Comanche is a Numic language of the Uto-Aztecan family. The Comanche were once part of the Shoshone people of the Great Basin, and Comanche later diverged from Shoshoni and became a separate language. The language’s own name is *nʉmʉ tekwapʉ*, meaning “language of the people.” The Comanche autonym *nʉmʉnʉʉ* means “the human beings” or “the people.” The language has a conventional writing system whose alphabet was developed by Dr. Alice Anderton and adopted as the official Comanche Alphabet by the Comanche Nation in 1994.

Most Comanche speakers are elderly. The source states that there were roughly 25–30 native speakers in July 2013 and fewer than nine fluent native speakers as of 2022. The sources describe boarding-school suppression of Comanche and current preservation efforts, but they do not describe Comanche religious beliefs, denominations, ceremonies, cosmology, or spiritual practices.

## Overview

The Tewa are a linguistic group of Pueblo Native Americans who speak the Tewa language and share Pueblo culture. Their homelands are on or near the Rio Grande in New Mexico north of Santa Fe. The six Tewa-speaking pueblos are Nambé, Pojoaque, San Ildefonso, Ohkay Owingeh, Santa Clara, and Tesuque; Hopi Tewa communities also live in Arizona, mostly in Tewa Village and Polacca on the First Mesa. Tewa is one of five closely related Tanoan languages spoken by Pueblo people of New Mexico. The sources describe cultivation, pottery, weaving, wood carving, jewelry, woven goods, religious life, language preservation, and changing relations with Spanish and United States authorities. A 1988 census recorded 4,546 Native Americans on New Mexico’s Tewa reservations.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Woven goods** — The sources identify woven goods as an alternative form of income and describe woven garments as part of the modern-day economy. They do not specify named textile patterns, weaving techniques, or distinctions from neighboring cultures.

**Cotton garments** — Cotton was made into clothing and shoes. The sources do not provide a vernacular name, named pattern, or detailed construction method.

**Hide clothing** — Hides from hunted animals, including deer and rabbits, were made into clothing and shoes. The sources do not describe named garments or decorative schemes.

The museum records include a beaded belt, beaded bandolier, beaded choker, beaded armbands, goat-hide leggings, hide moccasins, and feathered arm ornaments, but they do not identify these objects as Tewa.

### Clothing & dress

The sources state that cotton and animal hides were made into clothing and shoes. They do not distinguish everyday men’s and women’s garments, head coverings, named footwear, or ceremonial dress among the Tewa. The British Museum records describe an ensemble of powwow regalia containing a beaded belt, goat-hide leggings, hide moccasins, a beaded bandolier, a beaded choker, beaded armbands, an upper back bustle and bustle medallion, and feathered arm bustles. These catalogue records do not assign the ensemble to the Tewa.

### Architecture

The sources do not provide sufficient information about Tewa house forms, building materials, roof construction, named building types, or architectural decoration. They mention homes, pueblos, villages, kivas, and agricultural settlements, but do not describe their construction.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Pottery was the most influential art form described in the sources. The Tewa used pottery for storage, eating, cooking, and trading, and museum records document Santa Clara Pueblo and Tewa or Hano clay vessels. One Santa Clara Pueblo vessel is a black clay vessel with a stylized animal motif and a signature reading “Madeleine M, Santa Clara Pueblo.” Other records describe earthenware bowls with brown and red ornament on a yellow-white ground, and a painted bowl with a white ground and handle. The sources mention iron kettles and pots as introduced cooking objects, while pottery continued to be used for storage and dishes. No Tewa metalwork tradition is documented.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources identify jewelry as an alternative source of income before Spanish colonization and state that jewelry contributes to the modern-day economy. They do not name particular jewelry forms, materials, body-adornment practices, tattoos, hair practices, or ritual functions. The British Museum records describe beadwork in white, blue, yellow, orange, maroon, red, and other colours on regalia components, but do not identify the objects as Tewa.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not cover Tewa musical instruments, named song genres, musical performances, or performance contexts. They describe religion as encompassing mythology, cosmology, philosophy, and a worldview, and mention religious sodality leaders, but do not provide musical details.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover named Tewa dances, dramatic traditions, theatre, dance regalia, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment performances.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources describe marriage, childhood, religion, and Catholic ceremonies but do not provide an annual festival calendar. Marriage was primarily arranged through negotiation between families and was usually accompanied by an exchange of gifts. The ceremony could include a native ritual and might also include a nonnative ritual. Marriage within the community was monogamous, with sexual fidelity expected, although divorce and infidelity were observed. After marriage, the couple stayed in the husband’s mother’s home; after the first year, they established a permanent home in the community.

Children were tribal members from birth and were raised tolerantly. At the age of ten, boys and girls were divided into two groups to learn community roles. Children from primarily Catholic families also attended First Communion. The sources state that religious life includes respect and reverence for the Earth, the mountains, hills, water, and certain animals, birds, and plants. They also describe Catholicism as applied to the tribe alongside polytheist beliefs concerning supernatural spiritual forces and entities.

## Foodways

The sources describe the Tewa primarily as cultivators who used irrigation to grow maize, beans, and squash. They also hunted deer, bison, and elk, gathered berries and nuts, and processed plants and other natural flora into herbal teas and sometimes “potions.” During Spanish colonization, cows, pigs, and chickens were introduced, as were wheat, tomatoes, apples, pears, peaches, and chili. Pottery was used for cooking, eating, and storage. The sources do not name particular dishes, ceremonial foods, dietary rules, or tea and coffee customs.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources state that some Pueblo elders believe Tewa should be preserved through oral traditions alone, while many Tewa speakers consider literacy important for passing the language to children. Ohkay Owingeh published a Tewa dictionary, and Tewa-language programs have been established in most Tewa-speaking pueblos. TewaTalk was designed by students and professors at Worcester Polytechnic Institute to support language learning; it includes recorded speech and learning games. Children’s stories in Tewa have been digitized by the University of New Mexico. The sources do not provide named folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, or a documented storytelling cycle.

## Language & religion

Tewa is a Tanoan language spoken in the Rio Grande valley in New Mexico north of Santa Fe and in Arizona. It is also known as Tano or Tée-wah. The language has five related Tanoan languages in its wider linguistic context, although speakers of one cannot fully understand speakers of another. Tewa has dialect differences among Santa Clara, Tesuque, San Ildefonso, San Juan, and Nambé. It can be written with the Latin script, and orthographies developed independently across the pueblos. The sources describe disagreement over writing versus oral preservation, but also document dictionaries, language programs, digitized stories, and other revitalization efforts.

Tewa religion encompasses mythology, cosmology, philosophy, and worldview. It includes reverence for the Earth, mountains, hills, water, animals, birds, and plants. The sources describe polytheist beliefs concerning supernatural spiritual forces and entities alongside Catholicism. They name ’Agojo so’jo, associated with the Morning star and warfare, and Ponu’chona, a Hopi-Tewa deity associated with the morning star, animals, and hunting.
