## Overview

The Sauk, also called Sac, are Native Americans and Indigenous peoples of the Northeastern Woodlands. Their historical territory was near Green Bay, Wisconsin, while their history also includes the St. Lawrence River, Saginaw Bay, northern Illinois, Wisconsin, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, and Oklahoma. Today, three federally recognized tribes are based in Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, and Oklahoma: the Sac and Fox Nation of Missouri in Kansas and Nebraska, the Sac and Fox Nation in Oklahoma, and the Sac and Fox Tribe of the Mississippi in Iowa. The Sauk are closely allied with the Meskwaki. Their language belongs to the Algonquian language family. Sauk cultural life, as covered by the sources, includes clan organization, village life, hunting, farming, trade, lacrosse, oral traditions, language preservation, and material forms of dress and adornment documented in museum portraits.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Beaded necklaces and headdresses** — Museum records describe beaded necklaces and a beaded headdress worn by Sauk and Fox men in studio portraits. The catalogue records do not provide a named Sauk pattern system or a comparison with neighboring cultures.

**Fur and bear-claw necklaces** — Several museum portraits record necklaces made from fur and bear claws. These objects occur with shirts, blankets, leggings, moccasins, feather ornaments, and tomahawks.

**Embroidered moccasins** — Museum records describe embroidered moccasins worn by Big Bear, Dead Indian, and White Fish. The sources do not specify their construction, motifs, or regional distinctions.

**Leggings with decoration** — The catalogue records mention embroidered leggings, leggings with feather decoration, leggings with quill or bead decoration and fringe, and wool leggings with beadwork decoration.

**Blankets and wool blankets** — Portrait records repeatedly describe blankets wrapped around the body, waist, shoulders, or legs, including a wool blanket worn by the Sea and a wool blanket worn by Che-Ko-Skuk.

**Shell and cloth necklaces** — The museum objects include beaded and shell necklaces, cloth and shell necklaces, and dentalium shell necklaces. The sources do not describe a named textile technique associated with these objects.

**Quill or bead decoration** — The catalogue records identify quill or bead decoration on leggings and beadwork decoration on wool leggings, but do not provide further technical or stylistic information.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The museum catalogue records document shirts, cloth shirts, shirts with fringing, long-sleeved tops, blankets, wool blankets, leggings, embroidered leggings, decorated leggings, leg bands, moccasins, and decorated or embroidered moccasins. Men are shown wearing feather hair ornaments, eagle feathers, decorated fur headdresses, cloth wraps around the head, beaded headdresses, fur hats with eagle feathers, and cloth and shell necklaces. Other recorded adornments include ear ornaments, armbands, arm ornaments, beaded necklaces, fur and bear-claw necklaces, shell necklaces, cloth neck ties, scarves with gorgets, leather straps with conchos, and peace medals. The portraits also show men holding feather fans, feather pouches, walking sticks, ceremonial objects, and tomahawks. The sources do not describe women’s clothing, everyday dress, named garment types in the Sauk language, or a distinction between daily and ceremonial clothing.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Sauk house forms, building materials, roof types, architectural decoration, or named building traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources do not describe Sauk ceramics, houses, wooden household goods, cooking vessels, or named metalworking traditions. Museum records document peace medals, ear ornaments, dentalium shell ornaments, conchos, tomahawks, feather fans, feather pouches, and a walking stick. The Sauk historical account also describes boats used to cross a river and villages in which the people raised crops and traded with other tribes.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum catalogue records include ear ornaments, beaded necklaces, shell necklaces, dentalium shell necklaces, cloth and shell necklaces, fur and bear-claw necklaces, bear-claw necklaces, chokers made of dentalium, cloth neck ties with shells, scarves with gorgets, armbands, arm ornaments, leather straps with conchos, peace medals, and feather ornaments. Portraits also show eagle feathers, feather hair ornaments, decorated fur headdresses, and a fur hat with an eagle feather. The sources do not describe tattoos, body painting as a personal practice, hair-cutting customs, or ritual functions for the listed adornments. The Sauk clan system records charcoal as black and white clay as white in the symbolic painting of the two moieties.

## Music & performance

The sources do not identify Sauk musical instruments, song genres, musical scales, or named performance traditions. They record lacrosse as a practice associated with recreation, festivals, the preparation of young warriors for combat, and preparation for wars or raids. The sources do not explain whether music accompanied lacrosse or other ceremonies. The Sauk language article includes written language samples, including a greeting and a narrative about turtles, but does not identify them as songs or performance genres.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover Sauk dances, theatre, masked performance, dramatic traditions, or named dance forms. Lacrosse is described as a recreational and martial practice that was also part of festivals, but the sources do not classify it as dance or theatre.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not provide an annual festival calendar or named Sauk festivals. They state that lacrosse was played for recreation, as part of festivals, to toughen young warriors for combat, and as preparation for imminent wars or raids. The Sauk and Fox peoples were divided into two moieties, the *Kîshkôha* and the *Shkasha*, associated respectively with long hair and bravery. The moieties were symbolized through black charcoal and white clay. The tribe was governed by a council that included sacred clan chiefs, a war chief, heads of families, and warriors. Chiefs were categorized as civil, war, and ceremonial; only civil chiefs were hereditary. The sources do not describe birth, coming-of-age, marriage, funeral, healing, or annual agricultural rites.

## Foodways

The sources state that the Sauk lived in villages, raised crops, hunted American bison, and actively traded with other tribes after adopting a semi-sedentary lifestyle on the prairie. They do not name crops, dishes, cooking methods, food-preservation practices, drinks, dietary rules, or ceremonial foods. The sources therefore do not cover Sauk foodways in greater detail.

## Oral tradition & literature

Sauk traditions state that the tribe occupied the vicinity of the Saginaw River, and one tradition explains the name “Saginaw” through the Ojibwe expression “O-Sauk-e-non,” meaning “land of the Sauks” or “where the Sauks were.” The account of the Battle of Skull Island is presented as a legend in which Sauk people escaped by boat to an island before the river froze sufficiently for their attackers to cross. Some Ojibwe oral histories also place the Sauk in the Saginaw Valley before the arrival of Europeans. The Sauk language article records a written narrative about two turtles, a thunderstorm, rain, and a lake. The sources do not identify a Sauk epic, proverb tradition, riddle tradition, or named literary genre.

## Language & religion

Sauk is also known as *Thâkiwâtowêweni* or Thâkîwaki language. It is either a dialect of Fox or a distinct language and belongs to the Algonquian language family. It is closely related to the dialects spoken by the Meskwaki and Kickapoo, and Sauk and Meskwaki are described as mutually intelligible to a point. The Sauk once called themselves *asakiwaki*, “people of the outlet.” Sauk has a syllabic orthography; a Primer Book was published in 1975 based on a syllabary that existed in 1906, and a newer orthography was proposed around 1994. Five elders are described as fluent speakers, and Sauk is considered endangered. The sources do not describe Sauk religious beliefs, conversion history, or a current religious landscape.

## Overview

The Seneca, whose own name is *Onödowaʼga꞉ʼ*, are an Iroquoian-speaking Indigenous people historically associated with the southern shore of Lake Ontario and the territory between the Genesee River and Canandaigua Lake. They were the westernmost nation of the Haudenosaunee and were called “The Keepers of the Western Door.” In the 21st century, more than 10,000 Seneca live in the United States, with communities in western New York and Oklahoma, while approximately 1,000 live in Canada near Brantford, Ontario. Seneca communities are also documented in the Allegheny River region, the Niagara River area, Pennsylvania, and Ontario. Their folk-culture record includes longhouses, agricultural practices involving corn, beans, and squash, oral mythology, language revitalization, masks, rattles, moccasins, clubs, bowls, and other museum-held objects.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document named Seneca textile or pattern traditions in sufficient detail for this section.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no documented textile motif vocabulary.

### Clothing & dress

Seneca men and women wore clothing that included moccasins; museum records document pairs made from native-tanned skin, with porcupine quill, silk, or glass, and dating to ca. 1830 and ca. 1808. The British Museum records a photographic portrait of Lewis Bennett (Deerfoot), a Seneca man wearing moccasins, leggings, a fringed frock coat, and ear ornaments while holding a hat.

Men of both Seneca branches wore the same headgear as other Haudenosaunee people: hats with dried cornhusks on top. Seneca men wore theirs with one feather standing straight up. A museum catalogue records a Seneca headgear object from the United States, associated with Levi Cook, Seneca, Cattarangue. The sources do not describe women’s everyday garments in detail. Museum records also document brooches and a mother-and-child doll made of corn husk, cotton, wool, native-tanned skin, glass, and silk.

### Architecture

Seneca communities traditionally lived in longhouses, large buildings up to 100 feet long and approximately 20 feet wide. Related families shared them, and a longhouse could hold up to 60 people. Hearths stood in the central aisle, with two families sharing a hearth. Major villages were protected by wooden palisades. Ganondagan had 150 longhouses and was the largest Seneca village of the 17th century; Chenussio had 130 longhouses and was a major village of the 18th century.

Seneca towns were relocated every ten to twenty years as soil, game, and other resources were depleted. During the nineteenth century, many Seneca adopted log cabins similar to those of their American neighbors. The sources also describe villages near rivers and agricultural fields, with settlements extending through the Genesee River valley, around Seneca Lake, and along the Allegheny River.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Museum records document a wooden bowl from New York, United States, identified with the Seneca and the League of the Iroquois. The catalogue describes it as a wooden bowl or vessel and records that it was obtained through exchange with the Denver Art Museum. A British Museum record describes a wooden gunstock club ornamented with brass nails and fitted with a pointed, flat iron blade.

The Seneca economy included hunting and gathering, fishing, and the cultivation of corn, beans, and squash. Women processed medicinal plants, roots, berries, nuts, and fruit, while men cleared forests for fields and maintained hunting and fishing grounds. The sources do not provide a fuller account of Seneca ceramics or metalworking.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Museum records document Seneca and Haudenosaunee brooches. One is described as being shaped like a masonic cross, with a pattern on its front; another is a simple square with the pin attached at one corner. The catalogues associate these objects with Seneca individuals in Cattarangus, New York, and with Oneida and Seneca provenance.

The British Museum’s portrait record states that Lewis Bennett (Deerfoot) wore ear ornaments. The Seneca archery description records that bows were made of unbacked hickory and that arrows could be made from split hickory, dogwood, or Viburnum. The sources do not describe tattoos, hair practices, or named forms of ritual body adornment.

## Music & performance

The museum records document turtle-shell rattles associated with Seneca and Iroquois ceremonial life. One object is named *Kanyáhte’ ká’nowa’* and is described as a turtle-shell rattle. Another catalogue record identifies a rattle of tortoise shell from the eastern woodland area and states that it was used in the Iroquois religious society, where participants often used masks.

The rattles were used by the mask society and in the Great Feather Dance. One catalogue gives the phrase “ga no wa gusta we sa” for the object and states that it was used in dances and by the mask society. The sources also mention Seneca-language music broadcasts by the former Seneca-owned radio station WGWE, although the station broadcast primarily in English. It featured a daily “Seneca Word of the Day,” broadcast a limited amount of Seneca-language music, and occasionally used Seneca in its broadcasts.

The sources do not name Seneca instruments other than turtle-shell or tortoise-shell rattles, and they do not document named song genres or a detailed musical system.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name the Great Feather Dance and state that turtle-shell rattles were used in it. Museum records also associate rattles with dances and ceremonies of the mask society. A wooden mask catalogue record states that masks were used in dances and ceremonies by the “masksällskapet Seneca” in Cattarangua.

Another museum record describes two wooden false face masks. They were used by shamans and medicine men in secret ceremonies in which a person with poor health was healed from sickness. The catalogue identifies the objects with the eastern woodland area, Iroquois, and Seneca. The sources do not provide a fuller description of theatrical plots, named dramatic genres, choreography, or distinctions between entertainment and ceremonial performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not document an annual Seneca festival calendar or provide dates for recurring seasonal festivals. They do describe ritual and ceremonial contexts associated with the mask society, turtle-shell rattles, the Great Feather Dance, and wooden false face masks.

Seneca mythology records stories transmitted orally and later written down in the nineteenth century. It describes spirits, dreams, magical power, monsters, witches, and sorcerers. The museum catalogue states that false face masks were used by shamans and medicine men in secret ceremonies connected with healing. Another mask was used in dances and ceremonies by the Seneca mask society.

The sources also describe Haudenosaunee social organization through matrilineal clans. Seneca clans include Bear, Wolf, Turtle, Beaver, Deer, Hawk, Snipe, and Heron, divided between an animal side and a bird side. Children belonged to their mother’s clan, and the presiding elder was called the “clan mother.” The sources do not describe Seneca birth, coming-of-age, wedding, or funeral rites.

## Foodways

Seneca subsistence traditionally depended on hunting and gathering, fishing, and cultivating varieties of corn, beans, and squash. These vegetables were the staple of the Haudenosaunee diet and were called “the three sisters,” *työhe'hköh*. Seneca women generally grew and harvested them and also gathered and processed medicinal plants, roots, berries, nuts, and fruit.

Men hunted and fished in productive grounds away from towns and villages. These locations were altered and maintained to encourage game. The sources do not name prepared dishes, cooking methods, beverages, ceremonial foods, dietary rules, or food-related festivals. They also do not provide a detailed account of serving vessels, although a museum catalogue records a Seneca wooden bowl and describes it as a bowl, vessel, and a bowl-and-spoon object.

## Oral tradition & literature

Seneca oral history states that the people originated in a village called Nundawao near the south end of Canandaigua Lake, at South Hill. Seneca mythology was transmitted orally, and stories began to be written down in the nineteenth century. Jeremiah Curtin began transcribing stories in 1883, and Arthur C. Parker published *Seneca Myths and Folk Tales* in 1923.

Parker classified Seneca stories into six groups: “When the World was New,” “Boys who Defied Magic and Overcame it,” “Tales of Love and Marriage,” “Horror Tales of Cannibals and Sorcerers,” “Tales of Talking Animals,” and “Tales of Giants, Pygmies, and Monster Bears.”

Named figures include Eagentci, the Earth-mother or First Mother; Djieien, a man-sized spider; Djodiʼkwadoʼ, a horned serpent; Dagwanoenyent, a northern witch depicted as a whirlwind; Gaasyendietha, a fire-breathing dragon inhabiting Lake Ontario; Hagondes, a cannibalistic trickster and clown spirit; and Nyáʼkwaehe꞉h, a giant hairless bear. The sources also describe Seneca language revitalization efforts and the publication of language-learning tools.

## Language & religion

Seneca is an Iroquoian language of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy and is most closely related to Cayuga, Onondaga, Oneida, and Mohawk. The language is spoken primarily in western New York, on the Allegany, Cattaraugus, and Tonawanda reservations, and in Ontario on the Grand River Six Nations Reserve. The speech community has dwindled to approximately one hundred native speakers, while revitalization efforts are underway.

The Seneca Faithkeepers School was founded in 1998 as a five-day-a-week school teaching Seneca language and tradition. In 2013, middle school students served as announcers for a lacrosse match in Seneca. The sources state that many Seneca adopted Christianity during the nineteenth century. Seneca mythology describes spirits throughout nature, orenda or magical power, souls of living creatures, a heaven world, dreams as experiences of the soul, and monsters, wizards, witches, and sorcerers. Museum records connect masks and rattles with the mask society, healing ceremonies, and the Iroquois religious society.

## Overview

The Akimel Oʼodham, also called Akimel Oʼotham, are an Indigenous people living in central and southern Arizona and northwestern Mexico, in Sonora and Chihuahua. Their communities are associated especially with the Gila and Salt Rivers, including the Gila River Indian Community and the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community. The Akimel Oʼodham are closely related to the Ak-Chin Oʼodham, Sobaipuri, Tohono Oʼodham, and Hia C-ed Oʼodham. Their language, Oʼodham, is a Uto-Aztecan language spoken in southern Arizona and northern Sonora, Mexico. The Gila River Indian Community has more than 19,000 enrolled citizens. Their folk-culture significance in the sources centers on river-based life, irrigation, farming, basketry, textiles, dwellings, oral tradition, and the religious and ethical worldview called *himdagĭ*.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

*Himdagĭ* is described as an encompassing way of life rather than as a textile tradition, so the sources do not identify a separate named pattern system under this term.

**Basketry** — The Akimel Oʼodham were experts in textiles and produced intricate baskets as well as woven cloth. The museum records include coiled baskets, basketwork platters made with coil technique and geometric ornament, storage vessels with conventionalised designs in black, conical containers with ornamented rims, beaker-shaped baskets with black ornament, and a basketry basket with lid made of vegetable fibre.

**Basketry vessel** — Museum records describe straight-sided, coiled basketry vessels with black geometrical ornament.

**Carrying-sling jar** — A museum object is a jar with sling made of basketry, gum, and cotton cloth.

**Woven fabric cap** — Museum records show a woven fabric cap worn by a Pima chief in studio portraits.

**Woven cloth** — The Akimel Oʼodham produced woven cloth, but the sources do not provide a specific vernacular name, garment type, or technique beyond this description.

**Thatched lodge** — A museum postcard depicts an Akimel Oʼodham woman weaving a large basket in front of her thatched lodge.

**Geometric ornament** — The museum catalogue names geometric ornament, conventionalised black designs, black geometrical ornament, and an ornamented rim; it does not identify named motifs or explain their meanings.

### Clothing & dress

The sources provide little information about everyday or ceremonial clothing. Museum records describe a Pima chief wearing a western-style suit and a woven fabric cap with plaits hanging from it. Another portrait shows a Pima chief in a western-style suit with dreadlocks at the back of his head. The sources do not identify named Akimel Oʼodham garments, footwear, belts, ceremonial dress, or gender-specific clothing.

### Architecture

Traditionally, the Akimel Oʼodham lived in thatched wattle-and-daub houses called jacales. The source describes these as huts made from reed-grass mats cut in half and built in the form of a vault on arched sticks; the top was covered with mats thick enough to resist the weather. Inside were a petate for sleeping and gourds for carrying and storing water. Earlier villages were ranchería-style settlements consisting of a loose group of houses, with familial groups sharing a central ramada and kitchen area. Brush *Olas Ki:ki*, described as round houses, were built around this central area. The people also lived seasonally in temporary field houses while tending their crops.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources describe pottery pots and a basketry pot-like vessel in the museum catalogue, but do not provide named ceramic forms, pottery techniques, or information about firing. The Akimel Oʼodham historically used metal tools and trade goods after European contact. Museum objects include arrow-heads made of grey stone, red stone, and obsidian; wooden game-sticks consisting of four slats; pots made of pottery; baskets; platters; a jar with carrying-sling; and basketry containers. The sources do not describe metalwork traditions or named household forms beyond these records.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources do not document Akimel Oʼodham jewelry, named ornaments, tattoos, henna, ritual body decoration, or adornment practices. They mention plaits hanging from a woven fabric cap in a museum portrait and dreadlocks at the back of the head in another portrait, but do not explain these features as cultural practices.

## Music & performance

The sources do not identify named Akimel Oʼodham instruments, musical genres, or performance contexts. They do describe ceremonies that often include set speeches. In these speeches, the speaker recites portions of the people’s cosmic myth; the speeches are adapted for each occasion while retaining the same general context. Before American rule, such recitation was especially important in preparation for war. The language source includes a song from *Oʼodham Hohoʼok Aʼagida* and identifies it as an example of the “Storyteller dialect,” but it does not provide a separate name for a musical genre or instrument. The material supplied does not cover dance accompaniment, instrumental practice, or musical performance at weddings, funerals, or annual festivals.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not identify named Akimel Oʼodham dances, dramatic traditions, theatre forms, mask practices, or ceremonial dance contexts.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not provide an annual festival calendar or named festivals. They describe Akimel Oʼodham ceremonies involving set speeches and cosmic myth, and state that personal names have particular importance in society. From age ten until marriage, boys and girls were not allowed to speak their own names aloud because doing so could invoke bad luck for the children and their future. People also did not say aloud the names of deceased people, in order to allow them to move on and to call their spirits back among the living. The sources do not describe weddings, funerals, birth rites, initiation ceremonies, or seasonal festivals in detail.

## Foodways

The ancient Akimel Oʼodham economy was based primarily on farming, hunting, gathering, and extensive trading. They built an extensive irrigation system to compensate for arid conditions, and communities altered canal systems according to changing needs. The people cultivated foods and lived seasonally in temporary field houses while tending their crops. After European contact, new crops such as wheat, livestock, metal tools, and trade goods were introduced. The sources do not name specific dishes, beverages, cooking methods, dietary rules, or ceremonial foods. They state that the diversion of river water and the introduction of a non-native diet contributed to a high rate of diabetes among the Akimel Oʼodham.

## Oral tradition & literature

Akimel Oʼodham ceremonies often include set speeches in which a speaker recites portions of a cosmic myth. The people also gave children careful verbal instruction in moral, religious, and other matters. The language source reproduces a song from *Oʼodham Hohoʼok Aʼagida* (*Oʼodham Legends and Lore*) by Susanne Ignacio Enos, Dean Saxton, and Lucille Saxton, with an English translation. It also identifies *Taḏai* (“Roadrunner”) as an excerpt from the Oʼodham Piipaash Language Program and presents it in the Salt River dialect and in Saxton orthography. The sources do not identify an epic cycle, named folktale collection beyond this work, proverb tradition, or riddle genre.

## Language & religion

Oʼodham is a Uto-Aztecan language of southern Arizona and northern Sonora, Mexico. The language is also called Oʼodham ha-ñeʼokĭ, Oʼottham ha-neoki, Oʼodham ñiok, Oʼodham ñeʼokĭ, Oʼodham ñiʼokĭ, or Oʼotham ñiok, depending on dialect and orthography. The language has Akimel Oʼodham and Tohono Oʼodham dialect groupings, among others. Two common orthographies are Alvarez–Hale and Saxton. The Akimel Oʼodham way of life, *himdagĭ*, is centered on the holy river and encompasses religion, morals, values, philosophy, and worldview. Their religious beliefs and worldview focus on the natural world. The sources do not describe a separate organized religious institution.

## Overview

The Modoc are an Indigenous American people whose historical homeland lies in northeastern California and central Southern Oregon, including the Modoc Plateau, Tule Lake, Lower Klamath Lake, and the Lost River. Today, about 600 Modoc live in Klamath County, Oregon, while 200 live in Ottawa County, Oklahoma. They include the Klamath Tribes in Oregon and the Modoc Nation, formerly the Modoc Tribe of Oklahoma. The Modoc traditionally spoke a dialect of Klamath, also called Klamath–Modoc or Lutuamian, a Plateau Penutian language. Their material and intangible culture documented in the sources includes earthen dugout lodges, basketry, aquatic plant foods, fishing, seasonal hunting and gathering, ritual dance, sweat-lodge ceremonies, oral traditions concerning Kumush, and objects associated with Modoc people and the Modoc War.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Korgflätning** — The museum records identify Modoc caps, women’s caps, headgear, baskets, and a basket plate as made of basketry. The objects include an open, basket-like head covering, a basket used in games, and an unfinished basket.

**Wokas plants** — The Modoc built winter lodges near lake shores with reliable sources of seeds from aquatic wokas plants. The sources do not describe a named textile or pattern tradition associated with these plants.

**Earthen dugout lodges** — Winter dwellings were shaped like beehives, covered with sticks, and plastered with mud. The sources do not give a Modoc vernacular name for this house form.

The sources used do not document additional Modoc textile traditions, named patterns, moccasins, tule mats, burden baskets, or other pattern-bearing textile forms.

### Clothing & dress

The museum records identify a Modoc open, basket-like headgear, a basketry cap, and a basketry women’s cap. One catalogue record describes a cap as belonging to Captain Jack and as made of basketry. Other records concern necklaces made of glass beads and mussel shells or fruits. The British Museum photographs show Bogus Charley wearing a hat, a shirt, a cloth tied around his neck, trousers, and boots; Burgess Charley wearing a hat and a three-piece suit; Scar Faced Charley wearing a three-piece suit and bow tie; and Boston Charley wearing a shirt and jacket. Another photograph shows three Modoc men, including Donald McKay, wearing shirts and trousers. The sources do not describe ordinary or ceremonial dress systematically, nor do they provide Modoc vernacular names for garments, belts, footwear, or head coverings.

### Architecture

Until the 19th century, the Modoc built earthen dugout lodges for winter use. These structures were shaped like beehives, covered with sticks, and plastered with mud, and were located near lake shores with dependable sources of aquatic wokas seeds and fishing. The sources also mention a Modoc village near the Lost River built by Kintpuash’s band after leaving the reservation in 1870. No further architectural decoration, settlement plan, or Modoc vernacular building term is given.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources used do not document Modoc ceramics, metalwork, wooden objects, tools, or household goods beyond basketry objects. Museum records identify a basket, an unfinished basket, a basketry plate used in games, a basketry headgear, and basketry caps. The records do not describe their manufacture in detail or provide additional Modoc names for these forms.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Museum records identify a necklace made of glass beads and mussel shells that belonged to Hi-ne-ma Riaala, described as a heroine in the war of 1873, and another necklace made of fruits. The sources do not describe tattoos, hair practices, ritual functions, or a Modoc vernacular terminology for jewelry and body adornment.

## Music & performance

The sources do not document Modoc musical instruments, song genres, musical scales, performance ensembles, or musical occasions. They do record the *Shuyuhalsh*, a five-night dance rite of passage for adolescent girls. The number five figured heavily in Modoc ritual. The sources do not identify instruments used in the rite or describe its choreography, songs, or performers. A sweat lodge was used for purification and mourning ceremonies, but the sources do not state whether music formed part of those ceremonies. No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription concerns the Modoc or the United States in the supplied material.

## Dance & theatre

The Modoc *Shuyuhalsh* was a five-night dance rite of passage for adolescent girls. The sources identify it as a ritual but do not describe its movements, music, costumes, location, or participants beyond adolescent girls. They do not document Modoc theatre, masked performance, shadow puppetry, named entertainment dances, or dramatic traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not describe an annual Modoc festival calendar or festivals associated with fixed dates. They identify several ritual practices. The number five figured heavily in ritual, including the *Shuyuhalsh*, a five-night dance rite of passage for adolescent girls. A sweat lodge was used for purification and mourning ceremonies. The sources also describe the Modoc War, during which Kintpuash and his band resisted removal from their traditional homelands; Kintpuash was captured on June 4, 1873, and was executed with three warriors in October 1873. These events are historical rather than identified in the sources as annual commemorations. The sources do not describe birth, marriage, funeral, or other life-cycle ceremonies apart from the adolescent girls’ rite of passage and mourning ceremonies.

## Foodways

Before the 19th century, the Modoc caught salmon during salmon runs and migrated seasonally to hunt and gather other food. Their winter lodges were built near lake shores with reliable sources of seeds from aquatic wokas plants and fishing. The sources do not provide names of dishes, cooking methods, food restrictions, beverages, or ceremonial foods. They also do not document root digging, acorn processing, camas gathering, tule boats, or a Modoc food vocabulary beyond the reference to wokas plants and salmon.

## Oral tradition & literature

Kumush, also called Kemush, Kmukamtch, K’mukamtch, Gmok’am’c, Gmo’Kamc, or Kumukumts, is identified as the Modoc spirit of creation. The account describes Kumush as creating the Modoc tribe, giving things names, designating California as their home, and naming Mount Shasta and Tule Lake as the Modoc Garden of Eden. Recorded versions differ because the account was transmitted by different speakers in different circumstances. The sources identify Jeremiah Curtin’s *Myths of the Modocs*, published in 1912 from fieldwork conducted in the late 19th century, and Albert Gatschet’s *The Klamath Indians of Southwestern Oregon*, published in 1890. The Modoc Nation preserves a contemporary version, while H. L. Delaney’s *The Book of Spirals: Native Myths of the American West*, published in 2025, presents a twelve-part cycle in which Kemush appears as a culture hero and cosmological mediator.

## Language & religion

The Modoc traditionally spoke a dialect of Klamath, also called Klamath–Modoc or Lutuamian. Klamath is described as a Plateau Penutian language, itself a branch of the proposed Penutian language family. By 1998, only one native speaker remained; by 2003, the last fluent Klamath speaker living in Chiloquin, Oregon, was 92 years old. As of 2006, there were no fluent native speakers of either the Klamath or Modoc dialects, while revitalization efforts were underway as of 2019. The Modoc religion is not known in detail. Ritual practices documented in the sources include the five-night *Shuyuhalsh* and the use of a sweat lodge for purification and mourning. Kumush is identified as the Modoc spirit of creation.

## Overview

The Klickitat, also spelled Klikitat, are a Native American tribe of the Pacific Northwest. Most Klickitat are enrolled in the federally recognized Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation, while some are part of the Confederated Tribes of the Grand Ronde Community of Oregon. Their ancestral lands lay north of the Columbia River, at the headwaters of the Cowlitz, Lewis, White Salmon, and Klickitat rivers, in present-day Klickitat and Skamania Counties. They were a Shahaptian tribe whose eastern neighbors were the Yakama and whose western neighbors included Salishan and Chinookan tribes. The Klickitat were active and enterprising traders, serving as intermediaries between coastal tribes and communities east of the Cascade Mountains. Their name remains attached to Klickitat County, Klickitat, the Klickitat River, and other places and objects.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The supplied sources do not document named Klickitat textile or pattern traditions in sufficient detail for this section.

**Basket** — The museum records include a cooking basket made of woven osier stem with leather straps, a basketry bag made of basketry and cord, a basket with a thong made of basketry and leather, and a water basket made of osier.

**Parfleche envelope** — A rectangular parfleche envelope made from buffalo hide is painted with diamond and triangular designs in red, black, and much-faded blue, with heavy hide fringes along each vertical edge.

**Parfleche wallet** — A rawhide parfleche wallet carries painted geometric designs in green, red, and black.

**Motif vocabulary.** Diamond designs, triangular designs, geometric designs.

### Clothing & dress

The supplied sources do not describe everyday or ceremonial Klickitat clothing, named garments, head coverings, belts, footwear, or distinctions between men’s and women’s dress.

The museum catalogue records a woman’s necklace described as a “brave’s” dance necklace, made of deer toes. This object provides evidence of a named adornment associated in the catalogue with a woman and with dance, but the sources do not explain how it was worn, when it was used, or how it related to other forms of dress.

### Architecture

The supplied sources do not describe Klickitat houses, lodges, shelters, roof forms, building materials, decoration, or settlement layouts.

The historical sources identify Klickitat villages and locations, including Itkilak, also given as Ithlkilak, at White Salmon Landing; Nanshuit at Underwood; Shgwaliksh below Memaloose Island; Tgasgutcu near White Salmon Landing; and Wiltkun, whose exact location is unknown. Itkilak, Nanshuit, and Tgasgutcu were occupied jointly with the Chilluckquittequaw Tribe.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records two stone arrow-heads. One is flaked, white, triangular, and flat; the other is flaked, flat, light beige, and nearly translucent. It also records a smoking pipe made of stone and white metal.

The catalogue further identifies baskets made from woven osier stem, basketry, cord, leather, and osier. These include a cooking basket with leather straps, a basketry bag, a basket with a thong, and a water basket. The sources do not provide vernacular names, production contexts, dates, or comparisons with neighboring groups’ objects.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum catalogue records a woman’s necklace, described as a “brave’s” dance necklace, made of deer toes. The sources do not specify its date, construction method, symbolic meaning, ritual function, or relationship to other forms of body adornment.

No information is supplied about tattoos, hair practices, henna, earrings, belts, or additional jewelry types.

## Music & performance

The supplied sources do not name Klickitat instruments, song genres, musical systems, or performance settings. They do record a woman’s necklace described as a “brave’s” dance necklace, but they do not explain the dance, its music, or the circumstances in which the necklace was worn.

The Klickitat were encountered by the Lewis and Clark Expedition in 1805. The historical account states that two chiefs welcomed Lewis and Clark on their arrival, but it does not identify a musical performance, instrument, song, or ceremonial protocol associated with that meeting. No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription is supplied for the Klickitat or for the United States.

## Dance & theatre

The sources do not document named Klickitat dances, dramatic traditions, theatre forms, masks, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment performance.

The museum catalogue’s description of a woman’s “brave’s” dance necklace establishes an association between one necklace and dance, but gives no further information about choreography, participants, occasions, or meaning.

## Festivals & rituals

The supplied sources do not describe an annual Klickitat festival calendar, seasonal celebrations, life-cycle ceremonies, weddings, funerals, coming-of-age rites, or ritual observances.

The historical account states that the Klickitat joined in the Yakima treaty at Camp Stevens on June 9, 1855, after the Klickitat War erupted in 1855. They ceded their lands to the United States, and most settled upon the Yakama Indian Reservation, with a minority on the Grand Ronde Community. These are political and historical events rather than festivals or rituals, and the sources do not describe associated ceremonial practices.

## Foodways

The sources state that the Klickitat traded salmon, roots, and berries. They do not provide names for dishes, preparation methods, cooking recipes, dietary rules, beverages, ceremonial foods, or seasonal food calendars.

A museum record identifies a cooking basket made of woven osier stem with leather straps, indicating an object associated with cooking, but the catalogue does not specify what was cooked in it or how it was used. A water basket made of osier is also recorded, without further information about transport, storage, or preparation.

## Oral tradition & literature

The supplied sources do not present Klickitat folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles, or named storytelling genres. The Wikipedia article’s further-reading list includes Clarence Orvell Bunnell’s *Legends of the Klickitat: A Klickitat Version of the Story of the Bridge of the Gods*, but the source material does not summarize the narratives in that book.

The sources do document historical naming and language preservation. The Klickitat call themselves *Qwû'lh-hwai-pûm* or *χwálχwaypam*, meaning “prairie people,” with the form *X̣ʷáɬx̣ʷaypam* also given. The Yakama called them *Xwálxwaypam* or *L'ataxat*. These names are linguistic evidence rather than a described oral-literary tradition.

## Language & religion

The Klickitat are identified as a Shahaptian tribe. Their eastern neighbors, the Yakama, speak a closely related language. The supplied language article describes Sahaptin, also called Ichishkiin, as belonging to the Sahaptian branch of the Plateau Penutian family. It is spoken in the northwestern plateau along the Columbia River and its tributaries in southern Washington, northern Oregon, and southwestern Idaho, and is used by tribes connected with the Washington Reservations, including Yakama, Warm Springs, and Umatilla.

The Yakama Nation tribal cultural resources program has promoted *Ichishkíin Sɨ́nwit* as the traditional name of the language. The sources describe dialect names including *Ichishkíin*, *Ichishkínk*, *Chishkín*, *Čiškíin*, and *Ičiškíin*. They also state that Sahaptin has split ergative syntax, direct-inverse voicing, and applicative constructions. ## Overview

The Nez Perce, who call themselves *nimíipuu*, meaning “we, the people,” are an Indigenous people of the Plateau who live on part of their ancestral lands in the southeastern Columbia River Plateau of the Pacific Northwest. Their territory included parts of Washington, Oregon, Montana, and Idaho, with important associations with the Snake, Salmon, Clearwater, Grande Ronde, and Columbia rivers, the Bitterroot Mountains, the Blue Mountains, and the Wallowa Mountains. The tribe reports more than 3,500 members in 2021. The Nez Perce language belongs to the Sahaptian branch of the Plateau Penutian family. Their historical importance in folk culture is documented through seasonal subsistence, salmon fishing, horse breeding, trade, oral tradition, language preservation, woven bags, baskets, clothing, and beadwork.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Fibre bags** — British Museum records describe fibre bags made by a twining technique. The catalogue records do not identify a Nez Perce vernacular name for this form.

**Cornhusk wallets and bags** — Cornhusk bags and wallets were made with corn husk, hop twine, wool yarn, and deerskin. One wallet has a rectangular back, a flap, a purple geometric pattern, and a red rose with a green leaf; another has a diamond-shaped central pattern of black wool surrounded by dark areas containing an L-shaped design.

**Cornhusk bag from Kamiah** — A Museum of Ethnography object was identified as a gift from Elizabeth Wilson, Nez Perce, Kamiah, Idaho, 1960. It is a flat, rectangular plant-fibre bag with a twisted closing cord and geometric patterns in purple, pink, and blue on both sides.

**Baskets** — A Museum of World Culture record identifies a *korg*, or basket, associated with the Nez Perce and the Rocky Mountains in the United States. The supplied record does not specify its materials or construction technique.

**Grass bags** — British Museum records include bags made of grass and bags made of vegetable fibre.

**Twining** — The catalogue records document twining in fibre bags and corn-husk wallets. The supplied sources do not establish a distinct Nez Perce name for the technique or compare it with neighbouring cultures.

**Beaded clothing and bags** — Museum photographs describe a Nez Perce woman wearing a beaded dress and holding two decorated bags at Lapwai, Idaho. The sources do not provide a named textile tradition for this clothing.

**Motif vocabulary.** Geometric pattern, diamond shape, L-shaped design, red rose, green leaf.

### Clothing & dress

Museum photographs document a Nez Perce woman wearing a beaded dress and ornament while holding decorated bags at Lapwai, Idaho. Portrait records describe Jason, identified as *Kol-kol-shu-a-tash*, wearing a decorated fringed hide tunic, decorated hide leggings, moccasins, a shell choker, and a fur headdress. Timothy, identified as *Tomoson*, is described in a decorated fringed hide tunic, decorated hide leggings, moccasins, a shell and bear claw choker, and a headband with a feather. The sources also record an embroidered pouch worn across Timothy’s torso. The supplied sources do not distinguish everyday from ceremonial dress, or provide Nez Perce names for garments, belts, footwear, or head coverings.

### Architecture

The sources used identify a Nez Perce woman posing before a clap-board constructed structure, described in the catalogue as “house?” They do not provide enough information about Nez Perce house forms, roofs, building materials, named structures, decoration, or urban traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum records include a baby-carrier made of deer skin, leather, and brass; fibre bags; grass bags; corn-husk wallets; and a basket. Portrait records also show pipes, embroidered pouches, and canes. The sources do not document Nez Perce ceramics, named metalworking traditions, wooden objects, or tool-making practices.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum photographs describe shell chokers, a shell and bear claw choker, a fur headdress, a feathered headband, ornaments, and beaded clothing. The Nez Perce article explains that the name “Nez Percé,” meaning “pierced nose,” was applied by French Canadian fur traders, but that nose piercing was not practiced by the tribe. The sources do not document tattoos, hair practices, ritual functions of adornment, or named Nez Perce jewelry types.

## Music & performance

The Nez Perce language sources mention *wéeyekweʔnipse*, glossed as “to sing one’s spirit song,” and refer to Nez Perce spirit-singing as a subject of performance and metaphor. The Nez Perce language article also lists Nez Perce stories and language-learning materials, including *Titwáatit: (Nez Perce Stories)*. The sources do not name instruments, song genres beyond spirit-singing, musical scales, performance ensembles, or contexts such as weddings, funerals, courts, or festivals.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document named Nez Perce dances, theatrical traditions, mask performances, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not provide an annual Nez Perce festival calendar or describe named birth, coming-of-age, wedding, or funeral rites. They do document seasonal movement between permanent winter villages and temporary camps, usually returning to the same locations each year. Salmon fishing was important at Celilo Falls before the construction of The Dalles Dam in 1957, and the Nez Perce maintained seasonal relationships with fishing, hunting, and gathering places.

## Foodways

The Nez Perce were semi-sedentary hunter-gatherers, and the sources describe food procurement through foraging. Salmon was an important cultural and economic resource; hatching, harvesting, and eating salmon remain important to the Nez Perce through ownership or co-management of salmon fish hatcheries. The people also traveled to the Plains of Montana to hunt buffalo. The sources mention camas prairie sites and the importance of fishing and hunting grounds, but do not provide named dishes, recipes, cooking methods, beverages, dietary rules, or ceremonial food practices.

## Oral tradition & literature

Nez Perce oral tradition is mentioned in connection with the interpretation of the name *cú·pŉitpeľu*, although the supplied material does not provide a full narrative. The language sources list *Titwáatit: (Nez Perce Stories)* and describe documentation of Nez Perce texts, vocabulary, grammar, and language courses. The Nez Perce Tribe is undertaking a language revitalization program intended to reintroduce the language into native usage. The sources do not name a Nez Perce epic, proverb collection, riddle tradition, or specific storytelling ceremony.

## Language & religion

Nez Perce, also called *nimipuutímt*, is a highly endangered Sahaptian language related to the dialects of Sahaptin. It belongs to the Sahaptian sub-family of the Plateau Penutian family. The language has vowel harmony, a complex stress system, flexible word order, and polysynthetic verbs that can express information corresponding to an entire English sentence. The sources describe spirit-singing but do not provide a general account of Nez Perce religion, denominations, religious institutions, or a broader system of spiritual practices.

## Overview

The Iowa, also known as Ioway or *Báxoje*, are a Native American tribe whose ancestral movements took them from the Great Lakes region through present-day Iowa and the Great Plains. They historically spoke Chiwere, a Siouan-Catawban language, and today are enrolled in the Iowa Tribe of Oklahoma or the Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska. In 1837, many Iowa were moved to reservations in Brown County, Kansas, and Richardson County, Nebraska; later, a band settled south of Perkins, Oklahoma. The 2000 census recorded 2,258 people identified in Iowa categories described in the source. Their material culture includes bark lodges, tipis, earth lodges, moccasins, hide clothing, quillwork and bead decoration, while their language and recorded songs remain important aspects of cultural preservation.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

*Báxoje* is the Iowa name for the people and their language, translated in the sources as “grey snow.” The sources do not document an Iowa textile pattern tradition under this name.

**Hide clothing** — Bison and deer hides were used for clothing. The catalogue record for moccasins describes Plains hide preparation involving a mixture containing bone marrow, ground entrails and cactus juice, intended to make the hide supple and durable.

**Quill work** — British Museum records describe Iowa chiefs wearing leggings with quill work decoration. The sources do not describe the techniques, motifs or social meanings of this decoration.

**Beaded clothing** — Museum records describe beaded leg bands, beaded leggings and decorated moccasins in portraits of Iowa chiefs. The sources do not identify named beadwork patterns or explain their production.

**Wool blankets and cloth garments** — Museum portraits show Iowa chiefs wearing wool blankets, cloth shirts, cloth headdresses, tunics and wool leggings. The records document these objects but do not describe a distinctive Iowa weaving tradition.

**Moccasins** — The National Museum of World Cultures Foundation catalogue lists moccasins dated 1870. The sources do not provide an Iowa vernacular name or a detailed construction description.

No additional pattern-bearing textile traditions are documented in the supplied sources.

### Clothing & dress

Iowa clothing included garments made from bison and deer hide, while museum portraits also show cloth shirts, tunics, wool blankets, wool leggings and decorated moccasins. The catalogue records describe moccasins, beaded leg bands, beaded leggings and leggings with quill work decoration. Iowa men traditionally shaved their heads and decorated them with deer hide. Portraits identify several Iowa chiefs, including Deer Ham (*Ta réke*), British (*Nag-a-rash*), No Heart (*Nacheninga*) and Knife (*Mah-hee*), wearing combinations of cloth or fur headdresses, feathers, chokers, gorgets, ear ornaments, necklaces, peace medals, wrist decorations and blankets. The records also show Deer Ham holding a walking stick or tomahawk, and Knife holding a bow and arrows. The sources do not distinguish everyday and ceremonial dress in detail.

### Architecture

Historically, Iowa houses included bark lodges, *chakiruthan*, tipis and earth lodges. Earth lodges were oven-shaped buildings covered with earth to protect against extremes of temperature and oriented to a cardinal direction. A smoke hole provided ventilation from a central hearth. During hunting or warfare, the portable tipi was used. The sources do not describe decoration, interior furnishing beyond the hearth, or later urban architecture.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources describe Iowa manufacture of alum pipes, which were traded together with furs with French colonizers. The museum records document everyday and personal objects appearing in portraits, including walking sticks, rifles, bows and arrows, tomahawks, peace medals, gorgets and necklaces. The sources do not describe Iowa ceramics, metalworking techniques, wooden household objects or named domestic vessels.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Museum records describe chokers, gorgets, ear ornaments, necklaces, peace medals, wrist decorations, hair ornaments and feathers in portraits of Iowa chiefs. ## Overview

The Muscogee, also called Mvskoke, Mvskokvlke, Muscogee Creek, or Creek, are related Indigenous peoples of the Southeastern Woodlands in the United States. Their historical homelands included southern Tennessee, much of Alabama, western Georgia, and parts of northern Florida. Most were forcibly removed to Indian Territory, now Oklahoma, during the 1830s. Muscogee communities are also present in Alabama, Florida, and Oklahoma. Their languages belong to the Eastern Muskogean branch of the Muskogean language family. Muscogee society developed autonomous towns, confederated town networks, agriculture, craft specialization, hunting, trade, ceremonial grounds, and ballparks. Their history also includes Mississippian culture, moundbuilding sites, oral traditions, complex political organization, and continuing language programs.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Chief’s dress** — The British Museum catalogue records a complete dress of a Muscogie chief, including a hide jacket with fringe, a cloth belt, a chief’s bag made of worsted cloth and beads, fringed worsted-cloth garters with beads, and skin moccasins sewn with silk-thread decorations.

**Beaded accessories** — The catalogue identifies beads on the chief’s bag and garters, while the belt is made of worsted cloth. The available records do not describe particular patterns, motifs, or regional distinctions.

**Silk-thread moccasin decoration** — The recorded pair of chief’s moccasins is sewn of skin and decorated with silk thread. The sources do not specify the form or symbolism of the decoration.

**Fringe** — Fringe appears on the recorded hide jacket and garters. The sources do not describe a named fringe tradition or its ceremonial meaning.

**Cloth and hide clothing materials** — The museum records distinguish hide, skin, worsted cloth, beads, and silk thread in the chief’s dress. The sources used do not cover other documented Muscogee textile traditions.

**Finger weaving** — The sources used do not cover finger weaving as a Muscogee practice.

**Muscogee ribbon shirts** — The sources used do not cover Muscogee ribbon shirts.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no specific textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The museum catalogue records a chief’s dress consisting of a hide jacket with fringe, a worsted-cloth belt, a chief’s bag with a tassel, fringed garters made of worsted cloth and beads, and skin moccasins decorated with silk thread. A British Museum drawing depicts Hilis Hadjo, or Josiah Francis, wearing red head-gear, a military red coat with epaulettes, a waist belt with tassels, and shoes with spurs; he is also shown with a pistol and a long thin pipe. Other catalogue records depict Creek men in shirts, trousers, jackets, waistcoats, bow ties, watch chains, and suits. The sources do not describe ordinary women’s dress, named ceremonial garments, or a distinct Muscogee head-covering tradition beyond the recorded red head-gear.

### Architecture

The sources describe Muscogee towns, plazas, ballparks, and square ceremonial dance grounds, as well as complex cities with earthwork mounds and surrounding networks of satellite towns and farmsteads. They do not describe house forms, roofing, construction materials, wall decoration, or named domestic building types.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources mention pottery in connection with the Woodland period, when locals developed pottery and small-scale horticulture in the Eastern Agricultural Complex. They also record trade in firearms, gunpowder, axes, glass beads, cloth, rum, and European goods, and identify craft specialization among precontact Muscogee polities. The Metropolitan Museum of Art catalogue records a nineteenth-century drum made of wood, skin, and various materials. The sources do not provide named Muscogee ceramic forms, metalworking techniques, or household object types.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum records mention beads on a chief’s bag and garters, silk-thread decoration on moccasins, and tassels on a bag and belt. The sources do not describe named jewelry forms, shell ornaments, tattoos, hair practices, or ritual body adornment.

## Music & performance

Muscogee town life included square ceremonial dance grounds and ballparks. The sources also describe the *heles hayv*, or medicine maker, officiating at rituals and providing black drink for purification ceremonies. The *tustunnuggee* was a ranking warrior and principal military adviser, while micos and other leaders organized village life. Muscogee creation stories and legends include spoken narratives concerning human emergence, the Maker of Breath, the Sun, the Moon, Thunder, the Tie Snake, the Horned Serpent, and Corn Woman.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art catalogue records a nineteenth-century drum made of wood, skin, and various materials. The sources do not identify its performance context, construction beyond the catalogue description, or a named musical genre. They also do not describe named song forms, vocal styles, instrumental ensembles, dance accompaniment, or performance settings such as weddings or funerals.

## Dance & theatre

Muscogee confederated town networks were organized around plazas, ballparks, and square ceremonial dance grounds. The sources identify ball-play as an important activity: in 1790, the Muscogee and Choctaw settled a land dispute by playing a game involving nearly 10,000 players and bystanders. The sources do not provide a named dance, theatrical form, mask tradition, or detailed choreography.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not provide an annual Muscogee festival calendar or named seasonal festivals. They describe ceremonial dance grounds and several ritual practices. The *heles hayv*, or medicine maker, officiated at rituals, including the provision of black drink for purification ceremonies. Muscogee cosmology divided the universe into the Upper World, Middle World, and Lower World, with the Middle World understood as a balance between order and chaos.

Muscogee mythology includes creation stories in which humans emerge from beneath the earth in the West and journey eastward. Legends of the Tie Snake and Horned Serpent concern prohibited food, transformation, and the maintenance of cosmic balance. Stories of Corn Woman describe corn coming from her body and her sacrifice allowing corn crops to grow. The sources do not describe birth, marriage, funeral, or coming-of-age rites.

## Foodways

The sources identify corn, or maize, as central to the development of Mississippian agriculture, agricultural surpluses, and population growth. They also describe Muscogee farming, hunting, deer-hide exchange, and the use of black drink in purification ceremonies. Corn Woman legends connect corn with sacrifice, fertility, and the growth of crops.

The sources do not name Muscogee dishes, cooking methods, dietary rules, tea or coffee traditions, or ceremonial foods beyond black drink. They also do not provide a detailed account of food preparation or household foodways.

## Oral tradition & literature

Muscogee oral history describes a migration from places west of the Mississippi River, followed by settlement on the east bank of the Ocmulgee River. Creation stories from Kasihta, Kasihta-Chickasaw-Coweta, and Coweta origins describe humans emerging from beneath the earth in the West and travelling eastward. These stories refer to Hesaketvmesē, meaning “Maker of Breath” or “the One Above who holds life’s breath,” also called Epohfvnkv, “the Creator” or “the One Above us.”

Muscogee legends include the Tie Snake, the Horned Serpent, and Corn Woman. The sources also describe the Muscogee Nation’s language classes and immersion camps, including programs offered by the College of the Muscogee Nation and other educational institutions. The sources do not identify a named epic, proverb collection, riddle tradition, or modern literary movement.

## Language & religion

Muscogee, also called Muskogee or Mvskoke, belongs to the Muskogean language family and the Eastern Muskogean branch. Related languages and varieties include Hitchiti-Mikasuki, Koasati, and Alabama. The three main dialects identified in the sources are Muscogee proper, Oklahoma Seminole Muscogee, and Florida Seminole Muscogee. Muscogee uses a traditional alphabet adopted by interpreters and chiefs as the National Alphabet in 1853.

Muscogee grammar includes synthetic verbs, person markers, tense, aspect, mood, tone, nasalization, and subject–object–verb order. Muscogee mythology describes the Upper, Middle, and Lower Worlds and figures including the Maker of Breath, the Sun, the Moon, Thunder, the Tie Snake, and the Horned Serpent. The sources used do not describe a current religious denomination or institutional religious landscape.

## Overview

The Potawatomi are an Indigenous North American tribe of the Great Plains, the upper Mississippi River, and the western Great Lakes region. They are also First Nations in Canada and traditionally speak Potawatomi, a Central Algonquian language. The Potawatomi call themselves *Neshnabé* and *Bodéwadmi*, the latter referring to “keepers of the fire” within the Council of Three Fires alliance with the Ojibwe and Odawa. The Potawatomi first lived in Lower Michigan, later moved to northern Wisconsin, and eventually settled in northern Indiana and central Illinois. Today, federally recognized Potawatomi tribes exist in the United States, including Wisconsin, Michigan, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Illinois, while Potawatomi people are also connected with First Nations in Ontario. The sources do not provide a current total population.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document named Potawatomi textile traditions, patterns, or techniques such as ribbonwork, quillwork, floral beadwork, or bandolier-bag production.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no Potawatomi textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

Museum catalogue records document clothing in several photographic portraits. The Sucker (*O-ta-wa*), a Potawatomi councillor, is shown wearing a cloth shirt, leggings, moccasins, a cloth turban, and a blanket around his shoulders while holding a pipe. Thunder Coming Down To The Ground (*Mzhik-ki-an*), a Potawatomi chief, appears in one portrait wearing a cloth tie, shirt, jacket, trousers, shoes, and a blanket, and in another wearing a three-piece suit, neck tie, and blanket. White Bear (*Se-nadz-win*), a Potawatomi chief, is recorded wearing a bow tie, shirt, waistcoat, jacket, and trousers. The Flash Of A Sturgeon In Turning (*Wa-wa-suk*) wears a three-piece suit and neck tie.

Other catalogue records show Potawatomi people dressed for a Hiawatha play. A man wears a porcupine hair roach with an eagle feather, shell gorget, fringed shirt, beaded bandolier bag, armbands of decorated quill-work, beaded ling covering, and fringed trousers. A woman wears a decorated beaded headband with two feathers, beaded necklaces, bracelets, and a decorated fringed hide dress. The sources do not distinguish everyday and ceremonial dress beyond these records.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Potawatomi house forms, building materials, roofs, named buildings, settlement architecture, or architectural decoration.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources identify several museum-held objects: a staff from the mid-19th century made of wood, native-tanned skin, and deer dewclaws, and a prescription stick from the early 19th century made of wood and pigment. The Water Spider story describes a web-woven bowl used to carry a hot coal. The sources do not provide further information about Potawatomi ceramics, metalwork, household goods, tools, or named object types.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum catalogue records mention a shell gorget, decorated beaded headband, beaded necklaces, bracelets, an eagle feather, a porcupine hair roach, and armbands of decorated quill-work. The records do not explain their ritual functions or provide information about Potawatomi tattooing, henna, hair practices, or other body adornment.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not describe Potawatomi musical genres, named songs, musical instruments, dance music, or performance contexts. One museum catalogue record states that a Potawatomi man held a pipe, but it does not identify the object as a musical instrument. The sources therefore do not cover Potawatomi music in sufficient detail for a cultural profile.

## Dance & theatre

The museum catalogue records include two studio portraits of Potawatomi people dressed for a Hiawatha play. One man wears a porcupine hair roach with an eagle feather, shell gorget, fringed shirt, beaded bandolier bag, decorated quill-work armbands, beaded ling covering, and fringed trousers. One woman wears a decorated beaded headband with two feathers, beaded necklaces, bracelets, and a decorated fringed hide dress. The sources do not identify a Potawatomi dance, dramatic tradition, theatre form, or performance sequence.

## Festivals & rituals

Potawatomi religion is described as the traditional Native American religion of the Potawatomi people, practiced in Potawatomi communities in Canada and the United States. It has no formal leadership or organizational structure and displays much internal variation. Together with the Odawa and Ojibwe nations, the Potawatomi form a confederation called the Three Fires.

The Potawatomi instruct children in the Seven Grandfather Teachings: wisdom, respect, love, honesty, humility, bravery, and truth, directed toward their people and all creation. A related story tells of the Water Spider, who listens while other animals hesitate to retrieve fire. She eventually crosses the water with a bowl woven from her web, brings back a hot coal, and is honored for her bravery in a great celebration.

The sources do not provide an annual festival calendar, dates for ritual observances, or descriptions of birth, coming-of-age, wedding, or funeral rites.

## Foodways

The sources state that Allium tricoccum is consumed in traditional Potawatomi cuisine and that Vaccinium myrtilloides is eaten fresh, dried, and canned. The root bark of Vaccinium myrtilloides is also used for an unspecified ailment. The sources do not name Potawatomi dishes, staple grains, cooking methods, ceremonial foods, beverages, dietary rules, or food-related festivals.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Water Spider story embodies the Seven Grandfather Teachings and emphasizes patience and listening. In the story, animals face the cold after fire has been lost. The Water Spider listens as the others successively doubt their ability to retrieve it, then brings back a hot coal in a bowl woven from her web. The animals honor her bravery in a great celebration.

The sources also mention efforts to preserve Potawatomi language and cultural knowledge. Donald Neaseno Perrot, a native speaker who grew up in the Powers Bluff, Wisconsin, area, made Potawatomi videos and books. The Pokégnek Bodéwadmik Pokagon Band of Potawatomi began a master-apprentice program in January 2013, pairing language apprentices with fluent Potawatomi speakers. The sources do not identify a Potawatomi epic, proverb collection, riddle tradition, or wider literary corpus.

## Language & religion

Potawatomi is a Central Algonquian language of the Algonquian family and is most similar to the Odawa language. It has borrowed considerable vocabulary from Sauk and exhibits extensive vowel syncope. Potawatomi is spoken around the Great Lakes in Michigan and Wisconsin, as well as in Kansas, Oklahoma, and southern Ontario. The language is divided between Northern Potawatomi, spoken in Ontario and in Michigan and Wisconsin, and Southern Potawatomi, spoken in Kansas and Oklahoma. As of 2001, fewer than 1,300 people spoke Potawatomi as a first language, most of them elderly.

The most commonly used writing system is the Pedagogical System developed by the Wisconsin Native American Languages Program. In Kansas, the BWAKA system is used. A traditional syllabic writing system has also been used by Potawatomi, Odawa, Sauk, Meskwaki, and Ho-Chunk communities, but it has not been incorporated into the Unicode standards. Potawatomi religion has no formal leadership or organizational structure and varies internally.
