## Overview

The Mandan are a Native American people of the Great Plains who have lived primarily in what is now North Dakota and historically along the Upper Missouri River and the Heart and Knife rivers. They are enrolled in the Three Affiliated Tribes of the Fort Berthold Reservation; about half live in the reservation area, while others live elsewhere in the United States and in Canada. The Mandan developed a settled, agrarian culture in permanent villages of large, round earth lodges. They were a major trading nation whose corn surpluses were exchanged for bison meat and fat, horses, guns, and other goods. Their language belongs to the Siouan family and is closely associated historically with Hidatsa and Crow through long contact.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document Mandan textile or pattern traditions in sufficient detail for this section.

**Buffalo robes** — The museum records describe Buffalo Dance figures wearing buffalo robes. The same drawings show the buffalo figures elaborately painted and carrying rattles and long sticks.

**Painted buffalo figures** — British Museum catalogue records describe painted buffalo figures associated with the Buffalo Dance. The records do not specify the pigments or painting technique.

**Porcupine-quill embroidery** — The sources used do not document Mandan porcupine-quill embroidery.

**Geometric beadwork** — The sources used do not document Mandan geometric beadwork.

**Hide painting** — The sources used mention elaborately painted buffalo robes and painted buffalo figures, but do not provide further information about Mandan hide-painting methods or designs.

**Motif vocabulary.** Buffalo figures, buffalo robes, wheat bundle, rattle, long stick.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used provide very little information about everyday Mandan dress. The museum records identify a shoe from the Plains United States associated with the Mandan and preserve an inscription referring to “Chief Yonktonau Long mandan,” but they do not identify the shoe’s construction, material, or precise use. Catalogue descriptions of the Buffalo Dance show figures wearing buffalo robes, elaborately painted and carrying rattles and long sticks. No documented information in the sources distinguishes men’s and women’s daily clothing or identifies Mandan head coverings, belts, ceremonial footwear, or other named garments.

### Architecture

Mandan villages were permanent settlements containing large, round earth lodges, some 40 feet (12 m) in diameter, arranged around a central plaza. Matrilineal families lived in the lodges. The sources also describe defensive ditches and palisades around villages, including two trenches at Double Ditch Village and stronger fortifications at Huff Village. Double Ditch Village stood on the east bank of the Missouri River, north of where present-day Bismarck developed. Its remaining depressions mark former lodges and cache pits used to store dehydrated corn. Like-a-Fishhook Village was built upriver after the survivors of the 1837–38 epidemic joined the Hidatsa; the Hidatsa later moved some 20 miles north and constructed the village with common protection in mind.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The Mandan sources describe cache pits for storing dehydrated corn, defensive works, paddles, canoes, rattles, long sticks, and an object called the Ark or Big Canoe. A museum catalogue identifies a paddle from the Fort Berthold Indian Agency at Elbowoods, North Dakota, and describes it as intended for a canoe. British Museum records describe rattles and long sticks used in Buffalo Dance scenes. The sources used do not document Mandan ceramics, metalwork, pottery forms, or named household tools in further detail.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The Mandan sources mention a band called the Is’tope, glossed as “those who tattooed themselves.” They do not describe the tattoos’ designs, materials, social meaning, or techniques. The sources used do not document Mandan jewelry, amulets, hair practices, or other forms of body adornment.

## Music & performance

The sources identify rattles and a medicine pipe in Mandan ceremonial contexts. British Museum catalogue records describe buffalo figures in the Buffalo Dance holding rattles and long sticks. The dance represented in the drawing is connected to a Mandan account in which the Buffalos’ creation supplied the people with food during the coming year. Other catalogue records describe the Medicine Lodge, where the annual “Religious Ceremony” of the Mandans was held, and an Ark or Big Canoe standing in the centre of the village. The Master of Ceremonies is shown leaning against it with the Medicine Pipe in his hands.

The Mandan sources also mention the annual Okipa ceremony. George Catlin was permitted to watch it in 1832 after Four Bears invited him. The sources do not provide a complete account of its songs, instruments, choreography, or musical structure. David Thompson recorded that Mandan amusements included dancing and singing and that these were conducted with order and decorum. No other named Mandan instruments or song genres are documented in the supplied sources.

## Dance & theatre

The Buffalo Dance is represented in a series of British Museum drawings. One catalogue record identifies the scene as “Bel-lohk Na-pic (the Buffalo Dance)” and describes two of the eight Buffalos performing the dance. The Buffalo figures are elaborately painted, wear buffalo robes, and hold rattles and long sticks. Further drawings show the Evil Spirit, O-ke-hee-de, entering the area where the eight Buffalos are dancing after being defeated by the medicine pipe. The women and children then surround and pelt him with sticks and dirt, rejoicing over his defeat.

The sources also identify the Okipa as a sacred annual ceremony and describe the Medicine Lodge as the setting of the Mandans’ annual “Religious Ceremony.” They do not explain the full sequence of these ceremonies or distinguish all their ritual and theatrical elements.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources document the annual Okipa ceremony and an annual religious ceremony held in the Medicine Lodge. George Catlin attended the Okipa after Four Bears allowed him to watch it in 1832. During an attack on the Mandan village Nuptadi around 1785, the “turtles” used in the Okipa ceremony were saved; Mandan woman Scattercorn recounted that the turtles produced water that protected them.

The Buffalo Dance was connected with the creation of the Buffalos and with the supply of food during the coming year. In the Medicine Lodge, the Master of Ceremonies is shown with the medicine pipe beside the Ark or Big Canoe. The sources do not document a complete annual festival calendar, birth ceremonies, coming-of-age rites, weddings, funerals, or other life-cycle rituals. They do document epidemics, warfare, trade, and village relocation as major events in Mandan history, including the smallpox epidemics of 1781 and 1837–38.

## Foodways

Mandan foodways were based on settled agriculture and extensive farming carried out by women. Corn was a major crop and a principal article of trade. Mandan villages contained cache pits for storing dehydrated corn, and the Mandan exchanged large corn surpluses with other tribes for bison meat and fat. Crops and other goods circulated through Mandan-Hidatsa settlements, which were major trade centres in the Great Plains.

Bison products were important both as food and as trade goods. The Buffalo Dance was associated with the creation of Buffalos to supply the people with food during the coming year. The Mandan also traded for horses, guns, and other goods, and used horses for transportation, carrying packs, pulling travois, and hunting. The sources do not name specific prepared dishes, cooking methods, beverages, dietary rules, or ceremonial foods beyond these references to corn, bison, and buffalo products.

## Oral tradition & literature

Mandan oral tradition states that the Hidatsa were once nomadic until their encounter with the Mandan, who taught them to build stationary villages and cultivate agriculture. Mandan tradition also refers to an eastern place near a lake as an ancestral point of origin. Stories connected with the Okipa include the account of turtles producing water to protect people when Nuptadi Village was burned by the Sioux.

The Mandan winter count of Butterfly records warfare in 1835–1836, including the destruction of fifty Sioux tepees and the loss of thirty men in a war party. The sources also preserve statements attributed to Mandan people, including Scattercorn and Four Bears. Language-preservation work includes school programs, materials produced by the MHA Language Project, a vocabulary app, a dictionary, books in Mandan, a summer learning institute, and teacher materials. The 2020 documentary *To Save A Language* portrays Indrek Park’s efforts with Edwin Benson.

## Language & religion

Mandan, also called *Núu’etaa íroo* in the Mandan-language article, belongs to the Siouan language family. It has two main dialects, Núu’etaa/Nuu’etaare and Rúptaa/Rúptaare; the Mandan article also names Nuptare and Nuetare. Only the Nuptare variety survived into the 20th century, and its speakers were bilingual in Hidatsa. The sources describe Mandan as a separate branch of the Siouan family because long contact with Hidatsa and Crow obscured its exact relationship to other Siouan languages.

Mandan has grammatical forms that vary according to the sex of the addressee. The supplied sources describe medicine men as having their own secret language. Religious practices documented in the sources include the Okipa, the Medicine Lodge ceremony, the medicine pipe, the Ark or Big Canoe, and the Buffalo Dance. The sources do not describe a wider Mandan religious system or contemporary religious affiliation.

## Overview

The Karuk people, also called *káruk vaʼáraaras* or Karok, are an Indigenous people of California whose ancestral territory extends along the Klamath River from Bluff Creek near Orleans through Siskiyou County and into Southern Oregon. Happy Camp lies in the heart of this territory. The Karuk language is a language isolate, sometimes grouped with the proposed Hokan family, and the tribe maintains an active language revitalization program. According to the 2010 census, there were 6,115 Karuk individuals. Karuk cultural life includes hunting, gathering, fishing, basketmaking, ceremonial dances, plant knowledge, and the continued practice of ceremonies intended to heal and “fix the world.”

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Karuk basketry** — The sources document basketry made with plant and animal materials, including bear grass, spruce or willow roots, willow or hazel sticks, woodwardia fern, maidenhair fern, and porcupine quill. Objects in the museum records use twined technique and include ceremonial caps, hats, trays, lidded baskets, storage baskets, cooking baskets, tobacco baskets, and trinket baskets.

**Ceremonial basket caps** — The museum records describe basketry caps made from plant materials, often including bear grass, spruce or willow roots, willow or hazel sticks, and dyed woodwardia fern. Several have named designs, including “grizzly paw,” “friendship,” “house ladder,” and “snake nose.”

**Woman’s basketry hat** — One catalogue record identifies a woman’s hat made of basketry, with pine root listed as a possible material.

**Wooden and root trays** — A tray is recorded as made from wood, possibly willow or hazel, coniferous root, maidenhair and woodwardia fern, and porcupine quill.

**Lidded baskets** — The catalogue records lidded baskets made with wood, possibly willow or hazel, coniferous root, woodwardia fern, and bear grass. One basket is described as possibly the top or lid for a large seed basket.

**Tobacco baskets** — One recorded object is a trinket or tobacco basket with a lid, made from plant material and using twined technique.

**Motif vocabulary.** “Obsidian blade” or “flint,” “salt and pepper” or “stand-up,” “grizzly paw,” “friendship,” “house ladder,” and “snake nose.”

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe everyday or ceremonial clothing in detail. They identify a woman’s basketry hat and several ceremonial caps or basket hats, but do not provide documented information about garments, belts, footwear, or distinctions between men’s and women’s dress beyond the woman’s hat record.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Karuk houses, village architecture, roof forms, building materials, or named building types.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources used do not document Karuk ceramics or metalwork. They do record wooden trays and baskets used or described as storage, cooking, seed, trinket, and tobacco containers, as well as basketry caps and hats made with plant materials and, in some cases, animal material.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not describe Karuk jewelry, tattoos, hair practices, or other forms of body adornment. Porcupine quill appears in several museum catalogue descriptions as a material used in basketry objects.

## Music & performance

The sources describe ceremonial performances but do not identify musical instruments or provide detailed information about song genres. The Brush Dance, Jump Dance, and Pikyavish ceremonies last for several days. They are practiced to heal and “fix the world,” to pray for plentiful acorns, deer, and salmon, and to restore social goodwill and individual good luck. The film *Pikyáv (to fix it)*, produced in 2008 for the Truly California series, documents this subject.

Karuk language documentation includes recorded everyday conversations, songs, stories, and poetry. William Bright and Susan Gehr worked on a Karuk dictionary, published in 2005, while language documentation efforts also sought to preserve the cultural context of fluent speakers’ language use. The sources do not name instruments, specific song forms, or performance settings such as weddings, funerals, courts, or tea houses.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name the Brush Dance, Jump Dance, and Pikyavish ceremonies. These are ceremonial dances practiced over several days for healing, repairing the world, praying for plentiful acorns, deer, and salmon, and restoring social goodwill and individual good luck. The sources do not describe theatrical traditions, masks, dramatic genres, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment dance beyond this information.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not provide an annual festival calendar or dates for Karuk ritual events. They describe the Brush Dance, Jump Dance, and Pikyavish ceremonies as lasting several days and as serving purposes of healing, repairing the world, prayer for plentiful acorns, deer, and salmon, restoration of social goodwill, and individual good luck.

Karuk people traditionally cultivated a form of tobacco and were one among several California tribes to sow and harvest tobacco plants. The sources also describe continuing cultural practices of hunting, gathering, fishing, basketmaking, and ceremonial dancing. They do not cover birth rites, coming-of-age ceremonies, weddings, funerals, or other life-cycle rituals.

## Foodways

Karuk subsistence included hunting, gathering, and fishing along the Klamath River. The sources specifically connect ceremony with prayers for plentiful acorns, deer, and salmon. Karuk people developed detailed uses of plants and animals for food, tools, clothing, and pharmaceuticals.

The Karuk cultivated a form of tobacco. They also used fronds of the Coastal woodfern as anti-microbial agents while preparing eels for food consumption. The sources mention food harvesting from nature and the use of plant and animal materials, but they do not name dishes, grains, cooking methods, beverages, dietary rules, or ceremonial recipes.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not describe a specific Karuk epic, folktale cycle, proverb tradition, riddle tradition, or named traditional narrative. They do document language preservation through the recording of conversations, songs, stories, and poetry spoken by fluent Karuk speakers.

William Bright documented the Karuk language beginning in 1949 and later worked with Susan Gehr on a dictionary published in 2005. The Karuk Language Restoration Committee, established in 1990, created a plan involving the recording and writing of fluent speakers, training new speakers, raising awareness of the language’s cultural importance, receiving community feedback, and facilitating participation in programs where people practice and speak Karuk.

## Language & religion

Karuk, also called Karok, is the traditional language of the Karuk people around the Klamath River in Northwestern California. It is classified as a language isolate and has sometimes been grouped with the proposed Hokan family. The language has three tones—high, low, and falling—and is polysynthetic. Karuk has been written using several conventions, and a standardized writing system was adopted in the 1980s.

The sources describe ceremonial practices concerned with healing, repairing the world, prayer, social goodwill, and good luck, but they do not identify a formal religion, denomination, religious doctrine, or contemporary religious landscape. Karuk language revitalization includes the Karuk Language Restoration Committee, bilingual education, and a master–apprentice immersion program begun in 1992.

## Overview

The Yakama are a Native American tribe with nearly 10,851 members, based primarily in eastern Washington state. Today, Yakama people are enrolled in the federally recognized Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation, governed by a Yakama Tribal Council representing 14 tribes. Their reservation lies along the Yakima River and covers approximately 1.2 million acres (5,260 km2). Yakama territory historically extended across the Columbia River Plateau, from the Yakima River and its tributaries to the Columbia River, Lower Snake River, Wenatchee River, and the western side of the Cascade Range. Yakama is a northwestern dialect of Sahaptin, a Sahaptian language of the Plateau Penutian family. Hunting, gathering, salmon fishing, river territories, beadwork, regalia, and longhouse life are documented aspects of Yakama culture.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used document beaded clothing accessories and bags, but do not cover the seed traditions of wa'paas basketry, tule mat weaving, tule basketry, cedar-bark weaving, willow-bark weaving, sagebrush-fiber clothing, twined basketry, coiled basketry, or basket hats.

***Beaded skin gauntlets*** — British Museum records describe light brown skin gauntlets with fringed strips and glass beadwork. One pair has a geometric pattern in blue, red, black, and white, with a floral design below; another has a red rose with green leaves, a multicoloured peacock, and a pink flower.

***Beaded cloth bags*** — The catalogue records sewn cloth bags made from cotton, wool, velvet, or felted wool, with skin or braided skin straps. Their fronts carry glass-bead designs including flowers, roses, a parrot, a black bison, a brown deer, and a white and black eagle.

***Beaded purses and handbags*** — A cloth purse has a metal clasp, glass-beaded red roses on blue and white grounds, and a black cotton carrying strap.

***Beaded skin bag*** — One skin bag is lined with blue cotton printed with flowers and decorated with a white and black eagle above red and yellow flowers. Nine sets of leather tassels hang from its bottom, each decorated with four blue glass beads.

**Motif vocabulary.** Geometric pattern, red rose, green leaves, peacock, pink flower, parrot, black bison, brown deer, white and black eagle, red and yellow flowers.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not provide a general account of everyday Yakama clothing, footwear, belts, head coverings, or gender-specific dress. Museum records do document skin gauntlets, including one made of skin and another described as smoked skin, with skin fringe and glass beadwork. The catalogue also records photographs of Yakama men gathered in a longhouse “in regalia,” a studio portrait of five sons of a Yakama chief in regalia, and a Yakama husband and wife with child posing along the river. The sources do not identify the garments, ceremonial distinctions, or vernacular names of the clothing shown.

### Architecture

The sources used mention a longhouse in photographic catalogue records, where Yakama men are shown gathered in regalia at Toppenish, Washington, USA. They do not describe the longhouse’s construction, materials, roof, interior arrangement, decoration, or wider Yakama architectural traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources used do not document Yakama ceramics, wooden objects, tools, or household goods in general. The museum catalogue records metal clasps and metal snap closures on two textile objects, together with cotton, wool, velvet, felted wool, leather, skin, glass beads, and braided or sewn skin straps.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not document Yakama jewelry, tattooing, hair practices, or ritual body adornment. The museum objects include decorative glass beadwork, leather tassels, and fringed skin elements attached to gauntlets and bags.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not identify Yakama musical instruments, named song genres, or performance forms. They do document the Washane, described as the “Dreamer Religion,” associated with the Wanapum dreamer-prophet Smohalla, whose name is glossed as “Dreamer” or “Preacher.” Other prophets named in the source are Chief Homli of the Walla Walla, Kotiakan of the Pa'kiut'-ħlama local group of Lower Yakama, and Lishwailait and Ashnithlai, both identified as Klickitat. The source says that adherents included Chief Joseph and his Nez Percé followers, as well as Native people from other tribes in the region. No musical context, instrument, dance accompaniment, or performance setting is described.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover Yakama dances, theatre, dramatic traditions, or named entertainment forms.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not provide an annual festival calendar or descriptions of Yakama birth, coming-of-age, wedding, or funeral rites. They describe seasonal movement and fishing sites in historical Yakama territories: the area originally known as “Mool-mool” was a campsite for the summer and early fall seasons, and Priest Rapids was an important Wanapum settlement and fishing ground. The sources also state that Yakama people were hunters and gatherers known for trading salmon harvested from annual runs in the Columbia River. In the late 20th century, treaty-protected fishing rights were reaffirmed in United States v. Washington, known as the Boldt Decision, 1974, and United States v. Oregon, Sohappy v. Smith, 1969.

## Foodways

The sources used identify salmon as the principal foodway. The Yakama were hunters and gatherers known for trading salmon harvested from annual runs in the Columbia River. Historical Yakama territories included numerous important fisheries, including Prosser Falls, the Cowlitz Falls of Cowlitz River, and the Wanapum fishing grounds at Priest Rapids. The source explains that the Yakima River name Tapteal means “rapids,” referring to the waterfalls at Prosser, Washington. It also records place names associated with fish and fishing: Kachess Lake is glossed as “more fish,” Keechelus Lake as “few fish,” and Teanaway River as a “[salmon] drying place.” The sources do not describe recipes, cooking methods, named dishes, ceremonial foods, beverages, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not identify Yakama folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, or named literary cycles. They record the traditional language name *Ichishkíin Sɨ́nwit*, meaning “this language,” and state that the Yakama Nation tribal Cultural Resources program has promoted its use instead of the name Sahaptin. The sources also identify the Washane, or “Dreamer Religion,” and name Smohalla as its most prominent leader. Donald M. Hines’s *Ghost Voices: Yakima Indian myths, legend, humor, and hunting stories* is listed among the further-reading works in the Yakama article, but the supplied sources do not summarize its contents.

## Language & religion

Yakama is a northwestern dialect of Sahaptin, a Sahaptian language of the Plateau Penutian family. Sahaptin is spoken in parts of southern Washington, northern Oregon, and southwestern Idaho, and among the Yakama, Warm Springs, and Umatilla. In the Yakama dialect, the language is called *Ichishkíin Sɨ́nwit*, also spelled *Ichishkíin*, *Íchishkin*, *Íchishkink*, or *Chishkíin*. The source says that *Ichishkínk* and *Chishkín* mean literally “in this way/manner.” Sahaptin has a split ergative syntax, direct-inverse voicing, and applicative constructions. The sources document the Washane, or “Dreamer Religion,” led most prominently by Smohalla, but do not provide a broader account of current Yakama religious life.

## Overview

The Caddo people, also called *Hasí꞉nay* in the Caddo language, comprise the Caddo Nation of Oklahoma, a federally recognized tribe headquartered in Binger, Oklahoma. Historically, Caddo communities inhabited much of what is now northeast Texas, western Louisiana, southwestern Arkansas, and southeastern Oklahoma, especially the Piney Woods and areas near the Caddo River. About 6,000 people are enrolled in the Caddo Nation, including 3,044 living in Oklahoma. Caddo belongs to the Caddoan language family, which also includes Pawnee-Kitsai languages and Wichita. The Caddo are significant in the cultural history of the Southern United States because their ancestors formed the Caddoan Mississippian culture, built large earthwork mounds, developed extensive maize agriculture, and maintained distinctive religious, artistic, linguistic, and ceremonial traditions.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document Caddo textile or pattern traditions.

### Clothing & dress

The Caddo sources describe clothing production as part of women’s material work but do not identify named garments, weaving traditions, footwear, or head coverings. A Caddo woman named Zacado is said to have instructed the tribe in making clothing. The Caddo also practiced body ornamentation. Men favored painted skin, jewelry, pierced ears, and hair decorations such as braids adorned with bird feathers or animal fur. Women wore some jewelry and styled their hair similarly to men, while tattooing was especially associated with women and could cover most of the body, including the face.

Museum records show studio portraits of Caddo chiefs wearing western-style three-piece suits. Little Boy, also identified as Show-e-tat, is shown with a beaded waistband and metal ear ornaments. White Deer is shown with metal ear ornaments, while Warloupe, also identified as Nah-ah-sa-nah, is shown in a western-style three-piece suit.

### Architecture

Caddo settlements included villages, hamlets, and farmsteads distributed throughout the Caddo world. Leaders directed the construction of platform mounds, which served as temple mounds and platforms for residences of the elite. These flat-topped earthworks were arranged around leveled, large, open plazas that were usually kept swept clean and were often used for ceremonial occasions.

The Caddo lived mainly in the Piney Woods, a region of rolling hills, steep river valleys, and intermittent wetlands called “bayous.” The sources do not describe the form, materials, or roofs of ordinary Caddo dwellings.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Caddo women made wooden mortars, pots, and other utensils from clay. Wood and clay tools were carved and molded for daily tasks such as preparing food, and men and women were buried with objects they had made. A museum record describes a Caddo bottle or vessel with a globular body and narrow neck, found near Fayetteville. Its exterior, except for the bottom, was colored red with iron ochre. The record associates the vessel with a Caddo method of coloring pottery by dipping the vessel in ochre.

The Caddo also used handcrafted bows and arrows for hunting. An old Caddo man carried a drum, a pipe, and fire in the creation story, and tobacco was cultivated and used ceremonially.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Caddo body adornment included painted skin, jewelry, pierced ears, hair decorations, braids, bird feathers, and animal fur. Men are specifically described as favoring body modifications and ornamentation, while women used tattooing extensively. Tattoos could cover most of the body, including the face.

The museum portraits of Little Boy, White Deer, and Warloupe document metal ear ornaments, and Little Boy is additionally shown with a beaded waistband. The sources do not provide named jewelry types or describe the manufacture or ritual functions of these ornaments.

## Music & performance

Caddo culture includes songs and dances taught and performed by the Hasinai Society and the Caddo Culture Club. These organizations support the continuation of Caddo culture and its transmission to younger generations. The sources do not give specific names for the songs or dances, describe their musical structures, or identify a complete instrument tradition.

The creation story assigns continuing religious importance to a drum, a pipe, and fire. Tobacco was cultivated and used ceremonially. Caddo religious life developed a cycle of ceremonies around important periods of seasonal corn cultivation. In the late 19th century, the Caddo adopted the Ghost Dance religion, which practitioners believed would help restore traditional ways and halt European-American intrusions. John Wilson, a Caddo/Delaware medicine man who spoke only Caddo, became an influential Ghost Dance leader. In 1880 he became a peyote roadman and introduced the Big Moon ceremony, while the tribe already knew the Half Moon peyote ceremony. The Caddo Nation remains active in the Native American Church.

## Dance & theatre

The Hasinai Society and Caddo Culture Club teach and perform Caddo songs and dances as part of cultural preservation. The Ghost Dance was practiced by Caddo people in the late 19th century and was associated with hopes of returning to traditional ways and stopping European-American intrusions. The sources do not identify named Caddo dances beyond the Ghost Dance, nor do they describe theatrical, masked, or dramatic traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

Caddo religious practice centers on Kadhi háyuh, translated as “Leader Above” or “Leader in the Sky.” In earlier times, priests led the people, including a head priest called the *xinesi*, who was said to commune with spirits residing near Caddo temples. A cycle of ceremonies developed around important stages of seasonal corn cultivation.

The Caddo creation story says that the people emerged from a cave called *Chahkanina*, or “the place of crying,” at the confluence of the Red River of the South and the Mississippi River in northern present-day Louisiana. Their leader, Moon, instructed them not to look back. An old man carried a drum, a pipe, and fire, while his wife carried corn and pumpkin seeds. The wolf looked back, and the exit from the underground closed to those remaining below.

Tobacco was used ceremonially, and early priests drank a purifying sacrament made from wild olive leaves. The sources do not describe Caddo weddings, funerals, initiations, annual festivals with fixed dates, or other life-cycle ceremonies.

## Foodways

Caddo foodways were based on cultivated crops, hunting, gathering, and seasonal processing. Maize was particularly important, alongside sunflower, pumpkins, squash, beans, melons, and tobacco. Acorns and roots were gathered and processed for food during the cold seasons, when crops did not grow. Wild turkeys held cultural significance, and men hunted wild turkey, quail, rabbits, bears, and bison with handcrafted bows and arrows.

The Caddo were farmers, and by 1200 their villages, hamlets, and farmsteads had developed extensive maize agriculture. Agricultural surpluses supported denser settlement, while artisans and craftsmen developed specialized skills. Elderly women planted and cultivated the seeds for the seasonal crop, and younger and healthy women gathered fruits, seeds, and vegetables during warm seasons.

The sources do not identify named Caddo dishes, recipes, cooking methods, beverages, dietary rules, or food served at particular ceremonies. Tobacco was cultivated and used ceremonially, and wild olive leaves were used in a purifying sacrament drink by early priests.

## Oral tradition & literature

Caddo oral history preserves a creation account centered on emergence from *Chahkanina*, the “place of crying,” at the confluence of the Red River of the South and the Mississippi River. The story includes Moon, the wolf that looked back, the drum, pipe, fire, corn, and pumpkin seeds. It also recounts the westward movement of the Caddo along the Red River, called *Bah'hatteno* in Caddo, and the teachings of Zacado concerning hunting, fishing, dwellings, and clothing.

Caddoan oral traditions are described as an important part of Caddo culture. The Kiwat Hasí꞉nay foundation worked to record and digitally archive them, while the Caddo Nation Language Preservation Program, launched in August 2022, sought to archive resources, share them through community events and programs, and develop a curriculum. The sources do not identify a Caddo epic, proverb collection, riddle tradition, or named literary genre.

## Language & religion

Caddo, whose endonym is *Hasí꞉nay*, belongs to the Caddoan language family. Its commonly used dialects included Hasinai and Hainai, while Kadohadacho, Natchitoches, and Yatasi were also identified. The language is described as recently dormant, with the last native speaker dying in 2025; revitalization programs continue. The Kiwat Hasí꞉nay foundation offered language classes and created dictionaries, phrase books, and other resources. The Caddo Nation also developed language classes, recordings, digital archives, an Android app, and a language-preservation program.

Caddo religion focuses on Kadhi háyuh, “Leader Above” or “Leader in the Sky.” Priests, including the *xinesi*, were associated with temples and spirits. Ceremonies followed seasonal corn cultivation, and tobacco, fire, drums, pipes, and purifying drinks had religious importance. Later Caddo religious life included the Ghost Dance, the Half Moon peyote ceremony, the Big Moon ceremony, and continued activity in the Native American Church.

## Overview

The Otoe (*Jiwére* in Chiwere) are a Native American people of the Midwestern United States. Historically, they lived as a semi-nomadic people on the Central Plains along the Missouri River in Nebraska, Kansas, Iowa, and Missouri. The Otoe language, Chiwere, belongs to the Siouan family and is closely related to the languages of the Iowa, Missouria, and Ho-Chunk tribes. The Otoe lived in elm-bark lodges while farming and used tipis when traveling. They often left their villages to hunt buffalo, and the American bison became central to their diet and culture. Today, Otoe people belong to the federally recognized Otoe-Missouria Tribe of Indians, headquartered in Red Rock, Oklahoma.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Wool blankets** — Wool blankets appear in the museum records as clothing worn around the waist by Otoe chiefs. They are shown together with leggings, moccasins, necklaces, and other dress items.

**Beadwork** — Beadwork is documented on wool leggings worn by Medicine Horse and Buffalo Chief. The records describe beadwork decoration at the bottom of Medicine Horse’s leggings and beadwork decoration and fringe on Buffalo Chief’s leggings.

**Hide leggings** — Little Pipe is recorded wearing hide leggings with fringe in one studio portrait. The source does not provide a vernacular name or a fuller account of the technique.

The sources used do not document additional Otoe textile or pattern traditions.

### Clothing & dress

The museum records describe chiefly dress in studio portraits. Little Pipe, an Otoe Chief, wears a decorated fur turban with an eagle feather, ear ornaments, a beaded choker, necklaces, a checked cloth shirt, rings, and a wool blanket around his waist. In another portrait he wears hide leggings with fringe, while a wool blanket lies on the floor beside him.

Medicine Horse, an Otoe Chief, wears a decorated fur turban with an eagle feather, ear ornaments, beaded necklaces, a peace medal, wool leggings with beadwork decoration at the bottom, leg bands, and moccasins. Buffalo Chief wears a decorated fur turban with two eagle feathers, ear ornaments, a beaded choker, necklaces, a peace medal, wool leggings with beadwork decoration and fringe, a wool blanket around his waist, and moccasins.

The sources also record non-Otoe interpreters wearing brimmed felt hats, ties, shirts, vests, suit jackets, trousers, and leather shoes. They do not describe women’s dress or distinguish everyday clothing from ceremonial clothing.

### Architecture

The Otoe lived in elm-bark lodges while farming and used tipis while traveling. The sources identify these two building types and connect them with a semi-nomadic life on the Central Plains, but they do not describe roof forms, interior arrangements, decoration, or construction details beyond the use of elm bark.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources used do not document Otoe ceramics, metalwork, household goods, or craft traditions in this section. The museum records do show chiefs holding pipe tomahawks or tomahawks, and Medicine Horse and Buffalo Chief wear peace medals.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum records document ear ornaments, beaded chokers, beaded necklaces, rings, and peace medals in Otoe chiefly dress. The records also describe decorated fur turbans with eagle feathers: one feather for Little Pipe and Medicine Horse, and two feathers for Buffalo Chief. The sources do not explain the ritual functions of these objects or document tattooing, hair practices, or other forms of body adornment.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not document Otoe musical instruments, song genres, musical performances, or performance contexts. They mention a pipe tomahawk and tomahawks in museum portraits, but do not identify these objects as musical instruments or describe their use in music.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document Otoe dances, theatre, dramatic traditions, or performance settings.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not describe an annual Otoe festival calendar, seasonal ceremonies, life-cycle rites, funerals, weddings, or coming-of-age practices. They do state that the Otoe adopted the horse culture and semi-nomadic lifestyle of the Great Plains and that the American bison became central to their diet and culture, but they do not connect these subjects with named rituals.

## Foodways

The Otoe farmed, lived in villages, and often left their settlements to hunt buffalo. After adopting the semi-nomadic lifestyle of the Great Plains, the American bison became central to their diet and culture. The sources do not name particular dishes, cooking methods, staple grains, beverages, dietary rules, or ceremonial foods.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not document Otoe folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, or storytelling contexts. They identify Annette Arkeketa as a poet and playwright and Anna Lee Walters as an author. They also mention the Ioway-Otoe Language project of the Ioway Cultural Institute and the Baxoje, the Ioway Nation, on NativeWeb, but provide no further description of Otoe oral literature or language-preservation practices.

## Language & religion

The Otoe language is Chiwere, or *Jiwére*, and belongs to the Siouan family. It is closely related to the languages of the Iowa, Missouria, and Ho-Chunk tribes. The Otoe were once part of the Ho-Chunk and Siouan-speaking tribes of the Western Great Lakes and Upper Midwest. Around the 16th century, successive groups split off and migrated west and south, becoming distinct tribes including the Otoe, the Missouria, and the Ioway.

The sources mention Christian missionaries and a mission in connection with the Otoe during the 19th century. They do not provide a fuller account of Otoe religious beliefs, sacred practices, denominations, or ritual specialists.

## Overview

The Bannock were originally Northern Paiute but are more culturally affiliated with the Northern Shoshone. Their traditional lands included northern Nevada, southeastern Oregon, southern Idaho, and western Wyoming. Today they are enrolled in the federally recognized Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation of Idaho, located on the Fort Hall Indian Reservation. The Shoshone-Bannock live on the Fort Hall Indian Reservation in Southeastern Idaho, where Lemhi and Northern Shoshone also live. In the 2010 U.S. census, 89 people identified as having “Bannock” ancestry, including 38 “full-blooded” people; 5,315 people were enrolled in the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes. The sources present Bannock material culture, beadwork, dwellings, ceremonies, hunting, fishing, and food gathering, but do not identify a language family.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Beadwork** — After the introduction of glass beads, Bannock people transferred geometric designs from their petroglyphs to beadwork. A museum needle housing made by Lizzie Edmo in 1960 at Fort Hall, Idaho, is made of leather embroidered with light blue, darker blue, yellow, and red glass beads.

**Cornhusk bag** — A museum catalogue records a Bannock plant-fiber bag, possibly made from corn, with a square, flat form and leather-strap handles. Both sides carry geometric patterns including green, pink, yellow, and red, with varying motifs.

**Salmon-skin carrying bags** — The Bannock traditionally made carrying bags from salmon skin.

**Moccasin** — A Bannock moccasin from Fort Hall, Idaho, was given to the Museum of Ethnography in 1958 by Bessie Judson.

**Rawhide cradle** — A museum object identified as a Bannock rawhide cradle contains a doll lying in a partly untreated leather cradle.

**Baby carrier** — British Museum catalogue records show a Shoshone or Bannock baby in a baby carrier, with a beaded bag in front of the baby.

**Blanket** — A British Museum photographic record shows a Bannock man seated with a blanket over his legs.

**Motif vocabulary.** Geometric designs; geometric patterns; varying motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The sources do not provide a complete account of everyday or ceremonial Bannock dress. Museum records show Bannock people wearing cloth tunics in photographic portraits, while one portrait shows a man with a blanket over his legs. The sources also record moccasins and a baby carrier, but do not identify Bannock names for garments, footwear, belts, head coverings, or ceremonial clothing.

### Architecture

Before the late nineteenth century, Bannock people lived primarily in tipis made from buffalo hide during winter. During summer they built conical dwellings of brush and grass. The sources also identify sweat lodges and menstrual huts as Bannock building types. A British Museum photograph records a family group of six Bannock people sitting in a tipi at Medicine Lodge Creek, United States of America. The sources do not describe roof construction, interior organization, decoration, or urban architecture.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The Bannock traditionally made pottery, utensils from bighorn sheep horns, and tule reed rafts for water transport. The sources do not document Bannock metalwork. Museum records additionally identify a leather needle housing embroidered with glass beads, a plant-fiber bag with leather handles, and a rawhide cradle.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources do not document Bannock jewelry, tattooing, henna, hair practices, or named forms of body adornment. They do record glass beads used in beadwork and a beaded bag shown with a Shoshone or Bannock baby in a baby carrier.

## Music & performance

The sources do not identify Bannock musical instruments, song genres, musical scales, or performance settings. They name several Bannock ceremonies: the Scalp Dance, Grass Dance, Circle Dance, and Bear Dance. After acclimation to reservation life, the Bannock also practiced the Sun Dance. The sources describe religious practices involving worship and appeals to spirits, healing arts involving medicine men, and beliefs concerning the soul’s journey to the land of the dead after death, but do not explain the music associated with these practices.

## Dance & theatre

The Bannock’s named dances include the Scalp Dance, Grass Dance, Circle Dance, and Bear Dance. The Sun Dance was also practiced after acclimation to reservation life. The sources do not describe choreography, costumes, instruments, dramatic performance, theatre, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment contexts.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not provide an annual festival calendar or name festivals with dates. Bannock religious practices included worship and appeals to spirits and healing arts involving medicine men. The sources state that the soul was believed to undertake a journey to the land of the dead after death. The dead were wrapped in blankets and placed in rock crevices. Mourners practiced minor self-mutilation, sacrificed the deceased person’s horse, and destroyed the person’s tipi. The named ceremonies were the Scalp Dance, Grass Dance, Circle Dance, Bear Dance, and, later, the Sun Dance.

The sources also document historical events rather than ritual calendars. The Bannock War took place in 1878. A treaty signed at Soda Springs in 1863 established territorial boundaries and guaranteed annuities, but was never ratified. In 1869 Ulysses S. Grant ordered the Bannock to report to the Fort Hall Indian Reservation, and most complied.

## Foodways

Before the late nineteenth century, Bannock people fished for salmon on the Snake River in Idaho and hunted buffalo herds in the fall. In the 1870s they continued to hunt and gather food outside the reservation because provisions supplied by the U.S. government were not reliable enough to support them. The sources do not name dishes, staple grains, cooking methods, beverages, dietary rules, or ceremonial foods. They also do not document camas harvesting, root digging, or a named Bannock food tradition beyond salmon fishing, buffalo hunting, and general food gathering.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do not document Bannock folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, oral narratives, storytelling contexts, or literary preservation projects. They mention a Bannock Trail used to travel from Oregon, northern Nevada, southern Idaho, and western Wyoming to Montana and Canada to hunt buffalo, but do not describe oral traditions associated with it.

## Language & religion

The Bannock were originally Northern Paiute and are more culturally affiliated with the Northern Shoshone. The Wikipedia source gives the Northern Paiute terms *panaki* and *kutsutɨkaˀa* for the Bannock, but does not provide a language-family classification, dialect description, historical script, or current language situation. Religious practices included worship and appeals to spirits, healing arts involving medicine men, and the belief that the soul journeyed to the land of the dead after death. The sources do not identify a current religious denomination or broader religious landscape.

title: "Laguna"
subtitle: "United States"
region: "North America"
tags: [ethnography, north-america]

## Overview

The Pueblo of Laguna, also called *Kawaika* in Western Keres, is a federally recognized Native American Pueblo people in west-central New Mexico, in the Rio San Jose basin about 45 miles west of Albuquerque. Their reservation occupies parts of Cibola, Sandoval, Valencia and Bernalillo Counties and includes Encinal, Laguna, Mesita, Paguate, Paraje and Seama. The population figures given by the sources include 6,758 people who reported being exclusively Laguna and 8,358 who reported being Laguna either exclusively or in combination with another group on the 2010 census; the State of New Mexico gives a population of 7,700. Laguna traditionally speak Western Keresan, part of the Keres language family. Their cultural history includes farming along the Rio San José, pottery, Pueblo religious traditions, a historic Spanish mission, and continued transmission of Keresan language and artistic knowledge.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document a Laguna textile tradition sufficiently to describe its materials, techniques or distinctive patterns.

**Pottery** — Laguna people are described as skilled in pottery. Evelyn Cheromiah revived hand-coiled ceramic production in the 1970s by studying ancestral potsherds, identifying indigenous clay sources, restoring natural mineral and vegetal pigments, and reintroducing outdoor pit firing. Her vessels used stark white slips, precise geometric polychrome patterns, interlocking fine lines, and cloud or animal motifs.

**Museum vessels** — Museum records describe Laguna Pueblo vessels made from light or white clay, with red and black decoration. One vessel has a half-closed form with a strongly marked belly; another is small, closed, and has two openings separated by a handle. Other records describe a lerkärl with a broken handle and a pottery bowl with a white ground and dark-brown decoration.

**Motif vocabulary.** geometric patterns, interlocking fine lines, cloud motifs, animal motifs, red and black decoration, dark-brown decoration.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe Laguna everyday or ceremonial clothing, head coverings, belts, footwear, or gender-specific dress. A museum catalogue records a photograph of a Laguna woman nursing a child held in a carrier on her lap, but it does not provide a description of clothing or adornment. The sources also mention that Laguna residents in the Richmond boxcar community spoke Keresan, maintained community gardens, travelled to New Mexico for sacred ceremonies and annual Feast Days, and celebrated Grab Day, without documenting the clothing worn on those occasions.

### Architecture

The best-documented Laguna building is Mission San José de la Laguna, also called St. Joseph Church, constructed between 1699 and 1701. Its interior includes earthen-plaster murals with geometric and abstract Pueblo motifs made from hand-ground red, yellow and black native mineral pigments. The nave has exposed pine round-timber vigas covered by peeled-pole latillas arranged in a herringbone pattern. The sanctuary contains a hide-and-wood reredos, or altar screen, made between 1800 and 1808. The sources also refer to traditional Keresan kiva religious structures and to the old pueblo, now Old Laguna, but do not describe domestic houses in sufficient detail.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Laguna ceramic production uses hand-coiling, indigenous clay sources, natural mineral and vegetal pigments, and outdoor pit firing. During the mid-20th century, the craft had nearly reached extinction, and Laguna residents often relied on commercial goods or purchased utilitarian pottery from neighboring Acoma Pueblo. Museum records identify vessels and bowls from Laguna Pueblo, including light- and white-clay forms decorated in red, black or dark brown. The sources do not document Laguna wooden objects, tools, or household goods in detail. British Museum records do, however, identify a steel necklace and a steel bracelet associated with the material culture shown for this group.

### Jewelry & body adornment

A British Museum catalogue records a steel necklace consisting of a flexible band with hooks at both ends and 19 steel representations of squash blossoms. It also records a steel bracelet with two silver bands on the front, bisected by a zig-zag line representing mountains. The sources do not explain the social, ceremonial or ritual functions of these objects, and they do not document tattoos, henna, hair practices, or other forms of body adornment.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not document Laguna musical instruments, song genres, musical performance practices, or the contexts in which music is performed. They do state that Laguna residents travelled back to New Mexico to participate in sacred ceremonies and annual Feast Days, and that Keres is a sacred language traditionally understood as existing only in spoken form. These statements do not provide enough information to describe particular songs, instruments, dances, or performance structures.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover Laguna dance, theatre, dramatic traditions, masked performance, or named dances. Grab Day is described as a community celebration in which candies and gifts were thrown from boxcar roofs to village children, but the sources do not identify this as a dance or theatrical form.

## Festivals & rituals

Laguna residents of the Richmond boxcar community routinely returned to New Mexico for sacred ceremonies and annual Feast Days. They also celebrated Grab Day by throwing candies and gifts from boxcar roofs to village children. The sources do not give a calendar of Feast Days, dates for individual celebrations, or descriptions of the associated rites.

The historical sources describe continuing ties between Laguna religious life and the Roman Catholic Church, as well as traditional Keresan religious structures and altars. Mission San José de la Laguna combines Spanish colonial Catholicism with traditional Keresan iconography. Its altar screen depicts Saint Joseph at the centre, flanked by Saint Barbara and Saint John Nepomuk, while the sanctuary ceiling includes a rainbow, sun, moon and stars. The sources interpret this combination as a historical syncretism between Franciscan religious narratives and Pueblo cosmological oral histories. They do not describe Laguna birth, coming-of-age, wedding or funeral ceremonies.

## Foodways

The sources used do not document Laguna staple foods, named dishes, cooking methods, ceremonial foods, beverages, or dietary rules. They state that Laguna people historically farmed along the Rio San José and that the historic lake supported waterfowl including ducks, geese and swans, but they do not explain how these resources were prepared or consumed.

The Richmond boxcar community maintained community vegetable gardens, yet the sources provide no information about the crops grown, the foods prepared, or their ceremonial significance.

## Oral tradition & literature

Laguna oral history is mentioned as part of anthropological research demonstrating habitation of the area from 6500 B.C. to the present. The sources do not preserve named Laguna folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles or narrative genres. They also do not identify a Laguna literary canon.

Keresan religious beliefs are described as treating Keres as a sacred language that must exist only in spoken form. The sources connect the mission’s Pueblo celestial symbols with traditional Pueblo cosmological oral histories, but do not provide the content of those histories. The material and oral histories of the Richmond boxcar community are preserved in UC Berkeley’s Bancroft Library archives. Evelyn Cheromiah’s pottery teaching transmitted ancestral techniques to her daughters, Lee Ann Cheromiah, Mary Cheromiah-Victorino and Wendy Cheromiah, and to her grandchildren.

## Language & religion

Laguna traditionally speak Western Keresan, a variety of Keres. Keres is described as a Native American language spoken by Keres Pueblo people in New Mexico and as either a small language family or a language isolate, depending on analysis. The Western and Eastern groups differ significantly, while neighbouring Keres Pueblo varieties are mutually intelligible. Most Laguna elders do not speak English.

The language has a practical spelling system for Laguna, also called Kʼawaika in the language source, although Keresan traditionally has no unified orthographic convention. The sources describe Keresan as having tones, long and short vowels, and a complex consonant inventory. Keresan is generally verb-final, with flexible word order, and its verbs encode information including person, number, modality, polarity and aspect.

Laguna religious life historically includes Keresan kiva structures, community governance, traditional altars and ties to the Roman Catholic Church. Mission San José de la Laguna represents a combination of Spanish colonial Catholicism and traditional Keresan iconography. The sources do not identify a separate modern religious denomination or provide a complete account of present-day religious practice.

## Sources & further reading

- Barry M. Pritzker, *A Native American Encyclopedia: History, Culture, and Peoples*, Oxford University Press, 2000.
- Julia M. Keleher and Elsie Ruth Chant, *The Padre of Isleta: The Story of Father Anton Docher*, Sunstone Press Publishing, 2009.
- Laguna Pueblo, [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_Pueblo).
- Laguna language, [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laguna_language).
- The sources supplied identify no UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription for this group.

## Overview

Pueblo of Isleta, also known in Southern Tiwa as *Shiewhibak*, is a federally recognized tribe and an unincorporated community in Bernalillo County, New Mexico, United States. The pueblo lies in the Middle Rio Grande Valley, 13 miles (21 km) south of Albuquerque, on a knife-shaped lava flow crossing an ancient Rio Grande channel. It was originally established in the c. 14th century. The population was approximately 4,000 people, and the tribe owns 211,000 acres of land. The inhabitants traditionally speak Isletan Tiwa, one of the two varieties of Southern Tiwa, within the Tanoan branch of the Kiowa-Tanoan language family. Isleta is classified as an Eastern Pueblo because of its traditional dependence on irrigation and subsistence farming. Its documented cultural life includes matrilineal organization, kiva rituals, Kachina traditions, Catholic mission history, and distinctive pottery and clothing represented in museum collections.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document a named Isleta textile tradition, textile technique, or locally specific pattern system.

**Patterned blankets** — Museum catalogue records describe patterned blankets worn around the waist, upper torso, or body in studio portraits of Alejandro Padilla and Ambrosio Abeita. The sources do not identify their material, technique, or local production.

**Cloth shirts and jackets** — British Museum records describe cloth shirts and jackets worn by Isleta men in photographic portraits. The sources do not provide vernacular names or details of manufacture.

**Leg ornaments** — Alejandro Padilla is described as wearing leg ornaments in several photographic records. The sources do not state their material or construction.

**Motif vocabulary.** The museum records name patterned blankets and, on pottery, red diagonal diamonds and red and brown ornaments.

### Clothing & dress

The museum catalogue records document clothing worn by Isleta men in studio portraits. Alejandro Padilla, identified as an Isleta governor, appears in a cloth shirt, jacket, leggings, leg ornaments, boots or moccasins, and a patterned blanket around his waist; in one record he also holds a piece of cloth. Ambrosio Abeita is described in cloth shirts, jackets, leggings, boots or moccasins, and a patterned blanket around his waist. Hats appear on the knee or on a table in several portraits. A British Museum postcard depicts an Isleta woman seated in front of painted pottery, but it does not describe her clothing. The sources do not explain everyday and ceremonial distinctions, women’s dress, belts, head coverings beyond hats, or the production of the garments.

### Architecture

Pueblo of Isleta was built on a knife-shaped lava flow running across an ancient Rio Grande channel. The Isleta Pueblo Historic District is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The tribe maintains and operates a kiva as a sacred space for particular rituals and ceremonies. The Spanish Mission of San Agustín de la Isleta was built in the pueblo in 1613 by the Spanish Franciscan friar Juan de Salas, while the historic St. Agustin Mission Church is described as having been built by the Tiwa under the direction of a Spanish missionary in 1612. The sources do not describe the pueblo’s house forms, roof construction, building materials, decoration, or settlement layout in detail.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Museum of World Culture records document a small vessel with a cross handle and several pottery bowls from Isleta, New Mexico. One bowl is described as earthenware with exterior painting, a white ground, and red diagonal diamonds along the rim. Another is red on the exterior, with an interior white ground decorated in red and brown and having a wavy edge. The catalogue records state that the objects were obtained through an exchange with the Museum of Anthropology, University of California. A British Museum postcard shows an Isleta woman seated before painted pottery, with pottery placed on the ground in front of her. The sources also describe a turquoise cross mounted in silver, made by Isletans and given by Pablo Abeita to the King of Belgium in 1919.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources document a turquoise cross mounted in silver and made by Isletans. Pablo Abeita gave it to the King of Belgium during the royal visit to Isleta on October 26, 1919. The museum records also describe leg ornaments worn by Alejandro Padilla in studio portraits. No further jewelry types, ritual functions, body adornment practices, tattooing, henna, or hair customs are covered by the sources used.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not identify Isleta musical instruments, song genres, or musical performance traditions. They do document dances and celebrations in historical descriptions. Father Anton Docher wrote that a war captain and other officials had charge of various celebrations and dances, including the “dance of the kings” in January and the “tortoise dance” in February. The sources do not name instruments, describe musical structures, or explain who performs these dances, although the broader religious context includes masked Kachina dancers representing Kachinas at religious ceremonies. The inscription records supplied for this atlas contain no UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage element concerning Isleta Pueblo.

## Dance & theatre

Father Anton Docher’s 1913 description names the “dance of the kings” in January and the “tortoise dance” in February among the celebrations and dances overseen by a war captain and other officials. The sources do not describe their choreography, costumes, music, or participants. Religious practice includes Kachina dancers, who are masked members of the community representing Kachinas at religious ceremonies. The Kachina concept is described as having three aspects: supernatural beings, dancers, and small dolls carved in their likeness and given as gifts to children. The sources do not document theatrical traditions, masks outside the Kachina context, or performances intended solely as entertainment.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources name several ritual and seasonal contexts. Father Anton Docher described a “dance of the kings” in January and a “tortoise dance” in February. The tribe maintains and operates a kiva as a sacred space for particular rituals and ceremonies. Traditional religion involves the cult of the Kachinas, spiritual beings personifying aspects of the immaterial and natural worlds. Masked Kachina dancers represent these beings at religious ceremonies, while Kachina dolls are given as gifts to children.

Isleta social organization includes a moiety system in which one moiety is connected with winter practices and the other with summer practices and traditions. The Pueblo also has a Catholic mission history: the Spanish Mission of San Agustín de la Isleta was built in 1613, and the St. Agustin Mission Church remains part of the documented history of the community. The sources do not provide a complete annual festival calendar or descriptions of birth, marriage, coming-of-age, or funeral rites.

## Foodways

The sources describe traditional Eastern Pueblo subsistence farming as relying more heavily on irrigation than the dry farming practices more common in Western Pueblos. Maize, also called corn, was cultivated, while squash and beans were staple Pueblo foods throughout the region. The sources do not name Isleta dishes, cooking methods, ceremonial foods, beverages, dietary rules, or food-preparation utensils. The tribe’s later economic history includes cattle ranching: the Pueblo’s Comanche Ranch is described as running 1,000 head of cattle. No source used for this profile identifies a distinctive Isleta food or beverage tradition.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do not document Isleta folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, or a named oral-literary cycle. They do record the Southern Tiwa name *Shiewhibak*, meaning “a knife laid on the ground to play whib,” a traditional footrace. The sources also preserve historical descriptions by Father Anton Docher and museum catalogue identifications of Isleta people and objects. In August 2015, the tribe announced that the Tiwa language would be taught to children at Isleta Elementary School. In 2016, the Kellogg Foundation made grants totaling $148,000 for development of a dual-language Tiwa-English program for young children at the school. These educational efforts are the only documented language-preservation initiative in the supplied sources.

## Language & religion

The inhabitants traditionally speak Isletan Tiwa, one of the two varieties of the Southern Tiwa language. Southern Tiwa belongs to the Tanoan branch of the Kiowa-Tanoan language family. The other Southern Tiwa variety is spoken at Sandia Pueblo, while Northern Tiwa is spoken at Taos and Picuris Pueblos. The Southern Tiwa name for the pueblo is *Shiewhibak*, also written [ʃiexʷibʔàg]. The sources also give Western Keres *Dîiw'a'ane* and Navajo *Naatoohó* as names for the pueblo.

Traditional religion includes the cult of the Kachinas and the use of a kiva as sacred space for rituals and ceremonies. Kachinas are described as spiritual beings associated with immaterial and natural worlds, and Kachina dancers represent them during religious ceremonies. The sources also document Catholicism and the Spanish mission established at Isleta. They do not describe a historical script, current religious affiliation proportions, or detailed forms of religious syncretism.

- Julia M. Keleher and Elsie Ruth Chant, *The Padre of Isleta: The Story of Father Anton Docher*, Sunstone Press Publishing, 2009.
- James Mooney, “Isleta Pueblo,” *Catholic Encyclopedia*, Vol. 8, 1910.
- John L. Stoutenburgh Jr., *Dictionary of the American Indian*, cited in the Museum of World Culture catalogue records.
- [Pueblo of Isleta — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pueblo_of_Isleta)

## Overview

The Ponca people (Omaha-Ponca: *Páⁿka*) are an Indigenous nation of the Great Plains of North America, identified today with the Ponca Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma and the Ponca Tribe of Nebraska. Their historical homeland was around the mouth of the Niobrara River near its confluence with the Missouri River. The Ponca Tribe of Nebraska is headquartered in Niobrara, Nebraska, and has over 2,783 enrolled members; the Ponca Tribe of Oklahoma is headquartered in White Eagle, Oklahoma, and conducts business from Ponca City. Omaha–Ponca is a Dhegihan language of the Siouan–Catawban language family. Ponca history includes forced removal, the Ponca Trail of Tears, the civil-rights case Standing Bear v. Crook, and continuing efforts to revive cultural identity and language.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document named Ponca textile or pattern traditions.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name quill work, floral cloth, and beadwork only as descriptions of objects and clothing.

### Clothing & dress

Museum catalogue records describe Ponca men wearing shirts, long-sleeved tops, cloth shirts, waistcoats, blankets, leggings, hide leggings with quill work, and moccasins. A portrait of White Tail (*Cin'-de-cke*) records a cloth shirt, waistcoat, leggings, peace medal, bead choker, and trailer warbonner; his hair was arranged in two bunches wrapped in fur. The portrait of Iron Whip (*Wa-Sa-Ca-Pi*) records a bear claw necklace, ear ornaments, hide leggings with quill work, moccasins, a long-sleeved top, and a blanket wrapped around his legs. A portrait of four Ponca chiefs records headdresses, personal ornaments, shirts, wool blankets, leggings, moccasins, and tomahawks. The catalogue records do not distinguish everyday from ceremonial clothing beyond these descriptions.

### Architecture

The sources describe a prehistoric Ponca village excavated during an archaeological project conducted by the University of Nebraska and the Smithsonian Institution in the 1930s. It included large circular homes up to sixty feet in diameter, located almost two miles along the south bank of the Niobrara River. The sources do not specify the construction materials, roof forms, decoration, or a Ponca name for these houses.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources used do not document Ponca ceramics, metalwork, wooden household objects, or named tool traditions. Museum records do identify tomahawks, a sword, floral cloth, furs, blankets, bead and hide objects, and other personal possessions in photographic portraits.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Museum records describe bear claw necklaces, shell necklaces, bead chokers, beaded and shell necklaces, ear ornaments, peace medals, arm ornaments, bead and hide objects, and personal ornaments. One catalogue record describes a diadanum shell necklace, a bear claw necklace, an arm ornament, and leg ornaments including a fur leg ornament. The records also describe hair arranged in two bunches wrapped in fur and the use of headdresses, feathers, and warbonners. The sources do not explain the ritual functions of these forms of adornment.

## Music & performance

The sources identify three Ponca men—Frank Eagle, Louis McDonald, and McKinley Eagle—as co-founders of the Native American Church in 1918. They state that, as of 2024, the Native American Church was the most widespread Indigenous religion among Native Americans in the continental United States, Canada, and Mexico, with an estimated 300,000 adherents. The sources otherwise do not document Ponca musical instruments, song genres, musical structures, performance settings, or named musical traditions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document named Ponca dances, theatrical forms, dramatic traditions, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not describe an annual Ponca festival calendar or provide accounts of Ponca birth, coming-of-age, wedding, or funeral rites. They do record Standing Bear’s promise to bury his eldest son, Bear Shield, on the tribe’s ancestral lands. To fulfil that promise, Standing Bear left the reservation in Oklahoma and travelled toward the Ponca homelands, leading to his arrest and the habeas corpus case Standing Bear v. Crook in 1879. The United States District Court in Omaha, Nebraska, established in that case that Native Americans were “persons within the meaning of the law” of the United States.

## Foodways

The Ponca grew maize and kept vegetable gardens, unlike most other Plains Indians. Their last successful buffalo hunt took place in 1855. After forced removal to Indian Territory, the Ponca struggled with malaria, a shortage of food, and the hot climate; one in four members died within the first year. The sources do not name Ponca dishes, cooking methods, ceremonial foods, beverages, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

According to the sources, Ponca tradition holds that the people moved to the mouth of the Niobrara River from an area east of the Mississippi shortly before Columbus’s arrival in the Americas. The sources also describe traditions among related Siouan-speaking peoples concerning migration westward from east of the Mississippi River. The sources used do not document named Ponca folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles, storytelling genres, or a Ponca literary canon. Language preservation includes Louis Headman’s dictionary of the Ponca People, published by the University of Nebraska Press.

## Language & religion

Omaha–Ponca is a Dhegihan language of the Siouan–Catawban language family, spoken by the Omaha people of Nebraska and the Ponca people of Oklahoma and Nebraska. Its two dialects differ minimally but are considered distinct languages by their speakers. As of 2008, the sources report 50 fluent speakers of Omaha and 35 fluent speakers of Ponca, all elderly. The language has subject–object–verb syntax, definite articles that mark features including animacy, position, and number, and a tonal system using downstep. The sources mention language classes, Internet-based learning materials, the Umónhon Nation Public School, and language-revitalization partnerships. In 1918, three Ponca men helped co-found the Native American Church. The sources do not provide a fuller account of Ponca religious beliefs or practices.

## Sources & further reading

- James Owen Dorsey, *Omaha and Ponka Letters*, Government Printing Office, 1891.
- Stephen Dando-Collins, *Standing Bear is a Person*, Da Capo, 2004.

title: "Yokuts"
subtitle: "United States"
region: "North America"
tags: [ethnography, north-america]
