## Overview

The Huli are an indigenous Melanesian ethnic group living in Hela Province of Papua New Guinea, especially in the Tagari River basin and on the slopes of surrounding mountain ranges. Their homeland lies at an altitude of about 1,600 meters above sea level and includes primary forests, reed-covered marshes, kunai grasslands, scrub brush, rivers, streams, drainage ditches, and mounded gardens. They number over 250,000 people, based on the population of Hela at the time of the 2011 national census. They speak mainly Huli and Tok Pisin; many also speak surrounding languages, and some speak English. The sources present Huli material culture through tools, weapons, garments, wigs, belts, ornaments, and ceremonial costume, while their intangible culture includes oral histories, genealogies, traditions, and a specialized language used in bush activities.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources do not document named Huli pattern-bearing textile traditions.

**Carved chevrons** — One British Museum adze has carved chevrons on its quadrangular wooden upper section, with the incisions infilled with red pigment.

**Burned bamboo designs** — A bamboo tobacco-pipe has designs formed by burning.

**Red-pigment decoration** — Red pigment appears on several objects, including an adze, belts, arm-bands, a hornbill-beak neck ornament, and a tobacco-pipe.

### Clothing & dress

The catalogue records describe both garments and ceremonial costumes. Apron-type garments are made from vegetable fibre cord or woven brown vegetable fibre string. One has a fibre-cord fringe ending in short lengths of yellow cane, while another is roughly rectangular; another garment has a central woven panel. A belt may consist of bark overwrapped with brown fibre strips and decorated with brown and yellow fibre, or of curved rattan strips bound with fibre cord. Photographs describe Huli(?) men wearing plant-fibre skirts, bark loin cloths, plant-fibre arm ornaments, belts, and wigs. Women are shown wearing plant-fibre wigs, feather headdresses, shell ornaments, necklaces, and fur chest ornaments. Ceremonial costumes include black plant-fibre wigs, feather headdresses, plant-fibre skirts or loin cloths, arm ornaments, shell and pig-tusk necklaces, and decorated poles or weapons. The sources do not describe footwear.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Huli house forms, settlement architecture, roofs, or named buildings.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The catalogue records document wooden and cane tools and weapons, including axes, adzes, bows, and arrows. Axes have wooden hafts, cane bindings, and small polished stone blades. Adzes combine wooden pieces bound with cane; one has a cassowary(?) claw cutting point, and another has a claw secured with fibre string. Arrows are made of wood, cane, vegetable fibre, claw, and pigment. Bows are made of wood and cane. A bamboo tobacco-pipe has a closed node and burned designs. The sources do not document ceramics or metalworking traditions.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The objects include a polished pearl-shell breast ornament, cowrie-shell necklaces mounted on curved wooden strips, a hornbill-beak neck ornament, and ornaments incorporating pig tusks. Photographs show shell necklaces, pig-tusk necklaces, shell-chain nose ornaments, nose ornaments, beaded necklaces, fur chest ornaments, and arm ornaments. A photographed Huli(?) woman has yellow face paint, while a photographed Huli(?) man has a red-painted nose. Wigs combine vegetable fibre, human hair, feathers, cassowary feathers, bird of paradise feathers, leaves, snake skin(?), cuscus fur, and other materials. Some catalogue records also mention red ochre, bone, jaw(?), and metal springs.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not document Huli musical instruments, song genres, musical performance contexts, or named music traditions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document named Huli dances, theatrical forms, or dramatic traditions. The museum photographs do document ceremonial costumes and ceremonial poles or weapons with feather decorations.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not describe an annual festival calendar, life-cycle rites, marriage ceremonies, funerals, initiation ceremonies, or named ritual observances. The Huli are described as maintaining genealogies, traditions, oral histories, and cultural expressions, and the catalogue records include objects and photographs identified as ceremonial.

## Foodways

The sources do not describe Huli staple foods, cooking methods, signature dishes, dietary rules, or ceremonial meals. The Huli language article states that *tayenda tu ha illili*, glossed as “bush divide taboo,” is used while collecting karuka nuts, called *anga*, as well as while hunting or travelling.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Huli are described as being keenly aware of their history and folklore through knowledge of family genealogy and traditions. They recount lengthy oral histories relating to individuals and clans. The sources do not name particular folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles, or literary works, and they do not describe contemporary literary preservation projects.

## Language & religion

Huli is a Tari language spoken by the Huli people of Hela Province of Papua New Guinea. The sources state that Huli speakers mainly use Huli and Tok Pisin; many also speak surrounding languages, and some speak English. Huli has a specialized pandanus language called *tayenda tu ha illili*, used for collecting *anga*, hunting, and travelling, partly to evade malevolent bush spirits. Its grammar is nearly identical to ordinary Huli, but its vocabulary changes and may borrow words from Duna with altered meanings. Huli has a pentadecimal numeral system: *ngui* means 15, *ngui ki* means 30, and *ngui ngui* means 225. The sources do not cover the Huli language family, writing systems, or current religious landscape.

- “Huli language,” Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huli_language

- **Carved chevrons** — An adze has carved chevrons on its wooden upper section, with the cuts filled with red pigment.
- **Burned bamboo designs** — A bamboo tobacco-pipe has designs made by burning the bamboo.
- **Red-pigment decoration** — Red pigment appears on an adze, belts, arm-bands, a hornbill-beak neck ornament, and a tobacco-pipe.

### Clothing & dress

Huli clothing includes plant-fibre skirts, bark loin cloths, aprons, belts, wigs, and ceremonial costumes.

- **Fibre aprons** — Apron-like garments are made from vegetable-fibre cord or woven brown vegetable-fibre string.
- **Fibre-cord fringe** — One apron has a fibre-cord fringe ending in short pieces of yellow cane.
- **Bark and fibre belts** — Belts may use bark wrapped with brown fibre strips or curved rattan strips bound with fibre cord.
- **Plant-fibre skirts and loin cloths** — Photographs show Huli men wearing plant-fibre skirts and bark loin cloths.
- **Ceremonial costumes** — Ceremonial costumes include black plant-fibre wigs, feather headdresses, skirts or loin cloths, arm ornaments, necklaces, and decorated poles or weapons.

### Architecture

The sources do not cover Huli houses, settlements, roofs, or named buildings.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Huli tools and weapons are mainly made from wood, cane, fibre, claws, pigment, and polished stone.

- **Axes** — Axes have wooden hafts, cane bindings, and small polished stone blades.
- **Adzes** — Adzes combine wooden pieces bound with cane, and some have cassowary claws as cutting points.
- **Bows** — Bows are made of wood and cane.
- **Arrows** — Arrows are made from wood, cane, vegetable fibre, claw, and pigment.
- **Bamboo tobacco-pipe** — A bamboo tobacco-pipe has a closed node and burned designs.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Huli adornment combines shells, pig tusks, feathers, fibre, fur, paint, and other natural materials.

- **Pearl-shell breast ornament** — One object is a polished pearl-shell breast ornament.
- **Cowrie-shell necklaces** — Cowrie shells are mounted on curved wooden strips to make necklaces.
- **Hornbill-beak neck ornament** — A neck ornament is made with a hornbill beak and red pigment.
- **Pig-tusk necklaces** — Photographs and ceremonial costumes show necklaces made with pig tusks.
- **Composite wigs** — Wigs combine vegetable fibre, human hair, feathers, leaves, snake skin, cuscus fur, and other materials.

## Music & performance

The sources do not document Huli musical instruments, song genres, performance settings, or named music traditions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources do not document named Huli dances or theatre, but photographs show ceremonial dress and decorated ceremonial poles or weapons.

- **Ceremonial poles and weapons** — Ceremonial poles or weapons are decorated with feathers.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not describe a festival calendar or named rites, but they identify some objects and photographs as ceremonial.

- **Ceremonial costume** — Ceremonial clothing includes wigs, feather headdresses, plant-fibre skirts or loin cloths, arm ornaments, necklaces, and decorated poles or weapons.

## Foodways

The sources do not describe Huli foods or cooking, but they mention collecting karuka nuts during a bush taboo practice.

- **Bush divide taboo** (*tayenda tu ha illili*) — This special language is used while collecting karuka nuts, called anga, and while hunting or travelling.
- **Karuka nuts** (*anga*) — The Huli collect karuka nuts while using the bush divide taboo language.

## Oral tradition & literature

Huli people preserve history and folklore through family genealogies, traditions, and long oral histories.

- **Family genealogies** — Knowledge of family genealogy helps Huli people understand their history and folklore.
- **Clan oral histories** — Huli people recount lengthy oral histories about individuals and clans.

## Language & religion

Huli is a Tari language with a special pandanus vocabulary used during bush activities, while the sources do not describe the current religious landscape.

- **Huli language** (*Huli*) — Huli is a Tari language spoken by the Huli people of Hela Province.
- **Pandanus language** (*tayenda tu ha illili*) — This specialized language is used for collecting anga, hunting, and travelling, partly to evade malevolent bush spirits.
- **Pentadecimal counting** (*ngui*) — Huli uses a base-fifteen number system in which ngui means 15.
- **Thirty** (*ngui ki*) — In the Huli number system, ngui ki means 30.
- **Two hundred twenty-five** (*ngui ngui*) — In the Huli number system, ngui ngui means 225.

## Glossary

- *tayenda tu ha illili* — bush divide taboo language
- *anga* — karuka nuts
- *Huli* — the Huli language and people
- *ngui* — 15
- *ngui ki* — 30
- *ngui ngui* — 225

## Sources & further reading

- “Huli people,” Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huli_people
- “Huli language,” Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huli_language
- British Museum catalogue records for Huli objects and photographs, as supplied in the source material
- UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: no Papua New Guinea inscription is supplied in the sources used.

---
title: "Tolai"
subtitle: "Papua New Guinea"
region: "Oceania"
tags: [ethnography, oceania]
---

## Overview

The Tolai are the indigenous people of the Gazelle Peninsula and the Duke of York Islands of East New Britain, in the New Guinea Islands region of Papua New Guinea. They are ethnically close kin to peoples of adjacent New Ireland, including the Tanga people, and are thought to have migrated to the Gazelle Peninsula relatively recently, displacing the Baining people westwards. Approximately 100,000 Tolai speak Kuanua as their first language, while Lungalunga and Bilur each have approximately 2,000 first-language speakers. Tolai belongs to the Oceanic branch of the Austronesian language family. The sources document Tolai material culture through fishing equipment, tools, masks, dance-wands, drums, a figure and other museum objects, and describe continuing ceremonial beliefs associated with Tubuans and the Duk-Duk society.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document a Tolai textile or patterned-cloth tradition.

**Fishing net** — A British Museum fishing net is a long rectangular seine net made from vegetable fibre. It has twenty stone sinkers, two end sinkers encased in cane plaiting, and eighteen flat, oval-shaped orange wood floats.

**Decorated end floats** — The large spatulate wood floats at the ends of the net are attached with cane plaiting. Their two sides carry punctuated and painted designs representing a human figure, two turtles, one of two fish, and numerous fish and plant-like shapes.

**Dance-mask (‘lor’)** — A composite *lor* dance mask has a narrow, roughly triangular light-wood face with cut-out eyes, painted curved horizontal bands, a vegetable-fibre beard and hair, and a domed head. Above the face is a vegetable-fibre disk edged with white feathers and bearing a standing peacock figure with outstretched wings and displayed tail.

**Dance-wand** — One flat wooden polychrome dance-wand is carved and painted on both sides in the form of a human face with a tall fretwork headdress ending in a plume of white, yellowish and black feathers. It has pearl-shell, rubber and white-bead details, fibre beards and feather “hair.”

**Dance-wand fragment** — Another British Museum object is a triangular-shaped polychrome piece of wooden fretwork with feathers attached at the top. The wood is painted red, yellow, green and white, and the feathers are white, red, yellow and black.

**Carved mask** — A carved mask has a white-painted face made with natural pigments, a nose-pin and a fibre beard. Its hat is covered with red European textile, and a textile-covered snake emerges from the crown.

**Motif vocabulary.** Human figure, turtles, fish, plant-like shapes, peacock, concentric circles, tear-drop motifs, chevrons, fretwork headdress.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe Tolai everyday clothing, ceremonial garments, footwear, belts, or distinctions between men’s and women’s dress. They do document fibre beards and hair on masks, feather ornaments and headdresses on dance objects, nose-pins, and red European textile covering a mask’s hat. The catalogue records do not establish whether these elements correspond directly to human dress or body adornment.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Tolai houses, villages, buildings, roofs, construction materials, decoration, or urban traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The documented everyday and working objects include a vegetable-fibre fishing net, stone sinkers, wood floats, a wood elbow-shaped adze with a shell blade and coconut-fibre lashing, and a wood fish-hook for Ruvettus? with coconut-fibre binding below the point. The hook is attached to a wood rod by a coconut-fibre snood. The sources do not describe Tolai ceramics or metalwork. Other wooden objects include drums, slit-drums, dance-wands, masks and a stone ingut figure.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not describe Tolai jewelry, tattoos, henna, hair practices, or ritual body adornment. Museum objects include glass beads on a dance-mask, white beads and pearl-shell eyes on a dance-wand, a stick nose-pin on one face of the wand, and a nose-pin on a carved mask. These catalogue records do not explain their social or ritual functions.

## Music & performance

The Tolai sources document drums and slit-drums but do not provide names for them in a Tolai language. One British Museum object is a wood drum used in dance. It has an hour-glass shape, a lizard-skin (?) membrane, a handle and a detached cane coil that originally held the membrane in place. Its lower third is decorated with low-relief carving and European paint: three motifs of concentric circles, three green tear-drop motifs, a band of chevrons, and a green band at the base. The object is inscribed near the handle “Kai.Tupi.”

Another object is a small wood slit-drum with a circular cross-section, a central tongue and cylindrical handles at each end. The sources do not state how it is played, who plays it, or whether it accompanies particular songs, dances, ceremonies or life-cycle events. They also do not document song genres, vocal styles, musical scales, performance ensembles, weddings, funerals, courts, festivals or recording and preservation projects.

The Tolai language is described as the primary language of communication in the two major centres of East New Britain, Kokopo and Rabaul. The sources do not connect these centres with specific musical traditions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources document a Duk-Duk society and secret ceremonies performed by initiates. They also describe a continuing belief in the female spirits of the Tubuans. The sources do not explain the precise sequence, participants, meanings or calendar of these ceremonies.

Museum records identify a wood drum as used in dance, and several objects as dance equipment: a composite *lor* dance mask and two dance-wands. The *lor* mask includes a painted face, fibre beard and hair, feather-edged disk and peacock figure. One dance-wand represents a human face with a fretwork headdress, feathers, beads and fibre beards; the other is a polychrome wooden fretwork fragment with feathers.

The sources do not document named dances, dramatic plots, theatrical genres, audience arrangements, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment performances beyond the association of these objects with dance and the Duk-Duk society.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not provide an annual Tolai festival calendar, named seasonal festivals, or dates for recurring ceremonies. They do describe secret ceremonies performed by initiates of the Duk-Duk society and a belief in the female spirits of the Tubuans. They also record a belief in sorcery used either to gain someone’s love or to punish an enemy.

Christianity was introduced to the New Guinea islands region in 1875, when Methodist ministers and teachers from Fiji arrived. In 1878, some tribespeople ate four of the missionaries. George Brown, the Englishman who led the missionaries, directed and took part in a punitive expedition that resulted in a number of Tolais being killed and several villages being burnt down.

In August 2007, descendants of Tolai tribespeople who had eaten a Fijian minister and three Fijian teachers in 1878 publicly apologized to Fiji’s High Commissioner, Ratu Isoa Tikoca. The apology was accepted. At the event, Papua New Guinea’s Governor-General Paulias Matane spoke about the work of the early Fijian missionaries in spreading Christianity in the islands region.

The sources do not describe Tolai birth, coming-of-age, wedding or funeral rites.

## Foodways

The sources used do not describe Tolai staple foods, dishes, cooking methods, food taboos, ceremonial meals, beverages, dietary rules, or food production. The Tolai language source gives *minamai* as meaning “a small supply of betelnuts for chewing,” and lists *buai* as a Tok Pisin vocabulary item likely derived from Tolai, meaning “betelnut.” It also gives *mamai* as the Tolai verb “to chew betelnut.” No further foodways are documented.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not document Tolai folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, written literature, storytelling contexts, or contemporary literary preservation efforts. The Tolai language source provides example sentences and vocabulary, including *tinata*, “the language,” but does not identify an oral-literary genre. It states that Tolai is one of the major substratum languages of Tok Pisin and lists vocabulary items likely to come from Tolai or a closely related language, including *aibika*, *buai*, *diwai*, *guria*, *kawawar*, *kiau*, *lapun*, *liklik* and *umben*.

## Language & religion

The Tolai language, or Kuanua, is spoken by the Tolai people in the Gazelle Peninsula of East New Britain Province. The language is also referred to in literature as Tolai, although Tolai is the name of the cultural group. The Tolais themselves call their language *tinata tuna*, translated as “the real language.” Kuanua is apparently a word in Ramoaaina meaning “the place over there.”

Tolai belongs to the Oceanic branch of the Austronesian language family. Its most immediate subgroup is the Patpatar–Tolai group, which also includes Lungalunga and Patpatar. Tolai is described as a healthy language and as a prestigious primary language of communication in Kokopo and Rabaul. It has many Tok Pisin loanwords and has lost the phoneme /s/, although /s/ has been reintroduced through English and Tok Pisin loanwords.

The majority of Tolais speak Kuanua as their first language. The sources say that Tolais almost universally define themselves as Christian and are predominantly Roman Catholic and United Church, while older beliefs and traditions, including Tubuans, Duk-Duk ceremonies and sorcery, still persist.

## Sources & further reading

- The sources supplied do not provide book references, publishers, years, or named documentation projects.
- [Tolai people — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolai_people)
- [Tolai language — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolai_language)
- No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription was supplied for Papua New Guinea.
- British Museum catalogue records supplied for fishing net, adze, fish-hook, drum, slit-drum, *lor* dance-mask, dance-wands, carved mask and stone ingut figure.
- Metropolitan Museum of Art catalogue record supplied for a wood-and-paint mask dated to the mid to late 19th century.

## Material culture

Tolai material culture is known through fibre fishing gear, carved and painted wood objects, drums, masks, dance-wands, and tools.

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources do not describe a Tolai textile tradition, but they show fibre nets and richly decorated wooden dance objects.

- **Fishing net** — This long rectangular seine net is made from vegetable fibre, with stone sinkers and orange wood floats.

### Clothing & dress

The sources do not describe everyday Tolai clothing or ceremonial dress, but some dance objects use fibre, feathers, and European textile.

The sources do not describe Tolai houses, villages, buildings, roofs, or construction traditions.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources do not explain Tolai jewelry or body-adornment practices, but museum objects include beads, pearl shell, and nose-pins.

- **Glass beads** — Glass beads appear on a dance-mask.
- **Pearl-shell eyes** — A dance-wand has eyes made from pearl shell.
- **Nose-pin** — A stick nose-pin appears on one face of a dance-wand and on a carved mask.

## Music & performance

Tolai performance objects include drums and slit-drums, but the sources do not name their musical styles or uses in detail.

## Dance & theatre

The sources describe secret Duk-Duk ceremonies, Tubuan spirits, sorcery beliefs, and the later spread of Christianity.

The sources give only a few Tolai terms connected with chewing betelnut.

- **Betelnut** (*buai*) — Buai is a Tok Pisin word likely derived from Tolai and means betelnut.

title: "Mundugumor"
subtitle: "Papua New Guinea"
region: "Oceania"
tags: [ethnography, oceania]
---

## Overview

The Mundugumor, also known as Biwat, are an indigenous people of Papua New Guinea living on the Yuat River in East Sepik Province. They speak the Mundugumor language and Melanesian Pidgin. The Mundugumor language is also called Munduguma and Mundukomo and is spoken in Biwat village of Yuat Rural LLG, East Sepik Province. Margaret Mead studied the Mundugumor during fieldwork in Papua New Guinea from 1931 to 1933, and later studies described changes among people then called the Biwat. The sources present marriage, kinship, motherhood, agriculture, exchange, wooden ancestral figures, masks, drums, and slit-drums as parts of the documented cultural record. They do not provide a population figure or identify a language family.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document a textile or pattern-bearing tradition by a Mundugumor vernacular name.

**Braided vegetable fibre strap** — A British Museum drum is described as having a braided vegetable fibre strap. The sources do not identify this as a wider textile tradition or provide further information about its manufacture.

**Wicker frame** — A British Museum mask has a wicker frame behind the wooden mask. The catalogue does not give a vernacular name or describe a broader basketry tradition.

**Vegetable fibre tassel** — One British Museum mask has an ear threaded with a vegetable fibre tassel. The sources do not explain its name, technique, or social use.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe everyday or ceremonial clothing, named garments, footwear, belts, head coverings, or distinctions between men's and women's dress. They mention vegetable fibre in the construction of a drum strap, a mask tassel, and rigid strips of bamboo threaded through mask perforations, but these catalogue descriptions concern objects rather than clothing.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Mundugumor houses, village layouts, roof forms, building materials, named building types, or architectural decoration. They state that the Mundugumor lived in a village on the Yuat River and that a local mission's airstrip was closed after a land dispute.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The catalogue records document wooden drums, a wooden slit-drum, wooden masks, and carved wooden ancestral figures. One drum has incised decoration and handles carved in the form of heads, with a braided vegetable fibre strap. A slit-drum has a handle at each end in the form of a quadruped and is made of wood with cowrie shells and feathers. The sources do not document ceramics or metalwork.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum records describe cowrie shells, feathers, pearl shell, pigment, vegetable fibre, and bamboo as materials or decorative elements on objects. One mask has perforated pearl shell eyes, red, black, and white pigment, conical and flattish bosses, perforated ears, a vegetable fibre tassel, and rigid bamboo strips threaded through perforations. The sources do not document personal jewelry, tattoos, hair practices, or named forms of body adornment.

## Music & performance

The sources identify drums and slit-drums in museum catalogue records. One wooden drum has incised decoration and handles carved in the form of heads; another object is a wooden slit-drum with handles in the form of quadrupeds, cowrie shells, and feathers. The sources do not provide vernacular instrument names, musical terminology, song genres, performance contexts, rhythms, or information about who performs or hears this music. They also do not establish whether the drums or slit-drum are used in ceremonies, dances, warfare, exchange, marriage, funerals, or other settings. The Mundugumor language article mentions recordings of Biwat language in the Paradisec collection and recordings from Papua New Guinea, Australia, and the Pacific from Don Laycock that include Biwat materials, but the sources do not describe their musical content.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document named dances, theatrical forms, mask dances, dramatic performances, choreography, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment performance. They record wooden masks in museum collections but do not state how the masks were used.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not describe an annual festival calendar, seasonal festivals, harvest ceremonies, funerals, initiation rites, or named ritual occasions. They do document life-cycle and social practices concerning marriage, pregnancy, childbirth, and childhood. Marriage commonly involved brother-and-sister exchange, and a valuable flute could sometimes be used in an exchange. Affairs and elopements could lead to marriage, with relatives sometimes pursuing the woman and fighting. Around one third of Mundugumor marriages are said to have begun in this violent fashion. During pregnancy, intercourse was subject to a taboo associated with fear of one child turning into twins. When a child was not preserved, the infant could be thrown into the Yuat River or strangled before disposal. The sources also describe children being given as hostages to temporary trade allies before the Mundugumor village came under Australian governmental control.

## Foodways

The sources state that most food was produced through slash-and-burn agriculture. In later accounts, the main cash crops were tobacco and betel nut, while the Biwat also kept pigs and other livestock, including cattle. They travelled by motorized canoe along the Yuat River to buy and sell produce in nearby Angoram, Wewak, and Madang. The sources do not name staple dishes, grains, cooking methods, ceremonial foods, beverages, dietary rules, or food taboos. They describe mothers feeding and weaning children, including breastfeeding, but do not provide a named food tradition.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do not record Mundugumor folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles, oral genres, or storytelling settings. Margaret Mead's field notes and Reo Fortune's field notes were later revisited by Nancy McDowell. McDowell completed Mead's book after Mead's death in 1978, and the book was published in 1991 as *The Mundugumor: From the Field Notes of Margaret Mead and Reo Fortune*. The sources also mention a collection of recordings of Biwat language held by Paradisec and Biwat materials in recordings from Don Laycock, but they do not describe literary texts or oral performances in those collections.

## Language & religion

Mundugumor, also called Munduguma and Mundukomo, is a Yuat language of Papua New Guinea. It is spoken in Biwat village of Yuat Rural LLG, East Sepik Province. The people also speak Melanesian Pidgin. The sources do not identify the language family, dialects, historical scripts, or writing systems. Later studies state that most of the Biwat were Catholic, that many no longer understood the indigenous kinship terminology described by Mead, and that education was widely available. The sources do not provide further information about Catholic practice, earlier religious systems, or spiritual traditions.

## Sources & further reading

- Nancy McDowell, *The Mundugumor: From the Field Notes of Margaret Mead and Reo Fortune*, Smithsonian Institution Press, 1991.
- James McElvenny, *Notes on Mundukomo*, unpublished manuscript, Department of Linguistics, University of Sydney, 2007.
- Margaret Mead and Reo Fortune’s field notes, later examined by Nancy McDowell.
- Paradisec collection of Biwat language recordings, including materials from Don Laycock.

title: "Mundugumor"

region: "Oceania"

## At a glance
| | |
|---|---|
| Who | The Mundugumor, also known as Biwat, are an Indigenous people. |
| Where | They live on the Yuat River in East Sepik Province, Papua New Guinea. |
| How many | The profile gives no population figure. |
| Language | Mundugumor, also called Munduguma and Mundukomo, plus Melanesian Pidgin. |
| Religion | Later studies say most Biwat were Catholic. |
| Known for | Marriage and kinship practices · Slash-and-burn agriculture · Wooden ancestral figures · Masks · Drums and slit-drums |

## Overview

The Mundugumor live in and around Biwat village on the Yuat River. Their documented culture includes marriage, kinship, motherhood, farming, trade, wooden objects, masks, and drums. The profile gives little information about clothing, houses, dances, festivals, stories, or personal adornment. Later studies describe major changes, including Catholicism, education, and reduced knowledge of older kinship terms.

## Material culture

The documented material culture centers on carved wooden drums, slit-drums, masks, and ancestral figures, with shells, feathers, pigment, bamboo, and vegetable fibre used as details or fittings.

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources do not describe a wider textile tradition, but they record vegetable fibre and wicker on museum objects.

- **Braided vegetable fibre strap** — A British Museum drum has a braided vegetable fibre strap.
- **Wicker mask frame** — A British Museum mask has a wicker frame behind the wooden mask.
- **Vegetable fibre tassel** — One British Museum mask has an ear threaded with a vegetable fibre tassel.

### Clothing & dress

The sources do not describe everyday or ceremonial clothing.

### Architecture

The sources do not describe Mundugumor houses or village buildings.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The documented objects are mainly carved wooden drums, slit-drums, masks, and ancestral figures.

- **Wooden drum** — One drum has incised decoration and handles carved as heads, with a braided vegetable fibre strap.
- **Wooden slit-drum** — A slit-drum has handles shaped like quadrupeds and is decorated with cowrie shells and feathers.
- **Wooden mask** — Museum records document wooden masks.
- **Carved wooden ancestral figure** — Museum records document carved wooden ancestral figures.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources do not document personal jewelry or named body-adornment practices.

- **Pearl shell eyes** — One mask has perforated pearl shell eyes.
- **Pigment** — One mask uses red, black, and white pigment.
- **Bamboo strips** — Rigid strips of bamboo are threaded through mask perforations.

## Music & performance

Museum records identify drums and slit-drums, but give no musical names or performance settings.

- **Drum** — A wooden drum has incised decoration and handles carved as heads.
- **Slit-drum** — A wooden slit-drum has quadruped-shaped handles, cowrie shells, and feathers.

## Dance & theatre

The sources do not describe named dances, theatre, choreography, or mask use.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not describe annual festivals or named ritual occasions, but they record marriage, pregnancy, childbirth, and childhood practices.

- **Brother-and-sister marriage exchange** — Marriage commonly involved an exchange between brothers and sisters.
- **Flute exchange** — A valuable flute could sometimes be used in a marriage exchange.
- **Violent marriage beginning** — Affairs and elopements could lead to marriage, sometimes followed by relatives pursuing the woman and fighting.
- **Pregnancy taboo** — During pregnancy, intercourse was subject to a taboo linked to fear that one child could become twins.
- **Child hostage exchange** — Children were sometimes given as hostages to temporary trade allies before Australian government control.

## Foodways

Most food came from slash-and-burn agriculture, with later cash crops, livestock, and river trade.

- **Slash-and-burn agriculture** — Most food was produced through slash-and-burn agriculture.
- **Tobacco** — Tobacco was a main cash crop in later accounts.
- **Betel nut** — Betel nut was another main cash crop in later accounts.
- **Pig keeping** — The Biwat kept pigs and other livestock.
- **Motorized canoe trade** — They travelled by motorized canoe along the Yuat River to buy and sell produce.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do not record Mundugumor stories or oral genres, but they preserve field notes and language recordings.

- **The Mundugumor** — Nancy McDowell completed Mead's book after Mead's death, and it was published in 1991 as The Mundugumor: From the Field Notes of Margaret Mead and Reo Fortune.
- **Biwat language recordings** (*Biwat*) — The Paradisec collection holds Biwat language recordings, including materials from Don Laycock.

## Language & religion

Mundugumor is a Yuat language, and the people also speak Melanesian Pidgin; later studies say most Biwat were Catholic.

- **Mundugumor language** (*Mundugumor*) — Mundugumor is also called Munduguma and Mundukomo and is spoken in Biwat village.
- **Munduguma** — Munduguma is another name for the Mundugumor language.
- **Mundukomo** — Mundukomo is another name for the Mundugumor language.
- **Melanesian Pidgin** — The Mundugumor also speak Melanesian Pidgin.
- **Catholicism** — Later studies state that most of the Biwat were Catholic.

## Glossary

- *Mundugumor* — The people and their language
- *Biwat* — Another name for the people
- *Munduguma* — Another name for the language
- *Mundukomo* — Another name for the language
- *Melanesian Pidgin* — A language also spoken by the people

---
title: "Tahitians"
subtitle: "French Polynesia"
region: "Oceania"
tags: [ethnography, oceania]
---

## Overview

The Tahitians, called *Māʼohi* in Tahitian and *Tahitiens* in French, are Indigenous Polynesian people of Tahiti and thirteen other Society Islands in French Polynesia. The population figures in the sources concern different historical periods: Tahiti probably had around 110,000 people, or perhaps 180,000, at first European contact in 1767; by 1830 its population had fallen to 15,300, and the 1881 census recorded about 5,960 Indigenous Tahitians. The sources describe Tahitian society, historical change, clothing, adornment, barkcloth, featherwork, shellwork, quilts, healing, poetry, painting, and political identification. They do not provide the language family or a current population figure.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Barkcloth** — Barkcloth was made from paper mulberry bark and could be dyed and decorated with leaf designs pressed onto the cloth. One recorded length of fine white barkcloth bears fingerprints and handprints dipped in dye and is associated with the Tahitian Mourner’s costume.

**Mourner’s costume** — The Tahitian Mourner’s costume combined barkcloth, feathers, pearl shells, wood, coconut shells, plaited fibre, and coir. Its recorded components include an apron, cloak, poncho, belt, sash, head-rope, cap, mask, breast-plate, and head-dress.

**Tifaifai** — A *tifaifai* is a cotton quilt. One example has an appliquéd mid-blue fan design on a white background, while another, made for a baby, has an orange *Tiare Tahiti* flower design on a cream background.

**Matting** — Recorded garments include a dress of matting covered with tufts of fibre and a piece of plaited vegetable fibre matting, probably worn as a dress.

**Tiputa** — A *tiputa* is a poncho made of barkcloth and decorated with stripes.

**Motif vocabulary.** Fan (*evantail*) design; *Tiare Tahiti* flower design; leaf designs; red triangles; fingerprints and handprints.

### Clothing & dress

The sources document both everyday garments and ceremonial clothing, but they do not distinguish men’s and women’s daily dress in detail. Recorded garments include a barkcloth apron, a striped *tiputa*, a belt and sash of barkcloth, a fibre-matting cap, a dress of matting, and a garment probably worn as a dress. The Tahitian Mourner’s costume was more elaborate: its cloak was made of feathers bound to a fibre netted base, its mask combined pearlshell and tropic bird feathers, and its breast-plate combined wood, pearlshell, feather tassels, and an apron of thinly carved pearlshell sections. A head-dress consisted of plaited fibre with bunches of black and white feathers. No footwear is described in the sources. A photograph records a woman in Papeete wearing flowers in her hair and a garland around her chest.

### Architecture

The sources state that the original Tahitians cleared land for cultivation on fertile volcanic soils and built fishing canoes. They do not describe Tahitian houses, roofs, named buildings, settlement forms, architectural decoration, or urban construction.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources do not describe Tahitian ceramics, metalwork, pottery, or household vessels. They state that the tools of the Tahitians when first discovered were made of stone, bone, shell, or wood. A *Tahiri*, described as a handle for a fly whisk, is recorded from the 18th century and is made of whale ivory and coconut fiber. Fishing canoes are mentioned, but their construction is not described.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Recorded adornment includes a shell necklace made on a base of young coconut leaves. It has small yellow and apricot-coloured spiral shells, bands of small black spiral shells, medium-sized pearl shells, and a cowrie-shell clasp. A dance bra was made from two drilled coconut shells strung together with synthetic cord. The sources also record a woman wearing flowers in her hair and a garland around her chest, and describe a white *tiare* flower behind the left ear as signifying readiness to take a lover in one of Paul Gauguin’s paintings. Tattoos and tattooing are not covered by the sources.

## Music & performance

The sources do not describe Tahitian instruments, song genres, musical forms, or performance contexts. They mention Tahitian poets Henri Hiro, Charles Manutahi, Vaitiare, and Turo Raapoto, who in the late 1960s and early 1970s spearheaded anticolonial writing in Tahiti. Hiro’s *God of Culture* invokes Oihanu, described as the Tahitian god of culture and husbandry. No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription is supplied for French Polynesia.

## Dance & theatre

The sources provide little information on dance or theatre. A dance bra made of two coconut shells is recorded in the museum catalogue. The sources do not name a Tahitian dance, dramatic tradition, mask performance, or theatrical genre.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not provide an annual festival calendar or describe named seasonal festivals, weddings, coming-of-age ceremonies, funerals, or other life-cycle rites. They do record the Tahitian Mourner’s costume, whose components include feather, barkcloth, fibre, wood, coconut-shell, pearlshell, and tropic-bird-feather elements. The sources also mention a concept of irrational fear called *mehameha* and healers called *taʼata rāʼau* or *taʼata rapaʼau*. Tiurai, described as the most famous Tahitian healer, died at age 83 during the influenza outbreak on Tahiti in 1918.

## Foodways

The sources do not describe Tahitian staple foods, dishes, cooking methods, food restrictions, feasting, or beverage traditions. They state that the original Tahitians cleared land for cultivation on fertile volcanic soils and built fishing canoes, but provide no further account of agriculture, fishing practices, or cuisine.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources describe a modern anticolonial literary movement rather than a corpus of folktales or epic poetry. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, Henri Hiro, Charles Manutahi, Vaitiare, and Turo Raapoto spearheaded anticolonial writing in Tahiti. Hiro’s *God of Culture* calls on Oihanu, the Tahitian god of culture and husbandry, to empower the “new generation.” Michou Chaze, Chantal Spitz, and Vaitiare explored problems of Tahitian identification in contemporary French Polynesia. The sources do not describe named folktales, proverbs, riddles, epics, or storytelling settings.

## Language & religion

The sources identify *Māʼohi* as the Tahitian name for the people and *Tahitiens* as the French term. They do not specify the language family, dialects, historical scripts, or writing system. In the 1820s Protestantism became the main religion on Tahiti. The sources also mention Oihanu, the Tahitian god of culture and husbandry, and state that healers used herbal remedies; in the 19th century Tahitians added European medicine to their practice. Tahitians are French citizens and participate in French elections.

## Sources & further reading

- Wikipedia, “Tahitians”: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tahitians
- UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: no inscription for French Polynesia is included among the supplied sources.
- British Museum online collection records for Tahitian costumes, barkcloth, quilts, necklaces, photographs, and related objects.
- Metropolitan Museum of Art catalogue record for *Tahiri* (handle for a fly whisk), 18th century.

---
title: "Rapa Nui"
subtitle: "Chile"
region: "Oceania"
tags: [ethnography, oceania]
---

## Overview

The Rapa Nui are Indigenous Polynesian peoples of Easter Island and represent the easternmost Polynesian culture. About 60% of the current Easter Island population is Rapa Nui, with a significant portion living in mainland Chile. At the 2017 census, the island had 7,750 inhabitants, almost all living in Hanga Roa on the sheltered west coast. The Rapa Nui speak Rapa Nui and Chilean Spanish. Rapa Nui is an Eastern Polynesian language and is written in the Latin script. The culture is especially associated with moai, large human figures carved from rock, as well as oral traditions, tattooing, choral music, distinctive foods, wood carving, stone carving, and the preservation of Rapa Nui National Park.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

*Feather headdresses* were historically made by the Rapa Nui, but the supplied sources do not describe their construction or patterns.

*Bark cloth* is named among historical Rapa Nui arts, although the sources do not provide further information about its materials, techniques, or designs.

*Flätad påse* — a plait bag recorded by the Museum of World Culture was made from *Scirpus ripar var. paschalis*. The catalogue identifies its locality as Easter Island.

*Wood carvings* form part of Rapa Nui art. The sources state that adzes, described as blunt round stones, were used to complete wood carvings.

*Stone carvings* are also documented in Rapa Nui art and museum records. A Museum of Ethnography catalogue records stone sculptures from Easter Island.

**Motif vocabulary.** *moai*, human figures; *Moko*, lizardman figure; *Moai Kavakava*, male figure; *Moai Tangata*, male figure; *moai papa*, female figure; *rei miro*, gorget.

### Clothing & dress

The supplied sources do not describe everyday or ceremonial Rapa Nui clothing, distinctions between men’s and women’s dress, belts, footwear, or named garments. They do document feather headdresses and tattooing as aspects of Rapa Nui culture. Priests, warriors, and chiefs historically had more tattoos than the rest of the population, while both men and women were tattooed to represent social class. The tattooing process used bone needles and combs called *Uhi*, made from bird or fish bones. Ink was produced from natural materials, primarily through burning *Ti* leaves and sugar cane. The sources do not identify particular garments, head coverings, or footwear.

### Architecture

The supplied museum records identify houses of stone on Easter Island, but do not describe their plan, roof form, construction method, or decoration. The Rapa Nui culture section records large stone platforms called *ahu*, on which moai rested. The most famous named examples are Ahu Tongariki, described as the largest ahu, and Ahu Vinapu. Most settlements in the mythology source were located on the coast, and moai were erected along the coastline, facing their descendants in the settlements. The sources do not provide a fuller account of domestic architecture or urban organization.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources do not describe Rapa Nui ceramics or metalwork. They do document stone tools, including adzes described as blunt round stones, which were used in the completion of stone images and wood carvings. Museum records include dance paddles called *Rapa*, a plait bag, wooden *rei miro* gorgets, wooden figures, and figures made from wood, obsidian, bone, and, in one case, paint. The Rapa Nui language source also records *toki*, meaning axe, as a Mapuche/Rapa Nui cognate.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources describe tattoos and body painting as having a fundamentally spiritual connotation. Tattoos could be regarded as a receptor for divine strength or *mana* and were manifestations of Rapa Nui culture. Priests, warriors, and chiefs had more tattoos as a sign of hierarchy, while men and women were tattooed to represent social class. Tattoo designs combined anthropomorphic and zoomorphic imagery. Young people are described as bringing back Rapa Nui tattoos, with local artists basing their work on traditional motifs. The museum catalogue also records *rei miro*, a wooden gorget, but does not explain its use or social meaning.

## Music & performance

Rapa Nui traditional music consists of choral singing and chanting. The sources name conch shell trumpets, percussive dancers, accordions, and *kauaha*, a percussion instrument made from the jaw bone of a horse. Modern Rapanui music has produced new genres, including a Rapa Nui style of tango. *Matato'a* is identified as one of the most famous musical groups on the island and as a promoter of traditional styles of dance and music.

The sources do not describe a detailed calendar of musical performances, wedding or funeral contexts, or named song genres beyond these forms. They do, however, connect music with dance and identify traditional dance and music as central subjects of contemporary cultural promotion.

## Dance & theatre

The sources mention Rapa Nui dance in connection with traditional music and identify *Matato'a* as a group promoting traditional styles of dance and music. A Metropolitan Museum of Art catalogue records the *Rapa*, or dance paddle, a wooden object from the early 19th century. Another museum catalogue records clubs, staffs, and paddles from Easter Island, although the catalogue marks their identification as uncertain. The supplied sources do not describe named dances, theatrical genres, mask traditions, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment performances.

## Festivals & rituals

The supplied sources do not provide an annual Rapa Nui festival calendar or descriptions of weddings, funerals, birth rites, or coming-of-age ceremonies. They do describe the *Tangata manu*, or bird-man cult, which followed the Moai era after warfare and the cessation of statue construction. The competition involved eggs and selected the birdman who would remain sacred for five months. The cult’s chief deity was Make-make.

The mythology source states that the cult declined after the island population adopted Catholicism, although the birdman remained present in the decoration of the island’s church. Rapa Nui mythology also describes a former relationship between the living and the dead: deified ancestors were believed to provide health, fertility of land and animals, and fortune, while the living offered support intended to improve the dead’s place in the spirit world.

## Foodways

Rapa Nui or Pascuense cuisine combines Indigenous Rapa Nui and American influences. Named ingredients include fish, octopus or *heke*, eel, sea snails or *pipi*, crustaceans including lobster, sweet potato, taro, banana, pineapple, coconut, pumpkin, poultry, pork, and lamb. Traditional food called *umu* consists of meat, fish, vegetables, and fruit wrapped in banana leaves and roasted in *umu pae*, an earth oven.

*Po'e* is a pudding made from mashed bananas, pumpkin, and flour and baked in the *umu pae*. Other named dishes include *tunu ahi*, fish grilled on hot stones, ceviche, and pork or mutton ribs. The Easter Island cuisine section also records *Po`e* as a banana or cassava cake and *Umu Rapa Nui* as the Easter Island version of curanto.

Easter Island cuisine includes dishes of both Chilean and Polynesian extraction, a wider array of fish than mainland cuisine, and fruits and tubers unavailable in continental Chile. Ceviche may be made with soy or coconut milk and with *mata huira*, *toremo*, or *kana-kana*. The sources do not describe dietary rules, tea or coffee customs, or ceremonial food beyond the named cooking practices.

## Oral tradition & literature

Rapa Nui mythology includes stories of *Hotu Matu'a*, regarded as the legendary first settler and *ariki mau*, or supreme chief, and the *Tangata manu*. The mythology source describes Hotu Matu'a and his colonising party as Polynesians who landed at Anakena beach, after which his people spread across the island and divided it between clans claiming descent from his sons.

Other named figures and beings include Make-make, creator of humanity; Uoke, a tectonic deity; Aku-Aku, spirits of the dead; Manana Take; Haua; Hina-Oio; and the *Hanau epe*. The Rapa Nui people source also mentions the epic battle between the Hanau Epe and the Hanau Momoko. The source does not describe a formal epic-poetry tradition, proverbs, riddles, or storytelling occasions.

Rongorongo is described as a system of glyphs discovered in the 1800s and as a possible older form of the Rapa Nui language. Its decipherment remains incomplete, and it is not clear whether it is writing or another form of cultural expression.

## Language & religion

Rapa Nui, also known as Pascuan or Pascuense, is an Eastern Polynesian language spoken on Easter Island. It is a minority language, while Spanish is widely spoken and is the primary language of education and administration. Many adult Rapa Nui speakers also speak Spanish, and most Rapa Nui children now grow up speaking Spanish. Written Rapanui uses the Latin script. *Rongorongo* is a possible undeciphered script once used on Rapa Nui.

Rapa Nui mythology includes creator god Make-make, the *Tangata manu* cult, deified ancestors, and spirits of the dead. The living were believed to maintain a reciprocal relationship with the dead through offerings. The sources state that the bird-man cult declined after the adoption of Catholicism, while its memory remained visible in the decoration of the island’s church.

## Overview

The Rapa Nui are the easternmost Polynesian culture. Most island residents live in Hanga Roa, and many Rapa Nui also live in mainland Chile. The culture is known for moai, carving, tattooing, music, food, and oral traditions. Rapa Nui remains important, but Spanish is now widely spoken and most children grow up speaking Spanish.

## Material culture

Rapa Nui material culture includes stone and wood carving, feather headdresses, bark cloth, tattoo tools, dance paddles, and large stone platforms for moai.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Rapa Nui arts include feather headdresses, bark cloth, plaited bags, and carvings in wood and stone.

- **Plait bag** (*Flätad påse*) — A museum record identifies this Easter Island bag as a plaited object made from Scirpus ripar var. paschalis.
- **Wood carvings** — Wood carvings were completed with adzes described as blunt round stones.
- **Stone carvings** — Museum records document stone sculptures from Easter Island.
- **Human figure** (*moai*) — The moai motif shows human figures.
- **Lizardman figure** (*Moko*) — Moko is a lizardman figure motif.

### Clothing & dress

The sources give little information about clothing but describe feather headdresses and traditional tattooing.

- **Feather headdress** — Feather headdresses were historically made by the Rapa Nui, but the sources do not describe their form or patterns.
- **Tattoo comb** (*Uhi*) — Uhi were combs made from bird or fish bones and used in tattooing.
- **Ti leaf ink** (*Ti*) — Ti leaves were burned to help make tattoo ink.

### Architecture

Rapa Nui architecture includes stone houses and large coastal platforms that held moai.

- **Stone house** — Museum records identify houses of stone on Easter Island.
- **Moai platform** (*ahu*) — Ahu are large stone platforms on which moai rested.
- **Ahu Tongariki** — Ahu Tongariki is described as the largest ahu.
- **Ahu Vinapu** — Ahu Vinapu is another named moai platform.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources do not describe ceramics or metalwork, but they record stone tools, paddles, bags, gorgets, and carved figures.

- **Axe** (*toki*) — Toki means axe in a Mapuche/Rapa Nui cognate.
- **Dance paddle** (*Rapa*) — Rapa are wooden dance paddles recorded in museum collections.
- **Gorget** (*rei miro*) — Wooden rei miro gorgets are recorded in museum collections.
- **Stone adze** — Adzes made from blunt round stones were used to complete stone images and wood carvings.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Tattoos were spiritual signs of strength and social class, while body painting and wooden gorgets were also recorded.

- **Spiritual power** (*mana*) — Tattoos could be seen as a receptor for divine strength or mana.
- **Wooden gorget** (*rei miro*) — A rei miro is a wooden gorget, but the sources do not explain its use or social meaning.
- **Tattoo designs** — Traditional tattoo designs combined human-like and animal-like images.

## Music & performance

Traditional Rapa Nui music centers on choral singing and chanting, with shells, percussion, and newer musical styles.

- **Jaw-bone percussion** (*kauaha*) — Kauaha is a percussion instrument made from a horse jaw bone.
- **Rapa Nui tango** — Modern Rapanui music includes a Rapa Nui style of tango.
- **Matato'a** — Matato'a is a famous island music group that promotes traditional dance and music.
- **Conch shell trumpet** — Conch shell trumpets are named among Rapa Nui musical instruments.
- **Percussive dancers** — Percussive dancers are named among Rapa Nui performance traditions.

## Dance & theatre

Rapa Nui dance is linked with traditional music, and wooden paddles were used as dance objects.

- **Dance paddle** (*Rapa*) — The Rapa is a wooden dance paddle recorded from the early 19th century.
- **Dance group** (*Matato'a*) — Matato'a promotes traditional styles of Rapa Nui dance and music.
- **Clubs and staffs** — Museum records include clubs and staffs from Easter Island, although their identification is uncertain.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources describe the bird-man cult and offerings to ancestors but give no annual festival calendar.

- **Bird-man cult** (*Tangata manu*) — Tangata manu was a competition involving eggs that selected a birdman who remained sacred for five months.
- **Bird-man deity** (*Make-make*) — Make-make was the chief deity of the bird-man cult.
- **Ancestor offerings** — The living offered support to deified ancestors to improve the dead's place in the spirit world.

## Foodways

Rapa Nui food combines Indigenous Polynesian and American influences and uses fish, seafood, fruits, and tubers.

- **Earth-oven meal** (*umu*) — Umu is meat, fish, vegetables, and fruit wrapped in banana leaves and roasted in an earth oven.
- **Earth oven** (*umu pae*) — Umu pae is the earth oven used to roast traditional food.
- **Banana and pumpkin pudding** (*Po'e*) — Po'e is a pudding made from mashed bananas, pumpkin, and flour and baked in the umu pae.
- **Fish grilled on stones** (*tunu ahi*) — Tunu ahi is fish grilled on hot stones.
- **Easter Island curanto** (*Umu Rapa Nui*) — Umu Rapa Nui is the Easter Island version of curanto.

## Oral tradition & literature

Rapa Nui oral tradition includes settlement stories, gods, spirits, clan ancestors, and the unresolved Rongorongo glyph system.

- **First settler** (*Hotu Matu'a*) — Hotu Matu'a is regarded as the legendary first settler and supreme chief.
- **Supreme chief** (*ariki mau*) — Ariki mau means supreme chief.
- **Bird-man** (*Tangata manu*) — Tangata manu appears in Rapa Nui mythology as the bird-man figure and cult.
- **Epic battle** (*Hanau epe*) — The Hanau Epe fought an epic battle with the Hanau Momoko.
- **Glyph system** (*Rongorongo*) — Rongorongo is a system of glyphs whose meaning and purpose remain uncertain.

## Language & religion

Rapa Nui is an Eastern Polynesian language, while traditional beliefs include creator gods, spirits, ancestors, and a later Catholic influence.

- **Rapa Nui language** (*Rapa Nui*) — Rapa Nui is an Eastern Polynesian language spoken on Easter Island and written in the Latin script.
- **Pascuan language** (*Pascuan*) — Pascuan is another name for the Rapa Nui language.
- **Creator god** (*Make-make*) — Make-make is the creator god in Rapa Nui mythology.
- **Spirits of the dead** (*Aku-Aku*) — Aku-Aku are spirits of the dead.
- **Ancestor spirits** — Deified ancestors were believed to provide health, fertility, and fortune in return for support from the living.

## Glossary

title: "Dani"

## Overview

The Dani, also spelled Ndani, are an ethnic group of the Central Highlands of Western New Guinea, in the Baliem Valley of Highland Papua, Indonesia. Around 100,000 people live in the Baliem Valley, including Dani communities in the lower, middle, and upper parts of the valley. The areas west of the valley are inhabited by representatives of the Lani people, who are incorrectly called “Western Dani”; surrounding highland peoples include the Walak, Nduga, Mek, and Yali. The Dani call themselves *Hubula*, also recorded as Huwulra, Hugula, or Hubla. The name Dani became established after the 1926 Smithsonian Institution–Dutch Colonial Government expedition under Matthew Stirling. The group is known through ethnographic research, museum collections, and tourism in the Baliem Valley.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Nätväska** — Museum of World Culture records describe net bags made of string. Some are patterned by wrapping parts of the string with orchid fibre in yellow, reddish-brown, and brown-white shades. Recorded examples have carrying straps and heights of 42, 47, 48, 53, 55, and 57 cm.

**Vegetable-fibre bag** — A British Museum record describes a bag made of plaited vegetable fibre and decorated on one side with yellow orchid stems.

**Bag or pouch** — Another British Museum record describes a bag or pouch made of vegetable fibre, with a handle of the same material. A pattern follows the lip, and two small fibre knots are attached near the centre on one side.

**Snäckband** — Museum of Ethnography records describe a Dani shell band from the Baliem Valley made from plant fibre, kauri shells, seeds of Jobs tears, cuscus skins, and plastic thread. It is used as a bridal gift, a gift at cremation, on other occasions, and as a means of payment.

**Rope with shells** — A British Museum record describes a long rope of plaited vegetable fibre decorated with shells, including larger cowrie shells along the centre and smaller shells on either side. A tuft of light-brown fur and several attachments are also recorded.

**Nätväska with transverse bands** — Several museum records describe net bags whose fronts are patterned in transverse bands. Orchid fibre is wrapped around selected sections of the string in yellow, reddish-brown, and brown-white shades.

**Motif vocabulary.** transverse bands, yellow orchid fibre, reddish-brown orchid fibre, brown-white orchid fibre, cowrie shells

### Clothing & dress

The sources used describe body ornaments and carrying objects but do not cover everyday clothing, named garments, head coverings, belts, footwear, or a complete distinction between men’s and women’s dress. Museum records identify two bound pig tusks used as nose ornaments, with recorded heights of 8, 8.4, 8.5, and 9.5 cm. A shell necklace from the Baliem Valley is described as usually worn by men and sometimes by women. The Dani are described in the museum record as a highland people who obtain shells for ornaments through exchange with coastal peoples.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Dani house forms, roof construction, named buildings, settlement layout, decoration, or other aspects of vernacular architecture.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum records contain no ceramics or metalwork. They do document stone tools and blades collected during expeditions to New Guinea. These include a grey, slate-like stone tool with a particularly sharp long edge that can be used as a knife; a light-green stone tool described as a very thin slice that can also be used as a knife; a grey, slate-like tool with a worn, slightly concave inner edge; greenish stone tools; a greenish chisel; and axe blades of stone, including a blue-grey stone blade with a pointed back and a convex-convex section. Recorded lengths include 7.7 cm, 10 cm, 12 cm, 13.5 cm, 18 cm, 21.5 cm, and 28.5 cm.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Museum of Ethnography records describe necklaces from the Baliem Valley made with shells threaded on plant-fibre string. One is made from three kinds of shells and is usually worn by men, though sometimes by women. The record explains that shells are exchanged for stone between coastal peoples and the Dani highland communities, where shells for ornaments are not locally available.

Other necklaces in the Museum of World Culture records are made from small shells sewn onto a woven cane or similar foundation, grey-white seed shells threaded onto string, or seed shells arranged so that small cup-like forms project into one another. Recorded necklace lengths include 43 cm, 220 cm, and 430 cm. The records also describe bound pig tusks used as nose ornaments. A British Museum object is a shell-decorated rope with fur, feathers, hair-like tails, and empty cocoons attached.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not identify musical instruments, song genres, or a distinct Dani musical tradition. They do describe communal dance and victory performance. Robert Gardner’s ethnographic work records the Dani term *edai* for a two-day dance of victory held after an enemy was killed. The Dani terms *wim*, “dead birds,” and “dead men” refer to weapons and ornaments taken from an enemy during battle; these trophies were displayed during the *edai*.

## Dance & theatre

The sources identify *edai* as a two-day dance of victory following the killing of an enemy. Robert Gardner recorded the Dani of the Baliem River Valley in Kurulu District and Wita Waya District, Jayawijaya Regency, and created the film *Dead Birds* from this experience in 1965. The sources do not describe other dances, theatrical forms, masks, puppetry, or entertainment performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources describe communal feasting, warfare, and exchange but do not provide an annual festival calendar. Pig feasts are important for celebrating events communally. The success of a feast, and the standing of a village big man or organiser, is often gauged by the number of pigs slaughtered. Pigs are valuable and are reserved for special occasions rather than served regularly.

Sweet potatoes are important in local culture and are the most important tool used in bartering, especially in dowries. Museum records describe a shell band used as a bridal gift, a gift at cremation, on other occasions, and as payment. The sources do not cover birth ceremonies, coming-of-age rites, a complete wedding sequence, or other funeral practices.

Ritual small-scale warfare between rival villages was an integral part of traditional Dani culture. Much time was spent preparing weapons and treating injuries. In 1966, 125 people were killed in a massacre during an attack by an enemy clan. The emphasis of battle was typically to insult the enemy and wound or kill token victims rather than capture territory, property, or an enemy village. The sources state that this fighting is no longer done.

## Foodways

Sweet potatoes are a staple crop and an important medium of barter, particularly in dowries. The Dani use an earth-oven method called *bakar batu* or *barapen* to cook pigs and staple crops such as sweet potato, banana, and cassava.

The method begins by heating stones in a fire until they are extremely hot. Some of the stones line a pit. Cuts of meat and pieces of sweet potato or banana are wrapped in banana leaves and lowered into the pit. More hot stones are placed on top, and the pit is covered with grass and a cover to retain steam. After a couple of hours, the food is ready to eat. Pigs are too valuable for regular meals and are reserved for special occasions, especially communal feasts.

The sources do not cover beverages, tea or coffee traditions, dietary rules, food prohibitions, or further named dishes.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not identify Dani folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, or a named oral-literary cycle. They do record the Dani expressions *wim*, “dead birds,” and “dead men,” referring to weapons and ornaments taken from enemies during battle. Robert Gardner’s film *Dead Birds* emphasised death and people-as-birds in Dani culture.

The sources also list ethnographic books concerning the Dani, including Robert Gardner’s *Gardens of War: Life and Death in the New Guinea Stone Age*, Karl G. Heider’s *The Dugum Dani* and *Grand Valley Dani: Peaceful Warriors*, and Peter Matthiessen’s *Under the Mountain Wall*. These are documentation of Dani life rather than works identified by the sources as Dani oral literature.

## Language & religion

Linguists identify at least four sub-groupings of Dani or Baliem Valley languages: Wano, Nggem, Central Dani, Grand Valley Dani, Lani or Western Dani, Walak, and Ngalik. Grand Valley Dani includes Lower-Grand Valley Dani and Hupla, Mid-Grand Valley Dani, and Upper-Grand Valley Dani. The sources also list Nduga, Silimo, and Yali as part of the Ngalik grouping.

Dani languages distinguish two basic colour terms: *mili* for cool or dark shades such as blue, green, and black, and *mola* for warm or light colours such as red, yellow, and white. The sources used do not cover a language family, historical script, religious affiliation, or Dani spiritual practices.

## Sources & further reading

- Robert Gardner, *Gardens of War: Life and Death in the New Guinea Stone Age*, Random House, 1968.
- Karl G. Heider, *The Dugum Dani: A Papuan Culture in the Highlands of West New Guinea*, Aldine Publishing, 1970.
- Karl G. Heider, *Grand Valley Dani: Peaceful Warriors*, Wadsworth Publishing, 1996.
- Peter Matthiessen, *Under the Mountain Wall: A Chronicle of Two Seasons in Stone Age New Guinea*, Viking Press, 1962.
- Robert Gardner’s ethnographic documentation of the Dani and the film *Dead Birds*.
- [Dani people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani_people)
- [Dani language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dani_language)
- The supplied sources identify no UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription for this ethnic group.

The Dani live in the Baliem Valley of Highland Papua, Indonesia. They call themselves Hubula. Their culture includes sweet-potato farming, pig feasts, shell ornaments, net bags, and stone tools. Traditional fighting and the victory dance edai are also recorded.

## Material culture

Dani material culture includes plant-fibre bags, shell ornaments, stone tools, pig tusks, and earth-oven cooking.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Dani fibre work includes net bags, pouches, shell bands, and ropes with plant-fibre patterns and shell decoration.

## Overview

The Buginese, also called the Bugis people, are an ethnic group of South Sulawesi, Indonesia. Their language, Buginese or Bugis, is an Austronesian language spoken by about 4 million people, mainly in the southern part of Sulawesi. Most native speakers, around 3 million, are concentrated in South Sulawesi, while smaller groups live on Java, in Samarinda and east Sumatra, in east Sabah and the Malay Peninsula, and in the South Philippines. The language belongs to the South Sulawesi subgroup of the Austronesian language family. Buginese culture is represented in the sources through the Lontara writing tradition, historical records, the epic creation myth Sureq Galigo, and museum objects including kris, daggers, clothing, belts, musical instruments, jewellery, and photographs of Buginese people and vessels.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

*Sarong* — A museum catalogue records a Buginese sarong from Boni in South Celebes. It is a narrow cotton textile patterned in black and white and sewn together at the short ends. The catalogue gives its width as 52 cm and its length, when doubled, as 171 cm. It could also be worn by girls as a head covering.

**Man’s ceremonial sword belt** — A British Museum belt is tablet-woven from two shades of blue cotton yarn and padded except at the fringed end. It contains three sections of an identical Islamic inscription in Kufic (?) calligraphy, a long loop, very long fringes, and floral patterning within a rectangle on the reverse.

**Kris sheath** — Kris sheaths in the catalogue are made from wood, gold and silver thread, with floral decoration. Another sheath is made of rattan and wood and has a loop for attachment.

**Belt patterning** — The belt catalogue describes alternating reverse colourways, four separating bands, and patterns made at the same time on both sides using the same weft. The catalogue identifies this as a considerable technical achievement.

The sources name no further Buginese textile traditions or motif vocabulary.

### Clothing & dress

The catalogue records a Buginese sarong made of cotton and patterned in black and white. It was sewn into a short-ended garment and could also be worn by girls as a head covering. A British Museum catalogue records a man’s hat made of dyed and interlaced vegetable fibre. Its shape derives from the Middle Eastern fez, and it is described as an early form of the black velvet hat called “peci,” which became established men’s headgear following Indonesia’s independence in 1945. A man’s ceremonial sword belt was tablet-woven from cotton yarn, padded, ornamented with floral patterning, and furnished with fringes and a loop. The sources do not describe everyday footwear, women’s separate dress, or other named Buginese garments.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Buginese houses, roof forms, building materials, named building types, urban traditions, or architectural decoration.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum records focus on edged weapons and related objects. A Buginese kris from Sulawesi has a steel blade, a carved ivory hilt embellished with diamonds, and a wooden sheath decorated with gold and silver thread. Other kris are made of forged iron and steel, with brass or silver collars and carved wooden hilts. One Buginese kris has the blade shape *sepukal* and a “water melon skin” blade pattern. The catalogues also record Buginese thrusting daggers found in South Sulawesi, including a dagger with a silver sheath and silver handle, and another with a straight, single-edged blade of coarsely damascened steel and a handle covered with white metal decorated with driven and chased floral designs. A Buginese knife found in South Sulawesi is also recorded.

### Jewelry & body adornment

A Dutch catalogue records a set of two bracelets called *ponto lola* in Buginese or *ponto sipapa* in Makassarese. They are hollow, somewhat triangular rings made of gilded sheet silver. Each bracelet consists of two halves joined by a pin. Leaf and flower ornaments in filigree decorate the bracelets, and blue and green gemstones are set into them. The set includes a small bag decorated with round green beads and a border of transparent beads. The sources do not document tattoos, henna, hair practices, or ritual functions for these ornaments.

## Music & performance

The sources record two British Museum objects described only as musical instruments made of bamboo. They do not provide their names, construction details beyond the material, musical systems, song genres, performance contexts, or ceremonial uses. The sources therefore do not cover Buginese music beyond the existence of these bamboo instruments.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not describe Buginese dances, theatre, masked performance, shadow puppetry, court performance, or other dramatic traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not describe an annual festival calendar, seasonal celebrations, harvest rites, birth ceremonies, coming-of-age practices, weddings, funerals, or other life-cycle rituals. They also do not identify named Buginese festivals or ritual foods.

## Foodways

The sources used do not describe Buginese staple foods, dishes, cooking methods, drinks, dietary rules, or ceremonial foodways.

## Oral tradition & literature

The earliest written record of Buginese is identified as *Sureq Galigo*, the epic creation myth of the Bugis people. Another important written source is *Lontara*, a term referring both to the traditional script and to a historical record. The earliest historical record of Lontara dates to around the 17th century. Historians of Indonesia have described these records as “sober” and “factual” in comparison with records from other regions of Maritime Southeast Asia. They are generally written in a matter-of-fact tone, contain few mythical elements, and commonly include disclaimers before statements that the writers could not verify.

The sources also mention a Buginese poem painted on a wall near the Royal Netherlands Institute of Southeast Asian and Caribbean Studies in Leiden, Netherlands. They do not describe the poem’s contents or provide further information about Buginese folktales, proverbs, riddles, storytelling occasions, or contemporary literary preservation.

## Language & religion

Buginese, or Bugis, is an Austronesian language of the South Sulawesi subgroup. It is most closely related within that subgroup to Campalagian and the Tamanic outlier in West Kalimantan. In Buginese it is called *Basa Ugi*, while the Bugis people are called *To Ugi*. According to a Buginese myth, *Ugi* derives from La Sattumpugi, described as the first king of Cina, an ancient Bugis kingdom; *To Ugi* therefore means “the followers of La Sattumpugi.”

Buginese was traditionally written in the Lontara script, a member of the Brahmic family also used for Makassar and Mandar. The name Lontara derives from the Malay word for the palmyra palm, whose leaves were traditional manuscript material. The Buginese lontara is locally known as *Aksara Ugi*. Buginese is now often written in the Latin script. The sources do not describe the current religious landscape, religious affiliation, syncretism, or spiritual practices of the Buginese.

title: "Lampung"
subtitle: "Indonesia"
region: "Southeast Asia"
tags: [ethnography, southeast-asia]
