## Overview

The Nyakyusa, also called the Sokile, are a Bantu ethnolinguistic group living in the mountains of southern Mbeya Region of Tanzania and the Northern Region of Malawi. They speak Nyakyusa, a member of the Bantu language family. Nyakyusa is spoken around the northern end of Lake Malawi, including northern Karonga District in Malawi and areas near the border with Tanzania. The available sources provide information about the group’s regional distribution, language, traditional god, and several museum objects, but do not give a population figure, a more specific river or mountain name, or a broader account of Nyakyusa folk-culture significance.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Riabi or lyabi** — A woman’s loin-cloth made of barkcloth from Riabi tree bark. The catalogue identifies the garment by these vernacular names and materials but does not describe its pattern or distinguish it from textiles of neighboring cultures.

**Lufwalilo** — A woman’s waist-band made of barkcloth from Riabi tree bark. It has a geometric pattern in black; the available catalogue record does not provide further information about its use or regional comparisons.

The sources used do not document additional Nyakyusa textile traditions or named pattern systems.

### Clothing & dress

The museum catalogue records a woman’s loin-cloth called *riabi* or *lyabi*, made of barkcloth from Riabi tree bark, and a woman’s *lufwalilo* waist-band made of the same material. The waist-band has a geometric pattern in black. The sources do not describe men’s clothing, footwear, head coverings, ceremonial dress, or differences between everyday and ritual clothing.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Nyakyusa architecture, house forms, building materials, roof types, decoration, or named building traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records several objects associated with the displayed material culture. These include spears with iron heads and wooden shafts ornamented with an animal tail or hide, a wooden shield covered in cow hide, a composite bark-cloth-beater, and a wooden staff carved and decorated with metal studs. The bark-cloth-beater includes a section of cow’s horn cross-hatched on one end and a short wooden handle inserted into a hole at the centre. The sources do not describe ceramics, household arrangements, manufacture, or the social meanings of these objects.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not cover Nyakyusa jewelry, body adornment, tattoos, henna, hair practices, or ritual ornaments.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not document Nyakyusa instruments, song genres, musical performances, dances accompanied by music, or performance contexts. The Nyakyusa language article includes a sample text from the Bible in Nyakyusa, but it does not identify this text as a song or performance tradition.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover Nyakyusa dances, theatrical traditions, masked performances, dramatic forms, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The available sources do not describe an annual festival calendar, seasonal celebrations, life-cycle rites, weddings, funerals, initiation practices, or other Nyakyusa rituals. They state only that the traditional god of the Nyakyusa is called *Kyala*, the Nyakyusa-language name for God.

## Foodways

The sources used do not cover Nyakyusa staple foods, dishes, cooking methods, food preparation, ceremonial meals, beverages, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Nyakyusa language source states that the Language Mapping Survey for Northern Malawi contains a folktale, “the Tortoise and the Hare,” in Chinkhonde and other languages of Northern Malawi, together with comparative vocabulary. The source reproduces a sample text from the Bible in Nyakyusa and gives its English translation. It does not identify a Nyakyusa epic, proverb tradition, riddle tradition, storytelling context, or literary revival.

## Language & religion

Nyakyusa, also called Nyakyusa-Ngonde and, in Swahili, Kinyakyusa, is a Bantu language of Tanzania and Malawi. The source states that there is no single name for the language as a whole; its dialects are Nyakyusa, Ngonde or Konde, Kukwe, Mwamba or Lungulu, and Selya, also called Salya or Seria, of Tanzania. In Malawi, Nyakusa and Kyangonde are spoken in the northern part of Karonga District, while Nkhonde is spoken in the centre of the district, including Karonga. Other names include Konde, Nkhonde, Mombe, Nyekyosa, Nyikyusa, Sochile, and Sokili. The language is closely related to Kyangonde and Swahili and is related to Yao, Bemba, Mambwe-lungu, and Chichewa. The traditional god is called *Kyala*. The sources do not describe current religious affiliation, historical scripts, or other spiritual practices.

title: "Gogo"
subtitle: "Tanzania"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]

## Overview

The Gogo, also known as Gongwe or Wagogo, are a Bantu ethnic group based in the Dodoma Region of central Tanzania. In 1992, their population was estimated at 1,300,000. Gogo is spoken throughout Dodoma Region and into the neighbouring district of Manyoni. The group has a history of hunting and gathering, agriculture, cattle keeping, caravan trade, famine, and changing relations with Nyamwezi colonists and other neighbouring peoples. Gogo society places importance on homestead groups, kinship, neighbourliness, ritual leadership, cattle, and age-group defence. The sources also document Gogo musicians and a collection of material objects including beadwork, leather goods, pottery, fibre baskets, wooden weapons, a drum, a cowbell, and smoking equipment.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document named Gogo textile or pattern traditions.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no Gogo textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe everyday clothing, footwear, or complete ceremonial dress. They do document several forms of beadwork and leather adornment: a man’s beadwork belt on a hide base; a leather belt covered with red, white, and black beads; another man’s beadwork belt on a hide base; beadwork and leather armlets; and a necklet made of black, blue, red, and white beads with a frontal leather pendant. A composite warrior’s headdress is described as an oval of hide from which part of an animal’s tail projects. The catalogue records do not identify the occasions on which these items were worn.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Gogo houses, building materials, roofs, settlement plans, or named architectural forms. They state that the homestead group was fundamental to Gogo society and that a strange traveller could be accompanied many miles by the young men of a homestead. They also record that people who died in unusual circumstances were sometimes thrown into the bush or the trunk of a baobab tree because such a person was believed to lack a homestead and could become an “evil spirit” associated with sorcerers or witches.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum records include a dark-coloured, sub-globular pottery bowl and a conical fibre basket with a small flat concave base. Recorded metal and wooden objects include an iron axe with a wooden handle, a sword with an aluminium hilt, black horn tip, plain iron blade, and a painted wooden sheath, and several clubs. One club is a herdsman’s club carved from wood, slightly curved at one end to a large ball; another is a brown wooden throwing club with a slightly carved flat head. The collection also includes a composite smoking water pipe with a straight pottery bowl, wooden stem, and gourd water-cooler with leather and iron, as well as a composite iron cowbell with an iron striker.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Documented body adornment includes beadwork and leather armlets, beadwork belts on hide bases, a leather belt covered with red, white, and black beads, and a necklet made from black, blue, red, and white beads with a leather frontal pendant. Other catalogue records describe copper-wire ear ornaments twisted into a hairpin shape with biconical bead tips, wooden ear-plugs, ear ornaments made of wood and brass, and a wooden stick carrying coiled and plaited wire pendants. Women’s girdles are recorded in two forms: coiled copper wire and white metal wire coiled around a central core. The sources do not explain the social, ritual, or life-cycle functions of these adornments.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not describe a named Gogo musical genre, song form, dance accompaniment, performance structure, or musical instrument vocabulary. They do record a wooden drum with a skin membrane among the museum objects. Gogo musicians named in the biographical material include Hukwe Zawose, Mzee Mchoya Malogo, John Mtangoo, Patrick Balisidya, and Benard Michael Paul Mnyang'anga, also known as Ben Pol. Mzee Mchoya Malogo is described as a musician and leader of the Nyati group from Nzali.

The sources also identify Gogo as a major language of the Anglican Church of Tanzania and state that the language is spoken by both Christians and Muslims. They do not connect particular songs, instruments, musical forms, or performance contexts to weddings, funerals, initiation, rainmaking, courts, or other ceremonies. The separate article titled “Gogo music” concerns go-go, a funk subgenre originating among African-American musicians in Washington, D.C., and does not describe Gogo people.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document named Gogo dances, theatrical traditions, dramatic genres, mask performances, or shadow-puppet traditions. They also do not describe dance contexts or distinguish ceremonial from entertainment performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not provide an annual festival calendar or name Gogo festivals. They do document ritual leaders as central figures in traditional society. These leaders controlled rainmaking and fertility, provided medicines against natural disasters or hazards, prevented overuse of certain resources, presided over circumcision and initiation ceremonies, provided supernatural protection for undertakings, and acted as arbitrators in homicide, witchcraft accusations, and serious assault. They were not to leave their “country” and were expected to be rich in cattle.

Defence against the Kisongo, Maasai, and Wahehe was organized through age groups of warriors. This organization was mainly used for local defence but could also be used for cattle raids. When an alarm sounded, able-bodied men were expected to take up arms and run towards the call. The sources do not describe the associated ceremonies, clothing, songs, dances, or ritual calendar.

Marriage involved an agreement concerning the number of livestock included in bridewealth. Bridewealth was conventionally given entirely in livestock, and the payment or return of brideprice formed a high proportion of court cases. Most marriages took place within a day’s walking distance. While most Wagogo had only one wife at a time, polygyny was not uncommon among older, well-established men, and a reasonably wealthy man could have two or three wives.

## Foodways

The sources describe the Gogo as having become agriculturalists with cattle by 1890, following an earlier tradition of hunting and gathering. They do not name staple grains, dishes, cooking methods, beverages, dietary rules, or ceremonial foods. They state that unreliable rainfall and drought repeatedly caused famine in Ugogo. Recorded famine years include 1881, 1885, 1888–89, 1894–95, and 1913–14.

During the First World War, requisitioning, drought, military demands, and the destruction or removal of food and livestock intensified hunger. When the rains stopped in November 1917, the central region experienced three years of *mutunya*, described as a “scramble for food” and the worst famine in recorded Gogo history. One estimate placed deaths in Dodoma district at 30,000, nearly one in every five people. In the Dodoma market, starving calves were offered for one shilling each, and many people fled the region.

Ugogo and Uzigua later experienced food shortages in 1919–21, 1925–6, 1928–30, 1932–5, 1937, and 1939. The sources state that the government encouraged the cultivation of drought-prone maize rather than drought-resistant millet and promoted the export of food and animals for military use. They do not describe named Gogo dishes or food preparation.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not document Gogo folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, praise poetry, or named oral-literary cycles. They do record historical accounts by European writers, including Edward Hore, Henry M. Stanley, and Emin Pasha, and preserve a long quotation from Stanley’s *In Darkest Africa* concerning travel through Ugogo.

The sources describe the movement of Wagogo clans and the development of new family and clan names, affiliations, customs, cultural practices, and ritual functions. They do not explain how these histories were transmitted or performed. No contemporary literary revival or preservation project is identified.

## Language & religion

Gogo is a Bantu language spoken by the Gogo people in Dodoma Region and neighbouring Manyoni. The language has three described dialects: Nyambwa, also called Cinyambwa or West Gogo, spoken west of Dodoma and in Manyoni; Nyaugogo, also called Cinyaugogo or Central Gogo, spoken around Dodoma; and Tumba, also called Citumba or East Gogo, spoken to the east. Gogo is grouped with Kagulu and has stated lexical similarities with Hehe, Sangu, Kimbu, and Nilamba.

Gogo is spoken by Christians and Muslims and is a major language of the Anglican Church of Tanzania. The Gogo people were influenced by Islam through nineteenth-century caravan trade, and more people learned Swahili. The sources also describe Roman Catholic and Protestant missionary activity in Ugogo during the colonial period. Traditional ritual leaders were associated with rainmaking, fertility, medicines, supernatural protection, initiation, and the arbitration of witchcraft accusations.

- Wikipedia, “Gogo language”: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gogo_language

title: "Fipa"
subtitle: "Tanzania"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]

## Overview

The Fipa, also known as the Wafipa, are a Bantu ethno-linguistic group based in the Sumbawanga Rural and Nkasi districts of Rukwa Region in southwestern Tanzania. They live on and around the Ufipa Plateau, between Lake Tanganyika and Lake Rukwa, and speak Fipa and Mambwe. Their population was estimated at 200,000 in 1992 and 195,000 in the 2002 census. Historically, the Fipa, Wanda, and Nyika occupied a largely treeless plateau connected to eastern, central, and Congolese Africa. Fipa culture includes highly organized chiefdoms, hereditary ironsmithing, cotton spinning and weaving, agriculture based on millet, round-hut settlements, spirit shrines, sacred pythons, and oral performance.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Cotton cloth** — Spinning and weaving locally grown cotton was universal and was always performed by men. The cloth was open, heavy, strong, and durable, with a white ground, a black-striped border, and dimensions of five by six feet. It was sufficient for the toga-like dress worn by men and women.

**Black-and-white striped cloth** — In the settlements, everyone wore durable cotton cloth of black and white stripes measuring six by five feet. The source describes this cloth as a practical garment rather than as a named ceremonial textile.

**Loom weaving** — The museum catalogue includes two shed sticks for a loom made of wood. The Fipa historical account states that the local weaving industry later declined as trade patterns changed.

**Reed mats** — Women made reed mats for sleeping and for filtering beer. The mats were also placed on beds made from cow hide stretched over wooden frames.

No other documented Fipa pattern-bearing textile traditions are covered by the sources used.

### Clothing & dress

The Fipa wore durable cotton cloth of black and white stripes. Locally grown cotton was spun and woven by men, producing a strong, heavy, open cloth with a black-striped border. The cloth measured approximately five by six feet or six by five feet in the descriptions and served as toga-like dress for both men and women. The sources do not name separate everyday and ceremonial garments, head coverings, footwear, or distinctive jewelry. They state that men and women wore this cloth and that reed mats were used on beds and for filtering beer.

### Architecture

The Wafipa lived in concentrated, widely spaced settlements of twenty to thirty round huts. The huts stood no more than a few yards apart, housed three to five people each, and had two surrounding corridor walls for small livestock. An inner room was used for eating and sleeping. Men made beds from a single cow hide, or cow-hide strips, stretched over a wooden frame, with a reed mat placed on top before sleeping. Villages normally contained 100 people; settlements of 300–400 people were large and uncommon. During the harvest, people working distant fields built round huts for sleeping and shelter. The sources do not describe roof forms, architectural decoration, or named urban building types.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Ironworking was a hereditary specialization. Iron smelting and forging were closely connected with technical knowledge, magic, and particular ingredients obtained from doctors and sorcerers. A special bag of magical ingredients was passed from father to son. The Twa chiefs, members of the chief’s family, and all women were forbidden to visit a kiln or forge; other visitors had to acknowledge the smith’s authority by making a payment. The women made pottery using the coil method. Everyday objects described in the sources include hoes, cow-hide beds, reed mats, and wooden loom parts. The museum catalogue records iron arrow-heads, cane-and-metal arrows, a wooden bow with a hide string, a leather pouch with a belt, and a reed, wax, leaf, and rattan whistle.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources do not document Fipa jewelry traditions, tattoos, henna, hair ornaments, or named forms of bodily adornment. They state that unmarried girls traditionally extended their labia minora by constant manipulation, which was thought to enhance sexual attractiveness and favor giving birth.

## Music & performance

The sources do not name Fipa musical instruments, song genres, or formal musical ensembles. They do describe vocal and ritual performance in several contexts. During the death of a woman in childbirth, women wept and chanted inside the hut containing the corpse while men sat quietly outside. Dances were forbidden during an epidemic, children stopped playing noisy games, and water-pots were covered. The Fipa language bibliography includes a work titled *There was a certain man: Spoken art of the Fipa*, indicating a documented spoken-art tradition, but the sources used here do not describe its genres or performance structure. The museum catalogue includes a whistle made of reed, wax, leaf, and rattan, but does not identify its cultural or musical use.

## Dance & theatre

The sources do not name a Fipa dance, theatre form, dramatic tradition, mask performance, or puppet tradition. They state that dances were forbidden during an epidemic and that children ceased playing noisy games. No further information about dance occasions, choreography, performers, or entertainment contexts is provided.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not describe an annual Fipa festival calendar or provide dates for seasonal festivals. They do document life-cycle practices and ritual responses to illness, death, and unusual birth circumstances. The Fipa had no initiation ceremony for either sex apart from the extraction of two or four lower incisors before or after puberty. At the birth of a girl, her father brought firewood on his head; when a boy was born, he carried a bow and arrow in his right hand. If childbirth was difficult, midwives asked the name of the unborn child’s father because unconfessed adultery was thought capable of causing death in childbirth.

After death, a meeting of kin decided inheritance, and a widow was assigned to the heir if she was willing. If a woman died in childbirth, the unborn child was cut from the belly and placed on the dead mother’s back inside the grave. The women wept and chanted inside the hut, while men sat outside; after burial, the hut was totally destroyed.

Twins were considered divinities with special powers over rain and crops. They could also cause epidemics. They were publicly acclaimed, carried around the village on a tray, and honored through communal sacrifices at the new moon. During harvest time or epidemics, their parents erected an altar outside their hut, where sacrifices were offered.

## Foodways

Millet was the main crop. It was made into dry porridge and usually eaten with the fingers together with beans. The Fipa planted their principal crops on earth-covered compost piles of vegetation, often roughly a mile or more from a settlement. During harvest, people working in the fields built round huts for shelter and sleeping. Women drew water, cooked, winnowed and pounded grain, while men made and spread compost piles and threshed millet. Threshing was often carried out cooperatively by groups of kinsmen and neighbors.

The sources mention beer indirectly through the use of reed mats for filtering it, but do not name a beer, give a recipe, or describe brewing. Fishing was considered important around Lake Rukwa, Lake Tanganyika, and the surrounding rivers, although the sources do not provide named fish dishes or cooking methods. The sources do not describe dietary rules, tea or coffee traditions, ceremonial meals, or named dishes beyond millet porridge and beans.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Fipa language bibliography records *There was a certain man: Spoken art of the Fipa*, published by Roy G. Willis in 1978. The sources do not provide the text, names of particular tales, genres, proverbs, riddles, epics, or performance contexts. Oral historical material is also represented in accounts of chiefs, dynasties, and prophets. Prophet Kaswa was said to have prophesied the coming of Europeans, warning that terrible strangers would bring war and that the people would lose their country. The historical account also preserves statements attributed to Paul Reichard and H. H. Johnston, but it does not identify a broader Fipa literary canon or contemporary preservation program.

## Language & religion

Fipa is a Bantu language of Tanzania spoken on the Ufipa Plateau in Rukwa Region between Lake Tanganyika and Lake Rukwa. The ethnic group is larger than the group of Fipa-language speakers. On the Tanzanian side, people who speak Mambwe-Lungu may identify as Fipa and consider their language a dialect of Fipa. Lungu and Mambwe are also spoken in Zambia. The sources name the dialects Milanzi, also called IchiSukuuma, Kwa, also called Ichikwa, and Nkansi; they also list South Fipa, Kandaasi, Siiwa, Nkwaamba, Kwaafi, Ntile, and Peemba in the linguistic classification.

The Fipa recognized Umweele as the supreme god and creator, but there was no cult to Umweele. Worship also concerned Katai, localized spirits associated with hills, lakes, trees, rocks, and groves, and ancestral spirits thought to inhabit the thresholds of descendants’ huts. Sacred pythons represented the spirits of places and received offerings of millet porridge and meat. Hereditary priests conducted worship. Illness was attributed to sorcery, territorial or ancestral spirits, divinities, demons, sorcerers, or witches, and responses included sacrifices, ritual burning, and medicines.

## At a glance
| | |
|---|---|
| Who | The Fipa, also known as the Wafipa, are a Bantu ethno-linguistic group. |
| Where | The Ufipa Plateau in southwestern Tanzania, between Lake Tanganyika and Lake Rukwa. |
| How many | About 200,000 people in 1992 and 195,000 in the 2002 census. |
| Language | Fipa and Mambwe. |
| Religion | Umweele was the supreme creator; people also honored spirits, ancestors, sacred pythons, and other divinities. |
| Known for | Organized chiefdoms · Hereditary ironsmithing · Cotton spinning and weaving · Round-hut settlements · Spirit shrines and sacred pythons |

## Overview

The Fipa live on and around the Ufipa Plateau in southwestern Tanzania. Their culture includes organized chiefdoms, farming, cotton cloth, round-hut settlements, and hereditary ironworking. Millet was the main crop, and people also fished around nearby lakes and rivers. Religious life included spirit shrines, ancestral spirits, sacred pythons, and ritual specialists.

## Material culture

Fipa material culture centers on strong cotton cloth, round huts, ironworking, pottery, reed mats, and simple farming and hunting tools.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Men spun and wove strong cotton cloth, while women made reed mats.

- **Cotton cloth** — Men spun and wove locally grown cotton into heavy, strong, open cloth with a white ground and black-striped border.
- **Black-and-white striped cloth** — People wore durable cotton cloth with black and white stripes, usually measuring about six by five feet.
- **Loom weaving** — Wooden shed sticks were used for loom weaving, although the local weaving industry later declined.
- **Reed mats** — Women made reed mats for sleeping and for filtering beer.

### Clothing & dress

Men and women wore a large, durable cotton cloth as toga-like dress.

- **Toga-like cotton dress** — Men and women wore strong, heavy cotton cloth measuring about five by six feet or six by five feet.

### Architecture

Fipa settlements had groups of round huts with rooms and animal corridors.

- **Round-hut settlement** — Settlements had twenty to thirty round huts, usually spaced a few yards apart.
- **Livestock corridors** — Two corridor walls around each hut made space for small livestock.
- **Cow-hide bed** — Men made beds from cow hide or cow-hide strips stretched over wooden frames, with a reed mat on top.
- **Harvest hut** — People working far from home built round huts for sleeping and shelter during harvest.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Hereditary ironworkers made tools and weapons, while women made coil-built pottery.

- **Hereditary ironworking** — Iron smelting and forging passed through families and involved technical knowledge, magic, and special ingredients.
- **Coil-built pottery** — Women made pottery using the coil method.
- **Iron arrow-heads** — The museum catalogue records iron arrow-heads among Fipa objects.
- **Bow and arrows** — The catalogue includes a wooden bow with a hide string and cane-and-metal arrows.
- **Whistle** — A whistle was made from reed, wax, leaf, and rattan.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources do not describe jewelry, tattoos, or named decorative body arts.

- **Labial extension** — Unmarried girls traditionally extended their labia minora by constant manipulation, which was thought to increase sexual attractiveness and help with childbirth.

## Music & performance

Fipa vocal and ritual performance included chanting, while the sources do not name formal music genres.

- **Women’s death chant** — When a woman died in childbirth, women wept and chanted inside the hut while men sat outside.
- **Spoken art** — A 1978 work titled There was a certain man: Spoken art of the Fipa records a spoken-art tradition.
- **Reed whistle** — The sources list a reed, wax, leaf, and rattan whistle but do not explain its use.

## Dance & theatre

The sources do not name Fipa dance or theatre forms.

- **Epidemic dance ban** — Dances were forbidden during an epidemic, and children stopped playing noisy games.

## Festivals & rituals

Fipa ritual life focused on birth, death, twins, illness, and sacred powers.

- **Tooth extraction** — The Fipa had no initiation ceremony for either sex apart from removing two or four lower incisors before or after puberty.
- **Birth signs** — At a girl’s birth her father carried firewood on his head, while at a boy’s birth he carried a bow and arrow in his right hand.
- **Childbirth ritual** — If childbirth was difficult, midwives asked the unborn child’s father’s name because hidden adultery was thought able to cause death.
- **Twin acclamation** — Twins were treated as divinities, carried around the village on a tray, and honored with communal sacrifices at the new moon.
- **Funeral destruction** — After a woman died in childbirth, the unborn child was placed on her back in the grave and the hut was destroyed after burial.

## Foodways

Millet porridge and beans formed the main food, supported by farming, fishing, and communal threshing.

- **Millet porridge** — Millet was made into dry porridge and usually eaten with the fingers.
- **Beans** — Beans were commonly eaten with millet porridge.
- **Compost-pile farming** — Main crops were planted on earth-covered piles of vegetation, often far from the settlement.
- **Communal threshing** — Groups of relatives and neighbors often threshed millet together.
- **Lake and river fishing** — Fishing was important around Lake Rukwa, Lake Tanganyika, and nearby rivers.

## Oral tradition & literature

Fipa oral tradition includes spoken art, histories of chiefs, and prophetic accounts.

- **Spoken art of the Fipa** — Roy G. Willis recorded the work There was a certain man: Spoken art of the Fipa in 1978.
- **Prophecy of Kaswa** — Prophet Kaswa was said to have warned that terrible strangers would bring war and take the people’s country.
- **Chief and dynasty histories** — Oral historical material preserved accounts of chiefs, dynasties, and prophets.

## Language & religion

Fipa religious life joined a supreme creator with local spirits, ancestors, sacred pythons, and hereditary priests.

- **Fipa language** (*Fipa*) — Fipa is a Bantu language spoken on the Ufipa Plateau in Rukwa Region.
- **Mambwe-Lungu speech** (*Mambwe-Lungu*) — Some people who speak Mambwe-Lungu identify as Fipa and consider it a dialect of Fipa.
- **Supreme creator** (*Umweele*) — Umweele was recognized as the supreme god and creator, but had no cult.
- **Local spirits** (*Katai*) — Katai were localized spirits linked with hills, lakes, trees, rocks, and groves.
- **Sacred pythons** — Sacred pythons represented place spirits and received offerings of millet porridge and meat.

## Glossary

- *Fipa* — The Fipa language and people
- *Wafipa* — Another name for the Fipa
- *Mambwe* — A language spoken by some Fipa
- *Mambwe-Lungu* — Speech some Fipa consider a Fipa dialect
- *Kwa* — A Fipa dialect
- *Umweele* — Supreme god and creator
- *Katai* — Localized spirits of places
- *Ufipa Plateau* — The Fipa homeland plateau

## Overview

The Rangi, also called *Valangi* in their own language and *Warangi* in Swahili, are a Bantu-speaking ethnic group of mixed Bantu and Cushitic heritage in the Dodoma Region of central Tanzania. In 2022, their population was estimated at 880,000. The Rangi use *Kilangi* as the endonym for their language, while *Kirangi* is the common Swahili exonym. Rangi history includes differing accounts of their emergence as a distinct ethnic group, ranging from approximately 300 AD to around 1500–1700. Their culture reflects both Cushitic and Bantu heritage and historical interaction with surrounding peoples.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document Rangi textile or pattern traditions.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not document everyday or ceremonial clothing, head coverings, belts, footwear, or other forms of Rangi dress.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Rangi house forms, roofs, decoration, or named building types. The source list includes “Notes on Irangi Houses” by R.F. Gray, but provides no architectural details from that work.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records several objects associated with the Rangi. These include wooden spears with iron points, arrows made of wood and iron, poisoned arrows made of wood, sinew, and feathers, a poisoned arrow with a wooden point and feathers, and a bill-hook made of iron with a wooden handle. The catalogue also records a milking pail with a handle carved from one piece of wood, and a bugle made from a horn. The sources do not describe ceramics or the cultural uses of these objects.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not document Rangi jewelry, body adornment, tattoos, henna, hair practices, or ritual ornaments.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not document Rangi musical genres, named instruments, songs, or performance contexts. The museum catalogue records a bugle made from a horn, but gives no information about its musical use or significance.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document Rangi dances, theatre, dramatic traditions, mask performances, or other forms of staged entertainment.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources mention a Rangi circumcision ceremony titled “Blessing a New Grove” and a Wasi/Rangi ceremony titled “Blessing the Year,” but provide no descriptions of their proceedings, dates, seasons, participants, or ritual meanings. The sources do not document an annual festival calendar, weddings, funerals, birth rites, or other life-cycle ceremonies.

## Foodways

The sources used do not document Rangi staple foods, cooking methods, named dishes, ceremonial foods, beverages, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not document Rangi folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles, storytelling practices, or literary preservation efforts. The references include studies of Rangi culture, progress, natural history, social processes, and ecology, but the supplied material does not summarize their oral-literary content.

## Language & religion

Rangi or Langi is a Bantu language spoken by the Rangi people of Kondoa District in the Dodoma Region of central Tanzania. Its native name is *Kɨlaangi*, while *Kirangi* is the dominant Swahili form and *Kilaangi* is used as a self-referent term. Estimates of the number of Rangi-speakers range from 270,000 to 410,000. Two main varieties are identified: the Rangi Highlands variety, known in Swahili as *Irangi ya Juu*, and the Lowlands variety, *Irangi ya Chini*. They are mutually intelligible. Rangi has 19 noun classes and is written in the Latin alphabet with the letters ɨ and ʉ, alongside ch, ng', ny, and sh. The sources used do not document Rangi religious beliefs or practices.

## Overview

The Mambwe are an ethnic group from Mbala and Senga Hill district of Northeastern Zambia and Kalambo District of Rukwa Region, Tanzania. In 1987, the Mambwe population in Tanzania was estimated to number 63,000; the number in Zambia had not been independently estimated, although the combined number of Mambwe and Lungu people in Zambia was estimated at 262,800 in 1993. The Mambwe speak Mambwe, also called *Cimambwe*, a Bantu language and a dialect of Mambwe-Lungu. Mambwe-Lungu is also spoken in Rukwa region and southern Sumbawanga town in Tanzania, as well as in Mankato, Mpulungu and Senga district of Zambia. The sources document Mambwe political history, clans, music, ceremony, religious practices and museum-held objects.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document a Mambwe textile or pattern-bearing textile tradition.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name an incised geometrical ornament on a wooden belt and an incised leaf pattern on a gourd vessel, but do not identify these as Mambwe motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe everyday or ceremonial Mambwe clothing, head coverings, footwear or dress distinctions. They mention bark cloth in which babies were carried during a conflict with the Bemba, but provide no broader account of clothing practice. A museum catalogue records a wooden belt with incised geometrical ornament, without identifying its use in dress.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Mambwe houses, villages, roofs or other forms of vernacular architecture. They state that a shrine or temple called *kavua* was erected in each village and dedicated to the ancestors of local chiefs.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Museum catalogue records include an iron axe with a wooden handle, a wooden European machete with iron, an iron hoe with a wooden handle, a wooden stool with three legs, a stool with four legs cut from solid wood, a stool made of wood, a wooden head-rest, a wooden spatulate artefact possibly used as a pottery beater, a cane basket, three baskets made of coiled grass, and a gourd vessel ornamented with an incised leaf pattern. The sources do not state which objects are specifically associated with Mambwe manufacture or use.

### Jewelry & body adornment

A museum catalogue records an armlet made of ivory and repaired in two places with local vegetal fibre, and a string of 28 barrel-shaped beads made of agate (?). The sources do not describe their meanings, occasions of use, or broader Mambwe body-adornment practices.

## Music & performance

The Mambwe have a traditional music piece consisting of a dance called *Nsimba* and musical instruments called *Vingwengwe*. The sources also name Kalambo hit parade, Solo Kalenge and Esther Namunga as artists who perform Mambwe Lungu traditional music. No further information is provided about the construction of the instruments, the musical forms, the repertory, or the contexts in which performances take place.

The sources used do not document additional Mambwe song genres, instrumental classifications, performance institutions or named musical ceremonies. They state that traditional dances and music form part of the annual harvest ceremony described under Festivals & rituals.

## Dance & theatre

*Nsimba* is identified as a traditional Mambwe dance. Traditional dances and music are also included in the ceremony held to celebrate a successful harvest and pray for rains for the next farming season. The sources do not describe the movements, performers, costumes or distinction between ceremonial and entertainment dancing. They do not document Mambwe theatre, masked performance, puppetry or dramatic traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

The Mambwe and the Lungu of Tafuna hold an annual traditional ceremony to celebrate a successful harvest and pray for rains for the next farming season. It takes place every last Saturday of June on the shores of lake Chila in Mbala. During the ceremony, the wives of the Chiefs present samples of food grown in their chiefdoms. The Chiefs bless the food and give thanks to the ancestral spirits for a successful harvest. The Chiefs then taste the food, after which the subjects are free to eat. The ceremony also includes traditional dances and music.

Traditional Mambwe religion recognizes a supreme god called *Leza*, who created the earth and everything on it but is described as remote from human affairs and not worshiped. Worship is directed to spirits of chiefly ancestors, called *imipasi yamwene yafwe*. Natural objects such as hills, caves, large rocks and permanent pools of water are divinized and referred to as *mayao* or *maleza*. These land shrines are associated with ancestral spirits called *imipasi* and are visited once a year in normal times and when crops have been harvested. Part of each crop is left at the shrine and the ancestral spirits are thanked. The sources also state that chiefs and their people appeal to the shrines during drought, crop failure, locust invasion, outbreaks of disease and invasion of their country.

The sources used do not document Mambwe birth, initiation, marriage or funeral rites.

## Foodways

The sources state that, during the annual harvest ceremony, the wives of the Chiefs present samples of food grown in their chiefdoms. The Chiefs taste the food before the subjects are free to eat, and part of each crop is left at a shrine during thanksgiving to the ancestral spirits. The sources do not name particular crops, dishes, grains, cooking methods or beverages.

In the account of conflict with the Bemba, the Mambwe are described as having been reduced to starvation and forced to live on rats, dogs and bark cloth in which babies were carried. This is presented as an episode of wartime deprivation, not as a description of ordinary foodways. The sources used do not document dietary rules, tea or coffee traditions, or named ceremonial dishes.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources describe accounts of Mambwe origins involving the common people and the Chiefs. The ruling line is said to have been founded by Changala, who came from Kola and was a Mulua. Changala is said to have settled in the south of Mambwe country under the authority of Chindo, head of the Simwinga clan. The account explains the relationship between the commoner title Chindo and the senior royal title Nsokolo, and traces the royal line through Mwimbe and Nsokolo wa Chisenga.

Mambwe clan names include Sichula, Sichilima, Simpemba, Simwinga and Simpasa, among many others. A quotation attributed to William Watson describes the Mambwe as suspicious of strangers, hardy, resilient and attached to their independence. The sources also list Mambwe Proverbs by A. Werner and A. N. Tucker among relevant literature. They do not document a named epic, riddle tradition, contemporary literary revival or preservation project.

## Language & religion

The Mambwe speak Mambwe, also called *Cimambwe*, a Bantu language and a dialect of Mambwe-Lungu. The Mambwe and Lungu peoples living at the southern end of Lake Tanganyika in Tanzania and Zambia speak a common language with minor dialectical differences. Mambwe-Lungu is also spoken by people of Rukwa region and southern Sumbawanga town in Tanzania, and in Mankato, Mpulungu and Senga district of Zambia. It has close affinities with languages spoken by Pimbwe, Rungwa and Namwanga. The sources do not describe a historical script.

Most Mambwe people today are Christian, including many Jehovah Witnesses or Catholics. Traditional Mambwe religion recognizes Leza as the creator, while worship is directed toward chiefly ancestral spirits. Shrines called kavua were erected in villages for local chiefly ancestors, and natural places called mayao or maleza were associated with imipasi.

- [Mambwe people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mambwe_people)
- [Mambwe language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mambwe_language)

The sources do not document a Mambwe textile tradition.

- **Incised leaf pattern** — A gourd vessel has an incised leaf pattern, but the sources do not identify it as a Mambwe motif.

### Clothing & dress

The sources do not describe everyday or ceremonial Mambwe clothing.

- **Baby-carrying bark cloth** — Bark cloth was used to carry babies during a conflict with the Bemba.
- **Wooden belt** — A museum catalogue records a wooden belt with incised geometric ornament, but does not identify its use in dress.

### Architecture

The sources do not describe Mambwe houses or villages, but they mention village shrines.

- **Village shrine or temple** (*kavua*) — A kavua was erected in each village and dedicated to the ancestors of local chiefs.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Museum records list tools, furniture, baskets and vessels, without linking them specifically to Mambwe manufacture or use.

- **Iron axe** — A museum catalogue records an iron axe with a wooden handle.
- **Iron hoe** — A museum catalogue records an iron hoe with a wooden handle.
- **Three-legged stool** — A museum catalogue records a wooden stool with three legs.
- **Coiled-grass baskets** — A museum catalogue records three baskets made of coiled grass.
- **Gourd vessel** — A museum catalogue records a gourd vessel with an incised leaf pattern.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources record two adornments but do not explain their meanings or use.

- **Ivory armlet** — A museum catalogue records an ivory armlet repaired in two places with local vegetal fibre.
- **Agate bead string** — A museum catalogue records a string of 28 barrel-shaped beads made of agate, with some uncertainty.

## Music & performance

Mambwe traditional music includes the Nsimba dance and Vingwengwe instruments.

- **Nsimba** — Nsimba is a traditional Mambwe dance and part of a traditional music piece.
- **Vingwengwe instruments** (*Vingwengwe*) — Vingwengwe are musical instruments used in traditional Mambwe music.
- **Kalambo hit parade** — Kalambo hit parade is named as an artist performing Mambwe Lungu traditional music.
- **Solo Kalenge** — Solo Kalenge is named as an artist performing Mambwe Lungu traditional music.
- **Esther Namunga** — Esther Namunga is named as an artist performing Mambwe Lungu traditional music.

## Dance & theatre

Traditional dance appears in both Mambwe music and the annual harvest ceremony.

- **Nsimba dance** (*Nsimba*) — Nsimba is identified as a traditional Mambwe dance.
- **Harvest dances** — Traditional dances are performed during the ceremony celebrating a successful harvest and praying for rain.

## Festivals & rituals

The main named ceremony celebrates the harvest, gives thanks to ancestors and asks for rain.

- **Annual harvest ceremony** — The Mambwe and Lungu of Tafuna hold this ceremony every last Saturday of June on the shores of Lake Chila.
- **Chiefs’ food blessing** — Chiefs bless food samples presented by their wives, give thanks to ancestral spirits, taste the food and then allow people to eat.
- **Shrine thanksgiving** — People leave part of each crop at a shrine and thank the ancestral spirits after the harvest.
- **Appeal during hardship** — Chiefs and their people appeal to shrines during drought, crop failure, locust invasions, disease and invasion.
- **Land shrines** (*mayao; maleza*) — Hills, caves, large rocks and permanent pools of water are treated as sacred places associated with ancestral spirits.

## Foodways

The sources mention harvest food offerings and wartime starvation, but do not name ordinary dishes or crops.

- **Chiefdom food samples** — At the annual harvest ceremony, chiefs’ wives present samples of food grown in their chiefdoms.
- **Harvest thanksgiving food** — Part of each crop is left at a shrine during thanks to the ancestral spirits.
- **Wartime starvation foods** — During conflict with the Bemba, some Mambwe were forced to live on rats, dogs and baby-carrying bark cloth.

## Oral tradition & literature

Mambwe origin accounts trace the ruling line from Changala through Mwimbe and Nsokolo.

- **Changala** — Changala is said to have come from Kola, been a Mulua, and founded the ruling line.
- **Chindo** — Chindo was the head of the Simwinga clan and held a commoner title.

- **Mambwe Proverbs** — Mambwe Proverbs by A. Werner and A. N. Tucker is listed among the relevant literature.

## Language & religion

Mambwe is a Bantu language, while traditional religion centers on Leza, chiefly ancestors and sacred natural places.

- **Mambwe language** (*Cimambwe*) — Mambwe, also called Cimambwe, is a Bantu language and a dialect of Mambwe-Lungu.
- **Supreme creator** (*Leza*) — Leza created the earth and everything on it but is described as remote and not worshiped.
- **Chiefly ancestral spirits** (*imipasi yamwene yafwe*) — Worship is directed toward the spirits of chiefly ancestors.
- **Ancestral spirits** (*imipasi*) — Imipasi are ancestral spirits associated with land shrines.
- **Village ancestor shrines** (*kavua*) — Kavua shrines were erected in villages for local chiefly ancestors.

title: "Kaguru"
subtitle: "Tanzania"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"

## Overview

The Kaguru, also known as Kagulu, Megi, Wetumba, Solwa and Mangaheri, are a Bantu ethnic group indigenous to Gairo District, Mvomero District and Kilosa District in Tanzania’s Morogoro Region. They are bordered by the Ngulu, Luguru, Gogo and Sagara peoples. Their homeland, Ukagura, includes the Ukaguru Mountains, plateau and lowlands, and lies around 200 miles west of the Saadani and Bagamoyo seaports. The population was predicted to be 217,000 in 1987, with most Kaguru residing in Gairo District and engaging especially in small-scale agriculture. Their language is Kaguru, also called Kagulu, a Bantu language closely related to Gogo and Zaramo.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Glass bead aprons** — British Museum catalogue records describe glass bead aprons strung on fibre. One has a black and white bead girdle and a coloured triangular pattern on a white background; another has a triangular pattern of red and black.

**Beadwork waist bands** — A British Museum record describes a beadwork waist band made with white, pink, red, black and green beads and vegetable fibre.

**Glass bead head dresses** — The catalogue records several glass bead head dresses strung on fibre. Their designs include rectangular-pattern bands, black, red and white bands, and bead streamers ending in cowrie shells or large red beads.

**Glass bead head bands** — A glass bead head band strung on fibre is recorded with a pattern in blue, white and pink.

**Glass bead arm bands** — The recorded armbands are strung on fibre and use bands and edging in combinations of black, red, white, green and pink.

**Motif vocabulary.** Triangular pattern, rectangular pattern, bands, coloured pattern.

### Clothing & dress

Kaguru clothing and adornment are mentioned in the description of missionary condemnation of local customs, but the sources do not provide a full account of everyday garments, footwear or named ceremonial dress. They state that women wore skirts all the time, while men wore a toga-like garment even when showering, taking care not to appear naked. The museum records show glass bead aprons, bead girdles, waist bands, head dresses, head bands and arm bands. One head dress included a bead streamer ending in cowrie shells, while another ended in large red beads. The sources do not identify vernacular names for these garments or distinguish their use by age, status or ceremony.

### Architecture

Ukagura had big, fortified settlements in the highland during Captain Bauer’s era. The steep terrain contained valleys that were useful to people escaping raids, and the highland settlements provided defensive positions. A British Museum record shows a wooden model of a native hut with mud plaster on the roof. The sources do not explain the complete house plan, the construction of settlement compounds, or the decoration of buildings.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources mention iron smelting in Ukagura and the intense need for charcoal that accompanied the industry. The British Museum catalogue records winnowing trays made of basketry or plaited vegetable fibre, with cane or wooden rims, as well as a wooden spoon with burnt and incised ornamentation. It also records a wooden stick with a head carved to represent an antelope. No ceramics, metal objects or named Kaguru forms are described in the supplied sources.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Beads are prominent in the museum records. They appear in aprons, girdles, waist bands, head dresses, head bands and arm bands, using glass beads in combinations of black, white, red, green, pink and blue. Head-dress streamers are recorded with cowrie shells or large red beads. The Wikipedia source also mentions native jewelry, red ocher used for beauty products, haircuts and ear-piercing among practices condemned by Christian missionaries. It does not give names for jewelry forms or describe tattoos, henna or particular hairstyles.

## Music & performance

The Wikipedia source names Kaguru songs and music among the customs condemned by Christian missionaries. It also describes singing and dancing during female initiation. Women inside the initiation house sang obscene songs, laughed loudly at jokes and danced; after a night of singing and dancing, the initiate was taken into the nearby bush. A British Museum catalogue record identifies a musical instrument comprising a flat wood board, a bowed wood stick and a split cane striker or beater. The sources do not provide a Kaguru name for this instrument, explain its musical technique, or identify song genres, performance ensembles or occasions such as weddings and funerals.

## Dance & theatre

Dancing is described in connection with female initiation. Women in the initiation house danced after singing and joking, and the sources present this as part of the seclusion and preparation of a girl for suitors and marriage. Dancing is also listed among the Kaguru customs opposed by Christian missionaries. The sources do not name a Kaguru dance, theatrical form, masked performance or dramatic tradition.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not describe an annual festival calendar or named seasonal festivals. They do describe rituals connected with matrilineal clans, land and life-cycle transitions. Kaguru society consisted of about one hundred matrilineal clans, each associated with one or more pieces of land. Each year, a clan organized rituals intended to revitalize its land.

Male initiation was performed at puberty by men in a bush camp outside the settlement. The initiate remained there until he recovered, and the rite was understood as the death of childhood and rebirth as an adult. Female initiation took place in the seclusion of a house when a girl was around 14 years of age. Seclusion could last weeks to months, and the girl was expected to become beautiful, fat and pale. The sources also describe marriage, bridewealth, brideservice, divorce, birth and death. Most marriages were not considered complete until children were born. Following death, the spirit was believed to enter an alternative dimension called “ghostland,” where ghosts lived in villages. The graves of prominent ancestral ghosts received wheat flour and the blood of sacrificial animals.

## Foodways

The sources associate Kaguru subsistence with small-scale agriculture, livestock and relations of mutual support. In the cool, rainy highlands, people regularly produced vegetables, some rice, millet and plantains, while the source specifically states that the highlands contained no maize. The plateau had less rain, more warmth, scrubland and forest, and the largest livestock holdings were generally kept there. The lowlands had the least dependable agricultural conditions and were vulnerable to cattle diseases.

Food could also be borrowed or shared through social relationships. During lean times, people might share harvests, borrow livestock or receive permission to resettle. The sources do not name prepared dishes, cooking methods, beverages, dietary rules or ceremonial foods. They mention brewing as a possible source of income for an older childless woman, but do not describe the beverage.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do not describe Kaguru folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles or a named literary tradition. They do mention Kaguru songs and music, as well as obscene songs sung during female initiation. The sources also state that ancestral ghosts wished to be remembered, hear their names called out and receive sacrifices. No contemporary literary revival or preservation project is identified.

## Language & religion

Kaguru, also called Kagulu, is a Bantu language of the Morogoro and Dodoma regions of Tanzania. It is closely related to Gogo and Zaramo but is not intelligible with other languages. The Kaguru are described as matrilineal, tracing descent and inheritance through the female line. Christian missionaries established headquarters among the Kaguru and attempted to separate Christian recruits from pagans, but in most cases they failed to overcome opposition.

Earlier Kaguru religious practice included ancestral propitiation, rainstones and magical medicines. Kaguru communities understood the dead, the living and generations still to be born as part of one community. Ghosts could become angry, disturbed or confused, and rites were held to placate, cool or quiet them. Wheat flour and the blood of sacrificial animals were poured on the graves of prominent ancestral ghosts.

## Sources & further reading

- “Kaguru people,” Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaguru_people
- “Kaguru language,” Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaguru_language
- British Museum catalogue records for the model building, glass bead aprons, beadwork waist band, glass bead head dresses, head band, arm bands, winnowing trays, wooden spoon, carved stick and musical instrument described in the supplied source material.

## Overview

The Bondei, also known as *Wabondei*, are a Bantu ethnic group based in Muheza District and Pangani District in eastern Tanga Region, Tanzania. Most Bondei reside in Pangani District, while others live in eastern Muheza District. Their population is roughly 100,000. They speak Kibondei, a Northeast Coast Bantu language closely related to Shambala, and are culturally related to the Shambaa and Zigua. The name “Bondei” was given by rulers of the Kilindi dynasty after the Shambaa Kingdom’s conquest of the area. It referred to people living in the valley between the Lwengera Valley and the sea east of the Usambaras. Bondei history is also marked by resistance to Shambaa and Kilindi rule, population movement, tribute systems, slave raiding, and the Kiva insurrection of 1869.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Moa mats** — The museum catalogue records mats associated with Moa. They include grass or fibre mats with rounded corners and a slight fringe. One mat is black and white in broad stripes with small interwoven patterns of lozenges and zigzags. Other examples are made from fine strips of palm leaf plaited together, straw coloured with bands of interwoven dark brown patterns.

**Grass-plaited mats** — A catalogue description identifies a grass-plaited mat consisting of narrow strips sewn together, with black and white patterns and a marginal fringe. Another mat is woven from grass with geometric designs in black and white.

**Moa mat pattern samples** — The museum holds a group of seventeen samples of grass-weaving patterns dyed brown, red and green for Moa mats, as well as a group of three samples of grass-weaving patterns in black and white.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name lozenges, zigzags, stripes, bands, geometric designs, and interwoven patterns.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not cover Bondei everyday clothing, ceremonial dress, head coverings, belts, footwear, or gender-specific dress.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Bondei houses, roofs, settlements, building materials, architectural decoration, or named building types.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records smoking pipes with pipe-bowls made of black pottery. One smoking pipe has a wooden stem. The collection also includes wooden spoons, including one with an oval bowl, and a wooden cup with incised geometric decoration. A stringed musical instrument similar to a lute is made of wood and has a skin membrane and four strings tuned by pegs. The sources do not describe Bondei metalwork, tools, cooking vessels, gourd containers, or other household goods.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not cover Bondei jewelry, body adornment, tattoos, henna, hairstyles, ritual ornaments, or forms of bodily decoration.

## Music & performance

The museum catalogue records a stringed musical instrument similar to a lute. It is made of wood, has a skin membrane, and has four strings tuned by pegs. The sources do not give a vernacular name for the instrument, describe its musical scale, or identify its repertoire.

The sources used do not document Bondei song genres, instrumental ensembles, performance contexts, dance accompaniment, court music, religious music, wedding music, funeral music, or public entertainment. They also do not describe how the recorded instrument was played or who played it.

The historical material does, however, identify named political movements and events involving Bondei people. The Kiva insurrection of 1869 was described as the fourth and most significant popular movement in the breakdown of the Shambaa state. This is historical evidence concerning Bondei resistance, not a description of a musical performance tradition.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover Bondei dances, theatrical traditions, masquerades, shadow puppetry, dramatic genres, ceremonial movement, or entertainment performances.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not describe an annual Bondei festival calendar, seasonal festivals, harvest ceremonies, initiation rites, weddings, funerals, birth rituals, religious observances, or other life-cycle ceremonies.

The historical sources do describe political and social institutions. Under Shambaa rule, subjects were required to pay tribute in food and livestock to local chiefs, who forwarded part of it to the king. In 1853, missionary explorer Erhardt observed that Kilindi chiefs could not protect their Bondei subjects from Zigula attacks. In the following year, chiefs governing Bondei territories were reported to be selling Bondei individuals into slavery along the coast.

The Kiva insurrection of 1869 enabled the Bondei to reclaim their freedom and was connected with the restoration of the kingdom. In November 1925, the first election for a jumbe Mkuu was contested by Geldart Mhina and John Juma. According to the provincial commissioner, 95% of elders and headmen chose John Juma. The sources present these events as political history rather than ritual practice.

## Foodways

The sources used do not document Bondei staple foods, named dishes, cooking methods, food taboos, beverages, ceremonial meals, or dietary rules.

The sources do state that most Bondei people reside in Pangani District, where they engage in different activities, especially small-scale agriculture. The history of Shambaa rule also records tribute in the form of food and livestock. No particular crops, recipes, preparation techniques, or food terms are supplied.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not record Bondei folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles, praise poetry, storytelling genres, or literary works.

The historical material does preserve political statements connected with Bondei identity. Geldart Mhina disputed that he was the last surviving member of Bonde’s old kings, while his followers said that they were reminded of the Kilindi carnage during Kiva “every time we see a Kilindi on the throne.” The sources also report that Bondei developed the skill of presenting political assertions in terms of the past. These statements concern historical memory and political identity, but the sources do not describe a wider oral-literary tradition.

## Language & religion

Bondei speak Kibondei, a Bantu language. Bondei is described as a Northeast Coast Bantu language of Tanzania, closely related to Shambala. The people are culturally related to the Shambaa and Zigua. The name *Wabondei* is given as the Swahili form for Bondei.

The sources used do not cover Bondei religious affiliation, spiritual practices, ritual specialists, conversion history, sacred places, historical scripts, dialects, or religious coexistence. They also do not document the relationship between religion and Bondei material culture.

## At a glance

| Who | The Bondei, also known as Wabondei, are a Bantu ethnic group. |

## Overview

The Bondei live mainly in Pangani District and also in eastern Muheza District. They speak Kibondei and are culturally related to the Shambaa and Zigua. Their history includes conquest, tribute, slave raiding, population movement, and resistance. The Kiva insurrection of 1869 helped the Bondei reclaim their freedom.

## Material culture

The profile records patterned grass and palm-leaf mats, wooden household objects, pottery smoking pipes, and a wooden stringed instrument.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Bondei matmaking uses grass, fibre, and palm leaf to create striped and geometric patterns.

## Overview

The Kinga are an ethnic and linguistic group native to Mbeya Region and Makete District of Njombe Region in Tanzania, in the great Kipengere Range northeast of Lake Malawi. Their population was estimated at 140,000 in 2003. The Kinga speak the Kinga language, a Bantu language closely related to Magoma, although mutual intelligibility is low. They are primarily agriculturists who cultivate millet, beans, bananas, wheat and potatoes, and they also keep cattle, sheep and goats. Their mountain settlements, ironworking, agricultural practices and beer production are among the cultural subjects covered by the sources. Kinga structures were built around common spaces used for public meetings.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document Kinga textile traditions or a pattern vocabulary.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not document everyday or ceremonial Kinga clothing, garments, head coverings, belts, footwear or other forms of dress.

### Architecture

Kinga structures were built surrounding a common space used for public meetings. The sources also describe Kinga homesteads as containing cylindrical and conical-shaped huts, surrounded by hedges of thorn. No further information about building materials, roofs, named building types or architectural decoration is provided.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Kinga ironworking was regarded by the Nyakyusa as requiring secret skills. Kinga smiths produced iron-tipped spears, hoes and knives. Iron was heated, layered in charcoal until the slag drained off, and reduced to a solid spongy mass called bloom; the bloom was reheated and hammered in a forge. Each operation required a new furnace, charcoal, labor and skill. The production of only three hoes or spears could require a ton of charcoal and a long apprenticeship. The Nyakyusa made shields, while seeking Kinga iron-tipped spears after wood-tipped spears proved ineffective against tough shields during the invasion of the Ngoni.

The museum catalogue records an iron axe with a wooden handle and a wooden carved staff bound with iron at one end. It also records grass-plaited baskets used for beer, including close-weave baskets with orange or red decorative bands, openwork lattice-patterned baskets, and a natural-colour basket. A grass basketry bottle is closely plaited and patterned in red. A bamboo mug or cup has pokerwork in bands of triangles and possibly contained a maize-cob.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not document Kinga jewelry, body adornment, tattoos, henna, hair practices or ritual ornaments.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not document Kinga musical instruments, song genres, musical performances or performance contexts.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document Kinga dances, theatrical traditions, dramatic performances or named entertainment forms.

## Festivals & rituals

Kinga priests claimed an ancient heritage older than their chiefs. The priests also seemed to interpret subterranean water movement. The Nyakyusa watched with fear and dismay as pilgrims descended the mountain paths each year toward “Lwenbe’s” shrine. Beyond this account, the sources used do not document an annual festival calendar, seasonal celebrations, life-cycle rites, weddings or funerals.

## Foodways

The Kinga cultivate millet, beans, bananas, wheat and potatoes. They cultivate bamboo for a strong beer, and the sources describe a very pleasing beer made from bamboo. Museum catalogue records identify several grass-plaited baskets as used for beer. One catalogue record describes a bamboo mug or cup with pokerwork in bands of triangles, possibly containing a maize-cob. The sources used do not provide a named dish, cooking method, dietary rule, ceremonial food tradition or tea and coffee practice.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not document Kinga folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, literary works, storytelling contexts or contemporary literary preservation efforts.

## Language & religion

Kinga is a Bantu language spoken by the Kinga tribe in Tanzania. It is closely related to Magoma, but mutual intelligibility is low. The Kinga speak Kinga almost exclusively at home and usually know Swahili, although they are not fluent. The sources state that Kinga priests claimed an ancient heritage older than their chiefs and were associated with interpreting subterranean water movement. They also describe annual pilgrimages toward “Lwenbe’s” shrine. No further religious system, script, denomination or current religious landscape is covered by the sources used.

## Overview

The Kuria, also known as the AbaKuria, are a Bantu community in Tanzania’s Mara Region and southern Kenya. Their homeland extends between the Migori River and the Mara River estuary, from Migori County in Kenya to Musoma Rural District in Tanzania. In Tanzania they live in Serengeti, Tarime, Musoma Urban and Rural, and Bunda Districts. Lake Victoria lies to the north. The Kuria are traditionally a farming and pastoral community, growing maize, beans, cassava, coffee and sweet potatoes, and keeping cattle. Their population in 2024 was estimated at 1,500,000, including 608,000 in Tanzania and 892,000 in Kenya. Kuria is a Bantu language spoken mainly in Northern Tanzania, with speakers also in Kenya.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document Kuria textile or pattern traditions.

### Clothing & dress

The museum records include a man’s leather belt ornamented with chains and glass beads. A photographic print shows two adult males wearing neck-ornaments, cloths, arm-rings and ear-ornaments. The sources used do not describe everyday clothing, ceremonial dress, head coverings, footwear, or named Kuria garment types.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Kuria houses, settlements, building materials, roof forms, or architectural decoration.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records four finger-knives made of iron. The sources do not identify their use, manufacture, regional style, or relationship to Kuria daily life. The sources used do not document Kuria ceramics, wooden objects, household goods, or named craft forms.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum records describe a man’s metal ear ornament with glass beads suspended on leather thongs; a man’s ear ornament made of coiled metal, metal chains and white glass beads with two small hide thongs; a woman’s ornament; a necklace of glass beads with a leather pendant, cowrie shells and silver chains; a necklace with pendants and chains made of glass and silver beads, including a leather pendant covered with silver chains, beads and a cowrie shell; and a man’s soapstone armlet. A photographic print shows adults wearing neck-ornaments, arm-rings and ear-ornaments. The sources do not explain the ornaments’ social or ritual functions.

## Music & performance

The museum catalogue contains a photographic print of two adult males playing drums, one sitting and one squatting. The sources do not name the drums, songs, musical genres, performance contexts, or other Kuria instruments.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document Kuria dances, theatre, dramatic traditions, or performance distinctions.

## Festivals & rituals

The Kuria practice circumcision for both males and females until today, while the source notes the existence of modern practices. The sources used do not describe an annual festival calendar, wedding rites, funerals, birth ceremonies, or other life-cycle rituals.

## Foodways

The Kuria grow maize, beans and cassava as food crops. Coffee and sweet potatoes are described as cash crops, and the sources also list maize and yams among cash crops. The sources used do not document named dishes, cooking methods, ceremonial foods, beverages, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

Major Kuria clan traditions state that the ancestor of the Kuria was Mokurya and that his descendants migrated from Misiri (Egypt), eventually reaching Bukurya after wandering along Lake Victoria. These traditions divide the Kuria into the Abasai, descended from Mokurya’s elder wife, and the Abachuma, descended from his younger wife. The sources used do not document Kuria folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles, written literature, or preservation projects.

## Language & religion

Kuria is a Bantu language spoken by the Kuria people of Northern Tanzania, with some speakers in Kenya. Maho (2009) treats the Simbiti, Hacha, Surwa and Sweta varieties as distinct languages. The sources used do not describe a Kuria writing system, religious landscape, sectarian affiliations, or spiritual practices.
