---
title: "Yaka"
subtitle: "Democratic Republic of the Congo"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]
---

## Overview

The Yaka are an African ethnic group living in southwest Democratic Republic of the Congo, near the Angola border and in the forest and savanna region between the Kwango River and the Wamba River. They number about 300,000 and speak the Yaka language. The Yaka are related to the Suku people and have a matrilineal society that also includes patrilineal lineage as family name. Their villages are led by chiefs, while the paramount chief, or *kiambv*, governs through nobles and village authorities. Yaka cultural life includes farming, hunting, fishing, initiation, divination, ancestor reverence, mask performance, sculpture, basketry, wooden vessels, drums, whistles, and other tools and objects.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Raffia composite masks** — Yaka masks in the museum records combine wood, cane, raffia and raffia cloth. They may have painted faces, patterned caps, projections, cloth strips, geometric designs, or raffia fringes.

**Nkanda masks** — The *nkanda* initiation ceremony uses masks worn by initiates and teachers. The masks may include *mondo*, *ndemba*, *kapita* and *mbala*. They are worn atop the head and are judged for color, creativity and execution.

**Bweni** — The *bweni* is a woven raffia headpiece worn by earth chiefs as a sign of authority. It commonly has between one and three crests running from the front to the back of the head and is worn day and night as a communal charm.

**Tsala** — The *tsala* is a beaded hat worn by nobles. Its upper part forms a cone decorated with a tuft of feathers. *Tsala zi kanaangi* have white feathers and signify a higher rank than *tsala zi nduwa*, which have red feathers.

**Bweni and headrest ensemble** — Because *bweni* were also worn as charms while sleeping, they required a headrest called *musaw* or *m-baambu*. The headrests were carved from one piece of wood and could be decorated with a leopard, antelope, human figure or house with a pitched roof.

**Ceremonial mask coverings** — Museum masks include caps and conical cloth “hats” on fibre frames, sometimes with four projections, painted geometric designs and raffia fibre attached around the rim.

**Raffia cloth and fibre objects** — The catalogue records raffia cloth, vegetable fibre, string, palm leaf and woven fibre in masks, hats, wigs, baskets, purses, load-carriers and other objects.

**Motif vocabulary.** Leopard, antelope, buffalo, human head, human figure, house with a pitched roof, quadruped with pointed snout, crests, projections, geometric designs, upturned nose.

### Clothing & dress

The sources describe ceremonial and authoritative head coverings rather than a complete account of everyday clothing. Paramount chiefly authority was signified by coiled rings around the ankle and arm containing fibres and a sacrificial tendon wrapped in copper, called the *kazekedi* or *lukano*. Nobles wore *tsala*, beaded hats with conical tops and feathers. Earth chiefs wore woven raffia *bweni*. Museum records include a chief’s hat made of vegetable fibre, a wig or cap made of fibre, and a male figure with a crested hat or coiffure. The sources also record masks made from wood, cane, raffia and raffia cloth, sometimes with painted faces, caps, cloth strips and raffia fringes. They do not describe ordinary garments, footwear, or a separate everyday dress system for men and women.

### Architecture

The sources do not provide a general description of Yaka houses, villages as architectural forms, roof construction, workshops, or settlement plans. They mention villages governed by chiefs and record headrests carved with imagery of a house with a pitched roof. Many graves are constructed in dwellings or placed in enclosures where *n-saanda* and *n-yoombu* trees are planted.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Yaka material culture includes carved wooden objects, tools, vessels and household goods. Museum records include drinking cups, wooden double cups, vessels with two spouts, boxes, baskets, winnowing trays, fish traps, combs, headrests, load-carriers, pipes, slit drums and whistles. Metal appears in swords, spear points, adze fittings, brass studs, brass nails, copper wire, iron wire and tin-plating. A museum figure has a receptacle for medicine and a glass mirror, while another has a block of fetish material set into the stomach. A *mukoku* is a carved slit drum used in ritual and divination contexts.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources describe authority objects and protective adornment rather than a complete jewelry tradition. Paramount chiefs wore coiled rings around their ankles and arms, made with fibres and a sacrificial tendon wrapped in copper. Noble *tsala* hats used beads and feathers, with white and red feathers indicating rank. Museum figures include beads, metal fittings, cloth bags, cords and pendants. Yaka headrests and other objects could contain or carry charms intended to protect their owners from wicked influences. The sources do not describe tattoos, henna, footwear, or hair practices beyond crested hats and coiffures.

## Music & performance

Yaka musical instruments include drums, slit drums, whistles and miniature flutes. The carved slit drum called *mukoku* is regionally famous and is used in ritual dances. Diviners use *mukoku* slit drums topped with carved heads to provide rhythm for chants. The drums may have compartments used for mixing and serving medicines, may be struck with a baton attached by a cord, and may also be laid horizontally as stools.

Before a hunt, men are signaled several days in advance by a whistle or miniature flute called *kasengo-sengo*. The hunt leader carries an elongated whistle called a *yimbila* to call and signal the hunters. It has a side extension with a hole for altering its pitch, and its lower end is carved as a human head. A more spherical whistle with a similar but shorter side extension is called a *ndemba*. Museum records include ivory and wooden whistles, some surmounted by human heads, as well as friction drums and numerous slit gongs. The sources do not identify named song genres.

## Dance & theatre

Yaka masks are used by dancers and performers during ceremonies and rituals and are believed to communicate with the spirit world. Their sculptures called *mbwoolo* and their carved slit drum called *mukoku* are used in ritual dances. Masks are also central to *nkanda*, the initiation ceremony for young men after circumcision. During the ceremony, the initiates, called *tundansi*, wear masks including *mondo*, *ndemba*, *kapita* and *mbala*. The leading *mbala* mask is designed by the sculptor and wearer to amuse spectators. Masks may have bulging eyes, an upturned nose, an open mouth and exposed teeth, with wooden projections or elaborate headpieces. The sources do not describe a separate theatrical tradition.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not describe an annual festival calendar or festivals with fixed dates. They do describe *nkanda*, a coming-of-age ceremony for young men. Yaka boys are circumcised at puberty rather than at birth. After circumcision, they become *tundansi* and leave the village for one to three years, during which they learn skills and are taught how to become proper men. They are separated from other villagers and forbidden from seeing women.

The initiation ends when the teachers, called *tulombusi*, and the elders judge the initiates ready. Usually five participants appear, with pairs wearing similar masks and a leader wearing the *kapita*. The *mbala* is worn by the leader of the *tulombusi*. The masks are inspected and judged for color, creativity and execution. The sources also describe ancestor offerings, hunting rites, divination, funerary grave practices and ceremonies connected with reconciliation between Kongo and Lunda groups. No annual festival, wedding rite or birth ceremony is described.

## Foodways

The Yaka farm cassava, sweet potatoes and corn as staple foods and supplement these with fish and game meat. Hunting is also a social and masculine institution. Commonly pursued animals include duiker, antelope, buffalo and wild boar. Yaka hunters use bows and arrows, rifles, lances, snares, traps, long nets and dogs.

Before a group hunt, hunters send palm wine and kola nuts to the earth chief for approval and as offerings to the ancestors. Animals are divided according to hunting rules: the first arrow determines ownership, while owners of other arrows and the dog that tracked the animal also receive portions. The land chief and political chief receive the remaining portions. Skins, teeth or tusks from animals capable of killing humans are given as tribute to the paramount chief. Portions are also divided among dependents and lineage headmen.

The sources mention palm wine, dried meat, mushrooms, fish, game meat, cassava, sweet potatoes, corn and kola nuts. They do not name prepared dishes, cooking methods, tea or coffee traditions, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do not describe Yaka epic poetry, folktales, proverbs, riddles, written literature or contemporary literary preservation efforts. They do describe chants used in divination. During a divination session, the *ngoombu* chants about possible curses, while relatives may repeat the ends of the chants. The diviner later reveals the curse believed responsible for an affliction.

The sources also preserve historical narratives about the establishment of the Yaka kingdom, the movement of Lunda groups westward, relations between Kongo and Lunda communities, resistance to colonial administration, and the later role of the Bayaka in independence movements. These accounts include King Kabamba, the Kwango region, and the political organization of the kingdom.

## Language & religion

The Yaka speak the Yaka language. The language source identifies several languages using the name Yaka, including Yaka language of Congo–Angola, Yaka language of Kivu, Yaka language of Lékoumou, Yaka language of Ubangi, Yaka language of Cameroon, and Yaka as a dialect of West Teke language. It does not provide a language-family classification or historical writing system.

Yaka religious and ritual life includes ancestor reverence, divination, healing, protective charms, initiation and beliefs concerning witches. The *ngoombu* diviner investigates strange phenomena, misfortune, illness and untimely death. *Mbwoolo* statuettes assist with interpreting dreams, communicating with ancestors, healing and protection. The Cleveland Museum describes Yaka figures called *Biteki* as containers for magical ingredients that can become *minkisi*, or power objects; one example is associated with *Phuungu* and protection against witches. The sources do not identify a wider religious affiliation.

| Who | The Yaka are an African ethnic group. |

| How many | About 300,000 |
| Language | Yaka |
| Religion | Ancestor reverence, divination, healing, protective charms, initiation, and beliefs about witches. |
| Known for | Nkanda initiation masks · Mukoku slit drums · Raffia headpieces · Hunting · Wooden sculpture |

## Overview

The Yaka live in forest and savanna regions near the Angola border. They farm, hunt, fish, and make many wooden, fibre, and metal objects. Villages are led by chiefs, with a paramount chief called kiambv. Cultural life includes initiation, divination, ancestor reverence, masks, sculpture, basketry, drums, and whistles.

## Material culture

Yaka material culture uses wood, raffia, fibre, cane, beads, feathers, copper, iron, brass, and tin for objects of daily use, authority, ritual, and protection.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Raffia, fibre, beads, feathers, and geometric designs are important in masks, hats, baskets, and other objects.

- **Raffia composite masks** — These masks combine wood, cane, raffia, and raffia cloth, often with painted faces, patterns, projections, and fringes.
- **Nkanda masks** (*nkanda*) — These initiation masks may include mondo, ndemba, kapita, and mbala, and are judged for color, creativity, and execution.
- **Woven raffia headpiece** (*bweni*) — The bweni is a woven raffia headpiece with one to three crests, worn by earth chiefs as a sign of authority and as a communal charm.
- **Beaded noble hat** (*tsala*) — The tsala is a beaded conical hat with a feather tuft, and its feather color shows rank.
- **Ceremonial mask coverings** — Masks may have fibre-frame caps or conical cloth hats with projections, painted geometric designs, and raffia around the rim.

### Clothing & dress

The profile describes ceremonial and authority headwear more fully than ordinary clothing.

- **Authority rings** (*kazekedi; lukano*) — Paramount chiefs wore coiled rings around the ankle and arm, made with fibres, a sacrificial tendon, and copper.
- **Noble hat** (*tsala*) — Nobles wore beaded hats with conical tops and feathers.
- **Earth chief’s headpiece** (*bweni*) — Earth chiefs wore woven raffia headpieces.
- **Fibre chief’s hat** — Museum records include a chief’s hat made of vegetable fibre.
- **Crested hat or coiffure** — A museum figure has a crested hat or coiffure.

### Architecture

The sources give little information about Yaka architecture, but they mention chiefs’ villages, graves, and house imagery.

- **Chief-led villages** — Yaka villages are governed by chiefs.
- **Grave dwellings and enclosures** — Many graves are built in dwellings or placed in enclosures where n-saanda and n-yoombu trees are planted.
- **Pitched-roof house motif** — Some carved headrests show a house with a pitched roof.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Yaka makers produce many wooden, fibre, and metal tools, vessels, containers, and household objects.

- **Drinking cups and vessels** — Museum records include drinking cups, wooden double cups, and vessels with two spouts.
- **Baskets and winnowing trays** — Baskets and winnowing trays are among the recorded everyday objects.
- **Fish traps** — Fish traps are recorded among Yaka material objects.
- **Mukoku slit drum** (*mukoku*) — The mukoku is a carved slit drum used in ritual and divination contexts.
- **Metal tools and fittings** — Records include swords, spear points, adze fittings, brass studs, brass nails, copper wire, iron wire, and tin-plating.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Adornment often marks rank or carries protective power.

- **Chiefly copper-wrapped rings** (*kazekedi; lukano*) — Paramount chiefs wore fibre and tendon rings wrapped in copper around their ankles and arms.
- **Feathered noble hats** (*tsala*) — Tsala hats use beads and feathers, with white and red feathers showing different ranks.
- **Beads and pendants** — Museum figures include beads, metal fittings, cords, cloth bags, and pendants.
- **Protective charms** — Headrests and other objects could carry charms meant to protect their owners from wicked influences.

## Music & performance

Yaka music uses drums, slit drums, whistles, and flutes for ritual, divination, and hunting signals.

- **Ritual slit drum** (*mukoku*) — The mukoku provides rhythm for ritual dances and diviners’ chants.
- **Hunt signal whistle** (*kasengo-sengo*) — Men are warned several days before a hunt by a whistle or miniature flute called kasengo-sengo.
- **Hunting leader’s whistle** (*yimbila*) — The yimbila is an elongated whistle used by the hunt leader to call and signal hunters.
- **Spherical whistle** (*ndemba*) — The ndemba is a more spherical whistle with a short side extension.
- **Other instruments** — Museum records include ivory and wooden whistles, friction drums, and many slit gongs.

## Dance & theatre

Masks, figures, and slit drums shape Yaka ritual dances and initiation performances.

- **Ritual mask performance** — Yaka masks are worn by dancers and performers and are believed to communicate with the spirit world.
- **Mbwoolo ritual figures** (*mbwoolo*) — Mbwoolo sculptures are used in ritual dances.
- **Nkanda initiation performance** (*nkanda*) — Nkanda uses masks in the initiation of young men after circumcision.
- **Leading mbala mask** (*mbala*) — The leading mbala mask is designed by its sculptor and wearer to amuse spectators.

## Festivals & rituals

The best-described Yaka ceremony is nkanda, a long initiation for boys after circumcision.

- **Coming-of-age initiation** (*nkanda*) — Nkanda prepares young men for adulthood after circumcision at puberty.
- **Initiates** (*tundansi*) — After circumcision, boys become tundansi and leave the village for one to three years to learn skills and proper manhood.
- **Initiation teachers** (*tulombusi*) — Tulombusi teachers and elders decide when the initiates are ready.
- **Ancestor offerings** — The sources describe offerings to ancestors, including offerings before group hunts.
- **Divination and funerary rites** — Yaka ritual life includes divination, grave practices, hunting rites, and reconciliation ceremonies between Kongo and Lunda groups.

## Foodways

Yaka food comes from farming, fishing, hunting, and gathered foods, with rules for sharing game.

- **Staple crops** — The Yaka farm cassava, sweet potatoes, and corn.
- **Hunted game** — Hunters pursue duiker, antelope, buffalo, and wild boar.
- **Hunting equipment** — Hunters use bows and arrows, rifles, lances, snares, traps, long nets, and dogs.
- **Hunt approval offerings** — Before a group hunt, hunters send palm wine and kola nuts to the earth chief for approval and ancestor offerings.
- **Game-sharing rules** — The first arrow determines ownership, while other hunters, the tracking dog, chiefs, dependents, and lineage headmen receive assigned portions.

## Oral tradition & literature

The profile records divination chants and historical accounts rather than named epics or written literature.

- **Divination chants** — During divination, the ngoombu chants about possible curses and relatives may repeat the ends of the chants.
- **Curse investigation** (*ngoombu*) — The diviner later reveals the curse believed to have caused an affliction.
- **Yaka kingdom history** — Historical accounts describe the founding of the Yaka kingdom, its political organization, and King Kabamba.
- **Kongo-Lunda histories** — The accounts describe Lunda movements westward and relations between Kongo and Lunda communities.
- **Colonial and independence histories** — The sources describe resistance to colonial administration and the later role of the Bayaka in independence movements.

## Language & religion

Yaka religious life centers on ancestors, divination, healing, protective power, initiation, and fears of witchcraft.

- **Yaka language** — The Yaka speak the Yaka language, a name also used for several other languages and a West Teke dialect.
- **Diviner** (*ngoombu*) — The ngoombu investigates strange events, misfortune, illness, and untimely death.
- **Protective statuettes** (*mbwoolo*) — Mbwoolo statuettes help interpret dreams, communicate with ancestors, heal, and protect.
- **Power figures** (*Biteki; minkisi*) — Biteki figures can hold magical ingredients that become minkisi, or power objects.
- **Phuungu protection** (*Phuungu*) — One Biteki figure is associated with Phuungu and protection against witches.

## Glossary

- *nkanda* — initiation ceremony
- *bweni* — raffia headpiece
- *tsala* — beaded noble hat
- *kazekedi* — chiefly authority ring
- *lukano* — chiefly authority ring

- *yimbila* — hunt leader’s whistle
- *ndemba* — spherical whistle or mask
- *mbwoolo* — ritual sculpture or statuette
- *tundansi* — male initiation participant
- *tulombusi* — initiation teacher
- *ngoombu* — diviner
- *Biteki* — figures holding magical ingredients
- *minkisi* — power objects
- *Phuungu* — protective power associated with a figure

## Overview

The Mangbetu are a Central Sudanic ethnic group living in the northeastern province of Haut-Uele in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Their language, also called Nemangbetu, is one of the most populous Central Sudanic languages and is spoken in northeastern Congo. The sources do not provide a population figure, and they do not describe a specific river valley, city, oasis, or mountain range as the group’s general homeland. Mangbetu culture is represented in the sources through highly developed art and music, distinctive iron and copper work, pottery, figures, body adornment, textiles, royal imagery, and the Mangbetu harp or guitar. Historical accounts also emphasize the former practice of elongating babies’ heads, known as *Lipombo*, and elaborate women’s hairstyles.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Egbe** — *Egbe* were fashionable and practical garments made by aristocratic Mangbetu women for special occasions. They were made from plant fibers and dye, worn over a skirt, and tied onto a girdle with a frontal apron; their decorated flat portions displayed bold geometric motifs.

**Negbe** — A *negbe* was a back skirt or sitting pad, also described in the catalogues as a buttock cover. It was made from compressed leaf or bark and vegetal fibers, with woven, interwoven, crisscrossing, zigzag, lined, or chequered arrangements.

The sources do not identify additional Mangbetu textile traditions or provide comparisons with neighboring cultures.

**Motif vocabulary.** Geometric motifs; concentric circles; concentric bands; cartouches; crisscrossing and zigzag arrangements; chequered formations.

### Clothing & dress

The sources describe *Egbe* as garments worn by aristocratic Mangbetu women on special occasions. An *Egbe* was worn over a skirt and tied onto a girdle together with a frontal apron. Its curved interior piece rested on the lower back and cushioned the wearer when sitting; when she stood, the decorated flat section faced outward. Museum catalogues also record *negbe* buttock covers made from compressed leaf or bark and vegetal fibers. A British Museum record describes a large carved male figure wearing a vegetal-fiber apron, while another male figure wears a fiber skirt around the waist. The sources do not describe ordinary daily dress, footwear, belts beyond the girdle associated with *Egbe*, or a complete ceremonial costume. A dance-cap made from an elephant’s ear with feathers is also recorded.

### Architecture

The Wikipedia source states that Western photographs and films documented Mangbetu architecture, royal courts, and dances. The supplied sources do not describe Mangbetu house forms, building materials, roof types, settlement layouts, named building types, or architectural decoration in sufficient detail.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Mangbetu metalwork includes iron weapons and tools, including knives, axes, arm-daggers, swords, arrow-heads, spear-heads, spears, a chisel-shaped currency blade, and a musical horn made of elephant ivory. The Wikipedia source states that knowledge of iron and copper forging helped provide a military and economic advantage and was used to make weapons and fine ornaments. Museum records describe pottery vessels with human heads, tall headdresses, striated hats or coiffures, earrings, loop handles, spouts, and string-like ornament. Wooden objects include stools, seats, boxes, pipes, combs, fly-whisks, and carved figures.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources record necklaces made of pale bluish shell discs and brown seeds strung on vegetable-fiber cord, ivory hair-pins, wooden and ivory hair or hat pins, and a pottery vessel whose human head wears a brass-wire earring. A sword has a wooden handle formed as a female torso and head, with beads for eyes. The Wikipedia source describes women’s elaborate hairstyles and states that Mangbetu figures are recognizable in African art because of the traditional elongated-head appearance. Babies’ heads were formerly wrapped tightly with cloth in the practice called *Lipombo*; the practice began dying out in the 1950s under the influence of westernization. The sources do not describe tattoos, scarification, ritual jewelry functions, or other body-adornment practices.

## Music & performance

The Mangbetu are known for highly developed music, and the Mangbetu harp or guitar is an instrument associated with and named after them. Museum catalogues record bow-shaped harps with wooden necks, skin-covered resonators, sound holes, pegs, strings, and necks terminating in human heads or figures. One harp has a male figure forming the neck; another has a human head at the end of the neck. A musical horn made of elephant ivory, a rattle with a plaited vine-leaf cage and dried seeds or metal clappers, and conical ivory whistles are also recorded. The Museum of World Culture catalogue includes a record identified as *kundi* and a musical-instrument photograph.

Ethnomusicologists sought out the Mangbetu to make video and audio recordings of their music. The supplied sources do not name song genres, musical scales, performance ensembles, wedding or funeral repertories, court procedures, or other specific performance contexts. They also do not establish whether the recorded instruments were used in particular ceremonies, dances, warfare, or entertainment, apart from the catalogue description of a musical horn as used in war.

## Dance & theatre

The sources state that Western photographers and filmmakers documented Mangbetu dances and that a wooden dance mask painted in black and white is held in a museum collection. A dance-cap made from an elephant’s ear and feathers is also recorded. The sources do not name any Mangbetu dance, theatrical genre, dramatic tradition, dance occasion, or distinction between ceremonial and entertainment performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not describe an annual festival calendar, seasonal celebrations, harvest festivals, religious festivals, or rites connected with birth, initiation, marriage, or death. They record that babies’ heads were traditionally wrapped tightly with cloth in the practice called *Lipombo*, and they describe the practice as declining in the 1950s with westernization. The sources also mention royal courts, dances, local wives used in the political expansion of King Nabiembali, and the establishment of independent kingdoms after his death in 1859, but they do not provide ritual descriptions for these events.

## Foodways

The supplied sources do not describe Mangbetu staple foods, dishes, cooking methods, food prohibitions, ceremonial meals, beverages, or tea and coffee traditions. The language source gives *ná-mutali* as a word meaning “fish,” but it does not provide a foodways description or identify a named dish.

## Oral tradition & literature

The language source discusses oral tale texts and identifies the connective *bhe* as a discourse developmental marker in Meegye narrative development. The sources also list Robert Guy McKee’s works on Mangbetu and Meegye-Mangbetu tales, including *Mangbetu Tales of Leopard and Azapane: Trickster as Resistance Hero*, and works concerning storytelling for peace-building and death compensations. The supplied material does not summarize the tales, provide the names of additional characters or genres, or describe proverbs, riddles, epic poetry, performance settings, or contemporary literary revivals.

## Language & religion

Mangbetu, also called Nemangbetu, is a Central Sudanic language spoken by the Mangbetu people of northeastern Congo. The speakers and language are also identified as Amangbetu, Kingbetu, and Mambetto. The most widely understood dialect is Medje; other dialects named in the source are Aberu or Nabulu, Makere, Malele, Popoi or Mapopoi, and Lombi. About half of the population speaks Bangala, a trade language similar to Lingala, while some people in southern areas speak Swahili. Mangbetu is associated with the Asua, whose languages are closely related. The sources do not describe a historical script, current religious landscape, denomination, cosmology, or named spiritual practices.

## Overview

The Lunda, also known as Balunda, Luunda and Ruund, are a Bantu ethnic group whose historical homeland lay along the Kalanyi River in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo. They formed the Kingdom of Lunda in the 17th century under Mwata Yamvo, also called Mwaant Yav, whose capital was Musumba. Lunda communities spread through Katanga, eastern Angola, north-western Zambia, Gabon, the Republic of the Congo and the Luapula Valley of Zambia. The sources give approximately 800,000 Lunda in Angola, 1.1 million in the Congo and 600,000 in Zambia. Most speak Lunda, also called Chilunda, although the Kazembe-Lunda adopted Bemba. The sources present Lunda history through migration, political expansion, farming, fishing, trade, religious belief, ceremonial dress and material culture.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

*Bastsnöre* — A catalogue record describes a rectangular piece of crocheted bast cord as part of a Lunda dance costume. Its use is unidentified in the record, which also suggests hand protection.

*Dansdräkt* — The Museum of World Culture records a Lunda dance costume from Kassai, Belgian Congo, consisting of a mask, shirt, leg clothing, cords and crocheted bast elements. It was used by medicine men at circumcision festivals when the medicine man led the dance.

*Mitunda* — The catalogue records describe “mitunda” as a type of necklace made by local people, who were reluctant to sell it because it possessed considerable prestige value. The object was associated with Lunda material culture but the record also places this necklace type among several Central and southern African communities.

The sources do not name Lunda textile patterns or provide documented pattern vocabularies.

### Clothing & dress

The sources describe a ceremonial Lunda dance costume used by medicine men at circumcision festivals. Its components included a mask, a shirt, leg clothing, cords, a rectangular piece of crocheted bast cord and a set of ten fingers threaded onto two strings, with five fingers on each string. The catalogue does not identify all components or specify the material of every part. The dance costume was worn when the medicine man led the dance.

A British Museum photographic record shows a group of standing Lunda adult males wearing cloths around their lower bodies, personal ornaments, head-gear, vests or shirts; one man held a rifle. The seated adult male, identified in the record as a possible leader or ruler, also wore head-ornaments and had a beard. The sources do not describe ordinary women’s clothing, footwear, belts or daily dress.

A Lunda head-dress from Belgian Congo consisted of eight parts made from glass beads. Some ornaments were worn above the forehead and beside the ears, while others formed arches across the head. The record states that some parts were worn only on special occasions and others were worn continually.

### Architecture

The sources used here do not describe Lunda houses, villages, royal buildings, construction materials, roof forms or architectural decoration.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The catalogue records several Lunda or Lunda-associated household and working objects. Three vessels called *mulondo* are identified as Lunda or Lwena, also given as Balunda, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The records describe ceramic vessels with rounded or oval bodies, circular or absent feet, cylindrical necks, geometric ornament within rectangles on one vessel, and a clay lid on another. Their recorded heights include 27 cm and 28 cm.

Lunda-associated tools include a straight-edged, socketed axe used for cutting wood, a hoe used for working the soil, and a wooden “spade” used for stirring flour. A calabash was used for storing small objects, while a sieve was used for cassava flour. The catalogue also records a wooden club with a carved human head, a knife called *kisu*, and a bow made of tough wood with a twisted leather string, probably buffalo hide or the hide of another large animal. The bow was used in warfare between groups and for hunting.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources document head ornaments, necklaces and personal ornaments but do not provide a complete Lunda jewelry vocabulary. A Lunda head-dress from Belgian Congo was made of glass beads and consisted of eight parts: a cylindrical ornament above the forehead, ornaments beside the ears, and arched ornaments worn across the head. Some elements were reserved for special occasions, while others were always worn.

The catalogue record for a Lunda knife also describes a necklace type called *mitunda*. It states that these necklaces had substantial prestige value and that people who called them *mitunda* were unwilling to part with them. The source does not describe tattooing, scarification, hair practices or other forms of body modification.

## Music & performance

The sources document several Lunda musical instruments. The *sansa* is identified in Museum of World Culture records as a Lunda musical instrument used by men. It was tuned with small balls of wax and described as profane. The records give examples from the Lunda-Kassai area of Angola and include object measurements such as lengths of 18,5 cm, 25,3 cm and 17 cm, together with widths and heights.

The British Museum records a wooden and iron sansa with a rattle. Other catalogue records identify a carved wooden smoking pipe and several rattles. Museum of Ethnography records describe foot rattles made from rows of calabashes threaded onto sticks, with strings for binding them around the legs or ankles. The records include examples with three rows, four rows or two groups of calabashes.

A drum record from Angola describes a large wooden drum with a sound opening, wooden handles and straps. The catalogue material includes general information about musical instruments among the Shokwe, including tall, narrow, hollow drums covered with stretched skin and decorated with incisions or reliefs. The supplied sources do not establish that this general description is specifically Lunda.

The sources do not name Lunda song genres, musical scales, dances performed for entertainment, funeral music or court ensembles.

## Dance & theatre

The sources document a Lunda medicine man’s dance costume used during circumcision festivals. The medicine man led the dance while wearing a costume that included a mask, shirt, leg clothing, cords and crocheted bast elements.

Two Museum of World Culture records identify medicine-man masks used at circumcision festivals. The masks were made by particular people, according to the catalogue descriptions. One record states that the mask’s upper section had cracks and that its surface was deteriorating; another describes loose material and a fragile, cracked substance.

The sources do not name a Lunda dance, theatrical genre, dramatic cycle or performance text. They also do not describe shadow puppetry, court dance or secular stage performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources mention circumcision festivals as a ceremonial setting for Lunda medicine men, masks and dance. A medicine man led the dance while wearing a specific costume, and medicine-man masks were used during the festival. The catalogue records do not provide the festival’s vernacular name, date, season or duration.

The Lunda religion described in the Wikipedia sources centred on Nzambi or Nzamb Katang as the Supreme Creator. Religious practice did not address Nzambi directly but proceeded through the spirits of ancestors. The sources also state that Lunda kings had twenty to thirty wives.

The sources do not describe an annual festival calendar, harvest festival, wedding ceremony, funeral rite, birth ceremony or other life-cycle ritual apart from the circumcision-festival material. They do not give dates for Lunda festivals.

## Foodways

The Lunda heartland contained rivers, lakes, forests and savannah. The sources describe Lunda people as fishermen and farmers who grew maize, millet, yams, sorghum, squash, beans, sweet potatoes, oil palms and tobacco. They drank palm wine.

The supplied material does not name a Lunda dish, provide recipes or describe particular cooking methods. The sources do not specify how the listed crops were prepared, nor do they describe ceremonial food, tea or coffee traditions.

After the defeat of Ndongo, the Lunda are described as basing part of their diet on cows and pigs taken from the kingdom of Ndongo. The same historical account states that their income included the sale of Mbundu prisoners to Portuguese merchants. The sources do not describe dietary rules or restrictions.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used here do not record Lunda folktales, epic poems, proverbs, riddles, named storytelling genres or literary preservation projects. They mention that the Lunda religion involved the spirits of ancestors, but they do not provide the narratives, prayers or oral forms associated with those beliefs.

## Language & religion

Lunda, also known as Chilunda, is a Bantu language spoken in Zambia, Angola and, to a lesser extent, the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is used mainly in the north-western province of Zambia. The Lunda language and its dialects were spoken and understood by perhaps 8.6% of Zambians according to a 1986 estimate. Most Lunda speak Lunda or Chilunda, except for the Kazembe-Lunda, who adopted Bemba from neighbouring communities. A small number of Lunda dialects are represented in Namibia.

The language description states that vowel length is contrastive and that /w/ may also be heard as a bilabial glide. The Lunda Kingdom’s religious tradition identified Nzambi or Nzamb Katang as the Supreme Creator and approached this creator through ancestral spirits. The sources do not describe a historical script or a current religious affiliation.

## Overview

The Bembe people, plural Babembe, are based in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and western Kigoma Region of Tanzania, living mainly in Fizi Territory in South Kivu and also in Tanganyika Province, including Kalemie. The Bembe population was estimated at 252,000 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 1991 and around 1.5 million in 2005. The Bembe are of Bantu stock and are ethnically related to the Barega and other Bantu-speaking peoples. Their historical cultural region, Ubembe, lies west of Lake Tanganyika and includes Fizi Territory and the Itombwe Mountains. The Bembe speak Kibembe. Their documented folk culture includes mountain agriculture, hunting, fishing, drums, dance, cassava-based foods, fish, and named wooden, metal, ceramic, and textile-related objects.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Muzidi** — Museum catalogue records describe Bembe textile reliquary figures known as *muzidi*. These figures are generally seated, with long, narrow torsos and extended limbs ending in prominently articulated fingers and toes.

The sources used do not document further Bembe textile patterns, weaving techniques, or pattern distinctions from neighboring cultures.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe everyday or ceremonial clothing, footwear, belts, hairstyles, or gender-specific dress. A Museum of World Culture catalogue records a straw hat called *mpu yangara*, described as a Europeanized hat with a brim, associated with Babembe in the former Franska Kongo and the Madzia-området. The same catalogue records a neck ring worn by both sexes and a head or neck ring of iron associated with Babembe-bambamba.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Bembe houses, roofs, settlement layouts, named building types, architectural decoration, or urban traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Museum catalogue records document knives, axes, a crossbow, a chief’s staff, baskets, wooden spoons, wooden bowls, clay pots, a clay carafe, a snuff-bottle, a powder horn, bells, pipes, and a dance broom. Named forms include *kwiti* and *mbesi* knives, *pukweto* and *kikuba* axes, *Bisa* clay pots, *yuku* or *Yku* clay carafe, *Mpipi* wooden powder horn, *lukombo* wooden bowls, *Kipi* women’s pipe, and *madibu ma banganga* wooden bells. The records also describe iron blades, wood, brass and copper wire, snakeskin, hippopotamus hide, and wickerwork of bark.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Museum records describe iron neck rings with loops containing pieces of yellow metal, iron rings that can be opened by a simple hand movement, and yellow-metal arm or foot rings. One catalogue associates an arm or foot ring with Bakuta smiths and export to Basundi-babembe. A separate record describes a neck ring worn by both sexes. The sources used do not document tattoos, scarification, henna, hair practices, or ritual functions for these ornaments.

## Music & performance

Bembe folk music traditionally uses drums. The way the drum is played can be called a six-beat tune, and the music is performed in celebration of any sort. Folk music is accompanied by dance, and the sources state that it has also been adapted into more modern genres. A Museum of World Culture catalogue records *madibu ma banganga*, described as large wooden bells with three clappers, from Mpandi II and associated with Babembe. Other catalogue records include a women’s pipe called *Kipi* and a wooden powder horn called *Mpipi*. The sources used do not name Bembe song genres, provide musical scales or repertories, or describe funerary, wedding, court, or other specific performance contexts.

## Dance & theatre

The Bembe folk dance is called *Esuba*. It uses movements of the shoulder and waist and accompanies folk music played on drums. The sources used do not describe theatrical forms, masked performances, shadow puppetry, dramatic genres, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment dance.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not describe an annual festival calendar, named festivals, seasonal ceremonies, birth rites, coming-of-age rites, weddings, funerals, or other life-cycle rituals. They state only that Bembe music and its accompanying dance are performed in celebration of any sort.

## Foodways

Babembe cuisine consists of cassava-based foods and fish. Named fish include *Mkeke* or *Mkebuka* and *Dagaa*, described as a very small fish. Cassava is prepared as *Kyenge* and *eswaka*, both compared in the source to fufu, and the Wabembe are described as especially fond of *Kyenge*. Vegetable-based foods include *sombe*, a stew of pounded cassava leaves prepared preferably with ground-up nuts and palm oil, and *mlonda*. The sources used do not describe meal ceremonies, beverages, tea or coffee, dietary rules, or food associated with particular festivals.

## Oral tradition & literature

Genealogical accounts preserved by traditional griots trace the Babembe to a common ancestor named Mbondo, also written M'mbondo. These accounts describe Mbondo’s relationship with Leka and Bangu and connect them with the Babembe, Balega, and Bangubangu lineages. Oral traditions also recount that the name Kalembelembe originated from the declaration “Tunapenda Kalembe,” translated in the source as “We love peace,” and that Kalembelembe signified “abundant peace.” The sources used do not document named epics, folktale cycles, proverbs, riddles, written literature, or contemporary literary preservation projects.

## Language & religion

Bembe is a Bantu language spoken by the Bembe people of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and western Tanzania. The Bembe language is also identified as Kibembe, while the Wikipedia material distinguishes it from Bembe language in the Republic of the Congo. The sources state that languages in the region were classified by prefixing the noun-class marker *Ki* to the root of place names, giving Kibembe for the language of the Bembe. The historical material describes Christian missions, catechism, adult baptisms, and campaigns against slavery at Kibanga and Mpala, as well as Arab-Swahili Muslim customs among Wanguana. The sources used do not provide a complete account of the current religious landscape or Bembe spiritual practices.

title: "Yanzi"
subtitle: "Democratic Republic of the Congo"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"

## Overview

The Bayanzi, also called Yan, Yanzi, Yansi, Batende, Bayansi, Mbiem, Nkaan, Wachanzi, Yey and other names, are an ethnic group in the southwest of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. They number about seven million. Their territory has been described from the lower Kasai River to the Congo River and the Ubangi River confluence, including the Lower Kwilu River between the Kwenge and Kwango Rivers. The Yanzi speak Kiyansi, also called Eyans, a Bantu language. Their largest political unit is the chieftainship, with about 120 chieftainships under three traditional kings. Yanzi history is closely connected with river navigation, trading, colonial encounters at Bolobo, and the production and use of iron tools, weapons, ornaments, musical instruments and wooden figures.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document named Yanzi textile or pattern traditions.

**Raffia currency cloths** — The British Museum catalogue records six cloths woven from raffia with fringes on all sides and identifies them as currency cloths.

**Embroidered palm cloth girdle** — A British Museum record describes a man's girdle embroidered and made of palm cloth.

**Girdle ornaments** — The catalogue records women's girdle ornaments, including a string of five ornaments made from gourd, wood, animal tooth, vegetable-fibre string and cloth string, as well as a woman's girdle ornament made of wood with a loop.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no Yanzi textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The sources provide only limited information about Yanzi clothing and dress. A British Museum catalogue records a man's embroidered girdle made of palm cloth and women's girdle ornaments made from gourd, wood, animal tooth, vegetable-fibre string and cloth string. Another woman's girdle ornament is made of wood and has a loop. The catalogue also records a widower's cap made of fibre and feathers, and a male mourner's head ornament in the form of a fibre circlet. These records distinguish men's and women's adornment and identify mourning-related objects, but they do not describe everyday clothing, footwear, hairstyles, complete ceremonial dress or named garments in vernacular terms.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Yanzi house forms, roofing, settlement architecture, named building types or architectural decoration. They mention village organization, including an upstream district for elders and a downstream district for young families, but do not describe the buildings themselves.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Yanzi material culture in the catalogue is represented particularly by iron tools and weapons. British Museum records include machetes, knives, cleavers, swords and hunting arrows. A machete has an iron blade with an inner surface blackened, a brass-covered handle, a wire-bound hilt and a pommel ornamented by punched plates. A sword has an iron blade and wooden handle, while one knife has a broad forged iron blade and carved wooden hilt. Other objects include a powder-box of pale wood with an engraved exterior, a gourd purse, a cane and wood tobacco box, a wooden box, a fishing-net made of vegetable-fibre cord, and a wooden head-rest with brass edging and nails. The catalogue also records a brass halsring from Öfre Kongo, Afrika, associated with Ngala-Yanzi material.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources document body adornment through girdles, ornaments and a brass halsring. Women's girdle ornaments include gourd, wood, animal tooth, vegetable-fibre string and cloth string; another is made of wood and has a loop. A brass halsring is recorded by the Museum of World Culture, with a diameter of 23 cm. The British Museum also records a widower's cap made of fibre and feathers and a male mourner's fibre circlet. The sources do not document tattoos, scarification, hair practices, cosmetics or named ritual jewelry beyond these catalogue descriptions.

## Music & performance

The sources document several musical and signalling objects but do not name Yanzi musical genres or performance traditions. British Museum records include a side-blown trumpet made of antelope horn, pan-pipes made of cane, hide and fibre, and a side-blown horn made of wood. The latter is identified as a war, hunting and funerals instrument. A hunting whistle is made of wood, snake skin and vegetable-fibre string.

A historical account describes Bayanzi river travel and trading by canoe. In March 1888, a convoy of Bayanzi pirogues was described carrying goods beneath brightly coloured umbrellas. The rowers, numbering fifteen to twenty and including both sexes, paddled to the rhythm of a monotonous song led by a team leader standing at the back of the canoe with a rooster between his feet. The same account describes the canoes as sometimes over fifteen meters long and between eighty and ninety centimeters wide. The sources do not provide names for the song, musical forms, dances, performance specialists or occasions apart from war, hunting and funerals associated with one horn.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document named Yanzi dances, theatrical traditions, masked performances, dramatic genres or dance occasions. The account of Bayanzi canoe travel mentions paddling to the rhythm of a monotonous song, but it does not describe a dance or theatre tradition.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not describe an annual Yanzi festival calendar, seasonal festivals, initiation ceremonies, wedding rites, birth ceremonies or funeral rituals in detail. They record a wooden side-blown horn associated with war, hunting and funerals, and a male mourner's fibre head ornament. The social structure described in the sources includes dormitories in which adolescents of each sex lived, but no rites connected with residence in those dormitories are given.

The sources describe Yanzi social organization through kingship, chieftainship, villages and clans. The chieftainship had defined borders; male clans were aristocrats and produced chiefs, while female clans were free individuals who provided wives to the aristocrats. The Bayanzi were matrilineal: a child belonged to the mother's clan, and the father was responsible for finding wives from outside the clan for his children. Grandparents were thought to be reincarnated in their grandchildren, whether dead or still living.

## Foodways

The sources used do not document Yanzi staple foods, cooking methods, named dishes, drinks, dietary rules or ceremonial food. The historical material mentions palm-oil plantations and forced labour under Huileries du Congo Belge, but it does not describe Yanzi foodways. The catalogue records a gourd purse and other containers, but does not identify their culinary uses.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not document Yanzi folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles, written literature or contemporary literary preservation efforts. The Wikipedia material reports local traditions recorded by Jesuits concerning origins, migrations, a region called “Kimput,” a great river, and the land of Kong Mukoko. It also records a tradition that Bayanzi ancestors or grandparents were reincarnated in their grandchildren. These accounts are presented as traditions, but the sources do not provide their narrative texts, performance contexts or names of storytellers.

## Language & religion

Yans, or Yanzi, is a Bantu language spoken in the Democratic Republic of the Congo by the Bayanzi. Guthrie classified six language varieties as Bantu B.85: B.85A Mbiem, West Yansi; B.85B East Yans; B.85C Yeei; B.85D Tsong, also called Itsong, Nsong, Ntsuo or “Songo”; B.85E Mpur, also called Mput; and B.85F Tsambaan. According to Nurse, most belong to the Yaka languages, while one or two belong to the Boma–Dzing languages. Maho notes that Tsong is the then-unclassified “Songo” language and is the variety that does not belong with the rest; Glottolog likewise classifies Nsong-Mpiin separately from Yansi.

The sources state that Attilio Pécile described the Bayanzi, Bakales and Fans in 1887 as pagans, but they do not provide a current religious landscape, denominations, conversion history or detailed spiritual practices.

## Overview

The Boma are a Bantu ethnic group in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. They live mainly along the banks of the lower Kasai and Lukenié rivers. The sources give an estimated 38,000 native speakers, while noting that estimates vary. The Boma speak Boma, a Bantu language. The Boma formed the Boma Kingdom in the 17th century, which continued until Belgian colonial conquest. The population includes Boma Nku in the south, mainly in the Kasai region and the middle stretch of the Kasai River, and Boma Ngeli in the north, in the region of Mushie. Museum catalogue records document bows, a basket, a sword, a bronze ring, and photographs of Boma adults and children.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document Boma textile or pattern traditions.

**Ngondo** — A bronze ring recorded by the Museum of World Culture. The catalogue describes it as a coin and status symbol, and states that it formed part of the bride-price.

**Bamboma** — The Museum of World Culture catalogue includes the term “Bamboma” in a record associated with the Bakongo tribe and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources used do not name any Boma motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The British Museum photographic records show Boma male and female adults and children, most wearing cloths around the lower bodies. The photographs also record personal ornaments. The sources do not identify the garments by vernacular name, distinguish everyday from ceremonial dress, or document head coverings, belts, footwear, or other forms of dress.

### Architecture

A British Museum photographic record shows rectangular, single-storey, thatched-roof buildings associated with a small group of Boma adults and children. Another photograph shows trees and single-storey European buildings in the background. The sources used do not provide further information about Boma architecture, named building types, interior arrangements, decoration, or urban traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Museum records document a bow made of wood and string, a basket made of cane, and a sword with a skin-covered sheath. The sword record also identifies the object as a knife with a sheath and associates it with Boma. The Museum of World Culture catalogue records a bronze ring called “Ngondo,” described as a coin and status symbol. It states that rings of this kind were collected on bast cords or similar materials and could be melted down for practical use. No Boma ceramic tradition is described.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The Museum of World Culture catalogue describes the bronze ring “Ngondo” as a status symbol that formed part of the bride-price. It gives the diameter as approximately 6 cm and states that such rings were collected on bast cords or similar materials. The catalogue also records the term “Nsimbi,” explaining it through “simba,” meaning to hold, hold fast, or hold in. British Museum photographs show personal ornaments, but the sources do not identify their forms or materials. Tattoos, hair practices, and other body adornment are not documented.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not document Boma musical instruments, song genres, musical performances, or performance contexts.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document Boma dances, theatre, dramatic traditions, or ceremonial and entertainment performances.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not document an annual Boma festival calendar, seasonal celebrations, or named festivals. They also do not describe birth, coming-of-age, funeral, or wedding ceremonies in detail. The Museum of World Culture catalogue states that the bronze ring “Ngondo” formed part of the bride-price, but gives no further account of the associated ritual.

## Foodways

The sources used do not document Boma staple foods, cooking methods, dishes, ceremonial food, beverages, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Wikipedia source states that the Boma formed the Boma Kingdom in the 17th century and that it endured until Belgian colonial conquest. The sources used do not preserve or describe Boma oral traditions, folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles, storytelling contexts, written literature, or preservation projects.

## Language & religion

Boma is a Bantu language of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Maho (2009) considers Boma, B.821 Mpe (Kempee), and B.822 Nunu to be closely related languages. Mpe and Nunu do not have ISO codes, and the source distinguishes this Nunu from the Nunu dialect of Ngiri. The Boma Nku inhabit the south, mainly in the Kasai region, while the Boma Ngeli live in the north in the region of Mushie; both are described as coming from lands surrounding the upper reaches of the Lukenié River. The sources used do not document Boma religious beliefs, institutions, spiritual practices, or historical writing systems.

## Overview

The Alur are a Nilotic ethnic group belonging to the larger Luo group. They live in northwestern Uganda and northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, especially in Mahagi territory, mostly north of Lake Albert, and in the southern West Nile region and northeastern Ituri Province. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, they are densely concentrated in 5,216 square kilometres of Mahagi. The source records two million Alur living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2009 and around 800,000 in Uganda in 2014. Most speak Alur or another Luo language, while some also speak Lendu, Kebu, or Lugbara. Their folk-cultural profile includes hierarchical chiefdoms, royal ritual, farming and herding, fishing, hunting, grass-thatched homesteads, the royal Agwara dance, and a material culture of iron tools, weapons, bows, quivers, fish-hooks, and trumpets.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document Alur textile or pattern traditions.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe everyday or ceremonial Alur clothing, head coverings, belts, footwear, or named garments. They do record gendered domestic and economic responsibilities: men herded animals, grew crops, built huts, hunted, fished, and participated in political life, while women kept house, reared children, and cooked. The sources also state that men and women traditionally lived and slept separately, with husbands and wives occupying separate huts and eating separately. No clothing materials, dress forms, or adornment practices are described.

### Architecture

Traditionally, the Alur live in grass-thatched huts. Homesteads in Alur clans are located in the central part of their territory, a settlement pattern described as helping keep the territory under clan control. The sources do not provide a named house type, structural plan, dimensions, decorative program, granary, urban architecture, or building ritual. They state that men built the huts, but do not otherwise describe construction techniques or divisions within the homestead.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records show a material culture containing numerous iron implements and weapons. These include knives with iron blades, wooden handles, and ferrules wrapped in bands of iron or copper wire; a reaping knife whose grip is decorated with strips of copper and brass; and a chopper with a wide iron blade, a projection on one side, and a wooden handle bound with iron wire bands, some beaded. Other recorded tools are an iron blade for an adze or axe with a split hollow socket and an iron fish-hook made with string of vegetable fibre. The catalogue does not document Alur ceramics or named household vessels.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not document Alur jewelry, tattoos, scarification, henna, hair practices, or other bodily adornment. The museum records mention decoration on the grip of a reaping knife with copper and brass strips, and a trumpet ornamented with cowrie shells, leather strips, brass rings, and bells, but do not identify these as personal adornment.

## Music & performance

The sources document one musical or sound-producing object in the museum catalogue: a long wooden elephant trumpet bound with the skin of a monitor lizard or python and ornamented with cowrie shells. Leather strips form a handle at one end and terminate in brass rings and bells on plaited strips at the other end. The catalogue does not supply a vernacular name, performance genre, musical scale, repertoire, or occasion for this trumpet.

The Alur social and political sources describe community rituals and festivals as settings for the Agwara dance, but do not describe accompanying instruments or songs. The royal spear head bearing tradition is associated with the crowning of Alur kings, although the sources do not identify it as a musical practice. The sources used do not cover song genres, instrumental ensembles, court music, funeral music, wedding music, or musical apprenticeship.

The recorded weapons also indicate a material context connected with hunting and warfare: quivers made of hide covered with long black hair have hide carrying straps, while their arrows have cane or wooden shafts, fibre bindings, and iron heads. Wrapped bows are recorded in forms made from wood, hide, and reptile skin, or from cane, hide, and cord of fibre. These catalogue descriptions do not establish how the objects were used in performance.

## Dance & theatre

**Agwara dance** is described as a royal dance performed only in the presence of the king during community rituals or festivals. Both men and women perform it. The sources do not provide choreography, costume, accompanying music, sequence, or regional variation. They also do not describe theatre, dramatic traditions, masked performance, shadow puppetry, or other named dances.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources describe the Agwara dance as part of community rituals or festivals and state that it is performed in the presence of the king. The current king is referred to as the Rwoth, while the title Ubimu distinguishes the king from other chiefs in the kingdom. Alur kings are crowned according to the royal spear head bearing tradition.

The Alur Kingdom currently has 64 chiefdoms, eight in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and 56 in Uganda. The sources describe a ritual undertaken by the Atyak-Winam and PaNduru chiefs in October 2012 to officially lay to rest a conflict that had continued between the clans after a leadership conflict and subsequent war for territory. Reconciliation efforts had begun under Rwoth Ubimu Valente Keruyoma but halted after his death in 2000.

The sources do not provide an annual festival calendar, named seasonal festivals, birth ceremonies, coming-of-age rites, wedding rites, funeral rites, or religious observances. They do state that the king has organized cultural sports tournaments in recent years, in which both men and women participate.

## Foodways

The Alur were farmer-herders and grew millet, cassava, maize, sweet potatoes, spinach, and pumpkins. They herded cattle, goats, and chickens. Goat and chicken were important sources of meat. Salt, forest resources, and wild animals were also important, while fishing became important during the drought season. Large herds of animals were typically hunted as secondary sources of meat so that the Alur would not exhaust their own goat and chicken numbers.

The sources describe food as part of the social hierarchy. High-ranking men had first choice of food, especially prestige food such as meat and beer. Cattle were also important because bride price was paid in cattle. The sources do not name dishes, cooking methods, brewing techniques, food taboos, tea or coffee traditions, or ceremonial foods. They also do not specify whether millet or another crop was used to make the beer mentioned in the account.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not record Alur folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles, praise poetry, named storytellers, or literary preservation projects. They do, however, preserve accounts of clan and chiefly history, including traditions concerning the Atyak Kingdom, the foundation of the Ukuru Chiefdom, and the formation of Paidha and PaNduru. These accounts connect political identity with descent, migration, rivalry, territorial control, and royal succession.

Alur patrilineages maintain family trees, and the sources describe them as important social realities rather than merely fictional genealogies. The Parombo family in the Ukuru clan, for example, included 2,000 men in 1949. The sources do not describe the form in which these genealogies are transmitted or performed.

## Language & religion

Alur is a Western Nilotic language spoken in the southern West Nile region of Uganda and the northeastern Ituri Province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its subdialects are Jokot, Jonam or Lo-Naam, Mambisa, and Wanyoro. Highland Alur, also called Okoro, speak a somewhat different dialect from lowland Alur, also called Jonam, and mutual understanding may be difficult. Alur has nine vowels and 23 consonants.

The language has significant influence from neighbouring Central Sudanic languages. There is extensive bilingualism between Alur and Lendu, and Alur has also been influenced by Okebo and Madi. The language has no officially accepted orthography, although informal conventions appear in written materials and road signs. The sources used do not describe Alur religious affiliation, religious institutions, conversion history, ritual specialists, or a spiritual system.

## Overview

The Budu people, also called *Babudu*, are a Bantu people living in the Wamba Territory in the Orientale Province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. They live on both sides of the Nepoko River, where different dialects are spoken, although the people of the Ibambi side and those of the Wamba side consider themselves one people. Their territory lies within tropical rain forest and is isolated, with roads inaccessible to vehicles other than bicycles. They speak the Budu language, also called Ɨbʉdhʉ. The sources do not state the population size. They offer evidence of a subsistence economy, bark clothing, palm-leaf-thatched houses, patriarchal family organization, elder consensus, forest exchange with the Mbuti people, and a material culture including iron weapons, a war whistle, a necklace of human teeth, and an ivory armlet.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

*Budu bark loin cloth* — The sources state that people wear loin cloths made from beaten bark. They do not describe named patterns, decorative motifs, or distinctions from textile traditions of neighboring cultures.

**Second-hand western clothes** — The sources also report the use of second-hand western clothes, without describing their construction, decoration, or patterns.

The sources used do not name any additional Budu textile traditions or motifs.

### Clothing & dress

Budu clothing described in the sources consists of loin cloths made from beaten bark and second-hand western clothes. The sources do not distinguish men's and women's dress, and they do not mention vernacular garment names, head coverings, belts, footwear, hairstyles, tattoos, or ceremonial clothing.

### Architecture

The Budu live in square huts with mud walls and roofs thatched with palm leaves. The sources do not give a vernacular name for these huts and do not describe internal organization, decoration, settlement layout, construction ceremonies, or urban architecture.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records several iron objects associated with the material culture shown in this atlas. These include an arm-dagger with an iron blade, wooden handle, and sheath; a sword with an iron blade and wooden handle; spears with iron spear-heads and barbs; and several knives. The knives include parade or ceremonial knives with sickle-shaped iron blades, handles covered with iron wire, and plain wooden handles; knives with long iron blades curved at the point; knives with wooden handles bound with iron or iron wire; and a knife whose butt end is wrapped with hide. One catalogue record describes a sickle-shaped ceremonial knife with a copper blade and wooden handle. The sources do not describe ceramics or other household objects.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum catalogue records a necklace made of human teeth strung on twisted fibre cord and a circular armlet made of ivory, now brown with oil. The sources do not explain their names, occasions of use, ritual functions, or distinctions between everyday and ceremonial adornment. No tattoos, henna, or hair practices are described.

## Music & performance

The museum catalogue records a war whistle made of a long conical piece of hollow wood, bound at intervals with iron and copper strips, with a plaited fibre band added for suspension. The sources do not provide a vernacular name for this whistle, describe how it was played, or identify musical scales, songs, genres, dances, ceremonies, or performance contexts. They also do not document other instruments or music traditions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not describe Budu dances, theatre, masked performance, dramatic traditions, or ceremonial and entertainment distinctions.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not describe an annual festival calendar, seasonal festivals, harvest rites, birth ceremonies, coming-of-age rites, weddings, funerals, or other life-cycle rituals. They state that important decisions are made by a consensus of elders and that both the Catholic church and, later, WEC International, or Worldwide Evangelisation for Christ, have been active with the Budu. Charles Studd, the founder of WEC, died in Budu territory and is buried in Ibambi.

## Foodways

The Budu mainly live by subsistence agriculture. Their crops include cassava, yams, corn, rice, peanuts, plantains, and pulses. Palm oil is the main cash crop, giving an income per capita of about $120 a year. Animal husbandry is rare and is limited to poultry and some goats. The Budu obtain meat and other forest resources through trade with the Mbuti people, identified in the source as Pygmies, who share their language. The sources do not name dishes, cooking methods, ceremonial foods, beverages, dietary rules, or food-related festivals.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do not describe Budu folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, storytelling settings, written literature, or preservation and literary revival projects. They state only that the Budu speak the Budu language and that a variety of it called Matta is spoken locally both north and south of Maboma.

## Language & religion

Ɨbʉdhʉ, also called Budu, is a Bantu language spoken by the Budu people in the Wamba Territory in the Orientale Province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its orthography uses the special characters ɨ, ʉ, ɛ, and ɔ, as well as the modifier letters colon ꞉ and equal sign ꞊ for grammatical tone, marking past and future tense respectively. A variety called Matta is spoken locally both north and south of Maboma. The Budu live on both sides of the Nepoko River and speak different dialects; [z] occurs only in the Koya dialect, while /h/ can be heard as voiced [ɦ] or voiceless [h], and /ɗ/ can be heard as [l] or a tap [ɾ] in free variation. Both the Catholic church and WEC International have been active with the Budu. The sources do not describe earlier religious practices, syncretism, or spiritual traditions.

- Wikipedia, “[Budu language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budu_language)”.
