title: "Herero"
subtitle: "Namibia"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]
---

## Overview

The Herero, or *Ovaherero*, are a Bantu ethnic group living primarily in Namibia, with significant populations in Botswana and Angola and a small number in South Africa. In Botswana, communities are found in Maun and villages including Sepopa, Toromuja, Karee, Etsha, Mahalapye, Pilane, Tsabong, Omawaneni, Draaihoek and Makopong. The 2023 census identified 178,987 Namibians as Ovaherero. They speak Otjiherero, a Bantu language of the Niger–Congo family. The Herero are traditionally pastoralists whose economy and social life have been closely connected with cattle. Their material culture includes distinctive women’s dress, horn-shaped headdresses, cattle-related symbolism, metal and leather ornaments, wooden tools and weapons, and objects associated with pastoral life. Their history also includes German colonial rule, the 1904–1907 rebellion and the genocide committed by the German Empire between 1904 and 1908.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Ohorokova** — *Ohorokova* are floor-length dresses worn by married and older Herero women every day, while younger and unmarried women wear them mainly for special occasions. They are high-necked, have voluminous skirts gathered from a high waist or below the bust, use multiple petticoats and may incorporate up to ten metres of fabric.

**Patchworked dresses** — Everyday dresses may be ingeniously patchworked from smaller pieces of fabric, including material salvaged from older garments. Dresses made from a single material are reserved for special occasions.

**Ohorokova vivid fabrics** — The dress style derives from clothing worn by German missionaries in the late nineteenth century but is now made in vivid colours and prints. In urban Windhoek, designers and models are updating the dress with glamorous sheer and embellished fabrics.

**Otjikaiva** — The *otjikaiva* is a horizontal horned headdress worn with women’s dress. It is made to match or coordinate with the dress and can be formed from rolled-up newspaper covered in fabric.

**Ekori** — The traditional headdress *Ekori* symbolized the horns of cows, which were the main source of wealth for the people. Missionaries regarded its shape as a symbol of the devil and rejected it.

**Military-style ceremonial clothing** — On ceremonial occasions, Herero men wear military-style garments including peaked caps, berets, epaulettes, aiguillettes and gaiters. The style is connected with uniforms taken from German soldiers during the 1904–1907 war and is worn to honour fallen ancestors and preserve their memory.

**Leather and bead ornaments** — Museum records document leather, fibre, metal-bead, iron-bead, ostrich-eggshell and copper-bead ornaments associated with Herero, Namibia and German South West Africa.

**Motif vocabulary.** Horns of cows, vertical zig-zags, serrated edges.

### Clothing & dress

Herero women’s dress is characterized by the floor-length *ohorokova*, a high neck, a voluminous gathered skirt, multiple petticoats and long sleeves with sculptural volume. Sleeves may be puffed from the shoulders or frilled at the wrists, and coordinating neckerchiefs are knotted around the neck. Married and older women wear the dresses daily, while younger and unmarried women mainly use them for special occasions. Everyday garments may be assembled from smaller pieces of fabric, whereas single-material dresses are reserved for special occasions.

The most distinctive head covering is the horizontal horned *otjikaiva*, which pays homage to cows that historically sustained the Herero. Decorative brooches and pins may be attached to its centre front. Men’s ceremonial clothing includes peaked caps, berets, epaulettes, aiguillettes and gaiters in a military style. The sources describe women’s neckerchiefs and men’s ceremonial garments, but do not describe Herero footwear or a named everyday belt.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Herero house forms, building materials, roof types, named building traditions or architectural decoration.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Museum catalogue records document a range of Herero-associated objects from Namibia and German South West Africa. These include knives with iron blades and wooden handles, daggers with wooden sheaths, swords with straight iron blades and hard brown wooden hilts and sheaths, a wooden crossbow, an arrow and a wooden bottle. A wooden snuff-box is carved on the outside with vertical zig-zags and closed by a wooden disc at the end of a thong. A smoking pipe has a horn mouthpiece, a steatite bowl and a white-metal cover connected to the stem by a chain.

A museum catalogue also records a small meat barrel or plate with a flat bottom and short handles. Its recorded measurements are 17.8 centimetres in length, 8.8 centimetres in width and 5.7 centimetres in height. The inscription identifies it as being from Damara, South-Africa, while the catalogue associates the record with the Herero People and Damaraland.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Museum records document necklets, necklaces, bangles, armlets, leglets, girdles, neck ornaments, head ornaments and ankle rings associated with Herero, Namibia and German South West Africa. Materials include iron beads, copper beads, steel rings, leather, fibre, metal, ostrich eggshell and thongs.

One necklet consists of four strings of cylindrical iron beads with an oval leather plate at the front, ornamented with smaller iron beads. Another necklace is made of cylindrical copper beads with similar iron beads at intervals, threaded on a thong. A bangle or armlet is made of iron with serrated edges, while another is formed of steel rings. A woman’s leglet consists of seven leather loops threaded with iron rings and connected by a thong.

Museum records also describe girdles made of ostrich eggshell or leather, a neck ornament made of small ostrich-eggshell discs divided vertically by leather, a leather and fibre head ornament with metal beads, and a pair of copper ankle rings recorded as women’s marriage rings.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not identify Herero musical instruments, named song genres, praise-poetry forms, performance settings or specific musical traditions. They mention that Father Peter Heinrich Brincker translated theological works and songs into Herero, but do not provide the titles, forms or performance contexts of those songs.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not cover named Herero dances, dramatic traditions, theatrical forms or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The Herero religious tradition includes the holy fire *Okuruuo*, also called *OtjikaTjamuaha*. It is located at Okahandja and is understood as a link to ancestors through which they speak to Ndjambi on behalf of the people. During immigration, the fire was doused and quickly relit. From 1923 to 2011 it was situated at the Red Flag Commando.

On Herero Day in 2011, a group associated with Paramount Chief Kuaima Riruako claimed that the fire had faced eastwards for the previous 88 years, although it should face towards the sunset. They removed it and placed it at an undisclosed location, causing controversy within the Ovaherero community.

Cattle are involved in social and religious practices. In celebrations such as marriages, cattle are normally eaten, while religious or ancestral-veneration ceremonies involve the sacrifice of cows or other animals. The sources do not provide a complete annual festival calendar or detailed descriptions of birth, coming-of-age or funeral rites.

## Foodways

Cattle are the most valued domestic animals in Herero culture, and cattle herding and trading are described as the most significant activities. Men conduct cattle herding and cattle trading, while women milk cows, perform household work, harvest small field crops and care for young children. Women also carry out much of the trading through bartering for other goods.

The sour milk *Omaere* was prepared by women in pre-colonial times. The sources state that the worth of an *OmuHerero* woman was measured by milk. Cattle are normally eaten at marriages, while cows or other animals may be sacrificed in religious or ancestral-veneration ceremonies.

Goats and sheep are kept for meat. Goatskin is made into child carriers and household ornaments, and goat dung is considered medicinal and is normally used to treat chickenpox. Horses and donkeys are common means of transport, and some Herero people are believed to consume donkey meat. Dogs are used by men for hunting and herding. Chickens are kept for meat and eggs. The sources do not describe staple grains, named cereal dishes, cooking methods, tea or coffee traditions, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not describe Herero folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles or named storytelling traditions. They do record the importance of historical memory in ceremonial clothing: Herero men’s military-style dress is worn to honour fallen ancestors and keep memories alive.

The Herero genocide appears in several works of fiction listed by the source, including Uwe Timm’s *Morenga*, Thomas Pynchon’s *Gravity’s Rainbow* and *V.*, Mari Serebrov’s *Mama Namibia*, Guy Saville’s *The Afrika Reich*, Jackie Sibblies Drury’s 2012 play *We Are Proud to Present a Presentation About the Herero of Namibia, Formerly Known as Southwest Africa, From the German Sudwestafrika, Between the Years 1884–1915*, and Anthony Scholefield’s *The Eagles of Malice*, published in 1968. These are literary representations rather than descriptions of Herero oral literature.

## Language & religion

Otjiherero is a Bantu language in the Niger–Congo family and is spoken by the Herero and Mbanderu peoples in Namibia and Botswana, as well as by small communities in southwestern Angola. Between 2015 and 2018, there were 250,000 speakers in these countries. Its distribution includes Hereroland, the Omaheke region, the Otjozondjupa and Kunene regions, and communities in Windhoek.

Otjiherero is taught in Namibian schools as both a native tongue and a secondary language. It is used as principal material at the University of Namibia and is one of six minority languages used by Namibian State Radio. The language was transcribed in an alphabet based on Latin script after missionary Gottlieb Viehe translated the Bible into Herero. Father Peter Heinrich Brincker translated theological works and songs.

Herero religion includes belief in *Okuruuo*, the holy fire linking people with ancestors and Ndjambi. Modern-day Herero are mostly Christians, primarily Catholic, Lutheran and Born-again Christian.

## Overview

The Herero are traditionally pastoralists whose lives have long been closely tied to cattle. Their culture includes distinctive women’s dress, horn-shaped headdresses, metal and leather ornaments, wooden tools and weapons, and other pastoral objects. They live mainly in Namibia, with significant populations in Botswana and Angola. Their history includes German colonial rule, the 1904–1907 rebellion and the genocide committed by the German Empire between 1904 and 1908.

## Material culture

Herero material culture is strongly shaped by cattle, pastoral life, women’s dress, metal and leather ornaments, and wooden tools and weapons.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Herero clothing uses vivid fabrics, patchwork and patterns linked to cattle horns.

- **Ohorokova dresses** (*Ohorokova*) — These floor-length dresses may use up to ten metres of vivid fabric and several petticoats.
- **Horned headdress** (*Otjikaiva*) — The otjikaiva is made to match or coordinate with women’s dresses and may be formed from rolled-up newspaper covered in fabric.
- **Traditional horn headdress** (*Ekori*) — The Ekori symbolized cow horns, but missionaries rejected its shape as a symbol of the devil.
- **Patchworked dresses** — Everyday dresses may be made from small fabric pieces, including cloth saved from older garments.
- **Pattern motifs** — Named motifs include cow horns, vertical zig-zags and serrated edges.

### Clothing & dress

Herero women are known for full, floor-length dresses and horn-shaped headdresses, while men wear military-style clothes for ceremonies.

- **Women’s dress** (*Ohorokova*) — The ohorokova has a high neck, long sleeves, a full gathered skirt and multiple petticoats.
- **Horn-shaped headdress** (*Otjikaiva*) — Women wear the horizontal otjikaiva as a tribute to cows that historically sustained the Herero.
- **Ceremonial military clothing** — Men wear peaked caps, berets, epaulettes, aiguillettes and gaiters in a military style.
- **Women’s neckerchief** — Coordinating neckerchiefs are knotted around the neck.
- **Decorative dress pins** — Brooches and pins may be attached to the centre front of the otjikaiva.

The supplied sources do not describe Herero architecture.

- **Straight-bladed sword** — The sword has a straight iron blade and a hard brown wooden hilt and sheath.
- **Wooden crossbow** — A wooden crossbow is recorded among the objects.
- **Smoking pipe** — The pipe has a horn mouthpiece, a steatite bowl and a white-metal cover joined to the stem by a chain.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Herero ornaments use iron, copper, steel, leather, fibre, ostrich eggshell and thongs.

- **Iron-bead necklet** — One necklet has four strings of cylindrical iron beads and a leather front plate decorated with smaller beads.

Herero religious life includes the holy fire Okuruuo and ceremonies involving cattle.

- **Holy fire** (*Okuruuo*) — The holy fire at Okahandja links the people with ancestors, who speak to Ndjambi on their behalf.
- **Other name for the holy fire** (*OtjikaTjamuaha*) — OtjikaTjamuaha is another name for Okuruuo.
- **Relighting the fire** — During immigration, the holy fire was doused and quickly relit.
- **Marriage cattle feast** — Cattle are normally eaten during marriage celebrations.
- **Animal sacrifice** — Cows or other animals may be sacrificed in religious or ancestral-veneration ceremonies.

## Foodways

Cattle are central to Herero foodways, work and social life.

- **Sour milk** (*Omaere*) — Women prepared sour milk called Omaere in pre-colonial times.
- **Milk** — The worth of an OmuHerero woman was measured by milk.
- **Cattle meat** — Cattle are normally eaten at marriages.
- **Goat and sheep meat** — Goats and sheep are kept for meat.
- **Goat dung medicine** — Goat dung is considered medicinal and is normally used to treat chickenpox.

## Oral tradition & literature

The supplied sources do not describe Herero oral literature, but they record strong historical memory and fiction about the genocide.

- **Ceremonial historical memory** — Men’s military-style clothing honours fallen ancestors and keeps their memories alive.
- **Morenga** — Uwe Timm’s novel Morenga is a literary work about the Herero genocide.
- **Mama Namibia** — Mari Serebrov’s Mama Namibia is a literary work about the Herero genocide.
- **We Are Proud to Present a Presentation About the Herero of Namibia** — Jackie Sibblies Drury’s 2012 play is a literary representation of the Herero genocide.
- **The Eagles of Malice** — Anthony Scholefield’s 1968 work is a literary representation of the Herero genocide.

## Language & religion

Otjiherero is widely used in education and broadcasting, while Herero religion combines Christian practice with belief in the holy fire.

- **Herero language** (*Otjiherero*) — Otjiherero is spoken by Herero and Mbanderu people in Namibia and Botswana and by small communities in southwestern Angola.

The Hambukushu are associated with rain-making abilities in the Okavango Delta and with basket weaving, while their women are known for using traps to catch fish.

## Overview

The Tswana, or Batswana, are a Bantu ethnic group native to Southern Africa. They inhabit south and eastern Botswana and the North West, Northern Cape, Gauteng, Free State, and other provinces of South Africa; Tswana-speaking communities are also found in parts of Namibia and Zimbabwe. Ethnic Tswana made up approximately 85% of Botswana’s population in 2011, while Tswana speakers in South Africa numbered over 4 million in 2012. Their language, Tswana or Setswana, belongs to the Bantu languages and is closely related to Sepedi and Sesotho. Tswana society has historically been organised through chiefdoms, clan-based lineages, cattle-based wealth, customary law, craft production, public assemblies, initiation systems, music, and foodways.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Leteisi** — Batswana wear a cotton fabric known in Setswana as *Leteisi* and in Sotho as *Shweshwe*. The source associates it with wedding celebrations and other traditional celebrations.

**Mogagolwane** — *Mogagolwane* is a checkered small blanket worn by mothers during traditional baby-showers and by married women during traditional weddings. Batswana women also wear it during initiation ceremonies and funerals.

The sources used do not document further Tswana textile traditions or a comparative account distinguishing these fabrics from neighbouring cultures’ equivalents.

**Motif vocabulary.** Triangular patterns, incised dots, faint black painted decoration, chevrons, and incised oval motifs are named in the museum catalogue descriptions.

### Clothing & dress

Batswana women wear *mogagolwane*, a checkered small blanket, during traditional baby-showers, weddings, initiation ceremonies, and funerals. The source identifies *Leteisi*, also called *Shweshwe*, as a cotton fabric used for weddings and other traditional celebrations. A museum photograph describes adult women wearing skirts, head-cloths, and blouses in a Tswana village. Museum objects include a cloak made of ox hide, an apron made of beads, a leather sandal, a woven wire belt, waist-bands, and waist ornaments made with ostrich eggshell discs, leather, fibre cord, and coloured red ochre. A dance head-dress is made of porcupine bristles mounted on a leather band. The sources do not describe everyday men’s clothing in further detail.

### Architecture

Tswana settlements historically included circular stone-walled family compounds. Kweneng’ Ruins, occupied from the 15th to the 19th century CE, consisted of sizeable settlements spread over an area 10 km long and 2 km wide. A British Museum photograph shows a Tswana village with a circular, thatched-roof building. The museum catalogue also records a model house made of thatch, paper, board, and straw, placed on a marked-up base board. A Museum of Ethnography photograph describes a modern house in Seronga surrounded by a traditional wall associated with older building traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Traditional Tswana craft production included pottery, metalworking, woodworking, basket weaving, and leatherwork. Potters made clay pots for storing water and traditional beer and for cooking. Museum objects include an earthenware milk pot with a constricted neck, black and red triangular patterns, and incised dots; a wide red earthenware bowl with faint black decoration; a wooden tripod vessel with chevrons; and a wooden bowl with a short handle. Other recorded objects include a ladle, wooden headrest, soapstone smoking-pipe bowls, carved wooden toys, and clay models of quadrupeds. Metalwork includes iron-bladed daggers, knives, battle-axes, brass bangles, copper beads, and wire ornaments.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Museum records document necklaces made from alternating seeds and beads, ostrich eggshell pieces strung on twisted fibre, and ostrich eggshell discs combined with leather. Waist ornaments use ostrich eggshell discs, leather discs, fibre cord, hide, and red ochre. Armlets and bangles are made from brass coils, brass wire, copper beads, and bright iron wire. A charm is made of cane bound with string, with gourd ends and strings of buttons and beads. A snuff-box combines carved ivory, wood, a small bearded human head, incised oval motifs, and a leather strap; another snuff-flask or box is made from springbok horn. The sources do not document tattoos, henna, or hair practices.

## Music & performance

Traditional Tswana music is performed during feasts and special occasions, including beer gatherings, weddings, and initiation ceremonies. Tswana music is mostly vocal and may be performed without drums depending on the occasion. Vocal music is classified as *dipina*, or songs, according to its function within social institutions. Music produced during initiation ceremonies is called *moamo*. The songs may be *mainaane a segologolo*, described as folklore of great import, or contemporary songs by a known composer, a *motlhami*.

Tswana songs may be sung in unison, *pina e e kodunngwe*, or in two or more parts. Multipart songs commonly use call and response: the call is *segalodimo* and the response is *segalo tlase*. Traditional communal music is described as largely pentatonic and associated with rhythmic bodily movements. The source connects musical performance with the agricultural seasons: *Letlhafula* is associated with hoeing and work-party songs; *Mariga* with children’s fireside story songs; *Dikgakologo* with women and children singing in the fields; and *Selemo* with beer-brewing, beer-songs, and beer-dances.

Instruments include *Setinkane*, a miniature piano, *Segankure* or *Segaba*, *Moropa* or *Meropa*, and *phala*. The *segaba* is a one-string instrument resembling a violin, while the *setinkane* is made with varying forks and played like a keyboard. Bows include *lengope*, *senwana*, *setinkane*, and *nokukwane*. Other instruments include the drum *moropa*, antelope horn *lepapata*, leg rattles *mathlo*, and whistles called *lengwane*, *lethlaka noka*, *mothlatsa*, *naka*, and *palo llo*. Modern Tswana music includes Tswana rap known as *Motswako*.

## Dance & theatre

The sources connect Tswana music and dance with feasts, beer gatherings, weddings, initiation ceremonies, agricultural seasons, and group dancing. Group dancing may use the *moropa* drum, *lepapata* antelope horn, and *mathlo* leg rattles. Beer-dances are associated with *Selemo*, the summer season in the classification of Tswana music. The sources used do not document named dramatic traditions, theatre forms, or specific dances.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not identify an annual Tswana festival calendar or dated festivals. They do associate musical and communal activities with four agricultural seasons: *Letlhafula* or Autumn, *Mariga* or Winter, *Dikgakologo* or Spring, and *Selemo* or Summer. These seasons are linked respectively with hoeing and work-party songs, children’s fireside story songs, singing in the fields, and beer-brewing, beer-songs, and beer-dances.

Tswana life-cycle and initiation practices include *Bojale*, a female initiation practice through which girls were incorporated into female *mephato*. Its training included songs, community responsibilities, morality, and preparation for marriage and motherhood. Male initiation involved *bogwane*, a preparatory phase, followed by enrolment into initiation camps. Boys of 16 years were taken to a remote place and circumcised; after training, they were brought to the *kgotla*, given a regimental name, and presented with weapons, including specialized daggers. Marriage was formalised through *bogadi*, usually cattle, while negotiations called *patlo* were conducted between families. The sources mention weddings and funerals as occasions for dress, music, and food but do not provide funeral rites in further detail.

## Foodways

*Bogobe* is a staple food made from sorghum meal and eaten with meat or vegetables. The most popular sorghum porridge is *Ting*. *Bogobe jwa Logala* or *Sengana* is made from sorghum porridge mixed or cooked with milk. *Seswaa*, described as Botswana’s national dish, consists of pounded or shredded meat and is often served with *Bogobe*. The source associates it with weddings, funerals, and other celebrations.

*Madila* is sour cultured milk prepared from cow and goat milk until fully matured. Traditionally, it was prepared using *Lekuka*, a leather sack or bag used for processing and storing it. *Madila* is also eaten as relish with pap and used in *motogo*, a soft porridge. Museum records include a milk pot made of earthenware with a constricted neck and black and red triangular patterns. A museum photograph from Kanye, Botswana, shows a woman using a large wooden pestle and mortar. The sources do not describe dietary rules, tea or coffee traditions, or additional ceremonial foods.

## Oral tradition & literature

A famous Tswana proverb is “Mmualebe o a bo a bua la gagwe,” translated in the source as meaning that even the one who speaks “badly” must be allowed to speak. It is described as a cornerstone of *kgotla* governance, where people voice their opinions and the *Kgosi* brings different views together into a decision acceptable to the community.

Tswana oral traditions include creation myths concerning *Modimo*, *Badimo*, *Loowe*, *Tintibane*, and *Matsieng*. According to the source, the first man and animals emerged from a hole in the earth at Lowe near Mochudi, while Matsieng left giant footprints in sandstone. The sources used do not document a named Tswana epic, a literary cycle, or a contemporary preservation project.

## Language & religion

Tswana, also known by its native name Setswana, is a Bantu language indigenous to Southern Africa. It is spoken in Botswana and South Africa and is also found in Zimbabwe and Namibia. It is a lingua franca in Botswana and parts of South Africa, while *Sepitori* is an urbanised variety associated with Pretoria. Setswana orthography is based on the Latin alphabet. The first European description is associated with Hinrich Lichtenstein’s 1806 work among the Batlhaping; Robert Moffat published Setswana religious and educational works, and a complete Bible translation appeared in 1857.

Traditional Tswana belief systems centre on *Modimo*, a supreme spiritual force associated with creation and cosmic order. *Badimo*, or ancestral spirits, serve as intermediaries between the living and Modimo. Ritual relationships with ancestors include “cooling,” *go fola*, and libations, *go phasa*. Ancestors are believed to influence weather and the arrival of rain, *Pula*. Christianity spread through missionary activity, while ancestral veneration and indigenous rituals declined in influence in some communities.

## Overview

The Tswana are a Bantu people of Southern Africa. Their society has been shaped by chiefdoms, clans, cattle, customary law, craft work, public assemblies, and initiation systems. Music, food, clothing, and rituals are tied to weddings, funerals, seasons, and community life. Setswana is spoken mainly in Botswana and South Africa, and also in Namibia and Zimbabwe.

## Material culture

Tswana material culture includes textiles, leatherwork, pottery, woodwork, basketry, metalwork, beadwork, and objects made from ostrich eggshell, horn, ivory, and fibre.

Tswana textile traditions include fabrics and blankets worn for weddings, initiation ceremonies, baby-showers, and funerals.

## Overview

The Murle are a Surmic ethnic group inhabiting Pibor County and the Boma area in Greater Pibor Administrative Area, South Sudan, as well as parts of southwestern Ethiopia. Murle oral traditions describe a mythical origin at *Jen*, located beyond Maji on the Boma plateau, followed by migration southward along the Omo River to Lake Rudolf, now Lake Turkana. From there, traditions recall movement through Kolobaadh in Taposa territory, over Mount Kathiangor, also called Kather, and into the Maruwa Hills, with some groups continuing to Boma. The Murle speak the Murle language, a member of the Surmic language family. Their pastoral way of life, oral traditions, cattle-based marriage system, and material culture are documented unevenly in the supplied sources.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The supplied sources do not document named Murle textile or pattern traditions.

**Motif vocabulary.** The supplied sources do not name Murle textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The supplied sources do not describe everyday or ceremonial Murle clothing in general. A British Museum catalogue records a woman’s apron ornament made from hide and decorated with short strings of round black seeds, light brown berries, and sections of small round white shells. It also records a waist belt made from a strip of hide with white cowrie shells sewn on one side. No named garment, head covering, footwear, or male dress tradition is described in the supplied sources.

### Architecture

The supplied sources do not describe Murle houses, huts, shelters, roofs, building materials, settlement plans, or architectural decoration. Arensen’s *Sticks and straw: Comparative house forms in southern Sudan and northern Kenya* is listed among the references, but its contents are not supplied here.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records several wooden objects associated with the displayed material culture. These include a club made of wood with a thin round handle and flattish head, and a wooden throwing-club described as a missile weapon. A tobacco pouch consists of a wooden cylinder with a skin cover secured by a strap to a hole in the bottom. The catalogue does not describe Murle metalwork, pottery production, cooking vessels, agricultural tools, or other household goods.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The British Museum records several women’s lower-lip ornaments. They are made of earthenware pricked with circles and lines, wood, ivory, or rhinoceros horn. The catalogue includes a wooden lip ornament, a lip ornament made of ivory, and several ornaments identified as made of rhinoceros horn or possibly rhinoceros horn. The supplied sources do not explain the ornaments’ names, meanings, ritual functions, or relation to age, marriage, or status. No tattooing, henna, or hair practice is documented.

## Music & performance

Murle oral traditions are preserved in songs and myths. One song recalls the creation of Murle humanity at *Jen*, while another version connects the first union between spirit and woman with the birth of Murimaan. The sources also state that a song about creation was still performed at the time of the account. Murle songs and myths describe *Jen* as a mythical Eden and associate it with the arrival of the ancestors, black cattle, and sweet tobacco.

The supplied sources do not name Murle instruments, musical genres, dances performed with music, or performance institutions. They do record that the rat has a ceremonial association with Murle funerary rites, particularly the deaths of Kelenya chiefs and their senior wives. No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription concerns this ethnic group.

## Dance & theatre

The supplied sources do not describe named Murle dances, theatrical traditions, mask performances, shadow theatre, or entertainment genres. They mention songs and myths, including creation narratives and stories concerning Murimaan, Jen, Manidherbo, the Pleiades, and the Etiwur stories about the discovery of animals.

## Festivals & rituals

The supplied sources do not identify an annual Murle festival calendar or provide dates for seasonal celebrations. They describe several ritual and religious associations. In Murle cosmology, *Jen* is venerated as a sacred point of origin and symbolizes the East, the source of life, rainfall, and ancestral memory. The rat has an enduring ceremonial association with funerary rites involving Kelenya chiefs and their senior wives.

Marriage is connected to bride wealth: men can marry only after paying several dozens of cows. The sources describe this system as a major factor in Murle social and economic life. They also state that Murle practice a blend of animism and Christianity, and that elders and witches often function as trouble fixers. The supplied sources do not describe initiation ceremonies, birth rites, wedding procedures, annual observances, or named funerals in detail.

## Foodways

The supplied sources do not document named Murle dishes, staple grains, cooking methods, dietary rules, tea or coffee traditions, or ceremonial foods. They mention tobacco in Murle creation traditions, including a verse describing tobacco at *Jen* as sweet like cattle. The sources also describe pastoral dependence on cattle and note localized shortages of rain, drinking water, bush fruits, and cattle grass. No further food preparation or cuisine is covered by the supplied sources.

## Oral tradition & literature

Murle oral traditions, recorded by Bazzet Lewis, describe the community’s origins and migrations. *Jen*, beyond Maji on the Boma plateau, is presented as a sacred place of origin. One creation account describes women descending from the heavens to Jen, where a woman encountered a spirit hidden among grass. A second woman later gave birth to Murimaan, who became the founding ancestor of the Murle. Another version names Abei as the grandmother of all mankind and Murimaan as the progenitor of Murle chiefs.

The traditions also refer to Jok, a great spirit, and Tammu, a term denoting God, rain, and the sky. Other narratives concern Manidherbo, the Pleiades, and Etiwur stories about the discovery of animals. The sources state that these episodes are more fragmented and contain internal contradictions. Murle songs and myths also preserve memories of migration along the Omo River, through Kolobaadh, over Mount Kathiangor, and into the Maruwa Hills.

## Language & religion

Murle, also called Ajibba, Beir, Merule, Mourle, or Murule, is a Surmic language spoken by the Murle people in southeastern South Sudan near the Ethiopian border. A very small number of Murle live across the border in southwestern Ethiopia. Murle clauses have basic verb–subject–object order, and the morphology of the verb agrees with the person and number of the subject and can also indicate those of the object. Number marking on nouns is complex, and vowel length is distinctive. The New Testament has been translated into Murle.

The Murle are described as practicing a blend of animism and Christianity. Their cosmology includes Jok and Tammu, who are sometimes described as distinct but are often used interchangeably by Murle speakers. Jok is described as masculine and resident in heaven, while Tammu is more frequently invoked in general discourse. Elders and witches often function as trouble fixers.

## Overview

The Bamun are a people of Cameroon’s highlands. Their language is known as Bamum, *Shü Pamom*, *Shümom*, Shupamem, Bamun, or Bamoun. Bamum is an Eastern Grassfields language with approximately 600,000–700,000 speakers in 2025. The language is associated with an original script developed by King Njoya and his palace circle in the Kingdom of Bamum around 1895. Museum catalogue material identifies Bamun objects including brass figures, smoking-pipes, masks, a staff finial, a palm-wine bottle, a woven bag, and an arm-dagger with sheath.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document named Bamun textile or pattern traditions.

**Palm-wine bottle** — A museum catalogue records a palm-wine bottle with bead mosaic.

title: "Duala"
subtitle: "Cameroon"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]

## Overview

The Duala are a Bantu ethnic group of Cameroon, concentrated mainly in the Littoral Province, especially in the Moungo, Nkam, and Wouri divisions. Their settlements lie along the coast or just inland, with the Wouri estuary—where the Wouri, Mungo, and Dibamba Rivers meet—as the centre of Duala country. Douala is their traditional capital, and many Duala live in and around the city. The group is closely related to other Sawa or coastal peoples, including the Ewodi, Bodiman, Pongo, Bakole, Bakweri, Bamboko, Isubu, Limba, Mungo, Wovea, and Oroko. Duala belongs to the Bantu language family and the Niger–Congo language family. The Duala became prominent coastal traders by the 16th century and have remained influential through trade, education, Christianity, urban employment, and ownership of property.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document a distinctive Duala textile or woven-cloth tradition.

The museum records do, however, document several forms of carved wooden material culture:

**Carved wooden stools** — British Museum records describe rectangular stools with crescent-shaped seats, open-work bases, small or half-height backrests, and carved supports. One stool has female figures with raised arms supporting the seat; another has leopards carved at the front and back, circles of burnt decoration, and dark-brown staining.

**Serpent-supported stool** — One British Museum stool has an open-work base with two S-figured serpents and a curved seat.

**Inscribed stool** — A stool carved from a single block has a crescent-shaped seat, a bird and two leopards on one side of its support structure, and the inscription “KAMEFUN” on the other.

**Prestige seat** — The Metropolitan Museum of Art catalogue records a wooden prestige seat dating from the mid–late 19th century.

**Pigmented stool** — Another British Museum object is a pale-coloured, carved and pigmented wooden stool with letters on its seat.

**Motif vocabulary.** female figures with raised arms, leopards, bird figure, S-figured serpents, circles of burnt decoration.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe Duala everyday clothing, ceremonial dress, head coverings, belts, footwear, or named garments.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe a characteristic Duala house form, roofing system, building materials, courtyard arrangement, or named architectural type. They do state that many Duala live in and around Douala, that many still own parts of the city, and that urban property ownership allows some to live from rents and development.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Duala material culture in the supplied records is represented chiefly by carved wood. The British Museum catalogue lists stools made from wood, including rectangular stools with open-work bases, curved or crescent-shaped seats, backrests, carved animals, human figures, serpents, letters, inscriptions, staining, pigmentation, and burnt decoration. The Metropolitan Museum of Art records a wooden prestige seat from the mid–late 19th century.

A Museum of Ethnography record describes an instrument made from a wooden plate with iron keys and a small ornamented gourd attached by a string. The plate is recorded as 12.2 centimetres long and 8.8 centimetres wide, and the object is identified with Cameroon and Duala.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not document Duala jewelry, body ornament, tattoos, henna, hair practices, amulets, or named adornment types.

## Music & performance

The Duala language article identifies Duala as a tonal language with subject–verb–object word order and records its historical use in religious and informal contexts. The Duala people article states that, at least until the German period, Duala men used a kind of “drum language”: coded messages were tapped out to communicate news over long distances.

A Museum of Ethnography catalogue record describes a small instrument associated with Duala. It consists of a wooden plate with iron keys, identified in the record as being of a “sansatyp” type, with a small ornamented gourd forming the resonating bottom. The gourd was attached to the instrument by a string. The catalogue gives the plate’s length as 12.2 centimetres and its width as 8.8 centimetres.

Pirogue racing has traditionally been the most important Duala sport and has a performance dimension involving music, display, competition, and divination. During the German colonial period, races were held annually on 27 January, identified in the source as the Kaiser’s birthday. Under the French, races became semiannual and were held on 14 July and 11 November. A typical racing pirogue is 20–28 metres long, has no keel, and has a bow carved with intricate designs. Each vessel is manned by 40–50 canoeists, mostly men who work as fishermen. In the past, diviners interpreted race results to predict the future; the source states that a Christian priest presides instead today.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document a named Duala dance, theatre form, masquerade, dramatic genre, or dance costume.

The Duala people article does record traditional annual festivals as visible expressions of pre-Christian beliefs in modern life. It also describes the Ngondo as an assembly of important chiefs and mentions secret societies including the Ekongolo, Jengu, Losango, and Munji. The sources do not provide performance descriptions for these institutions.

## Festivals & rituals

The Duala have been mostly Christianized since the 1930s, with Evangelical denominations, particularly the Baptist church, dominant. Remnants of pre-Christian ancestor worship persist, and the sea has an important place in Duala belief. The sources state that Duala belief holds that ancestors live in the sea. Demi-human water spirits called *Miengu*, singular *Jengu*, live in the waters and mediate between worshippers and God.

Traditional festivals held each year are described as the most visible modern expression of these beliefs. The supplied sources do not name these festivals or give their ritual calendars. The Ngondo is identified as an assembly of important chiefs, but the sources used here do not describe its ceremonies, dates, or relationship to an annual festival.

Pirogue races were held annually on 27 January during the German colonial period. Under the French administration, they occurred twice yearly, on 14 July and 11 November. Until the late 1930s, a family on Jebale Island was said to be able to summon the Miengu water spirits to assist favoured participants in the races.

The sources used do not describe Duala birth ceremonies, coming-of-age rites, weddings, funerals, or other life-cycle rituals. They do state that Duala inheritance is patrilineal and that property was traditionally divided among male heirs after the father’s death. The Duala traditionally practiced polygamy, although the custom became rarer after the introduction of Christianity.

## Foodways

The sources used do not document Duala staple foods, dishes, cooking methods, beverages, dietary rules, or ceremonial food.

They do state that rural Duala work mainly as fishermen and farmers, usually at subsistence level, and that fishing is the trade of choice. The museum records include a photograph titled “Infödingar från Duala efter lyckat fiske,” described as people from Duala after successful fishing. The sources do not identify the fish caught, the methods used, or the foods prepared from them.

## Oral tradition & literature

Early Duala history is preserved in oral traditions. The Duala trace their ancestry to a man named Mbedi, who lived in an area called Bakota in what is today Gabon or the Republic of the Congo. His sons Ewale and Dibombo migrated north to Pitti on the Dibamba River, where they separated after a quarrel. Ewale’s followers moved toward the Wouri River estuary, while Dibongo and his companions travelled toward the Sanaga River and later divided into different groups. Ewale’s people became the Duala, and Dibongo’s became the Limba.

According to Duala traditions, the Bakoko and Bassa occupied the Wouri estuary when the Duala arrived. The source places their displacement inland in the late 17th or early 18th century.

The sources used do not document a named Duala epic, folktale cycle, proverb tradition, riddle tradition, contemporary literary revival, or formal oral-literature preservation project. They do record the early missionaries’ development of a written form of the Duala language, partly to translate the Bible.

## Language & religion

Duala is a Bantu language and belongs to a subgroup called Sawabantu. It is a dialect cluster spoken by the Duala and Mungo peoples. The cluster includes Duala proper, Bodiman, Oli, Ewodi, Wuri, Pongo, and Mongo; Maho also notes a Duala-based pidgin called Jo. Duala is tonal and has subject–verb–object word order. It is part of the Niger–Congo language family.

The language became a trade language through its spread by early missionaries, especially among neighbouring Wovea and Isubu communities. Alfred Saker completed the first translation of the Bible into Duala in 1870. The Basel Mission promoted Duala as a lingua franca in southern Cameroon after German colonization, although German was used increasingly in schools. In 1910, German educational policy restricted the use of Duala in schools and official communications. After World War I, French was ordered in schools in the French mandate, while English-medium schooling became standard in the British mandate.

Most Duala have been Christianized since the 1930s. Evangelical denominations, particularly the Baptist church, dominate, while ancestor worship and belief in Miengu or Jengu water spirits remain part of the documented religious landscape.

- **Keyed plate instrument** (*sansatyp*) — A small instrument uses iron keys on a wooden plate and a gourd as its resonating bottom.
- **Pirogue racing** — Racing combines music, display, competition, and divination.

## Dance & theatre

The sources do not document a named Duala dance or theatre form.

- **Annual festivals** — Traditional annual festivals are described as visible expressions of pre-Christian beliefs.
- **Secret societies** (*Ekongolo, Jengu, Losango, Munji*) — The sources mention these secret societies but do not describe their performances.

## Festivals & rituals

Duala religious life combines Christianity with ancestor worship and belief in sea spirits.

- **Miengu water spirits** (*Miengu*) — These demi-human spirits live in the water and mediate between worshippers and God.
- **Jengu** — Jengu is the singular form of Miengu.
- **Ngondo** — Ngondo is an assembly of important chiefs, but its ceremonies are not described.
- **Pirogue race divination** — In the past, diviners read race results to predict the future, while a Christian priest presides today.
- **Jebale Island spirit help** — Until the late 1930s, a family on Jebale Island was said to summon Miengu to help favoured racers.

## Foodways

Fishing is the main rural trade, but the sources do not name Duala foods or cooking methods.

- **Fishing** — Rural Duala mainly work as fishermen and farmers, usually at subsistence level.
- **Successful fishing** — A museum photograph shows people from Duala after a successful fishing trip.

## Oral tradition & literature

Duala history is preserved through stories about migration and descent.

- **Mbedi ancestry** (*Mbedi*) — The Duala trace their ancestry to Mbedi, who lived in Bakota in what is now Gabon or the Republic of the Congo.
- **Ewale and Dibongo migration** (*Ewale, Dibongo*) — Mbedi’s sons moved north to Pitti, then separated after a quarrel and led different migrations.
- **Duala and Limba origins** — Ewale’s followers became the Duala, while Dibongo’s followers became the Limba.
- **Written Duala** — Early missionaries developed a written form of Duala partly to translate the Bible.

## Language & religion

Duala is a tonal Bantu language shaped by trade, missionary work, and changing colonial school policies.

- **Duala language cluster** (*Duala, Bodiman, Oli, Ewodi, Wuri, Pongo, Mongo*) — The cluster includes several related speech forms used by the Duala and Mungo peoples.
- **Jo pidgin** (*Jo*) — Maho records a Duala-based pidgin.
- **Duala Bible** — Alfred Saker completed the first Bible translation into Duala in 1870.
- **Trade language** — Duala spread as a trade language among neighbouring Wovea and Isubu communities.
- **Christianity and older beliefs** (*Miengu, Jengu*) — Most Duala have been Christian since the 1930s, while ancestor worship and belief in water spirits remain documented.

title: "Masa"
subtitle: "Cameroon"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"

## Overview

The Masa, also called Massa, Masana, Banana, or Yagoua, are a Chadic ethnic group living in Cameroon and Chad. Their estimated population is 266,000 to 469,000, with the majority residing in Cameroon. Most speak the Massa language, which is also known as Masa or Masana and has approximately 200,000 speakers. Masa is spoken in southern Chad and northern Cameroon, including areas along the Logone River and parts of the Far North Region. The sources describe a society in which cattle ownership, fishing, sorghum cultivation, weaving, warfare, marriage exchanges, and religious affiliation all have important social roles. The group is also represented in museum collections by fishing equipment, armour, clothing, musical instruments, jewellery, and other objects.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document named Masa pattern traditions or distinctive motifs.

**Fishing devices** — The sources describe the Masa as good weavers who developed a broad range of fishing devices and techniques. Museum records include a fish trap made of reeds bound with string of vegetable fibre and a fishing net made of fibre netting fastened to a wooden frame.

**Woman’s dress** — A British Museum catalogue records a woman’s dress made of fibre string. The sources do not provide a vernacular name, pattern vocabulary, or comparison with neighbouring cultures.

**Basketry** — A greave in the museum catalogue is made in basketry using cane and leaf, while another recorded object is a basket made of leaf. The sources do not describe their patterns or production contexts.

**Loin-cloth** — A museum catalogue records a loin-cloth made of hide with metal fittings. No vernacular term, pattern, or ceremonial use is given.

**Cuirass** — The catalogue records a cuirass, or body armour, made of hide. The sources do not describe decoration or construction beyond its material.

**Shield** — The museum records include shields made of reed, and a shield made of reed, wood, and hide. No named designs or motifs are supplied.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no Masa motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The sources give limited information about Masa clothing. A British Museum catalogue records a woman’s dress made of fibre string and a loin-cloth made of hide with metal fittings. The same catalogue records armour and related equipment, including a hide cuirass, a bark-fibre war helmet, reed shields, and a greave made in basketry using cane and leaf. These records document materials and object types but do not distinguish everyday from ceremonial dress. They also do not provide vernacular garment names, information about footwear, belts, head coverings apart from the war helmet, or a detailed account of men’s and women’s clothing. The Wikipedia source states that men who participate in formalised fighting over livestock or honour have helmets and clubs, and that they fight in lines while encouraged by women.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Masa houses, settlement forms, building materials, roofs, decoration, named building types, or urban architectural traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources used do not describe Masa ceramics or named household forms. Museum records document objects made from several materials: a harp made of wood with wire strings; a basket made of leaf; a fish trap made of reeds bound with string of vegetable fibre; and a fishing net made of fibre netting fastened to a wooden frame. Metal objects include an iron anklet with engraved decoration, an iron collar, an iron bracelet, and circular lip-plugs made of tin. The catalogue also records rattles made of wicker, gourd, leather, and beads, as well as dance-rattles made of leather with seed pods attached.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum catalogue records an anklet made of iron with engraved decoration, a collar made of iron, a bracelet made of iron, and circular lip-plugs made of tin. These are the only documented forms of Masa body adornment in the supplied sources. The sources do not explain their social or ritual functions and do not discuss tattooing, scarification, body paint, hair practices, or other forms of adornment.

## Music & performance

The supplied sources document several musical instruments in the British Museum catalogue but do not identify their Masa names, performance settings, or musical genres. One harp is made of wood with wire strings. A pair of rattles is made of wicker, gourd, leather, and beads, and a pair of dance-rattles is made of leather with seed pods attached. The catalogue records do not explain whether these instruments are used in ceremonies, entertainment, religious practice, warfare, marriage exchanges, or other contexts.

The Wikipedia source states that women encourage men during formalised fighting over livestock or honour. It does not describe songs, instrumental music, chants, performance structures, or named musical traditions. The sources used therefore do not cover Masa song genres, musical theory, professional performers, or the relationship between music and social occasions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not describe named Masa dances, dramatic traditions, theatre, mask performance, shadow puppetry, or ceremonial dance. The museum catalogue records a pair of “dance-rattles” made of leather with seed pods attached, but supplies no information about the dances in which they are used or about their performers and contexts.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not document an annual Masa festival calendar, named seasonal festivals, dates, or religious celebrations. They also do not provide detailed accounts of birth ceremonies, initiation, funerals, or wedding rituals.

The sources do describe social and ritualised practices connected with cattle. Cattle ownership is central to many social activities, including bride prices, and a wife will cost a man cows. The Masa also participate in cattle lending, called *golla*, and use traditional cow-fattening cures called *gurna*. Formalised fighting can be caused by the theft of cows or by adultery. The fighting has rules: the wounded must be collected from combat, a man on the ground or a wounded man must not be hit, and the fighting must end at dusk. Women who participate in this kind of fight acquire prestige in Masa society.

## Foodways

The Masa cultivate early red sorghum, identified in the source as *Sorghum caudatum*, as a staple. They also engage throughout the year in fishing in the Logone River and its affluent. Over the last thirty years, the introduction of cash crops influenced the food economy through monetarisation and the extensive cultivation of rice, which is cultivated mainly by northern Masa. Groundnuts are also grown.

The sources state that the Masa settled on river banks in order to practise fishing. Their fish sauces are accompanied by sorrel, okra, and false sesame, which the source describes as producing a monotonous diet. The sources also describe the Masa as good weavers who developed fishing devices and techniques that enabled them to become traders in fresh and dried fish. No named dishes, cooking vessels, beverages, dietary rules, ceremonial foods, or food-related festivals are documented.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not document Masa epic poetry, folktale cycles, proverbs, riddles, written literature, or contemporary literary preservation efforts. They do record an oral historical tradition stating that the Massa left Sudan and arrived in northern Cameroon before the Tikar people. According to the same account, when Muslims entered the region to convert local populations, the Massa stayed while the Tikar fled south.

The sources also state that the Massa are said to be related to the Tikar and Bamileke peoples. The Musgum claim a Massa origin through a union between a Kotoko prince and a Massa woman. These accounts are the only documented oral or traditional narratives in the supplied material.

## Language & religion

Massa, also called Masana or Masa, is a Chadic language spoken in southern Chad and northern Cameroon by the Masa people. It has approximately 200,000 speakers. Dialects listed in the source are Bongor, Bugudum or Budugum, Domo, Gizay, Gumay, Ham, Walia, Wina or Viri, and Yagwa. Masa is spoken in the southern part of Mayo-Danay department in the Far North Region, including the arrondissements of Yagoua, Kalfou, Wina, Yele, and Guéré. Central Masa is spoken along the Logone River, while Western Masa includes Gizay around Guéré and Viri or Wina. The source also identifies Muzuk as a Masa dialect and states that its speakers are bilingual in Muzuk and Munjuk.

The sources state that 45% of the population is Muslim and another 45% is Christian. Thirty percent are mainline Catholics or Protestants, while another fifteen percent are Evangelical Christians. The sources also report clashes between different religious groups.

- [Masa language — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masa_language)
- UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: the supplied sources identify no inscription for this ethnic group.
- British Museum catalogue records supplied for the objects shown.

## Overview

The Mundang are an ethnic group in West Africa living in parts of Cameroon, Chad, and Nigeria. They speak Mundang, an Mbum language. In Cameroon, Mundang is spoken mainly in Mayo-Kani department, Far North Region, including Mindif, Moulvouday, and Kaélé, and by 44,700 speakers according to SIL 1982. Mundang is also spoken in southern Mayo-Kebi in Chad, in the east of Bibemi commune in Bénoué department, and toward the Chadian border. Mundang communities are documented as agricultural people whose material and intangible culture includes farming, cotton production, cattle and goats, pottery, weaving equipment, vernacular architecture, and music accompanying dance.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document a named Mundang textile or pattern tradition.

**Weaving equipment** — Museum catalogue records describe wooden and cane parts of looms, including a heddle pulley made of wood and leather, a shuttle, a weaving reed, a reed beater, and a wooden weaving implement. One canoe-shaped shuttle contains a piece of cane and a wooden cylinder wrapped with white cotton spun thread.

**Cotton thread** — The catalogue records cotton thread in connection with loom equipment, including white cotton spun thread and cotton thread wrapped around a wooden stick.

**Indigo-dyed cotton cloth** — An arm-dagger sheath is recorded as made of split cane bound with indigo-dyed cotton cloth and carrying a strap tied at the lower end with cotton thread.

**Motif vocabulary.** No named textile motifs are given in the sources.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not document Mundang everyday clothing, ceremonial dress, head coverings, belts, footwear, or named garments.

### Architecture

Mundang people in Léré built mud houses with straight roofs and polished interior walls. They also constructed circular corn silos or granaries that were accessed through the roof. The sources do not provide a vernacular name for these buildings, further architectural decoration, or information about courtyards, workshops, or urban building traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records pottery objects including a lamp with a round base tapering in, then out, then in, and flaring out for the rim; a round vase with a nearly vertical neck and a slightly flaring rim; a vase with a shoulder decorated with bands of alternating diagonal lines; and another vase made of pottery. Recorded iron objects include two knife blades, a sword, a comb cum razor, a razor blade, a double fish-hook, and decorative bands of iron wire on a club. Other objects include wooden throwing-clubs, ceremonial clubs, a fish trap made of fibre tied to a wooden frame, and a gourd held at the base of the net.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not document Mundang jewelry, personal ornaments, tattoos, henna, hair practices, or ritual body adornment.

## Music & performance

The Mundang people of Chad use the *billim* drum, described as a double-headed cylindrical drum with laced membranes. The drum accompanies dance rhythmically alongside an end-blown trumpet and a gourd-vessel wrattle. The drummer places the instrument on the ground and strikes each side with a hand.

The sources also describe families of musicians called griots by western writers. Sona Jobarteh is identified as a modern performing act outside of Africa who acknowledges her Mundang heritage and sees its influence in the bluesy sound of her music. The sources do not name specific song genres, repertories, performance ceremonies, or musical forms beyond the accompaniment of dance.

## Dance & theatre

The sources state that the *billim* drum is used to accompany dance rhythmically. They do not name a Mundang dance, theatrical tradition, mask performance, dramatic form, or distinction between ceremonial and entertainment dance.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not document Mundang festivals, annual ritual calendars, life-cycle rites, weddings, funerals, coming-of-age ceremonies, or ritual dates and seasons.

## Foodways

Historically, the Mundang were an agricultural people. At the beginning of the 20th century they grew and harvested peas, beans, potatoes, nuts, and durra. They also produced cotton and raised cattle and goats. Mundang communities brewed beer from millet. The sources do not provide named dishes, recipes, cooking methods, ceremonial foods, tea or coffee traditions, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not document Mundang folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, written literature, storytelling contexts, or literary preservation projects. They identify families of musicians called griots by western writers, but provide no account of their oral repertory.

## Language & religion

Mundang is an Mbum language of southern Chad and northern Cameroon, spoken by the Mundang people. The Gelama dialect of Cameroon may be a separate language. In Cameroon, Mundang is mainly spoken in Mayo-Kani department, Far North Region, in Mindif, Moulvouday, and Kaélé, and is also spoken to a lesser extent in the south of Mayo-Kebi, the east of Bibemi commune in Bénoué department, and toward the Chadian border. Mundang of Lere in Chad and Mundang of Cameroon, centered in Lara and Kaélé, are highly similar. Nasalization is marked by a tilde in the writing system. The sources used do not document Mundang religious traditions or spiritual practices.

## Foodways

Mundang foodways grew from farming, livestock keeping, and millet beer brewing.

## Overview

The Kapsiki, also called Ka-Tsepkye, are a people living on both sides of the border between North Cameroon and Northeast Nigeria. They are called Kapsiki in Cameroon and Kamwe, or Higi, in Nigeria, and together amount to about 120,000 people. In Cameroon they live on a plateau in the Far North Province, in the center of the Mandara Mountains; in Nigeria they live on mountain slopes and the western plain. They have lived in the area for five centuries and have maintained an isolated cultural setting. Their language, Psekiye or Kamwe, belongs to the Chadic language family. The Kapsiki are associated with village life, livestock farming, agriculture, and, particularly in Rumsiki, tourism. Their folk-cultural significance in the supplied sources is chiefly visible in their settlement history, language diversity, clothing objects, and resistance to Islamisation.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Beaded pubic aprons** — The supplied British Museum catalogue records describe pubic aprons made from multicoloured glass beads arranged in rows, pairs, or lozenge patterns on cotton string. The objects have cotton-thread waistbands and ties; some include larger plastic or glass beads, cowrie shells, cut seeds, nut shells, or large white glass beads suspended from the lower edge.

**Lozenge-patterned apron** — One catalogue record describes an apron made predominantly from red, yellow, green, and blue glass beads arranged in pairs to form lozenge patterns. Its lower edge has larger plastic and glass beads suspended on cotton-thread strings terminating in cowrie shells.

**Horned-quadruped apron** — Another recorded apron uses predominantly black, brown, yellow, white, and green glass beads arranged in rows. Its central design is a horned quadruped, with larger uncertain plastic or glass beads suspended from the lower edge.

**Bird-and-plant apron** — A further apron has multicoloured glass beads arranged in pairs in rows and a central blue, black, red, and yellow design of a bird in front of a tree or plant. The lower edge has larger plastic beads suspended on twisted cotton-thread strings terminating in cut seeds or nut shells.

**Triangular beaded apron** — One catalogue record identifies a triangular apron made from multicoloured glass beads arranged in lozenge patterns on cotton string. Cotton strings terminating in glass beads run around two sides.

**Motif vocabulary.** Lozenge patterns; horned quadruped; bird in front of a tree or plant.

### Clothing & dress

The supplied sources document pubic-cover aprons but do not describe everyday clothing, ceremonial dress, men’s garments, head coverings, belts, footwear, or gender-specific dress beyond the recorded apron objects. The catalogue records identify cotton-thread waistbands and ties, glass and plastic beads, cowrie shells, and possible seeds or nut shells as components of these aprons.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Kapsiki house forms, building materials, roofs, decoration, named building types, or urban architectural traditions. They state only that Kapsiki communities include villages of 2000–6000 people and that the Kapsiki live on a plateau in the Mandara Mountains, while the Kamwe live on mountain slopes and the western plain.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources used do not cover Kapsiki pottery, blacksmithing, ironwork, brasswork, funerary iron objects, wood carving, basketry, tools, or household goods. The museum records concern pubic-cover aprons made with glass beads, plastic beads, cotton string, cotton thread, cowrie shells, and possible seeds or nut shells.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not describe Kapsiki jewelry, tattoos, henna, hair practices, or ritual body adornment. The catalogue records document beadwork and suspended ornaments on pubic-cover aprons, including cowrie shells, large white glass beads, and possible seeds or nut shells.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not identify Kapsiki musical instruments, song genres, musical repertories, or performance contexts. The supplied material mentions a documentary and events organized by the Malima Project to promote educational activities in the area, but it does not describe their musical content.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not describe Kapsiki dances, theatre, dramatic traditions, masks, or performance distinctions. A supplied bibliographic note gives the title *The dancing dead: ritual and religion among the Kapsiki/Higi of north Cameroon and northeastern Nigeria*, but the supplied sources do not provide details of the dancing or ritual practices discussed in that work.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not provide an annual Kapsiki festival calendar or descriptions of birth, coming-of-age, wedding, funeral, seasonal, or harvest rites. They state that the Kapsiki resisted Islamisation during the Fulani jihad of Modibo Adama and Hama Yaji. The supplied material also gives the title *The dancing dead: ritual and religion among the Kapsiki/Higi of north Cameroon and northeastern Nigeria*, but contains no further account of ritual practice.

## Foodways

The sources used do not describe Kapsiki staple grains, dishes, cooking methods, brewing, dietary rules, ceremonial foods, or tea and coffee traditions. They state only that Kapsiki communities subsist on livestock farming and agriculture.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not identify Kapsiki folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles, storytelling contexts, or literary traditions. The Kapsiki language article records that a translation of the Bible into Psikyɛ, *Ghena ta Shala*, was published in 1988. The supplied sources also mention the Malima Project’s educational documentary and events, without describing their oral or literary content.

## Language & religion

Psekiye or Kamwe is a Chadic language with eleven dialects, including Nkafa, Sina, Ghye, Humsi, Dakwa, and Tilli. The language is also called Psikye, Psikya, or Kapsiki; varieties include Psikyɛ and Zləngə. In Cameroon, Psikya speakers use Margi for their own language and its three varieties, while in Nigeria it is called Higi. Psikyá is spoken in parts of Mokolo and Mogodé, including Roumzou, Mogode, and Roumsiki; Zléŋé and Wula are spoken in two neighborhoods of Oula. A Psikyɛ spelling developed by the Biblical Alliance of Cameroon uses additional letters and appears in the 1988 Bible translation *Ghena ta Shala*. In Cameroon, the Kapsiki are described as a Kirdi, or pagan, ethnic group because of their resistance to Islamisation during the Fulani jihad of Modibo Adama and Hama Yaji.

subtitle: "Burkina Faso"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"

## Overview

The Mossi, or Mosi, are a Gur ethnic group native to modern Burkina Faso, primarily in the Volta River basin. They constitute 52% of Burkina Faso’s population, or about 11.1 million people in 2010; significant numbers also live in Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Mali, and Togo. The Mossi speak Mooré, also known as Mossi, a Gur language of the Oti–Volta branch and part of the Niger–Congo family. Their society is organized hierarchically around family and state, with the Mogho Naaba as the highest political position, the Nakomse as a ruling class, and the Tengabisi as descendants of earlier farming peoples. Their masks, dolls, royal figures, textiles, and ceremonies are central subjects of the available material.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Cotton shawl** — A man’s prestige garment made of cotton, woven in thirteen narrow strips and hand sewn together. The warp and weft are hand spun and dyed indigo throughout; supplementary weft stripes and twisted warp-thread fringes decorate both ends.

**Indigo cotton textile** — A cotton textile from Ouagadougou shows stages of plain weaving and indigo dyeing. The catalogue records that it was knotted and dyed by a Mossi woman.

The sources used do not document additional Mossi pattern-bearing textile traditions.

### Clothing & dress

The sources document a man’s prestige garment described as a cotton shawl. It is made from thirteen narrow strips sewn together, with hand-spun cotton warp and weft dyed indigo throughout, supplementary weft stripes along the borders, and twisted warp-thread fringes at both ends. The sources do not describe everyday clothing, women’s clothing, head coverings, belts, footwear, or named ceremonial dress beyond this garment.

**Motif vocabulary.** Supplementary weft stripes; incised geometric designs on a wooden cap mask.

### Architecture

The sources do not describe Mossi house forms, compounds, roofs, walls, or urban architecture. Museum records include a weathered wooden house-post and a wooden tethering post, possibly for a chief’s house, surmounted by a carved human head with iron nails driven around the neck.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum records include an iron-headed hammer-club with a wooden shaft, a leather pull-out pouch with red fringes and stamped ornament, and a wooden tethering post possibly associated with a chief’s house. Other recorded objects include a bronze dancing figure holding a fan, an antelope figure made of metal, a wooden female figure with incised line patterns and a small iron band around the wrist, and a metal figure of a Fulani woman with a child at a well. The sources do not describe Mossi ceramics.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources do not provide a general account of Mossi jewelry, hair practices, tattoos, or ritual body adornment. A museum description of a Mossi mask records a female figure with scar tattoos on the body and face, while the Mossi doll entry mentions decoration with beads, pearls, shells, fabric, metal earrings, pieces of bone, or animal hide.

## Music & performance

The sources do not identify Mossi musical instruments, song genres, or a specific musical tradition. They do document performance in ritual and public contexts. Masks appear at burials, funerals, memorial services, and annual public festivals, and museum records state that a *wan-balinga* mask was worn and danced with at the funeral of a male or female elder and during annual memorial services.

The Friday Mogho Naaba court ceremony is connected with Mossi political history and the authority of the royal court. Its narrative concerns the Moro Naba’s sister fleeing north to Yadega, the kingdom called Yatenga, while carrying the amulets of power, or *nam*. The Moro Naba mounted a white horse three times and returned to the palace each time. The sources also state that bridles, saddles, stirrups, and other horse-related objects are important to the Nakomse, while carved wooden figures represent royal ancestors.

## Dance & theatre

Mossi mask performance is associated with funerals, memorial services, religious observances, rituals, and public festivals. The Nyonyose, described as the ancient farmers and spiritual segment of Mossi society, use masks, while the Nakomse, or chief class, do not. Masks accompany the deceased, observe whether proper funeral procedures are carried out, honor the dead, and verify whether the spirit merits admission into the world of ancestors.

A museum catalogue identifies the proper name of one mask as *wan-balinga*, a mythical figure who was the mother of the first Mossi ruler. The sources also record masks with elongated projections, horns, geometric designs, and animal forms. They do not describe a Mossi theatre tradition.

## Festivals & rituals

Ceremonies and celebrations pace Mossi life and express joy or suffering, as well as duties to the memory of ancestors. The Friday Mogho Naaba court ceremony recalls the flight of the Moro Naba’s sister to Yatenga with the *nam*, or amulets of power. The Moro Naba’s repeated departures on a white horse and returns to the palace explain why the kings of Yatenga claim to hold the power of Mossi rule.

Royal ancestors are represented by carved wooden figures displayed each year at royal festivals called *na possum*. At these festivals, the heads of households reaffirm allegiance and loyalty to the chief. The sources also name the International Art & Craft Fair, or Salon international de l’Artisanat de Ouagadougou, Week of the Culture, and the Atypical Nights of Koudougou as annual public festivals where masks from different Mossi regions appear.

Funeral and memorial practices are especially important. Masks appear at burials and at funeral or memorial services held at regular intervals during the years after an elder’s death. Without a proper funeral, the spirit is believed to remain near the home and cause trouble for descendants. The sources also describe a girl’s doll being placed in a hut after her excision ceremony and given to her younger sister on her wedding night.

## Foodways

The sources used do not cover Mossi staple foods, cooking methods, named dishes, ceremonial foods, beverages, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

Mossi history has largely been preserved through oral tradition, although Mossi records also exist and were primarily written using the Ajami script. Oral tradition tells of the marriage of Yennenga, a Mamprusi/Dagomba princess and warrior princess, and Rialé, a solitary Mandé hunter. Their son, Ouedraogo, is recognized as the father of the Mossi people.

The sources state that Yennenga was the daughter of Naa Gbewaa, a king of present-day northern Ghana. While exploring her kingdom on horseback, she lost her way and was rescued by Rialé. Gbewaa’s tomb is located in Pusiga in Ghana’s Upper East Region. The sources also mention *Contes du Larhallé*, followed by a collection of proverbs and devices of the Mossi country, as further reading.

## Language & religion

Mooré, also known as Mossi, is a Gur language of the Oti–Volta branch and one of the four official languages of Burkina Faso. It is spoken in Burkina Faso, Ghana, Ivory Coast, Benin, Niger, Mali, Togo, and Senegal, and is the main language in Ouagadougou. The language is closely related to Frafra and less closely related to Dagbani. Regional dialects are described for Yatenga, the northern region, Koupela, and Tenkodogo, though they are mutually intelligible. Mooré can be written with the national Burkinabé alphabet or the Goulsse alphabet.

Mossi spiritual life includes beliefs concerning ancestors, land, and ritual obligation. Ancestors are believed to influence life on earth and to help or punish descendants. Land is understood as a path to the ancestors and has a spiritual dimension. Masks are sacred links to the spirits of ancestors and nature. The sources do not provide a general account of contemporary religious affiliation.

## Sources & further reading

- Christopher D. Roy, *Art of the Upper Volta Rivers*, Chaffin, 1987.
- Christopher D. Roy, *Land of the Flying Masks*, Prestel, 2007.
- Yamba Tiendrébéogo and Robert Pageard, *Contes du Larhallé: suivis d'un recueil de proverbes et de devises du pays mossi*, 1963.
- Elliott P. Skinner, *The Mossi of the Upper Volta: The Political Development of a Sudanese People*.
- [Mossi people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mossi_people)
- [Mossi language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mossi_language)
- No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription for this ethnic group was included in the sources.
- British Museum, Museum of World Culture, and Cleveland Museum of Art catalogue records supplied for the objects shown.

## Language & religion

Mooré is the main Mossi language, while spiritual life centers on ancestors, land, masks, and ritual obligation.

- **Mooré** — Mooré, also called Mossi, is a Gur language of the Oti–Volta branch and one of Burkina Faso’s four official languages.
- **Mossi language** (*Mossi*) — Mossi is another name for Mooré, which is the main language in Ouagadougou.
- **Regional dialects** — Regional forms are described for Yatenga, the northern region, Koupela, and Tenkodogo, and they are mutually understandable.
- **Ancestor beliefs** — Ancestors are believed to influence earthly life and to help or punish their descendants.
- **Sacred masks** — Masks are sacred links to the spirits of ancestors and nature.

## Glossary

- *Mooré* — The Mossi language
- *Mossi* — Another name for Mooré

- *Ouedraogo* — Son of Yennenga and Rialé

---
title: "Lozi"
subtitle: "Zambia"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]
