## Overview

The Lozi, also known as Balozi, are a Bantu-speaking ethnic group native to Zambia and Zimbabwe. Their population is estimated at 1,562,000 in all countries combined. They refer to their land as *Bulozi* or *Barotseland*, centred on the floodplains of the Zambezi River. Most Lozi live on and around the Barotse Floodplain, and the annual movement between floodplain and higher ground strongly shapes their culture. Lozi society is organised around a monarchy whose reigning head, the Paramount King, is called the *Litunga*. The people include several tribes, among them the Bamakoma, Kwanda, Lukolwe, Bafwe, Batotela, Bayeyi, Mbowe, Bambukushu, Mishulundu, Muenyi, Mwanga, Ndundulu and Basubia. Their material culture includes pottery, basketry, woodcarving, musical instruments, masks and ceremonial dress.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document a distinct Lozi textile tradition in sufficient detail for this section.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name geometric decoration, zigzag decoration, geometric incisions, bands of raised geometric carving, rectangles, cross lines, cross rows, dots, rings, checkered-patterned squares, vertical bands and stripes.

### Clothing & dress

Lozi traditional dress distinguishes men’s and women’s clothing. The *siziba* is worn by men and consists of a shirt and a knee-length skirt. It is sometimes paired with a sleeveless jacket and *mashushu*, described as a red beret. Women wear the *musisi*, a garment possibly influenced by crinolines worn by wives of nineteenth-century missionaries. The supplied sources do not document Lozi footwear, belts, everyday clothing, hair practices or a separate catalogue of ceremonial dress beyond these garments and the *mashushu*. Museum records associated with Lozi *Makishi* describe round hats made of bark, willow and grass. One hat is recorded as 25.5cm high and another as 25cm high; both have traces of white and red on the outside and were used at *Makishi* dances.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Lozi houses, settlements, roofs, building materials, workshops or other vernacular architecture.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum records document a broad range of Lozi-associated household objects and tools. Pottery includes a water pot with a handle and painted decoration, a pottery vessel, a pottery mug with a loop handle and zigzag decoration, and a yellowish-brown pottery jar with grooves on the neck and shoulder, red ornament and ochre decoration. The jar was used for water or beer. Wooden household objects include bowls, pots, lids, a milk pot, a spoon, a dipper or ladle, a head-rest, a stool, a canoe model and a carved food-vessel lid. Basketry appears in baskets, bags, a receptacle with a cover, a mug and a rectangular receptacle. Metalworking is represented by iron axes, a dagger with a triangular blade, a razor, an adze with a steel blade and a double gong.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources document a composite neck ornament made from six lengths of coiled wire with a calabash pendant attached by string. An armlet consists of glass, ostrich eggshell and wooden beads on a vegetal-fibre cord. The museum records also describe charms made from materials including bone, wood, gum, *abrus* seeds, fibre, hair, antelope or duiker horn, feathers, calabash and glass. The sources used do not describe tattoos, henna, hair practices or the ritual functions of these ornaments and charms.

## Music & performance

The museum records identify numerous Lozi-associated musical instruments. These include a wooden xylophone called *sirimba*, with twelve keys, carved geometric decoration, fibre strings, iron screws and twelve calabash resonators. A pair of wooden beaters accompanies it. Other instruments include composite drums with wooden bodies, hide membranes and cords; a drum with a reptile-skin drumhead fixed with metal tacks; an antelope-horn hunting horn or trumpet; an ivory horn war-trumpet; an antelope-horn trumpet; a wooden-board *sansa* with metal keys and a gourd resonator; and an iron double gong. The catalogue also records a possible musical-instrument striker formed from a carved wooden rod with geometric incised decoration and brass-wire binding.

The sources do not identify named song genres, instrumental repertories or performance settings for these instruments. They do state that several Lozi dances were accompanied by singing and often by drums. *Liwale* and *Ngomalume* were ceremonial dances performed at royal events, while *Liimba*, *Lishemba* and *Sipelu* were performed in the evening. *Siyemboka* was performed at beer parties, festivals, ceremonies and girls’ initiations.

## Dance & theatre

The Luyana or Lozi had two main ceremonial dances. *Ngomalume* was a war dance performed by men, involving belly movement, while *Liwale* was performed by women. Neither was accompanied by singing, and both were performed at royal events. The account of *Ngomalume* includes the saying that “no hungry man can dance” it effectively.

Other dances included *Liimba*, *Lishemba* and *Sipelu*. These were accompanied by singing and often drums and were performed in the evening. In *Sipelu*, men and women stood in opposite lines, with only one or two pairs dancing at a time. *Siyemboka* was introduced by the Mbunda and was performed at beer parties, festivals, ceremonies and girls’ initiations.

The museum records document *Makishi* masks and hats associated with dance. A *Nalandile* mask was made of bark fabric stretched over a wicker frame, with a wooden face painted dark brown and small holes at the eyes, nose and forehead. Another mask had brown and white cross lines and six cross rows of brown and white dots. A further mask, 37cm in dimension, had lines and rings around the eyes and checkered-patterned squares on the cheeks.

## Festivals & rituals

Lozi culture is strongly influenced by the flood cycle of the Zambezi River. At the beginning of the wet season, annual migrations take place from the floodplain to higher ground. The most important of these events and festivals is *Kuomboka*, during which the *Litunga* moves from Lealui in the flood plain to Limulunga on higher ground. The event usually takes place in February or March. The annual floods displace hundreds of people every year.

The sources also connect performance traditions with royal events, festivals, ceremonies, beer parties and girls’ initiations. *Ngomalume* and *Liwale* were performed at royal events, while *Siyemboka* was performed at beer parties, festivals, ceremonies and girls’ initiations. The museum records identify *Makishi* masks and hats as objects used in *Makishi* dances and state that the hats were for initiands or initiators.

The sources used do not describe Lozi birth, wedding, funeral or other life-cycle rites in detail. They also do not provide a full annual festival calendar beyond *Kuomboka* and the listed performance contexts.

## Foodways

The supplied sources mention food and drink only in limited contexts. A museum catalogue records a pottery jar used for water or beer, while the Lozi mythology describes Kamunu killing animals and cooking their meat for food. Museum objects include a wooden milk pot and a wooden dipper or ladle. A carved wooden lid is identified as a lid for a food vessel.

The sources do not identify staple grains, named dishes, cooking methods, tea or coffee traditions, dietary rules or a wider ceremonial food system. They also do not document the preparation of beer or milk beyond the names and uses of the associated vessels.

## Oral tradition & literature

Lozi mythology describes Nyambe as a creator god whom the Lozi call Nyambe. Nyambe’s wife was Nasilele and his mother was Ngula. One founding account presents Kamunu as the first human being. Nyambe instructed Kamunu to name the other creations and told him that the animals were his siblings. Kamunu learned skills including mastery over fire, forging metal, moulding pottery, carving spoons, plates and canoes, sowing crops and domesticating animals. After Kamunu repeatedly killed animals, Nyambe withdrew from him and eventually moved from Earth into heaven, called *Litooma* in Lozi mythology.

Other versions describe Nyambe and Nasilele’s daughter Mwambwa as the first Luyi sovereign and founder of the nation. Her eldest daughter Mbuyu later took over the sovereignty. A further version presents Mwambwa as the first female chief of the Luyi people and gives her the title *Njemakati*, meaning “a woman from whom the kingdom originates.” The sources state that these myths exist in several versions and have changed through oral transmission.

## Language & religion

Lozi, also known as *Silozi* and *Rozi*, is a Bantu language of the Niger–Congo language family within the Sotho–Tswana branch of Zone S, identified as S.30. It is spoken primarily in southwestern Zambia and in Namibia. The language is closely related to Northern Sotho, Tswana, Kgalagari and Sotho. *Silozi* is the endonym used by native speakers, and Lozi is sometimes written as Rotse.

The origins of Silozi are traced to a mixture of Luyana and Kololo. The Luyana settled on the upper Zambezi floodplains, where they established a kingdom called Barotseland or Bulozi. In the 1830s, the Kololo conquered the Luyana and imposed their rule and language. By 1864, the indigenous population had overthrown the Kololo, but the original Luyana language had largely been replaced by the hybrid language Silozi. The sources describe Nyambe as creator god in Lozi mythology and record several accounts of creation, death and the origin of Lozi sovereignty. They do not describe the current religious landscape.

## Sources & further reading

- Harold Scheub, “Nyambe And The Origin of Death,” in *A Dictionary of African Mythology*, Oxford University Press, 2000.
- Harold Scheub, “Nyambe Moves Away from Aggressive Men,” in *A Dictionary of African Mythology*, Oxford University Press, 2000.
- Harold Scheub, “Nyambi Flees from Assertive Men,” in *A Dictionary of African Mythology*, Oxford University Press, 2000.
- [Lozi people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lozi_people)
- [Lozi mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lozi_mythology)
- [Lozi language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lozi_language)

## Material culture

Lozi material culture uses clay, wood, basketry, metal, fibre, horn, ivory, beads and calabashes for household objects, clothing, instruments and ceremonial items.

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources do not describe a distinct Lozi textile tradition, but they record many geometric patterns.

Traditional Lozi dress includes separate garments for men and women.

The sources do not describe Lozi houses, settlements or building traditions.

Recorded Lozi adornments use wire, beads, calabash, fibre and natural materials.

## Music & performance

Lozi musical instruments include xylophones, drums, horns, sansas and gongs.

Lozi dances include royal dances, evening dances, initiation dances and masked Makishi performances.

The flood cycle shapes Lozi movement, royal ceremonies and annual festivals.

- **Girls’ initiations** — Siyemboka is performed during girls’ initiations.

## Foodways

The profile records only a few Lozi food and drink vessels and one mythic account of cooking meat.

- **Water or beer jar** — A pottery jar was used to hold water or beer.

Lozi myths tell of Nyambe, the first human Kamunu and the origins of Lozi sovereignty.

---
title: "Luvale"
subtitle: "Zambia"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]
---

## Overview

The Luvale, also called Lovale, Balovale, Lubale, Lwena, or Luena, are a Bantu ethnic group living mainly in northwestern Zambia and southeastern Angola. In Zambia they are centered on Zambezi, formerly known as Balovale, and are also found in places including the Lukanga Swamp and Lusaka; in Angola they reside in the east of Moxico Province. They are closely related to the Lunda and Ndembu, and share cultural similarities with the Kaonde, Chokwe, and Luchazi. Luvale belongs to the Niger-Congo language phylum and is a west central Bantu language. The sources give approximately 168,000 speakers in Zambia and 180 thousand in Angola. Luvale culture is documented through matrilineal social organization, initiation ceremonies, mask traditions, basketry, musical instruments, ritual practices, and agricultural life.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Visalo** — Luvale are known for weaving mats called *visalo*. The sources identify these as part of Luvale craft production but do not provide further information about their materials, patterns, or techniques.

**Costume of coloured vegetable string** — A museum catalogue records a costume consisting of a complete tight-fitting net made from coloured vegetable string.

**Barkcloth makishi costumes** — During *mukanda*, makishi wear elaborate masks and dyed woven costumes made from barkcloth. The sources describe these costumes in connection with initiation and ancestral representation rather than as everyday clothing.

**Winnowing basket** — A British Museum record describes a reed and string plaited flat basket with a twilled pattern in dark and light colour, a stiffened rim, and a loop. It was used as a winnowing tray.

**Plaited basket** — Another catalogue record describes a reed-plaited basket with a neck in a black and brown twilled pattern, a round top, and a square bottom.

**Basket-work dish** — A porridge dish is recorded as being made of basket-work.

**Wooden double dish** — A museum record describes a carved wooden double dish, each dish having a lid; the upper lid carries a fish and the object is circular.

**Motif vocabulary.** Fish on a lid; geometric carving; human face; tall hair-do; dark and light twilled pattern.

### Clothing & dress

The sources describe both ordinary and ceremonial clothing only in limited detail. During *wali*, an initiate makes a girdle called a *zeva*, which she wears throughout the ceremony. When she returns to her village, she is covered in a traditional cotton cloth called *chitenge*. The *wali* initiate, or *mwali*, remains in seclusion and receives instruction from an older woman called a *chilombola*. During *mukanda*, male initiates and the makishi are associated with dyed woven costumes made from barkcloth. The sources do not describe ordinary Luvale garments, footwear, daily head coverings, or a separate men’s and women’s clothing system beyond these ceremonial items. A museum catalogue records a hemispherical head-dress made of bark string arranged in closely set projecting loops and covered with red earth and grease.

### Architecture

The sources do not provide a general description of Luvale houses, village layouts, roofs, or construction methods. They mention a grass hut called a *litungu*, which is built for a girl undergoing *wali* initiation after she has been taken into seclusion near a fig tree called *muulya*. The sources also describe an isolated bush camp used by boys during the seclusion stage of *mukanda*, but do not give its construction details.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Luvale are described as skilled in pottery, metalwork, basketry, mat weaving, and woodwork. Their wooden objects include stools, some made entirely of wood and others with a hide seat on a wooden frame called a *likupu*. Museum records include axes with iron or steel blades and carved or coloured wooden handles, an iron-bladed knife with a wooden handle, two wooden cassava ladles, and a wooden comb with ten teeth and a handle carved with a human face and tall hair-do. A chair of hard dark wood is made after a European model and has a hide-covered seat. Its legs carry carved male and female figures, while its back legs have brass studs. The sources do not describe Luvale ceramic forms beyond pottery generally.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources do not describe tattoos, henna, or named systems of body ornament. Museum records include an upper portion of a white helix-shell ornament covered with yellow-brown spots, pierced at the top, with a strip of hide inserted. Another record describes a pair of small U-shaped copper ornaments with bosses, repousse dots, hollow interiors, and small pieces of metal that produce a jingling sound; they are strung on fibre. During *wali*, the initiate is covered in oil and red ochre after performing dances. The sources also record beads as decoration on the wooden handle of an axe.

## Music & performance

Luvale musical instruments include the *jinjimba*, a xylophone, the *likembe*, a small hand piano, and various drums. Museum objects include a royal drum carved of wood, with a lizard-skin membrane at each end, four handles, and a gourd tube with a spider-web diaphragm. The drum is identified as a symbol of the Chief. Other catalogue records include a sansa with its resonator, a composite thumb-piano or sansa with eight iron keys and a carved wooden sounding board, a slit drum made from a hollow section of a tree trunk, and a composite double rattle of twigs and grass basketry with seed rattles on a central stick. The rattle was used for dancing.

Drumming forms part of **Likumbi Lya Mize**, the official traditional ceremony, which also includes speeches, masked dancing, and dances by girls who have undergone *wali*. In *mukanda*, the female character *Pwebo*, or *Mwanapwebo*, is responsible for the musical accompaniment of rituals and dances. The sources do not identify named song genres, instrumental ensembles, or performance settings beyond initiation ceremonies, the traditional festival, dancing, and social gatherings.

## Dance & theatre

Luvale mask performance is closely associated with initiation. During **Likumbi Lya Mize**, masked male dancers called *makishi* perform alongside girls who have undergone *wali*. The ceremony includes dancing, drumming, and speeches by the chief and government officials.

The completion of **mukanda** is marked by a graduation ceremony featuring the *makishi* masquerade and a pantomime-like performance. The makishi represent spirits of deceased ancestors who return to assist boys in the transition from childhood to adulthood. Masks are made of wood and decorated with plant fibre, cordage, beads, and other materials. Their forms convey age, gender, social rank, and power. The figures include *Chisaluke*, *Mupala* or *Kayipu*, *Pwebo*, *Chileya*, *Chiwigi*, *Chikungila*, *Utenu*, *Katoyo* or *Chindele*, and *Katotola*. After the ritual, masks are burned or buried, symbolically returning them to the world of the dead.

## Festivals & rituals

The official traditional ceremony is **Likumbi Lya Mize**, one of the popular traditional festivals in Zambia. It takes place during the last weekend of August and generally lasts a week. The name means “ceremony of the Mize”; Mize is the headquarters of the Luvale and is located in Zambezi in North Western Province. The ceremony includes initiation ceremonies for girls and boys, masked dancing by *makishi*, dancing by girls who have undergone *wali*, speeches, and drumming.

The female initiation ceremony **wali** begins when a girl experiences her first menstruation cycle. She is taken into seclusion and brought to a fig tree called *muulya*, where she remains until a grass hut called *litungu* is built. She receives protective medicine and instruction from a *chilombola*, and is assigned a younger helper called *kajilu* or *kasambibiijikilo*. Seclusion could last between four and six months, although in recent times it lasts from a week to a month. Instruction concerns hygiene, sex, domestic chores, and preparation for marriage. The initiate must observe restrictions involving movement, food, speech, fire, and contact with members of the opposite sex. Graduation includes dances, oil and red ochre, and presentation to a new husband.

The male coming-of-age ceremony **mukanda**, also called *kumukanda*, involves Luvale boys between the ages of 8 and 12 and typically occurs at the beginning of the dry season. It has preparation, circumcision, and seclusion stages. Boys live for one to three months in an isolated bush camp, learn practical skills and cultural instruction, and return through a graduation masquerade. The sources also describe marriage customs, including bride price called *matemo* or *vikumba*, a welcome celebration called *vitilekela*, and a pre-wedding kitchen party in modern times.

## Foodways

The Luvale have a largely agrarian economy. Their staple crops are manioc, cassava, yams, and peanuts. Tobacco and hemp are grown for snuff, while maize is grown for beer. Women do most of the farming and processing of agricultural products. Slash-and-burn techniques and crop rotation are practiced, and pigs, chickens, sheep, and goats are kept for domestic use.

A society of hunters called *yanga* is responsible for catching bigger game, while everyone contributes to catching small game. The sources state that game has become scarce in much of the region. Luvale are also described as renowned fishermen who export dried catfish to the mining centers of the Copperbelt. Museum records include two wooden cassava ladles and a basket-work porridge dish. The sources do not name additional dishes, cooking methods, dietary rules, or ceremonial foods.

## Oral tradition & literature

Luvale oral tradition holds that the first leader among migrants moving south from north of Lake Tanganyika was Kenga Naweji. The tradition continues with the Luvale dynasty’s origin from Konde Mateti and the descent of Chinyama cha Mukwamayi, the founder of the Luvale chieftainship. Clan history is preserved through legendary explanations of how each clan arose and through a clan recitation called *kulisasula jikumbu*, which identifies a clan member.

The *mukanda* curriculum includes *tusona*, described as an ancient form of design and calculus consisting of ideographic tracings made in sand. Luvale naming traditions also preserve meanings connected with birth circumstances, reincarnation, and misfortune. The sources give *Kahilu*, meaning “he who has returned/come back,” and the female version *Omba*. They do not describe a named epic, folktale cycle, proverb tradition, or contemporary literary preservation project.

## Language & religion

Luvale is a Bantu language within the Niger-Congo language phylum and is considered a west central Bantu language. It is spoken in Angola and Zambia, is closely related to Chokwe, and uses a modified form of the Latin alphabet in writing. In Zambia it is recognized as a regional language for educational and administrative purposes. The sources give approximately 168,000 speakers in Zambia as of 2006 and 180 thousand speakers in Angola as of 2024.

Luvale recognize Kalunga as a sky god of creation and supreme power. They also recognize *mahamba*, nature and ancestral spirits belonging to individuals, families, or communities. Offerings are made to maintain good fortune. Evil spirits may be activated by sorcerers called *orwanga* to cause illness, while a diviner called *nganga* attempts to identify the source of a patient’s problem. Basket divination involves tossing up to sixty individual objects into a basket and interpreting their configuration. A traditional healer called *chimbanda* may select a new name for a seriously ill child.

## Overview

The Luvale live mainly in northwestern Zambia and southeastern Angola. In Zambia they are centered on Zambezi, formerly known as Balovale. Their culture includes matrilineal social organization, initiation ceremonies, mask traditions, basketry, music, ritual practices, and agricultural life. They are closely related to the Lunda and Ndembu and share cultural similarities with the Kaonde, Chokwe, and Luchazi.

## Material culture

Luvale material culture includes pottery, metalwork, basketry, mat weaving, woodwork, barkcloth costumes, and carved objects.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Luvale craft production includes mats, baskets, barkcloth costumes, and woven vegetable-string clothing.

- **Woven mat** (*visalo*) — Luvale are known for weaving mats called visalo.
- **Coloured vegetable-string costume** — A museum catalogue records a tight-fitting net costume made from coloured vegetable string.
- **Barkcloth makishi costume** (*makishi*) — During mukanda, makishi wear dyed woven barkcloth costumes with elaborate masks.
- **Winnowing basket** — A reed and string plaited flat basket with a dark and light twilled pattern was used as a winnowing tray.
- **Plaited basket** — A reed-plaited basket has a neck, a black and brown twilled pattern, a round top, and a square bottom.

### Clothing & dress

The profile describes ceremonial clothing linked to wali and mukanda rather than everyday dress.

- **Initiation girdle** (*zeva*) — During wali, an initiate makes and wears a girdle called a zeva throughout the ceremony.
- **Traditional cotton cloth** (*chitenge*) — When a wali initiate returns to her village, she is covered with a traditional cotton cloth called chitenge.
- **Bark-string head-dress** — A museum catalogue records a hemispherical head-dress made of bark string, red earth, and grease.
- **Barkcloth costume** — During mukanda, male initiates and makishi are associated with dyed woven costumes made from barkcloth.

### Architecture

The profile names a grass hut for wali and an isolated bush camp for mukanda.

- **Initiation grass hut** (*litungu*) — A grass hut called a litungu is built for a girl undergoing wali initiation.
- **Fig tree** (*muulya*) — A girl entering wali seclusion is taken near a fig tree called muulya.
- **Boys’ bush camp** — During mukanda, boys live for one to three months in an isolated bush camp.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Luvale are described as skilled in pottery, metalwork, basketry, mat weaving, and woodwork.

- **Hide-seat stool** (*likupu*) — Some Luvale stools have a hide seat on a wooden frame called a likupu.
- **Carved double dish** — A carved wooden double dish has two lidded dishes, with a fish on the upper lid.
- **Iron-bladed axe** — Museum records include axes with iron or steel blades and carved or coloured wooden handles.
- **Cassava ladle** — Museum records include two wooden cassava ladles.
- **Human-face comb** — A wooden comb has ten teeth and a handle carved with a human face and tall hair-do.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The profile records shell, copper, beads, oil, and red ochre as forms of adornment.

- **Shell ornament** — A white helix-shell ornament has yellow-brown spots, a hole at the top, and a strip of hide.
- **Copper ornaments** — A pair of small U-shaped copper ornaments has bosses, repousse dots, hollow interiors, and jingling metal pieces.
- **Beaded axe handle** — Beads are used as decoration on the wooden handle of an axe.
- **Oil and red ochre body covering** — During wali, the initiate is covered in oil and red ochre after performing dances.

## Music & performance

Luvale music uses xylophones, thumb pianos, drums, rattles, and other instruments in ceremonies and dancing.

- **Xylophone** (*jinjimba*) — The jinjimba is a Luvale xylophone.
- **Small hand piano** (*likembe*) — The likembe is a small hand piano.
- **Royal drum** — A royal drum has a wooden body, lizard-skin membranes, four handles, and a gourd tube with a spider-web diaphragm.
- **Thumb piano** (*sansa*) — A sansa may have a resonator, eight iron keys, and a carved wooden sounding board.
- **Composite double rattle** — A composite double rattle made of twigs, grass basketry, and seed rattles was used for dancing.

## Dance & theatre

Luvale mask performances represent ancestors and are closely linked to initiation ceremonies.

- **Masked male dancers** (*makishi*) — During Likumbi Lya Mize, masked male dancers called makishi perform with girls who have undergone wali.
- **Pwebo mask figure** (*Pwebo*) — Pwebo, also called Mwanapwebo, is one of the makishi figures.
- **Chisaluke mask figure** (*Chisaluke*) — Chisaluke is one of the makishi figures in the mukanda masquerade.
- **Mupala mask figure** (*Mupala*) — Mupala, also called Kayipu, is one of the makishi figures.
- **Katotola mask figure** (*Katotola*) — Katotola is one of the makishi figures in the mukanda masquerade.

## Festivals & rituals

Luvale ceremonies mark initiation, coming of age, marriage, and the traditional year.

- **Mize ceremony** (*Likumbi Lya Mize*) — Likumbi Lya Mize takes place during the last weekend of August and generally lasts a week.
- **Female initiation** (*wali*) — Wali begins when a girl experiences her first menstruation cycle and enters seclusion for instruction and preparation for marriage.
- **Male coming-of-age ceremony** (*mukanda*) — Mukanda, also called kumukanda, involves boys between the ages of 8 and 12 and includes preparation, circumcision, seclusion, and graduation.
- **Marriage bride price** (*matemo*) — Bride price is called matemo or vikumba.
- **Welcome celebration** (*vitilekela*) — A marriage welcome celebration is called vitilekela.

## Foodways

Luvale foodways center on farming, hunting, fishing, and processing crops.

- **Staple crops** — Staple crops include manioc, cassava, yams, and peanuts.
- **Beer maize** — Maize is grown for beer.
- **Snuff crops** — Tobacco and hemp are grown for snuff.
- **Big-game hunting society** (*yanga*) — A society of hunters called yanga is responsible for catching bigger game.
- **Dried catfish** — Luvale fishermen export dried catfish to the mining centers of the Copperbelt.

## Oral tradition & literature

Luvale oral tradition preserves migration stories, dynastic history, clan identity, sand designs, and names.

- **Clan recitation** (*kulisasula jikumbu*) — The clan recitation called kulisasula jikumbu identifies a clan member.
- **Sand design and calculus** (*tusona*) — Tusona are ideographic tracings made in sand and are included in the mukanda curriculum.
- **First migrant leader** (*Kenga Naweji*) — Luvale oral tradition says Kenga Naweji was the first leader among migrants moving south from north of Lake Tanganyika.
- **Founder of the Luvale chieftainship** (*Chinyama cha Mukwamayi*) — Chinyama cha Mukwamayi is described as the founder of the Luvale chieftainship.
- **Returned person name** (*Kahilu*) — Kahilu means “he who has returned/come back,” and the female version is Omba.

## Language & religion

Luvale is a regional Bantu language, and Luvale religion includes a sky god, spirits, divination, and healing.

- **Sky god** (*Kalunga*) — Kalunga is the Luvale sky god of creation and supreme power.
- **Nature and ancestral spirits** (*mahamba*) — Mahamba are nature and ancestral spirits belonging to individuals, families, or communities.
- **Sorcerer** (*orwanga*) — Sorcerers called orwanga may activate evil spirits to cause illness.
- **Diviner** (*nganga*) — A diviner called nganga attempts to identify the source of a patient’s problem.
- **Traditional healer** (*chimbanda*) — A traditional healer called chimbanda may select a new name for a seriously ill child.

---
title: "Bambara"
subtitle: "Mali"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]
---

## Overview

The Bambara, also called Bamana, are a Mandé ethnic group native primarily to southern Mali, with communities also in Ivory Coast, Guinea, Burkina Faso and Senegal. They are the largest Mandé ethnic group in Mali, where about 80% of the population speaks Bambara regardless of ethnicity. The Bamana emerged as a royal section of the Mandinka people and later developed a state known as the Bamana Empire. Their history is associated with farming communities in Ouassoulou, between Sikasso and Ivory Coast, and with Ségou. Bambara culture is particularly represented in the sources through caste and age-group societies, ritual sculpture, masks, agricultural headdresses, textiles, music objects and wooden figures. Bambara art was often made for religious use and ritual display rather than solely for visual appreciation.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Bogolanfini** — Bogolanfini, or mud cloth, is made from hand-spun cotton woven in narrow strips and sewn together. British Museum records describe cloths decorated with the mud resist method, producing dashes, crosses, circles, zig-zags, stripes, diamonds, triangles and squares.

**Bambara weaving** — A Museum of World Culture record identifies a Bambara textile made of cotton and narrow strips sewn together before dyeing. It is described as white and dark brown-black and catalogued as “Bambara mud cloth” and “Bokolan fini cloth.”

**Discharge-dyed wrapper** — British Museum wrappers use natural-coloured cotton warp and weft, with brown patterns produced by discharge dyeing. One example has repeating concentric ovals in a wave design, while another has densely arranged geometric and abstract patterns.

**Woman’s wrapper** — Recorded wrappers include single-width cotton textiles, eight-strip woven textiles and seven-strip woven textiles. Some are hand spun and brown-dyed; one is embroidered with strips of recycled sardine tins attached with cotton thread.

**Circumcision cloth** — Several catalogue records identify bogolanfini as cloth or circumcision equipment. These textiles are constructed from eight narrow strips and may be divided into panels containing repeating blocks, crosses, zig-zags, chevrons, triangles, diamonds and circles.

**Carrying cloth** — A carrying cloth in the British Museum record is composed of four hand-woven narrow strips sewn together. Its mud-resist decoration divides the surface into four sections and creates a central diamond-chain pattern.

**Indigo-dyed blanket** — A cotton blanket called *munnyuure* is woven in ten wide strips sewn together. Its hand-spun cotton warp is indigo-dyed, while the weft includes white and indigo-dyed bands and supplementary white-weft patterns.

**Motif vocabulary.** Dashes, crosses, circles, zig-zags, stripes, concentric ovals, waves, diamonds, triangles, chevrons, squares, central diamond chains.

### Clothing & dress

The sources document cotton wrappers, skirts, blankets, carrying cloths and a poncho-type garment. A Museum of World Culture record describes a cotton garment from Ségou measuring 185 centimetres in length and 90 centimetres in width, with dark-brown patterning produced by a discharge method. British Museum records describe women’s wrappers made from cotton warp and weft, sometimes left with loose warp-thread fringes at both ends. Some textiles are brown- or yellow-dyed and decorated with mud or discharge resist. One married woman’s skirt is made from a single width of hand-woven cotton decorated with a five-by-eight grid of crosses, chevrons, zig-zags and triangles. The sources also record a cotton masquerade costume assembled from 22 narrow hand-woven strips, with a drawstring neckline, sleeves and two lower “sleeves” for the legs. Photographs show women wearing cloths, headgear, shirts and neck ornaments, but the sources do not describe ordinary footwear, belts or a complete everyday dress system.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Bambara house forms, building materials, roof types, granaries or urban architecture.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Bamana artistic traditions include pottery, sculpture, weaving, iron figures and masks. The sources describe wooden and metal locks, including locks carved as stylised human beings and a crocodile. A wooden and metal heddle pulley is carved in the shape of a woman’s head, and other loom pulleys are also recorded. A wooden slit-gong has a carved human head at one end and metal studs for the eyes. Other catalogue objects include a wooden whistle or flute, a calabash rattle or sistrum surmounted by a human head, a wooden guitar with six strings and a reptile-skin resonator, and a wooden trumpet used to summon people to dance. British Museum records also identify poisoned arrows with cane shafts, cane binding and triangular iron arrow-heads.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources mention bead neck ornaments, metal earrings, nose ornaments, metal teeth, cowrie shells and abrus seeds on objects and headdresses. A wooden Bambara statue is described as having a marked scarification pattern, while another has powerful scarification marks and a high, pointed hairstyle. The sources do not provide a general account of Bambara jewelry, tattooing, henna, hair practices or ritual body adornment.

## Music & performance

The sources identify several instruments and sound-producing objects. These include a wooden whistle or flute, a wooden guitar with six strings and a resonator covered with reptile skin, a curved metal rattle attached to the end of its stave, a calabash rattle or sistrum mounted on a bent stick and surmounted by a human head, a scraped wooden slit-gong, and a wooden trumpet. The Museum of World Culture records that the trumpet was used to summon people to dance.

Music is also connected to Bambara language and oral performance. The Bambara language article states that griots, called *Jeliw* in Bambara, are storytellers, praise singers and “human history books” who study singing and recitation for many years. Bambara oral literature is mainly passed on by these performers, and many of their songs are said to date back to the old empire of Mali. The language article also records Bambara-language singing by Malian artists including Oumou Sangaré, Sidiki Diabaté, Fatoumata Diawara, Rokia Traoré, Ali Farka Touré, Habib Koité and Amadou & Mariam. The sources do not describe named song genres, musical scales, performance ensembles or wedding and funeral repertoires.

## Dance & theatre

Bamana dance is associated with agricultural ceremonies, initiation and masquerade. The *Tyi Warra*, also written *ciwara*, is a headdress used at harvest time by young men chosen from the farmers association. Museum records describe wooden dance headdresses with antelope forms, horns, human figures, basketry, string, cane, cowrie shells and abrus seeds. One headdress is worn by young men during dances and ceremonies connected with agriculture. The associated animal is identified as an antelope, and the headdresses occur in male and female pairs.

The sources also describe masks and masquerade costumes. The *n’tomo* mask was used by dancers at male initiation ceremonies, while a Komo head-dress mask is built from clay on a carved-wood foundation and has an animal head, antelope horns, tusks and porcupine quills. A wooden mask is recorded as having been used by the N’Tomo society. The sources do not describe a named dramatic theatre tradition or a complete choreography.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not provide an annual Bambara festival calendar or dates for recurring festivals. They do document initiation, agricultural and masquerade rituals. The *n’tomo* mask was used by dancers during male initiation ceremonies. In southern Mali, statues were created for initiation among young men, including the *sonkalaniw*, performed by a group of Jo initiation known as *boso*, and the *nyeleniw*, used in blacksmiths’ Jo initiation.

Bamana society maintained age-group, sex-based and vocational associations known as *Tons*. Young men’s initiation rites could be organized by sex, while the Soli ton consisted of young men who lived separately from the community and provided farm labour before taking wives. Farming and hunting associations included the Chi Wara Ton and the Donzo Ton. The sources state that Ton societies continued as ways of socializing and passing on traditions, although their power and importance faded in the 20th century. The sources do not cover birth ceremonies, weddings, funerals or a dated annual ritual cycle.

## Foodways

The sources used do not describe Bambara staple foods, named dishes, cooking methods, drinks, ceremonial meals or dietary rules. One British Museum photograph shows adult women pounding “meal” with pestles in a mortar, sifting it into a calabash and carrying a child, but the catalogue does not identify the food.

## Oral tradition & literature

Bambara oral literature is mainly transmitted by griots, called *Jeliw* in Bambara. They are described as storytellers, praise singers and human history books who study the trade of singing and reciting for many years. Many of their songs are said to date back to the old empire of Mali. The sources do not name a Bambara epic, tale cycle, proverb collection or riddle tradition.

The language article gives the example of oral literature consisting largely of tales of kings and heroes. It also notes that written literature is slowly evolving because French has predominated as the “language of the educated,” while a substantial oral literature continues to exist. The sources do not describe contemporary literary preservation projects.

## Language & religion

Bambara, also known as Malian, Bamana or Bamanankan, is a Manding language in the larger Mandé family. It is spoken throughout Mali as a lingua franca and is most widely spoken east, south and north of Bamako. The language has two lexical tones and a subject–object–verb structure. Its dialects include Kaarta, Tambacounda, Beledugu, Bananba, Mesekele, Jitumu, Jamaladugu, Segu, Cakadugu, Keleyadugu, Jalakadougu and others named in the source.

Since 1967, Bambara has mostly been written in the Latin script with additional phonetic characters. N’Ko and Arabic script are also used, while Masaba was developed beginning in 1930. Most Bamana today adhere to Islam, but many continue traditional rituals, especially ancestor honouring. This syncretic Islam is described as rare, although conversions often occurred in the mid to late 19th century. Bamana art was frequently created for spiritual purposes, ritual ceremonies and offerings.

- Patrick R. McNaughton, “Bamana Blacksmiths,” *African Arts*, 1979.
- Richard L. Roberts, *Warriors, Merchants and Slaves: The State and the Economy in the Middle Niger Valley 1700–1914*, Stanford University Press, 1987.
- Louis Tauxier, *Histoire des Bambara*, P. Geuthner, 1942.
- Dominique Zahan, *Antilopes du soleil: Arts et rites agraires d’Afrique noire*, Edition A. Schendl, 1980.

---
title: "Senufo"
subtitle: "Mali"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]
---

## Overview

The Senufo, also known as Siena, Senefo, Sene, Senoufo, and Syénambélé, are a West African ethnolinguistic group living across northern Ivory Coast, southeastern Mali, and western Burkina Faso. The Nafana subgroup is found in north-western Ghana. Their highest population densities are between the Black Volta river, Bagoe River, and Bani River. A 2013 estimate places their total population over 3 million, with about 0.8 million in southeastern Mali. The Senufo languages form a branch of the Atlantic–Congo sub-family of the Niger–Congo languages. The Senufo are known for agriculture, music, wood sculpture, masks, figurines, textiles, and other handicrafts connected with cultural themes and religious beliefs.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

***Fila*, also called *filafani wii*** — A painted textile associated with Korhogo in northern Ivory Coast. The museum record describes cotton cloth with painted motifs; these motifs were historically associated with hunters, ritual dancers, and initiated Senufo people.

**Korhogo cloth** — The museum record identifies this textile as having historical origins in the village of Korhogo. Its painted motifs have strong significance and were connected with supernatural powers and people.

**Indigo-dyed wrapper** — A British Museum wrapper is composed of eight narrow strips sewn together, using hand-spun cotton warp and weft, indigo-dyed bands, chequerboard arrangement, supplementary weft patterns, and short warp-thread fringes.

**Figurative cloth** — Another British Museum cloth is composed of ten narrow strips sewn together and painted with figurative designs in mud and natural dye.

**Patterned cotton cloth** — A further British Museum textile uses white cotton, indigo-dyed weft stripes, orange- and grey-dyed cotton inserts, and pattern blocks.

**Motif vocabulary.** Painted motifs, figurative designs, pattern blocks.

### Clothing & dress

The sources describe no complete account of everyday or ceremonial dress. The museum record states that Korhogo painted textile motifs were formerly reserved for hunters, who had historical heroic status, ritual dancers, and initiated Senufo people. The Senufo are also described as wearing specially crafted brass jewelry, including pieces that imitate wildlife. The sources do not document specific garments, head coverings, belts, footwear, or gendered dress.

### Architecture

Senufo villages consist of small mud-brick homes. In rainy southern communities, thatched roofs are common, while flat roofs are prevalent in the dry, desert-like north. The sources do not provide a named Senufo building type, detailed settlement plan, courtyard arrangement, or architectural workshop tradition. A museum record describes a carved Senufo door from Ivory Coast with low-relief decoration, pivot projections, and a wooden lock; the door’s upper composition includes a turtle, two toucan-like birds, and a snake.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources describe wooden household and workshop objects rather than a developed ceramic tradition. Museum records include a wooden pot with three legs, carved lines, diamond shapes, and a lid topped by a bird; a wooden door lock with movable catches and a metal key; wooden loom pulleys carved with animal heads; a horse-shaped wooden seat; and a wooden dance staff with an animal head. Senufo artisans include blacksmiths, carvers, brasscutters, potters, and leather workers. Training to become an artisan takes about seven or eight years.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Senufo people wear specially crafted brass jewelry, including forms that imitate wildlife. Museum figures show scarification marks on the face, cheeks, breasts, abdomen, back, and around the navel. One seated female figure has a hairstyle incorporating a stylized bird head. The sources do not document specific jewelry names, tattooing rites, hair ceremonies, or other forms of body adornment in detail.

## Music & performance

The Senufo are regionally and internationally known as musicians. The sources classify their instruments into wind instruments, stringed instruments, and percussive instruments. Museum objects include a standing wooden drum with a hide head, relief figures, four feet, and six wedges used to tighten the drum skin. Its relief decoration includes a woman, snakes, a turtle, a lizard, and slave bracelets. Another drum has a carved wooden body, a hide top, wooden pegs, hide thongs, and reliefs including a mask, snake, bird, reptiles, a man with a vertical flute, and manacles.

Other museum records include a composite horn made from antelope horn with a wooden end and animal fur and skin. The sources do not name Senufo song genres, melodies, dances performed to particular instruments, or musical occasions such as weddings or harvest ceremonies. They do state that musicians form a recognized occupational group within Senufo society and that Senufo communities use several categories of instruments.

## Dance & theatre

The sources document masks, dance masks, figurines, and ritual equipment carved by Senufo artists. Museum records include animal-head masks, human-face masks, a hyaena-head dance mask with antelope horns and a bird on the forehead, a spotted quadruped dance mask, and a baboon-head dance mask coloured in white and red. A museum dance staff is described as a zoomorphic wooden sculpture.

The sources state that carved figures were used in a *tyekpa* funeral ceremony as dance sculptures, carried on the heads of dancers during the ceremony. They do not describe theatrical narratives, named dramatic genres, or distinctions between entertainment and ritual performance beyond these ritual and funeral references.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not provide an annual festival calendar or named seasonal festivals. They describe several ritual and institutional practices. Senufo villages traditionally have a male secret society called **Poro**, with elaborate initiation rituals held in a sacred forest. These rituals involve masks, figurines, and ritual equipment. The main function of Poro is described as guaranteeing a good relationship between the living world and the ancestors.

The **Sandogo** society governs divination and is generally associated with women. Men who inherit the profession through the matrilineal line may also become diviners. The Senufo also have **Wambele** and **Tyekpa**, which perform sorcery and rituals. Caryatid figures are used in ceremonies connected with advancement through the age-grade cycle, and carved figures were used in a *tyekpa* funeral ceremony. The sources do not describe birth rites, weddings, annual festivals, or a detailed funeral calendar.

## Foodways

The Senufo are predominantly agricultural people cultivating corn, millet, yams, and peanut. They also cultivate cotton and cash crops for the international market. The sources do not name prepared dishes, cooking methods, drinks, ceremonial foods, or dietary rules. They likewise do not document food exchange, feasting, or restrictions connected with Islam or traditional religion.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used for this profile do not cover Senufo folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, storytelling contexts, or literary preservation efforts.

## Language & religion

The Senufo or Senufic languages comprise around fifteen languages spoken in northern Ivory Coast, southern Mali, and southwestern Burkina Faso; Nafaanra is also spoken in western Ghana. They form their own branch of the Atlantic–Congo sub-family of the Niger–Congo languages. The sources describe suffixal noun classes, aspect-marked verbs, a mostly three-level tone system, borrowed words from Bambara and Jula, and subject–object–verb constituent order.

The Senufo are predominantly animists, with some Muslims. Traditional Senufo religion includes ancestral and nature spirits and a Supreme Being understood through a female Ancient Mother, Maleeo or Katieleo, and a male Creator God, Kolotyolo or Koulotiolo. Poro and Sandogo organize important spiritual and divinatory practices.

## Sources & further reading

- Bohumil Holas, *Les Sénoufo (y compris les Minianka)*, Presses Universitaires de France, 1957.
- Carol Spindel, *In the Shadow of the Sacred Grove*, Vintage, 1989.

title: "Senufo"
subtitle: "Mali"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]

## At a glance
| | |
|---|---|
| Who | The Senufo, also called Siena, Senefo, Sene, Senoufo, and Syénambélé, are a West African ethnolinguistic group. |
| Where | Northern Ivory Coast, southeastern Mali, western Burkina Faso, and north-western Ghana for the Nafana subgroup. |
| How many | Over 3 million people, including about 0.8 million in southeastern Mali, by a 2013 estimate. |
| Language | About fifteen Senufo or Senufic languages, including Nafaanra. |
| Religion | Mostly animist, with some Muslims. |
| Known for | Agriculture · Music · Wood sculpture and masks · Textiles · Handicrafts tied to cultural and religious themes |

## Overview

The Senufo live across parts of Ivory Coast, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Ghana. They are mainly farmers who grow corn, millet, yams, peanuts, cotton, and cash crops. Their culture is known for music, wood carving, masks, figurines, textiles, and other crafts. Poro and Sandogo are important spiritual and social institutions.

## Material culture

Senufo material culture centers on painted and woven textiles, carved wood, brass jewelry, masks, musical instruments, and useful household objects.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Senufo textiles include painted cloth from Korhogo and woven cloth made from narrow cotton strips with dyed bands and added patterns.

- **Painted Korhogo cloth** (*Fila; filafani wii*) — This cotton cloth has painted motifs that were linked with hunters, ritual dancers, and initiated Senufo people.
- **Korhogo cloth** — This painted textile came from the village of Korhogo, and its motifs were connected with supernatural powers and people.
- **Indigo-dyed wrapper** — This wrapper has eight sewn cotton strips, indigo bands, a chequerboard layout, added weft patterns, and short fringes.
- **Figurative cloth** — This cloth has ten sewn strips painted with figures in mud and natural dye.
- **Patterned cotton cloth** — This textile combines white cotton, indigo stripes, orange and grey inserts, and pattern blocks.

### Clothing & dress

The profile gives little detail about everyday dress, but painted Korhogo textiles once marked hunters, ritual dancers, and initiated Senufo people.

- **Reserved painted textiles** — Korhogo painted textile motifs were formerly reserved for hunters, ritual dancers, and initiated Senufo people.
- **Wildlife-like brass jewelry** — Senufo people wear specially made brass jewelry that can imitate wildlife.

### Architecture

Senufo villages use small mud-brick homes with roof styles suited to wet or dry regions.

- **Mud-brick home** — Senufo villages consist of small homes made from mud brick.
- **Thatched roof** — Thatched roofs are common in rainy southern communities.
- **Flat roof** — Flat roofs are common in the dry, desert-like north.
- **Carved Senufo door** — A carved door from Ivory Coast has low relief, pivot projections, a wooden lock, and figures of a turtle, two toucan-like birds, and a snake.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Senufo artisans make carved wooden household, workshop, and ritual objects, alongside work in metal, pottery, and leather.

- **Three-legged wooden pot** — This wooden pot has three legs, carved lines, diamond shapes, and a lid topped by a bird.
- **Wooden door lock** — This lock has movable catches and a metal key.
- **Animal-head loom pulley** — Wooden loom pulleys are carved with animal heads.
- **Horse-shaped seat** — One carved wooden seat is shaped like a horse.
- **Dance staff** — A wooden dance staff has an animal head.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Senufo adornment includes wildlife-like brass jewelry, scarification, and hairstyles with carved animal forms.

- **Wildlife-like brass jewelry** — Senufo brass jewelry includes forms that imitate wildlife.
- **Scarification** — Museum figures show scarification on the face, cheeks, breasts, abdomen, back, and around the navel.
- **Bird-head hairstyle** — One seated female figure has a hairstyle with a stylized bird head.

## Music & performance

Senufo musicians are well known, and their instruments include wind, stringed, and percussive types.

- **Standing wooden drum** — This drum has a hide head, four feet, six wedges for tightening the skin, and reliefs of a woman, snakes, a turtle, a lizard, and slave bracelets.
- **Carved relief drum** — Another drum has a carved wooden body, hide top, wooden pegs, hide thongs, and reliefs of masks, animals, a flute player, and manacles.
- **Composite horn** — This wind instrument is made from antelope horn with a wooden end and animal fur and skin.
- **Musicians** — Musicians form a recognized occupational group within Senufo society.

## Dance & theatre

Senufo dance uses carved masks, staffs, and figures, especially in ritual and funeral settings.

- **Hyaena-head dance mask** — This mask has antelope horns and a bird on the forehead.
- **Spotted quadruped dance mask** — This dance mask represents a spotted four-legged animal.
- **Baboon-head dance mask** — This mask has a baboon head and is colored white and red.
- **Animal-head masks** — Senufo artists carve masks with animal heads and human faces.
- **Funeral dance sculptures** (*tyekpa*) — Carved figures are carried on dancers' heads during a tyekpa funeral ceremony.

## Festivals & rituals

Senufo ritual life centers on secret societies, initiation, divination, sorcery, and relationships with ancestors.

- **Poro society** (*Poro*) — This male secret society holds elaborate initiation rituals in a sacred forest and helps maintain a good relationship between living people and ancestors.
- **Sandogo divination society** (*Sandogo*) — Sandogo governs divination and is generally associated with women, though some men inherit the profession through the mother's line.
- **Wambele sorcery society** (*Wambele*) — Wambele performs sorcery and rituals.
- **Tyekpa rituals** (*Tyekpa*) — Tyekpa performs sorcery and rituals, including a funeral ceremony with carved dance figures.
- **Age-grade advancement figures** — Caryatid figures are used in ceremonies connected with advancement through the age-grade cycle.

## Foodways

The Senufo are mainly farmers who grow staple crops, cotton, and cash crops.

- **Corn farming** — Corn is one of the crops cultivated by the Senufo.
- **Millet farming** — Millet is one of the crops cultivated by the Senufo.
- **Yam farming** — Yams are one of the crops cultivated by the Senufo.
- **Peanut farming** — Peanuts are one of the crops cultivated by the Senufo.
- **Cotton and cash crops** — The Senufo grow cotton and other cash crops for the international market.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do not describe Senufo folktales, poetry, proverbs, riddles, storytelling, or literary preservation.

## Language & religion

Senufo languages form their own branch of Niger–Congo, while Senufo religion centers on spirits, ancestors, and a Supreme Being.

- **Senufic languages** (*Senufic*) — About fifteen Senufo languages are spoken across northern Ivory Coast, southern Mali, and southwestern Burkina Faso.
- **Nafaanra** — Nafaanra is spoken in western Ghana.
- **Atlantic–Congo branch** (*Atlantic–Congo*) — Senufo languages form a branch of the Atlantic–Congo sub-family of Niger–Congo languages.
- **Ancient Mother** (*Maleeo; Katieleo*) — The Supreme Being is understood through a female Ancient Mother called Maleeo or Katieleo.
- **Creator God** (*Kolotyolo; Koulotiolo*) — The male Creator God is called Kolotyolo or Koulotiolo.

## Glossary

- *Fila* — Painted Korhogo textile
- *filafani wii* — Another name for Fila
- *Poro* — Male secret society
- *Sandogo* — Divination society
- *Wambele* — Society linked with sorcery and rituals
- *Tyekpa* — Society and funeral ritual
- *Senufic* — Senufo language branch
- *Nafaanra* — Senufo language of western Ghana
- *Atlantic–Congo* — Language sub-family branch
- *Maleeo* — Female Ancient Mother
- *Katieleo* — Female Ancient Mother
- *Kolotyolo* — Male Creator God
- *Koulotiolo* — Male Creator God

---
title: "Soninke"
subtitle: "Mali"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]
---

## Overview

The Soninke, also called Sarakolleh, are a West African Mande-speaking ethnic group found in Mali, southern Mauritania, eastern Senegal, The Gambia, and Guinea, especially Fouta Djallon. They are concentrated in the valley of the upper Senegal River and along the Mali–Senegal–Mauritania border between Nara and Nioro du Sahel. Their contemporary population is estimated at over 2 million. The Soninke language is a Mande language, also known as Serakhulle or Azer. Soninke communities and culture were spread through migration, trade networks, French colonial labor migration, and Wangara mercantile confederations. The Soninke are associated historically with the ancient Ghana or Wagadu Empire and maintain cultural practices involving Islam, social stratification, marriage, circumcision, agriculture, trade, foodways, textiles, and body adornment.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources do not document named Soninke textile traditions beyond the museum catalogue descriptions of indigo-dyed and embroidered cloth.

**Indigo stitch-resist-dyed cotton cloth** — British Museum catalogue records describe skirts made from five or six wide strips of plain-weave cotton, hand sewn together. The cloth is dyed dark indigo and decorated with alternating bar, dot, geometric, linear, triple-dot, and semi-circle patterns, with plain indigo borders and unworked warp-thread fringes.

**Indigo tie-dyed and stitch-resist-dyed shawls** — The catalogued women’s shawls are made from cotton woven in six or seven wide strips and hand sewn together. They use alternating indigo-dyed and black warp stripes, dot and line patterns, deep indigo borders, and loose warp-thread fringes.

**Indigo checkerboard shawl** — One catalogue record describes a cotton shawl woven in ten wide strips, with indigo-dyed hand-spun cotton warp and alternating indigo-dyed and natural-coloured cotton bands aligned as a checkerboard. A narrow red-dyed cotton weft stripe runs through each weft band.

**Indigo herringbone-patterned skirt** — One skirt is made from eight narrow machine-spun cotton strips, hand sewn together. Plain-weave strips are resist-dyed in indigo to create lighter herringbone patterns, with zig-zag patterns along one short end.

**Indigo-dyed embroidered gown** — A man’s gown, identified as a boubou or *tobe*, is made from four sheets of European cotton sheeting dyed indigo in Africa and sewn into a rectangular garment with square sleeves. It has a pocket and extensive hand-sewn embroidery in white, green, peach, red, light blue, dark blue, and yellow cotton thread.

**Motif vocabulary.** Triple dots, linear patterns, dotted semi-circles, bars, dots, geometric patterns, herringbone patterns, zig-zags, checkerboard bands, knives, stars, and spirals.

### Clothing & dress

The museum records show women’s skirts and shawls made from indigo-dyed cotton, together with a man’s rectangular gown identified as a boubou or *tobe*. The gown has square sleeves, a pocket, and embroidered decoration on the front and back. The catalogue records also document photographs of Soninke women, men, children, older women, and boys from the village of Garawol in The Gambia. These records mention women’s head coverings and garments, but do not describe their construction in detail. One photograph shows a woman wearing large, heavy gold earrings; another records gold rings attached to a head covering at the forehead. The sources do not document Soninke footwear, belts, or a separate ceremonial dress system.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Soninke architecture, house forms, roofing, building materials, or urban construction traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources used do not provide a general account of Soninke ceramics, wooden objects, tools, household goods, or metalworking. They do document gold earrings and gold rings in museum photographs, and mention pottery workers within the hereditary caste category called the tage or numu.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Museum catalogue records from The Gambia describe Soninke women from the village of Garawol wearing gold earrings and gold rings attached to head coverings. One record states that large, heavy gold earrings were a sign that a woman was married, while unmarried women wore considerably smaller gold earrings. Another records small rings attached to the head covering, at the forehead, or at the sides when women married. A related photograph identifies the earrings and the ring at the forehead as gold. The sources do not document tattoos, henna, or other hair practices. They do record boys with shaved heads during a circumcision ceremony.

## Music & performance

The sources describe music and performance in connection with circumcision and with hereditary social categories. During the circumcision period, boys circumcised the previous year organize *tam-tams* for the new boys in order to prepare them psychologically. During the ceremony, the boys sit around a drum called the *daïné*. Other teenagers, young girls, women, men, and slaves form a circle around them, while the boys are surrounded by scarves called *disa sing*.

The social hierarchy includes the *fune*, described as a bard, and the *gesere* or *jeli*, described as griots and singers. The sources also mention the *karikompe*, a wedding event accompanying the marriage contract, but do not identify its musical form or instruments. They do not document a broader repertoire of named song genres, instrumental ensembles, funeral music, court music, or professional performance settings.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document named Soninke dances, theatre, masked performance, shadow puppetry, or other dramatic traditions. The circumcision account describes a circle formed around the boys and the use of *tam-tams*, but it does not identify a dance.

## Festivals & rituals

The Soninke practice Islamic rites of marriage and circumcision. Marriage follows Islamic practices, and cousin marriage is common and preferred. When both families agree, the couple becomes engaged, described as *i na tamma laga*, in a mosque. Each month after the engagement, the man pays the woman’s family a bridewealth dower called *nakhafa*. The marriage, called *futtu*, is completed through a marriage contract mentioning the dower and a wedding event called *karikompe*. The couple has advisers: the man’s is called *khoussoumanta-yougo* and the woman’s *khoussoumanta-yakhare*. After one week of celebration, women meet to show gifts received by the couple from their parents, especially from the woman’s mother.

Circumcision is called *birou*. Boys circumcised the previous year organize *tam-tams* for the new boys, who sit around the drum called *daïné*. The boys are surrounded by scarves called *disa sing*. The sources also state that female genital mutilation has long been practiced among the Soninke as a ritual of social acceptance and that it continues in Mauritania and Senegal despite being illegal in contemporary law. The sources do not describe an annual festival calendar or provide dates for festivals.

## Foodways

Soninke breakfast foods include *fonde*, a porridge made of millet, sugar, milk, and salt, and *sombi*, a porridge made of rice, millet, or corn. Lunch foods include *demba tere* and *takhaya*, both containing rice and peanuts. *Dere* is a stew made from millet and beans. The sources identify rice, millet, peanuts, corn, sugar, milk, and salt as ingredients in these foods. The Soninke traditionally engage in agriculture, and during the rainy season men and women cultivate crops, while women usually remain at home to cook and care for children. The sources do not document cooking vessels, named cooking methods, tea or coffee traditions, ceremonial foods, or dietary rules beyond the group’s predominantly Muslim religious context.

## Oral tradition & literature

Soninke oral tradition identifies Dinga as the ancestor of the Soninke. His sons included Dyabe Sisse, described as the founder of the Wagadu kingdom with its capital at Kumbi. Another Soninke tradition indicates migration from Aswan, Egypt. The sources also record a traditional proverb: “Cousins are made for each other.” The historical tradition of the Soninke includes their role as founders of the ancient Ghana Empire, also called the Wagadu Empire.

The sources mention the tradition of epic storytelling among Soninke blacksmiths in the bibliography through Badoua Siguine’s *La tradition épique des forgerons soninké*. They also list a work on the supernatural in Soninke tales, *Le surnaturel dans les contes soninké*. No specific epic title, riddle tradition, contemporary literary revival, or preservation project is described in the supplied material.

## Language & religion

Soninke is a Mande language spoken by the Soninke people of West Africa. It is also known as Serakhulle, Azer, or Maraka, and the language is called *Sooninkanxanne* in Soninke. The language has an estimated 2.3 million speakers, primarily in Mali and Mauritania, and is also spoken in Senegal, Ivory Coast, The Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, and Guinea. It is a national language of Mauritania, Mali, Senegal, and The Gambia. Dialects include the Berber-inflected Azer dialect. Long vowels are written double: aa, ee, ii, oo, uu.

Most Soninke are Muslims. The rulers and people of the Ghana Empire converted to Islam in the 11th century, and Soninke people have been Muslim ever since. They typically adhere to the Maliki school of Sunni Islam. Islamic practices appear in marriage, circumcision, and other rites of passage. The sources do not document historical scripts or additional forms of religious syncretism.

## Sources & further reading

- François Manchuelle, *Origins of Black African Emigration to France: The Labor Migrations of the Soninke, 1948–1987*, University of California, Santa Barbara, 1987.
- M. T. Abéla de la Rivière, *Les Sarakolé et leur émigration vers la France*, Université de Paris V, 1977.
- Mahamet Timera, *Les Soninké en France : d’un histoire à l’autre*, Karthala, 1996.
- Christian Girier, *Parlons soninké*, L’Harmattan, Paris, 1996.
- Badoua Siguine, *La tradition épique des forgerons soninké*, Université de Dakar.
- [Soninke people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soninke_people)
- [Soninke language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soninke_language)

The profile documents indigo cotton clothing, embroidered gowns, and gold jewelry, but gives little information about buildings, pottery, tools, or household goods.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Soninke foodways center on millet, rice, peanuts, corn, milk, sugar, and salt.

region: "Sub Saharan Africa"

## Overview

The Bobo, sometimes called Bobo Fing, are a Mande ethnic group living primarily in Burkina Faso, with some communities in Mali. Their major southern community is Bobo-Dioulasso, the second-largest city of Burkina Faso and its old French colonial capital. Further north are Fô and Kouka, while Boura lies in the extreme north in Mali. The Bobo number approximately 110,000 people, with the great majority in Burkina Faso. They speak Bobo, a Mande language with Northern and Southern dialects. Bobo culture includes farming, masks, wooden sculpture, drums, and decentralized social organization based on lineages and elders.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document Bobo textile or pattern traditions.

**Bobo masks** — Bobo masks have detailed wooden structures extending above the main body. They are traditionally painted red, black, and silver/white, and are repainted at the beginning of each season.

**Wooden stools** — British Museum records describe stools made of wood, with handles in the form of human heads, three or four legs, and, in some examples, incised geometric patterns.

**Palls** — A Museum of World Culture record describes a one-piece wooden pall from Bomborokuy, associated with Bobo Ule. It was owned by the same family for at least three generations and was carried hooked over one shoulder.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name incised geometric patterns, animal and human features, bird heads, triangles, rhombs, crosses, and checker patterns.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe everyday or ceremonial Bobo clothing, head coverings, belts, footwear, or gender-specific dress. One museum record states that a wooden pall from Bomborokuy was carried hooked over one shoulder, but it does not identify this as clothing.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Bobo houses, compounds, roofs, villages, defensive architecture, workshops, or other forms of the built environment.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The documented objects are chiefly wooden masks, stools, palls, drums, and sculptures. A Museum of Ethnography catalogue records a small metal human figure from Mali, described as copper or possibly bronze, with a round pointed hat and a bent implement over one shoulder; the record associates it with the Bobo Fing-folket. Another metal object is a reddish crocodile, probably copper, associated with the Bobo Fing-folket. The sources do not document Bobo ceramics.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not document Bobo jewelry, amulets, tattoos, henna, hair practices, or other forms of body adornment.

## Music & performance

The museum catalogue records several drums from Bomborokuy, Övre Volta, associated with Bobo Ule. They are made of wood and skin. Some are played with a drumstick, while another is described as a “tambourine” played with the hands. The records describe drums with heights of 24 cm, 45 cm, 47 cm, and 91 cm, and diameters of 15 cm, 16,5 cm, 20 cm, and 26 cm.

The sources do not provide names for Bobo musical genres, songs, dances, or ensembles. They also do not describe the social contexts in which the recorded drums are performed. One Cleveland Museum of Art record describes Bolo masks as being danced for entertainment during communal occasions such as funerals, male initiations, and harvest celebrations, but the record does not provide a Bobo-language name for a musical tradition.

## Dance & theatre

A Cleveland Museum of Art record states that Bolo masks are primarily danced for entertainment during communal occasions such as funerals, male initiations, and harvest celebrations. The mask combines animal and human features and is always worn by a male dancer. A Museum of World Culture record states that a tall Bobo Fing mask with two faces and nine carved bird heads keeps evil spirits away.

Another Museum of World Culture record describes a horned helmet mask associated with Bobo Fing. The mask bearer personifies the protective spirit “Do”, acts as a police figure, and drives away those who threaten to disturb death rites or fertility ceremonies. Each clan makes its own particular type, and animal motifs are common.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not give an annual Bobo festival calendar or festival dates. They describe several ritual and communal contexts. Bolo masks are danced during funerals, male initiations, and harvest celebrations. The horned helmet mask associated with Bobo Fing is used in connection with death rites and fertility ceremonies.

Bobo religious belief describes two important epochs: the time of Wuro, when the universe was created, and the contemporary time, when Wuro gave humanity his son Dwo. Blacksmiths traditionally worship Dwo. Bobo masks honor Wuro and have a spiritual role in erasing evil and balancing the sun, earth, and rain.

## Foodways

Farming is of primary importance among the Bobo and is described as the essential component of day-to-day existence. Major food crops are red sorghum, pearl millet, yams, and maize. The sources state that the Bobo also cultivate cotton, which is sold to textile mills in Koudougou, while cotton and peanuts function as primary cash crops.

The sources used do not describe Bobo dishes, cooking methods, ceremonial foods, beverages, dietary rules, or food preparation.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources state that the Bobo are descendants of an ancient aggregation assembled around a number of core clans, none of which preserved oral traditions of immigration into the area. They also state that more than 41% of Bobo lineages claim a foreign origin while saying that they are autochthonous.

Bobo cosmogony describes the creation of the world by Wuro and the ordering of his creations into opposing pairs, including man and spirits, male and female, village and bush, and culture and nature. According to legend, Wuro created the first man, who was a blacksmith and received the first mask. The sources do not document Bobo epics, folktales, proverbs, riddles, or literary preservation projects beyond these statements about oral tradition and cosmogony.

## Language & religion

Bobo is a Mande language of Burkina Faso and Mali. It has Northern and Southern dialects; the Northern dialect is also known as Konabéré. Northern and Southern Bobo share only 20%–30% intelligibility according to Ethnologue and are considered separate languages by that standard. The terms Bobo Fing, meaning “Black Bobo”, and Bobo Madaré distinguish them from Bobo Gbe, meaning “White Bobo”, and Bobo Oule, meaning “Red Bobo”, of Burkina.

The Bobo traditionally follow a pagan, animist religion. Wuro is the creator god who formed the earth from a ball of clay. He cannot be described and is not represented by sculptures. Wuro’s son Dwo is important in the contemporary epoch, and blacksmiths traditionally worship Dwo. Some Bobo have converted to Christianity or Islam.

## Sources & further reading

- Guy Le Moal, *Les Bobo. Nature et fonction des masques*, Musée royal de l’Afrique centrale, Tervuren, 1999.
- [Bobo people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobo_people)
- [Bobo language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobo_language)

No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription for this group is included in the supplied sources.
