## Overview

The Ndau are an ethnic group indigenous to south-eastern Zimbabwe, especially the districts of Chipinge and Chimanimani. They are also found in parts of Bikita, the Zambezi valley, central Mozambique along the coast, and central Malawi. Their presence in these regions was first documented in the 1500s by Portuguese missionary João dos Santos. The Ndau have historical and cultural connections with the Kalanga, Venda, and Shona peoples, including through the Mapungubwe trading network, while Nguni influences became strong in modern times. As of 1997, an estimated 581,000 people spoke Ndau in Mozambique. Ndau is a Bantu language and a Shona language, mutually intelligible with other Shona languages, and received official-language status in Zimbabwe in 2013.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Mpalu** — A textile traded by the Ndau in the Mapungubwe-centered trade networks. It was described as a distinctive red cloth.

**Njeti** — A traded Ndau textile distinguished in the source as a white cloth.

**Vukotlo** — A traded Ndau textile described as a distinctive blue cloth.

These textiles were among the Ndau trade goods exchanged with various groups, including the Khoisan peoples and Arab traders. The sources do not describe their fibers, weaving techniques, looms, production settings, or later use in clothing.

### Clothing & dress

The sources state that the Ndau traded textiles called *Mpalu*, *Njeti*, and *Vukotlo*, described respectively as red, white, and blue cloths. They also traded animal skins and bones. The sources used do not describe everyday clothing, ceremonial dress, gendered garments, head coverings, footwear, or the ways these cloths were worn.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Ndau house forms, roofing, building materials, architectural decoration, named building types, or urban traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The historical account identifies traditional herbs, spiritual items, animal skins, bones, textiles, and golden beads among Ndau trade goods. The museum catalogue records objects associated with divination equipment: flasks and containers made of gourd, a container made of gourd, skin with hair, cord, and metal, a basket made of cane, a chief’s ornament made of porcelain, and other divination objects. The records do not identify the objects as specifically Ndau or describe their manufacture, use, or place of origin beyond these catalogue descriptions.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources mention golden beads as historical trade goods. The museum catalogue records a chief’s ornament made of porcelain, a head-band made of cowrie shells, leather, and string, a belt with thongs made of glass beads, leather, and cord, a necklet made of glass beads, cloth, and string, and a fly-whisk with a ring made of wood, horse tail, cord, and glass beads. The sources used do not describe tattoos, scarification, ear piercing, hair practices, or the ritual meaning of these ornaments.

## Music & performance

The Ndau language article records songs and musical traditions preserved in publications by C. Kamba Simango, Franz Boas, and Natalie Curtis Burlin. In 1922, Simango, described as a Vandau ethnographer, worked with Franz Boas to publish a collection of 20 Ndau fables and 29 Ndau proverbs with English translations in the Journal of American Folklore.

The collection Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent, published in 1920, included Ndau texts and translations supplied by Simango. It contained Ndau lyrics, English translations, and transcriptions of the music. The named ritual songs include *Mate'ka*, identified as “Song of the Rain Ceremony,” and *Manthi'ki*, identified as “Spirit Song.” Other named songs include *Lum'bo Lgo Lu'do*, identified as “Love-Song,” and *Mafu've*, identified as “Dance of Girls.” The same account lists “Children's Songs,” “Laboring Songs,” and “Dance Songs,” together with *Kufa'mba*, a mocking song, and *Chili'lo*, a lament.

The sources also mention songs in the folktale “How the Animals Dug Their Well,” and songs forming part of the “Legend of the Daughter and the Slave” and the “Legend of the Sky-Maiden.” An appendix provided an interlinear word-for-word rendering of Ndau proverbs and song lyrics into English. The sources used do not name musical instruments or describe performance ensembles, venues, or musicians beyond these publications.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name *Mafu've* as a “Dance of Girls” and refer more generally to “Dance Songs.” They also identify *Mate'ka* as a song of the rain ceremony. The sources used do not describe Ndau dance movements, costumes, dramatic forms, theatre, masks, puppetry, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not provide an annual Ndau festival calendar or dates for festivals. They do describe several ritual and spiritual practices. *Mate'ka* is identified as a “Song of the Rain Ceremony.” Ndau n'anga are traditional healers who communicate with spirits and use traditional medicine, called *mushonga*, to heal or harm people. They may be male or female, although the source says they are more often female.

When resolving a case of spirit aggression, an n'anga determines the nature of the spirit and whether it was sent by a witch or another n'anga. Spirits can be captured in a ceremony called *ukufemba*, in which the spirit introduces itself and explains how it entered a family. N'anga are also called upon to manipulate weather during droughts or floods by appealing to the *nzuzu*. They practice divination by inviting *madzvoka* to possess them, enabling them to perceive remote places and events and to determine the perpetrator of a crime, locate lost people or objects, or discover whether someone is lying.

## Foodways

The sources used do not describe Ndau staple foods, grains, dishes, cooking methods, ceremonial foods, tea or coffee traditions, dietary rules, or food taboos. The historical account states only that traditional herbs were among the goods traded by the Ndau in networks centered around Mapungubwe.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Ndau language article records 20 Ndau fables and 29 Ndau proverbs published in 1922 by C. Kamba Simango and Franz Boas. The proverbs include “Simba lo ngwena lili mumfula,” translated as “The strength of the crocodile is in the water”; “Chipanga achizivi vatendji,” translated as “The knife does not know its owner”; “Hove djinotevela mulambo wadjo,” translated as “Fish follow their river”; and “Manthede a·novengana pakurga, napamfumfu anobesana,” translated as “Baboons quarrel over food, but in danger help one another.”

Simango also supplied Ndau texts and translations for Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent, published by Natalie Curtis Burlin in 1920. The book included Ndau songs, folktale songs, English translations, musical transcriptions, commentary, and an interlinear rendering of the proverbs and lyrics. Named narratives include “How the Animals Dug Their Well,” the “Legend of the Daughter and the Slave,” and the “Legend of the Sky-Maiden.” The sources do not describe a contemporary literary movement beyond the recorded publications and the 2013 rejuvenation of the ChiNdau identity in Zimbabwe.

## Language & religion

Ndau, also called chiNdau, Chindau, Ndzawu, Njao, and Chidanda, is a Bantu language and a Shona language. The language article states that it is spoken by 2,400,000 people and is mutually intelligible with Manyika, Zezuru, and Karanga. In Zimbabwe, Ndau is mainly spoken in Chipinge and Chimanimani districts. In Mozambique, it is spoken in parts of Sofala Province, including Machanga, Chibabava, Machaze, Buzi, Nhamatanda, Dondo, and Beira, and to a lesser extent in Mambone and Mossurize. Ndau also uses L, Q, and X in its orthography, with sounds acquired from neighboring Nguni languages.

Traditional Ndau identify themselves as one people through Musikavanthu/Mlambo, regarded as a common ancestor and as a rainmaker and earthly embodiment of the Creator of the Universe, known as “Mwari Musikavanthu” or “Musikavanhu.” Many Ndau people have also embraced Christianity through missionary activity. The sources used do not describe a historical script.

- Natalie Curtis Burlin, *Songs and Tales from the Dark Continent*, 1920.
- Christy Schuetze, *Spirit Wives and Church Mothers: Marriage, Survival, and Healing in Central Mozambique*. University of Wisconsin Press, 2023.
- Carin Vijfhuizen, *The People You Live With: Gender Identities and Social Practices, Beliefs and Power in the livelihoods of Ndau women and men in a village with an irrigation scheme in Zimbabwe*. Wageningen University, 1998.
- British Museum catalogue records for Ndau-associated objects: stopper; flask and containers forming part of divination equipment; basket; chief’s ornament; head-band; belt; necklet; and fly-whisk.

title: "Karamojong"
subtitle: "Uganda"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]

## Overview

The Karamojong, also called Karimojong, are a Nilotic ethnic group living mainly in north-east Uganda, in the southern part of the region known as Karamoja. Their population is estimated at 475,000 people. Their language, Ngakarimojong, belongs to the Nilotic language family and the Nilo-Saharan language family. The Karamojong are agro-pastoral herders whose principal livelihood is livestock herding, while crop cultivation is secondary and possible only in suitable areas. Their culture is organized in part through a generation-based age system, pastoral transhumance, wrestling connected with marriage, traditional dance, and the social importance of cattle. Museum records document objects associated with Karamoja, Moroto, Kangole, Amudat, Nakipiripirit, and Nabilutuk.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources do not describe named Karamojong textile or pattern traditions in sufficient detail for this section.

**Beaded women’s aprons** — A British Museum catalogue records an apron made of glass beads arranged in patterns on a hide backing with hair. The beads are pale, mid, and dark blue and red, with some iron beads.

**Women’s hide dress** — A Museum of World Culture record identifies a front piece of a married woman’s dress from Nakipiripirit, made of hide. The record states that unmarried women’s front pieces were decorated with cowrie shells and beads and were smaller.

**Cowrie-shell girdles** — Museum records document a woman’s girdle from Nakipiripirit with cowrie shells, as well as British Museum records of a leather waist-band decorated with cowrie shells and a girdle made of pale hide with ostrich eggshell discs and glass beads.

**Married woman’s tail-piece** — A British Museum record describes a tail worn behind by a married woman, made of vegetable fibre and decorated with pink and white glass beads and larger blue and white glass beads.

**Hide arm ornaments** — A British Museum catalogue records an arm ornament made from five plaited hide strips, with a tassel of loose strips, some decorated with coils of aluminium wire.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name linear motifs on one calabash stopper, but do not provide a broader Karamojong motif vocabulary.

### Clothing & dress

The sources document clothing and adornment for both women and men, but do not provide a complete account of everyday dress. Women’s garments include hide front pieces and aprons made from glass beads arranged on hide. The Museum of World Culture record for Nakipiripirit distinguishes the front piece of a married woman’s dress from the smaller front piece worn by unmarried women, which could be decorated with cowrie shells and beads. British Museum records describe a married woman’s fibre tail-piece, a leather waist-band decorated with cowrie shells, a girdle of hide and ostrich eggshell discs, and open sandals made of buffalo hide.

Men’s and women’s headgear are represented by catalogue records. A composite headdress consists of black ostrich feathers mounted on cow hide with a fibre chin strap. Another head-dress, called “Chignon” in the record, is made of human hair and clay and painted brown, blue, and grey. A Museum of World Culture record describes a man’s helmet made of mixed materials. The sources do not describe named vernacular garment terms beyond *rungu* for a club.

### Architecture

The sources do not describe Karamojong houses, settlements, fences, roofing, or other forms of vernacular architecture.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Museum records document several household and working objects associated with Karamoja. These include iron knives, a finger-knife with a leather guard, spears, arrows with leaf-shaped iron heads, and clubs called *rungu*. The collections also include clay pots without ears from Kangole, calabash bowls, a milk vessel, a carved wooden spoon, a fly-whisk made from a cow’s tail, wooden vessels, and water vessels made from gourds with leather straps.

Several vessels are identified as drums used for storing food. Records from Nakipiripirit describe cylindrical vessels made from wood or other materials, with dimensions including 15 cm in diameter and 24,5 cm in height, and 20 cm in diameter and 31 cm in height. A calabash bottle from Nakipiripirit has a woven carrying covering made from strips.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum records document body ornaments made from hide, cowrie shells, glass beads, metal, hair, clay, and other materials. These include necklaces, bracelets, waist ornaments, neck ornaments, arm ornaments, earrings, and a man’s lip ornament made from white stone. A child’s bracelet consists of aluminium and copper spirals on a metal core. A woman’s neck ornament is made of iron with rolled ends, while another waist ornament consists of five loops of predominantly black glass beads.

Hair and head adornment are also represented. The British Museum records a frontal head ornament made of felted human hair and clay, painted, and a “Chignon” made of human hair and clay. The sources do not document tattooing, henna, or a broader named system of body decoration.

## Music & performance

The sources do not describe named Karamojong musical genres, instruments, song forms, or performance contexts in detail. A Museum of World Culture collection category called “Horisonter - Musik” includes several objects identified as drums, but the catalogue descriptions state that these were vessels for storing food rather than providing a musical function. One Museum of World Culture record identifies a dance bell worn below the knee by a girl. The Wikipedia article states that Karamojong traditional dance is remarkable and has stood the test of time, but does not name a dance form or describe its musical accompaniment.

## Dance & theatre

Karamojong traditional dance is described in the Wikipedia source as remarkable and enduring. A museum catalogue records a dance bell worn below the knee by a girl. The sources do not name particular dances, theatrical forms, dramatic genres, or performance occasions.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not identify an annual Karamojong festival calendar or named seasonal festivals. They do describe several social and ritual practices. Livestock herding involves pastoral transhumance: for 3–4 months in a year, people move their animals to neighboring districts in search of water and pasture. The availability of food and water affects interaction with other ethnic groups.

Wrestling is a rite of passage into manhood and a requirement connected with engagement. A young Karamojong man must wrestle the woman he wishes to marry. If he wins, he is considered a man and may marry her; dowry negotiations can then begin. A non-Karamojong man who wishes to marry a Karamojong woman is also required to undergo the ceremony. The sources do not describe funeral rites, birth ceremonies, named initiation ceremonies, or festival dates.

A Museum of World Culture record describes a goat-hide strap worn within a family during an offering against illness and accidents. This is the only explicitly described ritual object in the museum records.

## Foodways

The sources state that the Karamojong are cattle-keeping people and that livestock herding has social and cultural importance. Crop cultivation is a secondary activity undertaken only where practicable. Water and food availability are persistent concerns. Museum records identify milk vessels, calabash bowls, pots, and several drums or vessels used for storing food. A Museum of World Culture record describes a milk vessel from Nabilutuk, while several objects from Nakipiripirit are identified as food-storage vessels.

The Karamojong language article records *ŋakipi* for water and *ŋakile* for milk. It also states that traditional liquids such as water and milk are feminine plural forms in the language, while bottled beer is a more recently introduced masculine singular term. The sources do not identify staple grains, named dishes, brewing traditions, cooking techniques, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources describe Karamojong and Teso Cluster migration traditions. According to the Wikipedia accounts, the group is said to have migrated from Abyssinia between 1600 and 1700 AD as a single group before fragmenting into several peoples. Another account places the wider migration from present-day Ethiopia around 1600 A.D. The name Karamojong is derived from the phrase “ekar ngimojong,” explained as “the old men can walk no farther.” The language article gives a related explanation, approximating the name as “the old men sat down,” referring to a migration more than 300 years ago.

The language source mentions selected Ngakarimojong proverbs but does not reproduce them. It also records the greeting *Ejoka?*, the response *Ejok-nooi*, and other phrases. The sources do not describe a named epic, folktale cycle, riddle tradition, contemporary literary movement, or formal preservation project.

## Language & religion

Ngakarimojong is a Nilotic language of the Nilo-Saharan language family spoken by the Karamojong in north-east Uganda. It is also written as ŋaKarimojoŋ or ŋaKaramojoŋ in Karamojong, and as Ngakarimojong or N'Karamojong in English. Closely related languages and dialects are associated with the Jie, Dodoth, Teso, Turkana, Tesyo, Jiye, Toposa, and Nyangatom. These peoples are described as part of the Karamojong cluster, also called the Teso cluster.

Written Ngakarimojong uses the Roman alphabet. Spelling rules were established by missionaries in the 1960s, and the orthography was created mainly by British Anglicans and Italian Roman Catholics. The language has three basic tones and three contour tones. The vocabulary source records *Akuj* for God, while noting that its root also means “north” and “up.” It states that traditional religious beliefs are reflected in the language. The sources do not describe the current religious landscape in detail.

## Sources & further reading

- John Lamphear, *The Traditional History of the Jie of Uganda*, Clarendon Press, 1976.
- Diane Lesley-Neuman, *ATR Harmony in Karimojong: Justification for a Stratal Optimality Theory*, University of Colorado, 2007.
- P. Logiro and J. Ilukori, *A Simplified Ngakarimojong-English English-Ngakarimojong Dictionary*, Fountain Publishers, 2007.
- Bruno Novelli, *A Grammar of the Karimojong Language*, D. Reimer, 1985.
- [Karamojong people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karamojong_people)
- [Karamojong language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karamojong_language)

title: "Baganda"
subtitle: "Uganda"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]
---

## Overview

The Baganda are a Bantu ethnic group who share a common culture, history, language, and clan system. They are primarily native to Buganda, a subnational kingdom within Uganda. The Baganda comprised 15.3 percent of Uganda’s population at the time of the 2024 census, and the population in Uganda is estimated at 16.3 million. A single person is a Muganda, while several people are Baganda; the people are also called Abaganda, and Ganda appears in older English texts. They traditionally speak Luganda, and every Muganda belongs to a clan. The Kabaka, the king of Buganda, has a central place in social and political life. Organized Baganda communities also exist in Canada, South Africa, Sweden, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Lubugo** — Barkcloth, also called olubugo or Lubugo, was the most common form of attire used throughout Buganda. It was made from the bark of at least 20 tree species, especially the Mutuba tree, and different trees produced colors and textures ranging from yellow and sandy brown to dark red-brown. The finest quality was rusty brown cloth called Kimote; a species producing white cloth was reserved for the Kabaka.

**Barkcloth manufacture** — Museum records describe barkcloth made from the bark of certain cultivated Ficus species. Barkcloth beaters were wooden clubs with cylindrical, grooved or serrated heads. One recorded beater has a head decorated with pointed patterns made by carving.

**Decorated barkcloth** — Museum examples include a red-brown barkcloth dress or cloak with bands of geometric patterns in black dye, barkcloth with geometric patterns stencilled in black, and large rectangular terracotta-coloured barkcloth with seams, repairs, and stains.

**Barkcloth tools** — The Museum of World Culture records a wooden barkcloth beater, 27 centimetres high, with a ribbed cylindrical head and carved pointed decoration. Other records describe barkcloth beaters with different coarse and fine grooves.

Barkcloth also served as bedding and for wrapping goods. Museum records include a strip on which beating had just begun and a finely corrugated rectangle with patchwork repairs.

**Motif vocabulary.** Geometric patterns, pointed patterns, bands, chequer plaiting.

### Clothing & dress

The traditional dress of Baganda women is the Gomesi, while the Kanzu is the traditional dress of Baganda men. Barkcloth, or Lubugo, is the traditional fabric and is made from the bark of the Mutuba tree. Historical descriptions state that Baganda covered the body from head to toe and regarded nudity as disgusting and shameful. Bark cloaks could resemble yellow corduroy cloth and were carefully made, crimped, and set as though stiffened with starch.

Museum records add garments made of goat skin, composed of several pieces sewn together and pierced with small holes around the edges, as well as a robe made from white gazelle skin. Recorded adornments include a headband of fibre and red, white, and blue glass beads, and a waist belt made of fibrous material covered with small blackened wooden rings. The sources do not describe footwear or a separate everyday dress tradition.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Baganda houses, architectural forms, roofing, decoration, or named building types.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Museum records include red pottery bottles blackened with plumbago, including milk-vessels with incised and coloured red-and-white bands, long slender necks, cup-shaped lips, and globular bodies. Other objects include a wooden pot with a plaited cap, a basketry beer strainer, a small coiled basket apparently made from bark strips, and a snuff-container made from two brass cartridge cases soldered together.

Recorded weapons and tools include wooden shields with bosses, cane wicker-work shields, shields with basket-work ornamentation, a knife with a large curved iron blade, and a metal bill-hook with a carved wooden handle. Museum photographs document Ganda men making cooking-pots by coiling clay and another Ganda man pounding grain with a wooden pestle and mortar.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Museum objects include necklaces made from elephant-tail hair and red glass beads, neck-rings made of iron or beads, an ivory child’s anklet, a silver armlet with hinged construction, and a dance anklet or rattle consisting of an iron bar with nine iron beads. Other recorded ornaments include a waist ornament composed of 102 strands of plaited fibre covered with white, red, and blue glass beads, a metal miniature-shield amulet, and an oval circlet covered with plaited dried leaf.

A snuff-bottle is made of blue glass and has a cover of red, white, and black glass beads ending in small cowrie shells. The sources state that Baganda men rarely kept facial hair and that women carefully shaved their armpit hair, except under a custom connected with a husband’s absence. They also state that the Baganda traditionally avoided scarification, tooth extraction, pierced ear lobes, and circumcision.

## Music & performance

Baganda music is a musical culture developed by the people of Uganda. Its instruments include the Amadinda and Akadinda xylophones, the Ennanga harp, the Etongoli lyre, drums, and the Kadongo lamellophone, whose plural is budongo. Amadinda, akadinda, ennanga, entongoli, and several types of drums were used in the courtly music of the Kabaka. The kadongo entered Baganda music more recently, dating to the early 20th century, and budongo music is not part of traditional court music.

Baganda music is based on an approximately equidistant pentatonic scale. The octave, mwànjo, is divided into five intervals of approximately 240 cents, or 2.4 semitones. The music is not harmony-based, chords are not used, and only octaves are consonant. Performances often use noisy or buzzing timbres: metal rings can be placed around kadongo lamellas, while scales of a kind of goana can be fixed to the ennanga so that the strings touch them.

The amadinda is a log xylophone with 12 wooden bars placed on two fresh banana stems. It is played by three musicians called omunazi, omwawuzi, and omukoonezi. The parts are called okunaga and okwawula, while the third musician performs okukoonera. The correct way of playing is called Okusengejja. Named advanced or mistaken techniques include Okudaliza, okusita ebiyondo oba ebisenge, Okubwatula, Okugugumula, Okuyiwa, and Okwokya.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not describe named Baganda dances, theatrical genres, masked performances, or dramatic traditions. They state that dancing forms part of the twin-naming ceremony called okuzina abalongo.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not describe an annual Baganda festival calendar or seasonal festivals. They do describe rites connected with naming, marriage, death, and the confirmation of twins.

In the former naming ceremony called okwalula abaana, a child was named and confirmed as a member of the clan. A saved piece of the child’s umbilical cord was used in confirming connection to the father. Twin-related names and titles include ssaalongo for the father of twins, nnaalongo for the mother, and particular surnames for older and younger twins. The naming and confirmation of twins is called okuzina abalongo and involves drinking, eating, obscene words, promiscuity, and dancing. Some participants may undergo a cleansing ceremony called okukansira.

Traditional marriage involves several rites. These include a visit to the bride-to-be’s paternal aunt, Ssenga; Okukyala, the visit to the bride-to-be’s parents; Okwanjula, the introduction ceremony; Akasiki, held the night before the wedding reception; Kaasuze katya, held on the morning of the reception; Embaga, the wedding reception; Okuzza omuzigo, a show of appreciation; and Okugenda mu kisenge, a honeymoon lasting roughly six days. In modern times, some ceremonies are skipped or merged.

Death rites include Okubika, the announcement of death; a communal wake; preparation of the body; Okuziraga, a ritual involving oil or water rubbed on the forehead or face; and Okwabya Olumbe, which marks the end of mourning and is usually held days or months after burial.

## Foodways

The sources used do not describe Baganda staple foods, named dishes, cooking traditions, ceremonial meals, beverages, or dietary rules. They mention eating and drinking as parts of the twin-naming ceremony and record a wooden pestle and mortar used by a Ganda man for pounding grain.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Baganda creation myth identifies Kintu as the first man on earth and in Buganda. Kintu married Nnambi, the daughter of the god Ggulu, and the Baganda are described as the descendants of Kintu and Nnambi. Nnambi’s jealous brother Walumbe is responsible in the myth for human disease, sickness, and death. Kayikuuzi tried to protect humans from Walumbe and continues trying to capture him from the underground where he hides. On the basis of this myth, the Baganda are called abaana ba Nnambi, or Nnambi’s children.

The sources also record a Ganda proverb: “He who makes you shed tears, you make him shed blood.” They describe clan traditions, mythological names, and songs whose titles refer to associated texts. The sources used do not describe a Baganda epic, riddle tradition, contemporary literary revival, or preservation project.

## Language & religion

Luganda is the traditional language of the Baganda and is described as a tonal language. Its tones significantly influence music: the progression of tones in a song text partly determines possible melodies, and musical patterns can evoke new text associations for Luganda speakers. The sources also state that the words Ganda, Abaganda, and Omuganda are connected with concepts of brotherhood, unity, and the clan or people.

According to the 2002 Census of Uganda, 42.7 percent of Baganda were Roman Catholic, 27.4 percent Anglican, 23 percent Muslim, and 4.3 percent Pentecostal. The sources state that most Baganda belong to Abrahamic religions, while some also secretly follow the traditional Kiganda religion. Traditional religious references include the Lubaales, Ggulu, Walumbe, and Kayikuuzi. Clan members are believed to share common ancestors, and each clan has a totem animal, plant, or thing that its members must not eat or harm.

## Sources & further reading

- [Baganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baganda)
- [Baganda music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baganda_music)
- UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: no Uganda inscriptions were supplied in the sources.
- British Museum collection records supplied for shields, barkcloth, clothing, musical instruments, tools, pottery, jewelry, and photographs.
- Museum of World Culture and Museum of Ethnography catalogue records supplied for Baganda barkcloth beaters and barkcloth.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Barkcloth, especially Lubugo, was the most common traditional cloth in Buganda.

- **Barkcloth beater** — Wooden barkcloth beaters had grooved or serrated heads, and some had carved pointed patterns.
- **Decorated barkcloth** — Some barkcloth had black geometric patterns, bands, seams, repairs, and stains.
- **Barkcloth patterns** — Recorded motifs include geometric patterns, pointed patterns, bands, and chequer plaiting.

### Clothing & dress

The Gomesi and Kanzu are the traditional clothes of Baganda women and men.

- **Women’s dress** (*Gomesi*) — The Gomesi is the traditional dress of Baganda women.
- **Men’s dress** (*Kanzu*) — The Kanzu is the traditional dress of Baganda men.
- **Bark cloak** (*Lubugo*) — Bark cloaks could look like yellow corduroy and were carefully crimped and stiffened.
- **Goat-skin garment** — Some recorded garments were made from several pieces of goat skin sewn together and pierced around the edges.
- **Gazelle-skin robe** — Museum records include a robe made from white gazelle skin.

### Architecture

The sources do not describe Baganda houses or named building types.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Baganda everyday objects included pottery, baskets, snuff containers, shields, knives, and grain-pounding tools.

- **Red pottery milk vessel** — Some pottery bottles were blackened with plumbago and had long necks, cup-shaped lips, globular bodies, and red-and-white bands.
- **Wooden pot with cap** — A recorded wooden pot had a plaited cap.
- **Beer strainer** — A basketry beer strainer is among the recorded household objects.
- **Cartridge-case snuff container** — One snuff container was made from two brass cartridge cases soldered together.
- **Shield** — Recorded shields were made from wood, cane wicker-work, or basket-work and could have bosses or ornamentation.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Baganda adornment used hair, beads, iron, ivory, silver, fibre, leaf, and cowrie shells.

- **Elephant-tail necklace** — Some necklaces were made from elephant-tail hair and red glass beads.
- **Ivory anklet** — An ivory child’s anklet is among the recorded ornaments.
- **Silver armlet** — A recorded silver armlet had a hinged construction.
- **Dance anklet** — A dance anklet or rattle was made from an iron bar with nine iron beads.
- **Beaded waist ornament** — One waist ornament had 102 strands of plaited fibre covered with white, red, and blue glass beads.

## Music & performance

Baganda music uses xylophones, harps, lyres, drums, and lamellophones in a pentatonic musical system.

- **Log xylophone** (*Amadinda*) — The amadinda has 12 wooden bars placed on two fresh banana stems and is played by three musicians.
- **Court xylophone** (*Akadinda*) — The akadinda was used in the courtly music of the Kabaka.
- **Harp** (*Ennanga*) — The ennanga was used in courtly music and could have scales fixed to its strings to create buzzing sounds.
- **Lyre** (*Etongoli*) — The etongoli lyre was used in Baganda music and courtly music.
- **Lamellophone** (*Kadongo*) — The kadongo entered Baganda music in the early twentieth century and is also called budongo in the plural.

## Dance & theatre

The sources do not describe named dances or theatre traditions, but dancing is part of the twin-naming ceremony.

- **Twin-naming dance** (*Okuzina abalongo*) — Dancing forms part of okuzina abalongo, the naming and confirmation ceremony for twins.

## Festivals & rituals

Baganda rites mark naming, twins, marriage, death, and the end of mourning.

- **Child naming rite** (*Okwalula abaana*) — In okwalula abaana, a child was named and confirmed as a member of the clan using a saved piece of the umbilical cord.
- **Twin-naming ceremony** (*Okuzina abalongo*) — Okuzina abalongo confirms twins and includes drinking, eating, obscene words, promiscuity, and dancing.
- **Bride’s introduction ceremony** (*Okwanjula*) — Okwanjula is the traditional introduction ceremony for the bride-to-be.
- **Wedding reception** (*Embaga*) — Embaga is the wedding reception in traditional marriage.
- **End of mourning rite** (*Okwabya Olumbe*) — Okwabya Olumbe marks the end of mourning days or months after burial.

## Foodways

The sources give little detail about Baganda food, but mention eating, drinking, and pounding grain.

- **Grain pounding** — A recorded photograph shows a Ganda man pounding grain with a wooden pestle and mortar.
- **Eating and drinking at twin rites** — Eating and drinking are parts of the twin-naming ceremony.

## Oral tradition & literature

Baganda origin stories trace the people to Kintu and Nnambi and explain death through Walumbe.

- **First man** (*Kintu*) — Kintu is described as the first man on earth and in Buganda.
- **Mother of the Baganda** (*Nnambi*) — Nnambi was the daughter of Ggulu, wife of Kintu, and the Baganda are called her children.
- **Cause of death** (*Walumbe*) — Walumbe is Nnambi’s jealous brother and is blamed in the myth for disease, sickness, and death.
- **Protector and pursuer** (*Kayikuuzi*) — Kayikuuzi tried to protect humans and continues trying to capture Walumbe underground.
- **Proverb** — A recorded Ganda proverb says, “He who makes you shed tears, you make him shed blood.”

## Language & religion

Luganda is a tonal language, and Baganda religious life includes Abrahamic faiths, traditional beliefs, clans, and totems.

- **Traditional language** (*Luganda*) — Luganda is the traditional tonal language of the Baganda, and its tones influence song melodies.
- **People of the clan** (*Muganda*) — A single Baganda person is called a Muganda.
- **The Baganda people** (*Abaganda*) — Abaganda is another name for the Baganda.
- **Traditional gods and spirits** (*Lubaales*) — The Lubaales are among the traditional religious references of the Baganda.
- **Clan totem** — Each clan has a totem animal, plant, or thing that members must not eat or harm.

## Glossary

- *Kimote* — Finest rusty-brown barkcloth

- *Kanzu* — Traditional men’s dress

- *Nnambi* — Kintu’s wife and ancestor of the Baganda

## Overview

The Gisu people, also called the Bamasaba people of Elgon, are a Bantu-speaking ethnic group of the Masaba people in eastern Uganda. They live mainly in Mbale District, on the slopes of Mount Elgon. The 2014 National Census of Uganda estimated their population at 1,646,904, or 4.9% of the total population. They are closely related to the Bukusu people of Kenya, and their language is mutually intelligible with Bukusu. The Gisu are agriculturalists whose cultural life includes the Imbalu initiation ceremonies, a two-year cycle of circumcision ceremonies, Lumasaba language traditions, banana-based foodways, bamboo-shoot gathering, and material objects such as pottery vessels, wooden tools, shields, ornaments, and rattles.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document Gisu textile or pattern traditions.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources used do not name Gisu textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe everyday clothing, ceremonial dress, footwear, head coverings, or named garments. They do record several forms of body adornment and warrior ornament: a girdle made of strings of seed, warrior’s head ornaments made from pierced tusks and attached with leather thongs, an iron necklet, and a leather leglet bound with cotton cloth and fitted with an iron rattle.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Gisu houses, settlements, roofs, building materials, decoration, or named architectural forms.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records a range of pottery vessels and household objects. These include a reddish pottery vase with one handle, a spheroidal pottery beer pot with five mouths, a pottery vessel with a black interior and everted lip, a pottery vase with three necks, a vase with two necks, a pottery vase with a spout and strainer, and plain or reddish pottery bowls. One bowl has nine holes, while another has ten holes in the bottom. The catalogue also records a small wooden and wicker shield with a central boss; a single-edged, curved iron knife with a wooden handle; and a wooden whistle bound with iron and brass wire.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The catalogue records an iron necklet with ring ends, a girdle made of strings of seed, and a leather leglet bound with cotton cloth. The leglet has an attached iron rattle containing two metal balls. Two warrior’s head ornaments are made from tusk: one is pierced four times and attached with a leather thong through two holes, while the other is pierced twice and attached through the holes with a leather thong. The sources do not describe tattoos, henna, hair practices, or the ritual functions of these ornaments.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not provide a documented account of Gisu music, named song genres, musical ensembles, or performance settings. They do record a wooden whistle bound with iron and brass wire, but give no information about its playing technique, musical use, or performance context. The sources also mention the book *African Musics in Context: Institutions, Culture, Identity*, but do not provide a description of Gisu musical practice in the supplied material.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not describe Gisu dances, theatre, dramatic traditions, masked performances, or entertainment forms. The supplied material does not identify named dance traditions or distinguish ceremonial performance from recreation.

## Festivals & rituals

The principal named ritual in the sources is *Imbalu*, the initiation ceremony undergone by men among the Bagisu. The initiation ceremonies among the Bamasaaba are held every two years during August. The source describes circumcision as an old culture practiced by the Bamasaaba in eastern Uganda and states that the culture was adopted from the Maasai people, who were described as the Bamasaba’s in-laws. The supplied account connects the adoption of circumcision with the story of Masaba, who migrated from the Ethiopian Mountains via Lake Turkana to Sironko and settled around Bududa. He fell in love with a Maasai girl known as Nabarwa, and her family required him to undergo their rite of circumcision before marrying her. The sources do not describe birth, wedding, funeral, annual harvest, or calendrical festivals beyond the August timing of Imbalu.

## Foodways

Banana is the staple food of the Gisu people and is commonly referred to as “Matoke.” The sources also state that the Bamasaba ancestors lived on bamboo shoots, known as *Malewa* in the Lumasaba language. These shoots are collected from bamboo trees on top of Mount Elgon. The sources do not describe recipes, cooking methods, ceremonial foods, dietary rules, beverages, or meal customs. Agricultural communities among the Bagisu grow Arabica coffee, cotton, tobacco, maize, beans, millet, sorghum, yams, and cassava. Those living as far as 5000 feet above sea level grow Arabica coffee, much of which is sold to Bugisu Co-operative Union.

## Oral tradition & literature

The supplied sources preserve an origin tradition concerning the ancestors Mundu and Sera, whom the Masaba, Bukusu, and Luhya people believed to be their ancestors. A related account tells of Masaba’s migration from the Ethiopian Mountains via Lake Turkana to Sironko and his settlement around Bududa. Masaba’s first son with Nabarwa was Mwambu, who was nicknamed Nkisu by his Maasai uncles after they had stolen his father’s cows. Masaba failed to pronounce the nickname and called his son Mugisu; the account presents this nickname as the origin of the name Bagisu. The sources do not describe a named epic, proverb corpus, riddle tradition, or contemporary literary revival.

## Language & religion

Masaba, also called Lumasaaba and sometimes Gisu or Lugisu after one of its dialects, is a Bantu language spoken by more than two million people in East Africa. The Gisu dialect in eastern Uganda is mutually intelligible with Bukusu, spoken by ethnic Luhya in western Kenya. Varieties listed in the source are Gisu, Kisu, Bukusu, Syan, Tachoni, Dadiri, and Buya. Dadiri is spoken in the north, Gisu in the center, and Buya in the center and south of Masaba territory in Uganda. Masaba has a five-vowel system and around eighteen noun classes. The Bamasaba speak a dialect of Lumasaba that is fully understandable by other dialects and is also understood by the Bukusu.

The majority of the Bagisu are Christians, mainly Anglican through the Church of Uganda, estimated at 45.7%. Roman Catholics account for an estimated 29.1%; around 14% follow Islam according to the 2002 Census of Uganda, and 5.3% are Pentecostal. The sources do not describe traditional religious practices beyond the ancestor tradition and the Imbalu initiation ceremony.

## Overview

The Betsileo are a highland ethnic group of Madagascar and the country’s third-largest ethnic group by population. They occupy the south of the Madagascar plateau, from the north of the Mania River to the foot of the Andringitra Massif, between the Bongolava chain, the Eastern Forest and the neighboring territories of other Malagasy groups. Much of the region lies within the Malagasy province of Fianarantsoa, whose capital has the same name. Their territory is traditionally divided into Northern, Central and Southern Betsileo areas. The Betsileo speak a dialect of Malagasy, a Malayo-Polynesian language derived from the Barito languages of southern Borneo. Their folk culture is associated with rice terraces, zebu raising, woodcarving, woven textiles, ceremonial practices and the continued combination of Christian and ancestral traditions.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Woven cotton textiles** — The museum records include cotton cloths with stripes, geometric patterns, fringes and embroidery. One waist-band is woven from off-white cotton with brown, green and pink stripes, with braided bands sewn to its ends.

**Burial cloths** — The catalogue records burial cloths woven from cotton. One consists of dark brown, light brown, orange and white wide stripes, thin green stripes and a geometric pattern woven along the ends; another uses off-white cotton with red stripes and red geometric patterns.

**Striped Betsileo tissue** — A Museum of Ethnography record describes a Betsileo tissue sewn at the middle, striped in different colours, with silk embroidery and fringed warp threads.

**Brown embroidered cloth** — A British Museum record describes a rectangular brown cotton cloth with fringe on all sides and an embroidered silver geometric pattern with the initials “EB” at the centre.

**Basketry** — The catalogue records hats, covers, mats and baskets made of basketry, as well as a hat made of vegetable fibre.

The sources used do not name additional Betsileo textile traditions or vernacular pattern names.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used record a waist-band woven from cotton, several basketry hats, a hat made of vegetable fibre and a cap made of plaited grass. They also record cotton burial cloths and other woven cloths with stripes, fringes, geometric patterns and embroidery. The sources do not distinguish everyday and ceremonial clothing by gender, and they do not provide vernacular garment names, footwear traditions or detailed accounts of dress practices.

### Architecture

Betsileo traditionally lived in huts made of vegetable fibre, while wooden huts were reserved for nobles. Both types could be decorated with motifs or the horns of zebu, following Malagasy architectural norms. Mud and brick houses are more common today. The Betsileo region around Fianarantsoa is characterized by hills and valleys whose sides contain rice paddies formed into elaborate terraces. The sources used do not provide a vernacular name for a house type, or details of roofs, interior plans or urban architecture.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum records include a water flask made of burnished red pottery in the shape of a double gourd, a pottery bowl, an earthenware pot, a clay cooking vessel, a wooden spoon, a wooden plate, a shallow wooden dish, a gourd bottle, a palm-leaf fan, basketry mats, a basket, a pandanus-leaf cup and a wooden candlestick-holder. They also include a paddle-shaped spade made of hard brown wood, a pump drill and a tinder-box made of horn, wood, cord and bone. The sources do not describe local names or specific production techniques beyond the materials and forms recorded in the catalogues.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum records include a pair of silver earrings set with coral studs. The sources used do not document tattoos, henna, hair practices, ritual jewelry or other forms of body adornment.

## Music & performance

The British Museum catalogue records a musical instrument with the native name *Valiha*, described as a tube zither or guitar made from a section of bamboo. It has numerous strings formed from the bark or peel of the bamboo and raised on small bridges at both ends. The catalogue also records reed, bark and bamboo flutes, as well as an unfinished reed or bamboo musical instrument described as a snuff-box. These records establish the presence of string and wind instruments associated with the museum’s Betsileo material, but the sources do not describe musical genres, repertories, performance settings, song forms or musicians.

The sources describe the role of diviners, astrologists and witch doctors in Betsileo society. Astrologists and diviners are consulted to set dates for ceremonies or read people’s futures, while witch doctors are believed to manipulate magic and converse with ancestors. The sources do not connect these practices to named musical performances.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not describe Betsileo dances, theatrical traditions, dramatic genres, mask performances or other forms of staged entertainment.

## Festivals & rituals

One of the most significant Betsileo ceremonies described in the source material is *famadihana*, translated there as “turning of the bones.” During the ceremony, the remains of Betsileo ancestors are taken from their tombs, wrapped in new linens and celebrated. The sources do not provide a calendar date or season for this ceremony.

Betsileo religious life combines Christian practices with ancestral traditions and religious tenets. Much of the Malagasy population converted to Christianity after the arrival of European missionaries in the nineteenth century, and the source states that about 94% of Betsileo are Christians. Most Betsileo are described as either Protestant or Catholic, while ancestral traditions continue to be observed alongside or in combination with Christian practices.

Pre-Christian beliefs recognized ancestral spirits, ghosts and nature spirits, as well as a creator deity named Zanahary, who is still invoked for ceremonial purposes. The sources used do not describe birth rites, coming-of-age ceremonies, weddings, funerals apart from *famadihana*, annual festivals or a complete ritual calendar.

## Foodways

Rice cultivation is the Betsileo economic mainstay, and rice is described as a staple food in Madagascar. The Betsileo diet almost invariably consists of rice accompanied by livestock such as beef, chicken or duck, and secondary crops such as cassava, beans and other farm vegetables. Cattle raising is also important, although the source describes it as less significant than among neighboring groups such as the Bara.

The Museum of World Culture catalogue includes a photograph identified as a rice field in Betsileo, Madagascar, with the printed description “Rice Fields in terraces in the Betsileo.” The sources used do not name Betsileo dishes, cooking methods, ceremonial foods, drinks, dietary rules or food-related festivals.

## Oral tradition & literature

The different Betsileo kingdoms, including Fandriana, Fisakana, Manandriana and Isandra, had oral traditions dating back to the 17th century. The sources used do not preserve the contents of specific tales, epics, proverbs or riddles, and they do not identify a Betsileo literary revival or preservation project.

## Language & religion

The Betsileo speak a dialect of Malagasy. Malagasy is described as a branch of the Malayo-Polynesian language group derived from the Barito languages spoken in southern Borneo. The sources do not provide a Betsileo writing system, historical script or named literary language.

About 94% of Betsileo are Christians, most being either Protestant or Catholic. Christian practice exists alongside ancestral traditions and religious tenets. Earlier Betsileo beliefs recognized ancestral spirits, ghosts, nature spirits and the creator deity Zanahary. Diviners, astrologists and witch doctors remain significant in society: they are consulted about ceremonies, health issues, poisoning and the future, and witch doctors are believed to communicate with ancestors.

- The sources used do not identify a named scholar or documentation project for Betsileo culture.
- [Betsileo people — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsileo_people)

## Overview

The Sakalava are an ethnic group primarily found along the western edge of Madagascar, from Toliara in the south to the Sambirano River in the north. They constituted about 6.2 percent of Madagascar’s population, or about 2,079,000 people, in 2018. Their territory extends over about 128,000 square kilometers, from the Onilahy River in the southwest to Nosy Be in the north. Sakalava society includes regional groups with distinct customs and two principal dialects: the northern dialect of Boina and the southern dialect of Menabe. Their history includes Austronesian and Bantu settlement, Arab and European trade, royal dynasties, cattle pastoralism, royal ancestor worship, Tromba ceremonies, and the historical formation of Sakalava kingdoms in western Madagascar.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The museum catalogue records a shawl woven from raffia. It has blue, green and beige warp stripes down the centre, green and beige stripes along the outside edges, and two bands of ikat-dyed patterns showing men riding horses, animals and geometric designs. Braided fringe finishes each short end.

The sources used do not provide a vernacular name or further description of Sakalava textile traditions.

**Motif vocabulary.** Men riding horses, animals, geometric designs.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not provide a general account of Sakalava everyday or ceremonial dress. The museum catalogue records clothing on several figures, including cotton-cloth garments, a tunic tied at the waist with a hide belt, and a garment of cotton cloth tied with grass. A photographic record depicts an adult male wearing head-gear, a tee-shirt and shorts while riding an “ombi” or humped cow. The catalogue also records a shawl woven from raffia with striped and ikat-dyed decoration.

### Architecture

A museum photographic print shows a settlement with rectangular thatched shelters, with small palms and eucalyptus trees in the foreground. The sources used do not describe the construction, internal arrangement, decoration, or regional variation of these shelters. The religious sources describe a *doany* as a place of worship containing shrines dedicated to royal ancestors; the Doany of Mahajanga is also described as a gravesite for royal ancestors.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records spears with socketed iron or copper heads, hard-wood shafts, and, in one case, a copper spur at the butt. It also records wooden staffs, including one with a horse-and-rider handle and another carved with zigzags. Other objects include a wooden guitar or zither with a gourd resonator and vegetable-fibre strings, silver earrings, animal-horn charms, raffia string, cotton cloth, and glass beads. The catalogue also includes model rifles and powder-flasks carried by male warrior figures. The sources do not describe Sakalava ceramics.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum catalogue records an ear-ring made of silver. It also records charms made from animal horn, clay, fibrous matter, wooden pegs, red-dyed cotton cloth, raffia string, and red and black or many-coloured glass beads. One charm is identified as being against thieves and contains seven wood shavings and chips of wood. The sources do not document tattoos, henna, hair practices, or a broader system of jewelry and body adornment.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not identify Sakalava musical genres or describe a detailed performance repertoire. They do record a guitar or zither made of wood, with a gourd resonator and vegetable-fibre strings.

The principal named performance tradition in the sources is **Tromba**. It is a ceremony in which dady priests divine the spirits of deceased royal ancestors and communicate their words to Sakalava people. Tromba has also historically involved ceremonies and processions for deceased royalty, functioning both as a religious event and as a form of community celebration and identity affirmation. The practice has a long association with the Sakalava royal dynasties. It also spread to Mayotte through Andriantsoly and farther to Tanzania through Comorian migration to Zanzibar.

The sources do not describe song forms, musical ensembles, dance accompaniment, instruments used in Tromba, or performance venues beyond the religious and processional contexts mentioned above.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not describe Sakalava dances, theatrical forms, dramatic genres, or named dance performances. They state that Tromba includes ceremonies and processions for the spirits of deceased royalty, but do not specify choreographic forms.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not provide an annual festival calendar or dates for seasonal celebrations. They describe several religious and royal practices. About 60% of the Sakalava are said to follow Fomba Gasy, a traditional religion centred on royal ancestor worship and the noble dady lineage, which preserved the remains of deceased rulers.

During Tromba, dady priests divine the spirits of dead ancestors and communicate their words. The Sakalava visit memorial sites of royal ancestors to clean and maintain them. A devoted *toñy* is a tree or stone assigned to a spirit in its honour. In a doany, visitors wait until a guardian guides them to the shrines, joins them in prayer, and helps summon ancestral spirits. Visitors may offer money and receive a small piece of limestone called a *tanifoty*, understood in the source as a physical manifestation of an ancestor’s blessing. A white dot is placed on the visitor’s chest before departure.

The sources also describe royal succession, exile, burial, and the transformation of rulers into ancestors who can possess mediums known as the *saha* during Tromba. They do not describe birth, marriage, initiation, or funeral rites in general.

## Foodways

The sources used do not describe Sakalava dishes, staple foods, cooking methods, ceremonial meals, beverages, or dietary rules. They state that the Sakalava have historically been pastoralists with large zebu cattle herds, traditionally allowing them to graze freely over grasslands in the northwestern region. The sources do not provide further information about the use of cattle in foodways.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources describe Sakalava history through local tradition, oral histories, and documents. According to local tradition, the founders of the Sakalava kingdom were the Maroseraña, also called Maroseranana, princes described as “those who owned many ports,” from Fiherenana, now Toliara. Merina oral histories and documents in Comoros mention annual expeditions by Sakalava slave raiders through the end of the eighteenth century.

The sources used do not record a Sakalava epic, named folktale, proverb, riddle, or specialist storytelling context. The Sakalava language article states that Malagasy has a tradition of oratory arts and poetic histories and legends. Its best-known national epic is *Ibonia*, about a Malagasy folk hero of the same name, but the source does not identify it as specifically Sakalava.

## Language & religion

Sakalava communities speak at least two distinct Malagasy dialects. The Sakalava of Boina speak a northern Malagasy dialect, while the Sakalava of Menabe speak a southern Malagasy dialect. Southern Sakalava is more closely related to Masikoro, while Northern Sakalava shares linguistic features with Tsimihety. Malagasy is an Austronesian language and dialect continuum, and Sakalava dialects belong to its western varieties.

Malagasy is written in the Latin script, which Western missionaries introduced in the early nineteenth century; the Sorabe script, a local development of the Arabic script, was previously used. The Sakalava religious landscape includes Fomba Gasy, royal ancestor worship, Tromba, Sunni Islam, and Christianity. Sunni Islam arrived through Arab traders and was adopted by Sakalava rulers in the eighteenth century in connection with military support from the Omani and Zanzibar Sultanates. Christianity arrived with European traders and missionaries. The sources state that many Sakalava converts continued traditional practices such as spirit worship.

## Overview

The Antaisaka, also known as Tesaka or Tesaki, are an ethnic group of Madagascar traditionally concentrated south of Farafangana along the south-eastern coast. They have since spread more widely throughout the island, and an estimated 600,000 Malagasy identified as Antesaka in 2013. The group forms about 5% of Madagascar’s population. Antesaka speak a dialect of Malagasy, a branch of the Malayo-Polynesian language group derived from the Barito languages spoken in southern Borneo. Their folk-cultural profile is documented especially through marriage taboos, funeral rites, rice cultivation, fishing, and the use of local plant materials in houses and objects.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document named Antaisaka textile or pattern traditions.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources used do not name Antaisaka motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe everyday or ceremonial clothing, head coverings, footwear, or named garments. A British Museum catalogue record identifies a woman’s belt made of off-white woven cotton folded lengthwise into several layers, with a wallet sewn at the centre and woven of vegetable fibre. The record does not provide an Antaisaka vernacular name or explain the belt’s social or ceremonial use.

### Architecture

Antaisaka villages contain rectangular, one-room houses made of local plant material. These houses have an extra door on the eastern side, used only for removing a corpse from the living quarters. Funeral architecture includes the *kibory*, a communal burial house hidden in a sacred forest called the *ala fady*. The *ala fady* is restricted to men. The sources do not describe roofs, decoration, settlement plans, or urban architecture.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records several objects associated with the material culture shown in the atlas: a wooden shield; a raffia basket; a carrying radio basket made of raffia; a wooden and fibre crab trap; and a bark winnowing tray. It also records a metal-and-wood bill-hook. The sources do not describe pottery, ceramic production, decorative metalwork, carving styles, or the cultural meanings of these objects.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not document Antaisaka jewelry, body adornment, tattoos, henna, hair practices, or ritual ornaments.

## Music & performance

Music appears in the documented funeral rite. After a corpse has been dried for two to three years, it is moved to a separate house accompanied by the women of the village. The women cry together on cue and then begin to dance. Meanwhile, village children dance to drum music outside until morning, when the corpse is moved to the *kibory*. The men gather in the house of the village leader and take turns going to the corpse house, where they affix money to the deceased using a specified type of oil. The sources do not name the drums, identify song genres, or describe musical performance outside the funeral context.

## Dance & theatre

Dance is documented as part of the funeral ceremony. Women begin to dance after collectively crying beside the corpse, while children dance to drum music outside the corpse house until morning. The sources do not name these dances or describe theatre, mask performance, shadow puppetry, court dance, or entertainment traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not describe an annual festival calendar or seasonal festivals. They do document several life-cycle and communal rites. Family life and marriage are regulated by numerous *fady*, or taboos. Twins are regarded as taboo and were traditionally killed after birth or left in the forest to die; although this practice has been outlawed, it persists among some traditional communities, and twins are not permitted to be buried alongside their family members.

Funeral customs involve drying a corpse for two to three years before transferring it to a communal burial house called a *kibory*. Before this transfer, the village performs a ritual called *tranondonaky*. Women accompany the corpse while crying and dancing, men attach money to the deceased with a specified oil, and children dance to drum music outside. Men finally transport the body to the sacred forest, where they privately speak their last words to the deceased. The sources do not describe weddings beyond marriage taboos, coming-of-age ceremonies, initiation, or annual celebrations.

## Foodways

The principal Antaisaka economic activities documented in the sources are the cultivation of coffee, rice, and bananas. Women are primarily responsible for the rice harvest in accordance with local tradition. People living along the coast often rely on fishing as a principal source of income. The sources do not name specific dishes, cooking methods, food restrictions, ceremonial foods, or coffee-preparation traditions. They also do not document a distinctive cuisine beyond the cultivation of these crops and coastal fishing.

## Oral tradition & literature

The history of the Antesaka is preserved in oral history. According to this tradition, the founder of the clan was named Andriamandresy. He was born Repila in Tsiarepioky, near Mahabo, later changed his name to Ihazorango, and finally adopted the name Andriamandresiarivo in anticipation of being named king. Oral history also recounts that Ratongalaza killed or exiled his brothers to secure the throne. The sources do not provide named folktales, epic poems, proverbs, riddles, literary works, or contemporary preservation projects.

## Language & religion

Antesaka speak a dialect of Malagasy. Malagasy is described as part of the Malayo-Polynesian language group and as derived from the Barito languages spoken in southern Borneo. The sources do not describe a historical script or a separate Antaisaka writing tradition.

The documented spiritual and ritual framework includes *fady*, or taboos, and sacred forests. The *ala fady* is a sacred forest restricted to men and contains the *kibory*, the communal burial house. Funeral practices include drying the corpse, collective crying and dancing, attaching money to the deceased with a specified oil, and privately speaking last words to the deceased. The sources do not identify a formal religious affiliation, denomination, priesthood, divination system, or named healing tradition.

### Architecture

Antaisaka villages have simple one-room houses, while the dead are placed in a communal burial house in a sacred forest.

- **Communal burial house** (*kibory*) — The kibory is a communal burial house hidden in a sacred forest.

Recorded Antaisaka objects include plant-fibre containers, wooden tools, a trap, and a metal-and-wood bill-hook.

The sources do not document Antaisaka jewelry or body-adornment traditions.

Music is documented mainly in funeral rites, with children dancing outside to drum music until morning.

Antaisaka foodways center on growing coffee, rice, and bananas, along with coastal fishing.

---
title: "Nuba"
subtitle: "Sudan"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]
---

## Overview

The Nuba are indigenous inhabitants of southern Sudan, comprising 50 various indigenous ethnic groups who inhabit the Nuba Mountains of South Kordofan state. They live in one of the most remote and inaccessible areas of Sudan, particularly in the foothills of the Nuba Mountains and in villages and towns in and around the mountains. Population estimates vary widely; the Sudanese government estimated that they numbered 2.07 million in 2003, while most of the rest of the 1,000,000 Nuba people are described as living in mountain villages and towns. Their languages belong chiefly to the geographic Kordofanian group, primarily within the Niger–Congo family, while several languages belong to the Nilo-Saharan family. Nuba culture is represented in the sources through farming, herding, wrestling, body painting, domestic architecture, oral traditions, and material objects connected with initiation, fighting, music, and adornment.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources do not document named Nuba textile or pattern traditions in sufficient detail for separate entries.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name complex body-painting patterns and decorations, but provide no individual motif names.

### Clothing & dress

Muslim men wear a sarong and occasionally a skull cap. Older Muslim men wear skull caps and grow beards. Older women and young women wear beads and wrap a sarong over their legs; they sometimes wear a cloak tied on the shoulder. Women and girls braid their hair in strands and string it with beads. Both sexes practice scarification. The museum catalogue records several forms of ceremonial and initiation dress: an initiation skirt made of grass; an initiation girdle made of a bull’s tail, with rope and fibre; a leather-fringe girdle with glass beadwork, cowrie shells, and snailshells; and belts worn by young men while wrestling or on ceremonial occasions. These belts use root, reptile skin, snake skin, brass rings, the carapace of a tortoise, and a projecting piece of gum arabic covered with monitor-lizard skin. A head-dress is made of two cow horns joined by cow skin. The sources do not document Nuba footwear.

### Architecture

Nuba villages consist of family compounds. A family compound is a rectangular enclosure containing two round mud huts thatched with sorghum stalks and facing each other. This hut arrangement is called a *shal*. The *shal* is fenced with wooden posts interwoven with straw, and two benches run along its sides around a central fire where families tell stories and oral traditions. In front of it is the larger yard, the *tog*, whose fence is made from strong tree branches as high as the hut roofs. Goats, chickens, and donkeys are kept there. Tall conical granaries called *durs* stand on one side of the *tog*, while maize and vegetables such as pumpkin, beans, and peanuts are grown in a small yard at the back.

The museum catalogue describes Nuba homesteads as groups of small round clay shelters with conical thatched roofs. It also records a Lafofa homestead under construction, with circular clay buildings, thatched roofs, impressed decoration, and a structure probably serving as a granary.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum objects include bowls made of earth and gum, decorated with ochre, gypsum, and charcoal. Weapons and tools include iron-bladed spears, arm-daggers, knives or swords, axes or adzes, fighting sticks, clubs, and throwing sticks. Their handles and shafts are made from wood, bamboo, or other plant materials; some objects have leather bindings, sheaths, brass wire, ferrules, or tassels. Shields are made from hide and have notched edges, a conical boss, a stitched hide handle, and a twisted leather lanyard. Other recorded objects include a snuff-box made from a nut with a gourd stopper, a body-stamp made from a gourd, and cow bells made from baobab nuts with wooden clappers.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Women wear beads, and the museum catalogue records glass beadwork in green, blue, saffron, and white, together with cowrie shells and snailshells. Initiation and ceremonial objects include bracelets made from a cow’s tail, a girdle made from a bull’s tail with rope and fibre, and belts ornamented with brass rings and the carapace of a tortoise. The catalogue also records a bracelet classified as religious or ritual equipment.

Both sexes practice scarification. Young men spend hours painting their bodies with complex patterns and decorations; the source connects this practice with Nuba ideas about the power and importance of strength and beauty. Women and girls braid their hair in strands and string it with beads. The sources do not name particular scarification designs, jewelry forms, or body-painting motifs.

## Music & performance

The museum catalogue records several instruments. A lyre is made of wood, with a framework of three sticks tied into a U-shape, a gourd attached to the open end, cow skin stretched across the gourd, and twisted fibre strings tied to the framework. Other instruments include a trumpet made from the horn of a roan antelope, a musical horn made from a gourd, and a composite trumpet made from a kudu horn and a wax extension decorated with abrus seeds. Another trumpet is made from a roan antelope horn.

Initiation performance is represented by a pair of leg rattles made from palm-leaf rattles attached to a two-ply twisted palm-fibre string. The catalogue also records an initiation whip made of fibre with a wooden handle, initiation bracelets, and other initiation objects. A pair of cow bells made from baobab nuts has wooden clappers attached by string.

The Wikipedia source describes family storytelling around the fire in the *shal*, where stories and oral traditions are told. It does not provide names for songs, genres, musical ensembles, or performance repertories. No UNESCO inscription concerns Nuba music.

## Dance & theatre

The sources do not document named Nuba dances or dramatic traditions. They describe athletic competition, especially traditional wrestling, as a distinctive cultural practice. Strong young men compete with athletes from other villages to promote personal and village pride and strength; in some villages older men take part in club- or spear-fighting contests. The museum catalogue includes wrestler’s belts, belts worn by young men while wrestling, and ceremonial belts, but does not describe choreography, dance steps, or theatrical forms.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not provide an annual Nuba festival calendar or named festivals. They describe initiation-related objects, including an initiation skirt, initiation girdle, initiation whip, initiation horn, initiation bracelets, and initiation leg rattles. The catalogue also records belts worn on ceremonial occasions, especially wrestling.

Traditional ritual specialists and priests are described in areas of the Nuba Mountains where Islam has not deeply penetrated. They hold authority alongside clan elders and are responsible for rain control, keeping the peace, and rituals intended to ensure successful crops. Some guard shrines containing objects used to secure positive ritual outcomes, including rain stones associated with rain magic, and some undergo what they recognize as spiritual possession.

The sources also describe scarification and circumcision for boys and female genital mutilation for girls. They do not provide detailed accounts of weddings, funerals, birth ceremonies, or named coming-of-age rites.

## Foodways

The Nuba are primarily farmers and also herders who keep cattle, chickens, and other domestic animals. They maintain gardens near their homes for vegetables requiring constant attention, such as onions, peppers, and beans. Fields farther up the hills are used for quickly growing crops such as red millet without irrigation, while more distant farms produce white millet and other crops. In household compounds, maize and vegetables such as pumpkin, beans, and peanuts are grown behind the main enclosure.

The sources do not name prepared dishes, cooking methods, beverages, food-preservation techniques, ceremonial foods, or dietary rules. They also do not document a distinctive Nuba cuisine beyond the crops and domestic animals described above.

## Oral tradition & literature

Families tell stories and oral traditions around the fire in the *shal*. The sources do not record the names of Nuba folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles, or poems. They also do not identify a Nuba literary script or a contemporary literary revival.

The article describes several documentary and photographic representations of Nuba life. These include *Nuba Conversations* (2000), a documentary and ethnographic film directed by Arthur Howes; Leni Riefenstahl’s photographic collections *The Last of the Nuba* (1973) and *The People of Kau* (1976); and Roopa Gogineni’s documentation of Bisha TV, a satirical muppet show popular throughout the Nuba lands. The sources describe Bisha TV as an example of comedy used to deal with authoritarian rule.

## Language & religion

The Nuba speak various languages that are not closely related to one another. Most speak one of the many languages in the geographic Kordofanian language group of the Nuba Mountains, primarily within the Niger–Congo language family. Several Nuba languages belong to the Nilo-Saharan family. Over one hundred languages are spoken in the area and are considered Nuba languages, while many Nuba also speak Sudanese Arabic, described as the common language of Sudan.

Islam is the primary religion of many Nuba people, alongside Christianity and traditional shamanistic or animistic beliefs. The majority of Nuba living in the eastern, western, and northern parts of the mountains are Muslims, while those living to the south are described as Christians or practitioners of traditional animistic religions. Ritual specialists and priests conduct rain-control and crop-success rituals, guard shrines, and may undergo spiritual possession.

## Sources & further reading

- R. C. Stevenson, *The Nuba people of Kordofan Province: an ethnographic survey*, Graduate College, University of Khartoum, 1984.
- Samuel Totten, *Genocide by Attrition: The Nuba Mountains of Sudan*, Routledge, 2012.
- Mohamed Salih, *Environmental Politics and Liberation in Contemporary Africa*, Springer Netherlands, 1999.
- Nanne Op ’t Ende, *Proud to be Nuba: Faces and Voices: Stories of a Long Struggle*, Code X Publishing, 2007.
- *Nuba peoples*, Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuba_peoples

---
title: "Bassa"
subtitle: "Liberia"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]
