## Overview

The Bassa are a West African ethnic group primarily native to Liberia and a subgroup of the larger Kru peoples of Liberia and Ivory Coast. They form a majority or significant minority in Grand Bassa, Rivercess, Margibi, Montserrado and Bong counties. Small communities are also found in Sierra Leone and Ivory Coast. Their overall population is described as about 1.1 million, making them the second-largest ethnic group in Liberia at 18 percent. The Bassa language is a Kru language within the Niger-Congo family. Bassa culture includes lineage-linked villages, farming, lagoon fishing, craft occupations, initiation societies, masks, brasswork, oral traditions and an indigenous writing system. Their material culture is represented in the cited museum records by masks, a brass-related regional context, a skin quiver with arrows, a woven fish trap and a small wooden mask from Grand Bassa.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Geometric ornament on a skin quiver** — A museum record describes a skin quiver from Grand Bassa with an outer leather covering ornamented at the top in geometric patterns. The record does not identify a named Bassa textile tradition or compare the decoration with neighboring cultures.

**Woven basket construction** — The sources state that some Bassa masks are fastened to the forehead area of a woven basket worn by the performer. The museum records do not identify a vernacular name for this basket or describe its weaving technique.

**Braided bonnet** — Bassa mask performers are described as wearing a braided bonnet fastened at an angle to the forehead. No further information about its fibers, pattern vocabulary or production is given.

The sources used do not document additional named Bassa textile or pattern traditions.

### Clothing & dress

The sources provide little information about everyday clothing. They describe special clothing associated with masks: a performer may wear a braided bonnet fastened at an angle to the forehead, or a woven basket to which a mask is attached. A British Museum record describes a wooden helmet mask whose edges are pierced for attachment to a costume. The sources do not identify named garments, daily dress, footwear, belts, women’s clothing or men’s clothing. They also do not provide a vernacular name for the costume associated with mask performances.

### Architecture

Inland Forest Bassa villages are intentionally arranged in clusters of huts that appear disorganized but are placed so that a person looking in any direction encounters huts and has difficulty establishing bearings. The layout lacks a main road and includes empty lots, making movement through the village difficult for outsiders. The selection of a village location depends on access to fresh water, good farmland and certain reeds used as roofing material. The sources do not name a house type or provide detailed information about wall construction, foundations, internal rooms or urban architecture.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The Bassa are described as having occupational categories including farmers, barterers, traders, lagoon fishermen, blacksmiths, carvers, weavers, potters and other craftsmen. Their brasswork includes *ma go*, meaning “small head,” miniature brass-cast masks made for the Dan, with protruding open lips, flared nostrils, pierced slit eyes and a tattoo pattern extending from forehead to chin. Another object is the Brass Finial, an iron rod cast over with brass. Its top features a woman’s head with five rows of hair running from front to back and an encircling herringbone pattern. The museum records also describe a skin quiver with five arrows, iron barbed points, an inner wooden quiver and an outer leather covering, and a woven fish trap from Grand Bassa.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources discuss brass jewelry primarily in relation to the neighboring Dan. Dan women wore substantial brass jewelry, including anklets and bracelets, and the quantity of brass was associated with the husband’s wealth. The jewelry was banned in the late 1930s by Liberia’s minister of health, Rudolf Fuszek, after which surplus brass was melted down and recast. The sources connect Bassa production of *ma go* miniature masks with this surplus brass. They do not document Bassa jewelry types, tattooing, scarification as a bodily practice, hair fashions or other named forms of Bassa adornment beyond the mask-related features and the woman’s head represented on the Brass Finial.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not document Bassa musical instruments, song genres, instrumental ensembles, dance music, musical performance contexts or named music traditions. They describe performance in relation to masks. Some masks are intended to project reverence and fear through monstrous faces with protruding eyes, swollen lips and contorted human and animal features. Other masks are portrait masks made by skilled carvers according to sculptural laws passed down by masters of the craft. Ancestor masks embody concepts of beauty and are intended to give leniency, peace and promises of peace to heirs; they are deliberately not made to resemble specific individuals. “Devil” masks are worn by soothsayers and performers such as acrobats and jugglers, who are described as agents of social control. One mask type was made to resemble a disfigured person so that a performer could dance before crowds and tell jokes, giving the person’s features a positive association and helping prevent social exclusion.

## Dance & theatre

Bassa mask performance includes dancing, crowd interaction and joking. A mask made in the likeness of a disfigured person was used by a performer who danced with crowds and told jokes as part of a deliberate social act. “Devil” masks were worn by soothsayers and performers including acrobats and jugglers. Other masks represented spirits from the darkest parts of the forest or ancestor figures. The sources do not name a Bassa dance, theatre genre, dramatic cycle or choreographic vocabulary, and they do not distinguish a formal annual dance calendar from other performances.

## Festivals & rituals

The Bassa are among the peoples who practice the women’s initiation society called *Sande*, also referred to as *Bondo*. The practice includes rituals involving special helmet masks. The mask is worn by a society official during special ceremonies and represents the idealized beauty of a female primordial ancestor spirit believed to reside in bodies of water. The sources state that the primordial ancestor spirit originates from a body of water during a sacred journey by a society member or official. The mask itself is not given a separate name; *Sowei* or *sowo* refers to the title of the association official who wears the helmet mask.

The sources also describe secret rites of passage for men and women connected with the Sande society and other initiation traditions. They do not provide a calendar of annual festivals, dates for ceremonies, wedding customs, funerary practices, birth rites or harvest festivals.

## Foodways

The Bassa are traditionally settled farmers who grow yam, cassava, eddoes and plantain. Before colonial occupation, their occupational categories also included lagoon fishermen, farmers and barterers or traders. The sources do not provide names for dishes, cooking methods, drinks, food taboos, ceremonial foods or rules concerning meat and other ingredients. They also do not describe food preparation, serving customs or seasonal food festivals.

## Oral tradition & literature

Bassa oral history recounts movements from Ivory Coast through Eastern Guinea, Grand Gedeh and the coast. The sources associate the original name *Gbooh* or *Gbɔ̌ɔ̀* with the meaning “People of the East.” They also relate the name Bassa to *Bassa Sooh Nyombe*, translated as “Father Stone’s people,” and describe early European traders shortening the phrase. One account names Ɓǎ Gìà-xwí Sàwá, Ɓǎ vɛ̀nɛ̀, and Ɓǎ Sɔ́ɔ́ as leaders associated with the journey and with relations between Bassa traders and Europeans. The sources also describe oral history concerning the Nyanya kingdom or state, the Dii artifact and conflicts among Kru groups.

A Bassa legend says that the Brass Finial was the walking stick of a mythical ancestor named Sma Vlen, who migrated toward the coast during the 16th century. The sources do not provide named epics, folktale collections, proverbs, riddles, oral poetry genres or contemporary literary preservation projects.

## Language & religion

Bassa is a Kru language within the Niger-Congo family. The Bassa language is described as a dialect continuum with Western, Central, Rivercess and Eastern Bassa clusters. The sources name an indigenous writing system called Ehni Ka Se Fa and also describe the Vah alphabet, associated with Thomas Flo Lewis. Vah is described as alphabetic, with 30 consonants, seven vowels and five tones indicated by dots and lines inside vowels. The IPA has largely replaced Vah in publications, although Vah remains respected and is used by some older men for record keeping. The first Bible was translated into Bassa in 1922, and the entire Bible was published in Bassa in 2005.

Traditional Bassa religion has a moral and ethical foundation that reveres ancestors and supernatural spirits. Christianity arrived during the colonial era, and Christian ideas were fused with the traditional idea of a Supreme Being and powerful first ancestor. Contemporary Bassa people predominantly practice Christianity while retaining elements of traditional religion.

- British Museum catalogue records for wooden face masks and wooden helmet masks.
- Museum of Ethnography catalogue record: “Bassa mask,” 1998.10.0002; reference to Meneghini, 1972.

title: "Grebo"
subtitle: "Liberia"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"

## Overview

The Grebo, also called Glebo, are an ethnic group or subgroup within the larger Kru group of Africa. In Liberia they are found primarily in Maryland County and Grand Kru County in the southeastern part of the country, and also in River Gee County and Sinoe County. Grebo communities in Côte d’Ivoire are known as the Krumen and occupy its southwestern corner. A 2001 estimate gives approximately 387,000 Grebo in Liberia and an estimated 48,300 in Côte d’Ivoire, not counting refugees. Precise numbers are lacking because many people were displaced by the civil war in Liberia during the late 20th and early 21st century. Grebo culture includes ritual passages, shrines, divine beliefs, carved masks, age-group organization, bush schools, ceremonial clothing, drums, and practices associated with ancestors and the surrounding world.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

*Lappa* is a ceremonial wrap-around cloth used in Grebo culture. The source compares it with material made from raffia, but does not describe its production technique or provide a fuller account of its patterns.

The museum catalogue records include Grebo masks decorated with cowrie shells, metal inlays, raffia-like material, vegetal fibre, animal hair, animal skin, beads, nails, and painted markings. These records document adornment on masks rather than a separate textile tradition.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name spirals, zig-zag lines, parallel lines, spots, stripes, and incised motifs. They do not identify a specifically Grebo textile motif vocabulary.

### Clothing & dress

The source describes *lappa* as a ceremonial wrap-around cloth, similar to material made from raffia. It contrasts this clothing with the pants that most common men had access to wear. The sources do not provide a fuller account of everyday clothing, women’s garments, head coverings, belts, footwear, or clothing distinctions between different social groups.

Bodios and Jide are described as wearing black attire. The source states that the Bodio was a high priest guided by the gods and that his wife, the Jide, was subject to restrictions concerning public appearance and contact with objects. The museum records describe masks with raffia-like or vegetal-fibre attachments, wooden beards, animal hair, and animal skin, but do not establish these as ordinary dress.

### Architecture

The sources describe a building known as a *takae*. It was built by the followers of a Bodio and served as his place of seclusion and residence. The source does not specify its construction materials, roof type, plan, decoration, or relationship to other Grebo houses. The sources used do not otherwise cover Grebo domestic architecture, settlement form, workshops, or urban traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Grebo ritual and communal objects include carved wooden masks, stools, stones, brass rings, drums, trumpets, horns, chairs, and mortars. Shrines may include stools, stones, and brass rings known as *nitien*. These rings were associated with protection, healing, punishment, and sacred power. Large brass rings were used as ritual objects for protecting villages from “spirits, sicknesses, war and other people’s witchcraft.”

The museum catalogue records a bronze ring from Grand Cess, Liberia, with four raised elements, spiral, zig-zag, and parallel-line decoration, and a surface partly covered by green corrosion. The catalogue also records wooden masks and a wooden human-head figure. The sources do not describe Grebo ceramics.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Bodios often wore a heavy brass ankle ring placed on them by a blacksmith and worn until death. These anklets were considered animate and were regularly fed human blood. Large brass rings more generally served as ritual objects for village protection and were reportedly given power through human sacrifice.

Grebo masks and head-dresses were decorated with horns, beads, cowrie shells, nails, metal studs, raffia-like material, vegetal fibres, animal hair, fur, and painted or incised details. Museum records describe a wooden mask from Maryland County with a beard, metal inlays around the eyes, and cowrie shells on the forehead. The sources do not document tattoos, henna, or specific hair practices apart from hair-like and fibre attachments on masks.

## Music & performance

Instruments crafted in Liberia are described as connecting communal life with communication, entertainment, battle, and the signaling of danger. Grebo communities are associated with some of the largest drums described in the source. These drums are painted and carved, can be used for a town and for war, and are still maintained in some villages for communication. They may measure up to six or seven feet tall and are commonly used in pairs, sometimes with chairs or mortars used to reach them.

The source distinguishes a lower hum associated with male sound from a higher pitch associated with female sound. Trumpets and horns also signal and communicate with laborers beyond their entertainment use. The sources do not give names for particular drum types, songs, musical genres, or dances, and they do not describe musical notation, performance ensembles, or occasions such as weddings.

The Grebo language is a Kru language of Liberia. Tone is extremely important: *né* with a high or high-mid tone is the first-person pronoun “I,” while *nè* with a low tone is the singular form of “you.” The Grebo music article supplied with the sources concerns a United Kingdom indie-rock subculture rather than Grebo people and is therefore not used as evidence for Grebo musical culture.

## Dance & theatre

Grebo masks were worn in ceremonies to mediate or propitiate spirits. Dancers wearing carved masks were daubed with white clay, which marked a *ku* or spirit. Masks most often appeared at funerals and dances and were especially associated with warriors and warfare. Their representations embodied designated members even into death and were intended to appear striking and frightening to enemies while empowering those around them.

Most masks were not worn to conceal the wearer’s identity. They were placed on basket-like structures above the head and functioned more as helmets than as coverings. They could have horns, fibrous hair-like material, carved teeth, round protruding eyes, multiple sets of eyes, and sharp, flat, projecting noses. The sources do not identify named dances, dramatic genres, theatrical performances, or a separate theatre tradition.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not describe an annual Grebo festival calendar or provide named festivals and dates. They do describe ritual practices connected with shrines, masks, priests, divination, warfare, funerals, and initiation.

Traditional Grebo people had bush schools known as *poro* for males and *sande* for females. These schools and their associated societies continued as part of Grebo culture. Historically, poro societies adapted to new conditions by establishing Masonic lodges of the European-American style of fraternal society.

Grebo masks were used in ceremonies connected with spirits, funerals, dances, warriors, and warfare. White clay applied to participants denoted a *ku* or spirit. Ritual masks were made by highly initiated specialists who retained detailed knowledge of their forest-zone myth culture. Performers wore the masks within the forest, where rituals and ceremonies took place, and only occasionally displayed them to outsiders.

Divination was practiced by scrying. Spirits were believed to exist only in natural objects, and shrines could use large rocks, medicine, offerings, rituals, and sacrifices. Food was prepared for spirits and alcohol was poured at shrine sites to appease them and provide luck and fortune. A person accused of witchcraft, usually a woman, could be subjected to trial by ordeal through forced drinking of a decoction made from the bark of the sasswood or sassywood tree or vine.

## Foodways

The sources do not describe Grebo staple foods, cooking methods, named dishes, ceremonial meals, tea or coffee traditions, or dietary rules. They state only that offerings at shrines could include preparing food for spirits and pouring alcohol. These offerings were intended to appease spirits and provide luck and fortune.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do not describe Grebo folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, named cycles of stories, or contemporary literary revivals. They state that the makers of ritual masks retained detailed information about their forest-zone myth culture. The sources also refer to oral histories in connection with the classification of Grebo language varieties, but they do not record their contents.

## Language & religion

Grebo is a Kru language of Liberia. Grebo speakers live in the extreme south-west of Liberia, on the coast and inland, between the rivers Cavally and Cess. In Côte d’Ivoire, Krumen is the usual name for the Grebo languages. The Grebo language area contains speech varieties forming an extensive language continuum with cultural centers of gravity usually organized around town clusters. The internal classification of these varieties is difficult to delineate precisely.

Tone is extremely important in Grebo. A high or high-mid tone in *né* marks the first-person pronoun “I,” while a low tone in *nè* marks the singular form of “you.” Bilingualism or bidialectalism is common for exogamy and commercial interaction.

Grebo religious practice includes divine beliefs, ancestors, shrines, spirits, ritual priests, offerings, sacrifices, and divination. The Bodio was a high priest guided by the gods. Shrines were associated with natural objects, especially large rocks, and with ancestors and deities. The sources describe ritual objects and sacred places but do not assign Grebo religious practice to a named world religion.

- Jean-Baptiste Bacquart, *The Tribal Arts of Africa*, Thames and Hudson, 1998.

- **Protective brass rings** (*nitien*) — Nitien were brass rings used at shrines for protection, healing, punishment, and sacred power.
- **Large village-protection rings** — Large brass rings were used to protect villages from spirits, sickness, war, and other people’s witchcraft.
- **Bronze ring from Grand Cess** — A museum record describes a bronze ring from Grand Cess with four raised elements, spiral, zig-zag, and parallel-line decoration.
- **Carved wooden masks** — Carved wooden masks were important ritual objects and were decorated with many added materials.
- **Wooden head figure** — Museum records include a wooden human-head figure.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Brass rings and richly decorated masks are the most distinctive forms of Grebo adornment described.

- **Bodio’s ankle ring** — A Bodio often wore a heavy brass ankle ring placed by a blacksmith until death, and it was regularly fed human blood.
- **Cowrie-shell mask** — A wooden mask from Maryland County had a beard, metal inlays around the eyes, and cowrie shells on the forehead.
- **Horn and bead head-dress** — Grebo masks and head-dresses could include horns, beads, cowrie shells, nails, metal studs, fibres, hair, fur, and painted or incised details.

## Music & performance

Large painted drums linked community life with communication, entertainment, battle, and danger signals.

- **Large village drums** — Some Grebo drums are painted and carved, used for towns and war, maintained in villages, and reach six or seven feet in height.
- **Paired tall drums** — The largest drums are commonly used in pairs, sometimes with chairs or mortars used to reach them.
- **Trumpets and horns** — Trumpets and horns were used for signaling and communication with laborers as well as for entertainment.
- **Male and female sound** — The source links a lower hum with male sound and a higher pitch with female sound.

## Dance & theatre

Masked dancers appeared mainly at funerals and dances, where the masks represented spirits and warriors.

- **Spirit-marked masked dancers** (*ku*) — Dancers wearing carved masks were daubed with white clay, marking a ku or spirit.
- **Helmet-like masks** — Most masks sat on basket-like structures above the head and worked more like helmets than face coverings.
- **Warrior masks** — Masks were especially linked with warriors and warfare and were meant to frighten enemies and empower those nearby.

## Festivals & rituals

Grebo ritual life includes bush schools, masked ceremonies, shrines, divination, offerings, sacrifices, and ordeal practices.

- **Men’s bush school** (*poro*) — Poro was a traditional bush school and society for males.
- **Women’s bush school** (*sande*) — Sande was a traditional bush school and society for females.
- **Masked forest ceremonies** — Highly initiated specialists made ritual masks, and performers wore them in forest rituals connected with spirits, funerals, dances, warriors, and warfare.
- **Spirit divination** — Divination was practiced by scrying, and spirits were believed to exist only in natural objects.
- **Sasswood ordeal** (*sasswood*) — A person accused of witchcraft could be forced to drink a decoction made from sasswood bark or vine in a trial by ordeal.

## Foodways

The sources mention food and alcohol only as offerings at shrines.

- **Food offerings** — Food was prepared for spirits at shrine sites to appease them and provide luck and fortune.
- **Alcohol offerings** — Alcohol was poured at shrines to appease spirits and provide luck and fortune.

## Oral tradition & literature

The profile records myth knowledge and oral histories but gives no stories, poems, proverbs, or named literary works.

- **Forest-zone myth culture** — Mask makers retained detailed information about the forest-zone myth culture.
- **Oral histories** — Oral histories were used in classifying Grebo language varieties, but their contents are not recorded.

## Language & religion

Grebo is a tonal Kru language, and religious life centers on gods, ancestors, spirits, shrines, priests, offerings, sacrifices, and divination.

- **Grebo language** — Grebo is a Kru language spoken in southern Liberia, with related languages called Krumen in Côte d’Ivoire.
- **First-person pronoun** (*né*) — Né with a high or high-mid tone means “I.”
- **Singular second-person pronoun** (*nè*) — Nè with a low tone means the singular form of “you.”
- **High priest** (*Bodio*) — The Bodio was a high priest guided by the gods.
- **Priest’s wife** (*Jide*) — The Jide was the Bodio’s wife and faced restrictions on public appearance and contact with objects.

## Glossary

- *lappa* — ceremonial wrap-around cloth
- *takae* — Bodio’s seclusion house
- *nitien* — brass ritual rings
- *Bodio* — high priest guided by the gods
- *Jide* — Bodio’s wife
- *ku* — spirit marked by white clay
- *poro* — men’s bush school and society
- *sande* — women’s bush school and society
- *sasswood* — bark or vine used in ordeal drinks
- *né* — “I” with high or high-mid tone
- *nè* — singular “you” with low tone

## Sources & further reading

- Mary H. Moran, *Liberia: The Violence of Democracy*, University of Pennsylvania Press, 2006.

## Overview

The Baggāra, also known as Chadian Arabs, are a nomadic confederation whose members have mixed Arab and Arabized indigenous African ancestry. They inhabit part of the Sahel, mainly between Lake Chad and the Nile river near south Kordofan, with the largest populations in Chad and Sudan and smaller minorities in Niger, Central African Republic, South Sudan, Cameroon, and northern Nigeria. The source gives a population of over six million. They are known as Baggara and Abbala in Sudan and as Shuwa Arabs in Chad, Cameroon, and Nigeria. Their common language is Chadian Arabic, and their traditional livelihood is nomadic cattle herding, although many now lead settled lives. Baggara groups are associated with seasonal movement between wet-season grazing lands and river areas during the dry season.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

*Jibba* — A man’s cotton tunic recorded in the British Museum catalogue, with applique panels in dyed cotton and wool on both sides and embroidery at the neck, cuffs, and pockets.

*Tob* — A patterned cloth worn by women in several photographic records from South Darfur. The photographs show women wearing patterned or light-coloured floral tobs.

*Darangal* — A large roll-up bed made from numerous thin sticks of *bashom* wood bound with strips of cowhide called *seyur*.

*Dabia* — A bottle-shaped leather storage bag with a long, narrow neck, a plaited hanging loop, and a wider body made from sewn sections of red and plain leather. The catalogue records its use for millet, sorghum grain, or their flour.

*Boursa* — A round gourd transformed into a storage vessel, with a separate lid. Its low neck and lid use plaited vegetable fibre and leather thongs.

The sources do not identify named Baggara motifs or provide comparative pattern terminology.

### Clothing & dress

The catalogue records a man’s *jibba*, made of cotton cloth and decorated with applique panels in dyed cotton and wool, together with embroidery at the neck, cuffs, and pockets. Photographs from South Darfur show women wearing patterned *tob*, including light-coloured floral cloth. Other photographs show women wearing cloths, neck-ornaments, ear-ornaments, and nose-ornaments. A photographic record shows a bearded man wearing a *jellabiya* and turban, while another shows an older man wearing a turban and carrying a cane under his left arm. The sources do not describe everyday footwear, belts, trousers, or a separate ceremonial dress system.

### Architecture

The museum photographs show thatched roof buildings, wooden supports, and woven mats in South Darfur. One photograph places a young woman outside a thatched roof building, while another shows wooden supports and woven mats behind a woman. The sources do not provide a vernacular name for the house form, a description of its complete construction, or information about urban architectural traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum records include two long spears associated with the Baggara. One has a broad, leaf-shaped iron blade, a wooden shaft made of reed or bamboo, and an iron spiral at the butt; its recorded length is 264 cm. A second spear has a broad, leaf-shaped iron point, a reed shaft, and a spiral-like metal fitting; its recorded length is 256 cm. The British Museum catalogue also records two drums with skin coverings suspended from wooden stakes, a tray with a jug and glasses, and household storage objects made from leather, gourds, vegetable fibre, and wood. The sources do not describe Baggara ceramics.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The photographic catalogue records women wearing neck-ornaments, ear-ornaments, and nose-ornaments. Neck-ornaments are described as carrying amulets. A decorative *gilada* is recorded as a rectangular red-leather neck-piece for a riding bull, decorated with lines of cowrie shells, plaited leather edges, and long leather tassels. The sources do not describe tattoos, henna, hair practices, or named human jewelry types beyond these catalogue descriptions.

## Music & performance

The sources do not describe Baggara musical genres, named songs, or performance contexts. Museum photographs show groups of men and boys gathered around two skin-covered drums suspended from wooden stakes. Two men hold wooden sticks used to beat the drums, and the stakes also carry a string of amulets and a piece of light-coloured fabric. Another photographic record shows a woman speaking or singing with her eyes closed while wearing a patterned *tob*. These records document drums and vocal activity but do not identify the instruments by a Baggara vernacular name, explain their construction in detail, or state whether the performances belong to ceremonies, festivals, weddings, funerals, or other occasions.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not describe Baggara dances, theatrical forms, mask traditions, shadow puppetry, or named performance genres.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not provide an annual Baggara festival calendar or describe birth, coming-of-age, wedding, or funeral rites. They do record seasonal movement: nomadic groups migrate between grazing lands during the wet season and river areas during the dry season. The historical account also describes the Mahdist period from 1883 to 1898, when tens of thousands of Baggara migrated to Omdurman and central Sudan and supplied troops for the Mahdist armies. These movements are historical and subsistence-related rather than descriptions of ritual festivals.

## Foodways

The museum catalogue records the *dabia* leather storage bag as an object usually used for storing millet and sorghum grain, or flour made from these grains. The sources also describe Baggara subsistence as nomadic cattle herding and identify cattle ownership as central to the political use of the term Baggāra in Sudan. They state that Baggara groups migrate seasonally between wet-season grazing lands and river areas during the dry season. The sources do not name prepared dishes, cooking methods, beverages, ceremonial foods, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do not describe Baggara folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, or named storytelling traditions. They do record historical claims of ancestry from the Juhaynah Arab tribe and a documented letter from 1391 concerning Arab settlements and raids in the region. Braukämper dates the formation of Baggara culture to the 17th century in Wadai, between Bornu and Darfur, where camel-herding Arabs encountered cattle-rearing Fula people migrating east. These are historical accounts rather than recorded oral-literary genres.

## Language & religion

The Baggara mostly speak a distinct dialect known as Chadian Arabic. The language has also been called Shuwa Arabic, although the source describes *Shuwa* as a geographically and socially parochial term that has fallen into disuse among linguists specializing in the language. The term is said to be of Kanuri origin. Baggara communities in Southern Kordofan have Sudanese Arabic influence in their dialect because of contact with sedentary populations and Sudanese Arab camel herders. The sources used do not describe the group’s religious landscape, religious institutions, spiritual practices, or historical scripts.

## Sources & further reading

- Ulrich Braukämper, “Notes on the origin of Baggara Arab culture with special reference to the Shuwa,” in Jonathan Owens, ed., *Arabs and Arabic in the Lake Chad Region*, Rüdiger Köppe, 1994.
- Samuel Decalo, *Historical Dictionary of Niger*, Scarecrow Press, 1979.
- Alex de Waal and Julie Flint, *Darfur: A Short History of a Long War*, Zed Books, 2006.
- Yusuf Fadl Hassan, *The Arabs and the Sudan: from the seventh to the early sixteenth century*, Edinburgh University Press, 1967.
- Baggara Arabs, Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baggara_Arabs
- No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription for this group is identified in the supplied sources.

## Overview

The Bagirmi, also spelled Baguirmi or Barma, are a Central African ethnic group inhabiting the Chari-Baguirmi region of Chad. They are one of Chad’s major ethnic groups. Their language, Bagirmi, belongs to the Central Sudanic family and was spoken by 44,761 people in 1993, mainly in the Chari-Baguirmi Region and the Mokofi sub-prefecture of Guéra Region. Bagirmi society has a royal family whose king is known as *mbang*, a tradition dating to the Sultanate of Bagirmi. The available sources document agriculture, livestock raising, language, religious history, and museum objects associated with hunting, music, dance, and household use.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document Bagirmi textile or pattern traditions.

### Clothing & dress

The museum catalogue records two dancing skirts associated with the objects shown: one is made of hide and decorated with cowrie shells, and the other is made of strings of reed. The sources do not identify their vernacular names, who wore them, or whether they were used by men or women. No information is provided about everyday clothing, head coverings, belts, footwear, or other forms of dress.

### Architecture

The sources used do not document Bagirmi houses, other buildings, construction materials, roof forms, decoration, or urban architectural traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The catalogue records a jug made of pottery, as well as throwing-knives, throwing-clubs, a ceremonial axe, a ceremonial throwing-knife, a sheath for throwing weapons, and a curved wooden throwing-stick. The iron throwing-knives include examples with leather grips, while the sheath is made of leather and leopard skin. The ceremonial axe is made of wood with a two-pointed head that is lozenge-shaped in section. The catalogue also records small brass figures of a horseman, a giraffe, and an ostrich.

Four Museum of Ethnography records describe *Kastkniv*, a knife associated with Bagirmi in Chad. The catalogue states that it was used for hunting, thrown after running animals and aimed at their bones. Its blade is curved backward at a blunt angle, with a sharp edge along the front and a protruding handle. These records associate the objects with Gösta Moberg’s first expedition to North Africa in 1924–1925.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not document Bagirmi jewelry, body adornment, tattoos, henna, hair practices, or ritual ornaments.

## Music & performance

The museum catalogue records a drum carved in wood with a hide membrane tied on with leather thongs. It also records a “flute” or clarinet made of tin, brass, cowrie shells, leather, and bamboo, and a harp made of wood with horse-hair strings. The sources do not provide vernacular instrument names, musical genres, song forms, performance contexts, or information about whether these instruments were used at court, in ceremonies, or for entertainment.

The sources do record dancing skirts, but they do not describe the associated music, choreography, occasions, or performers. No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription concerns this ethnic group in the supplied material.

## Dance & theatre

The catalogue records two dancing skirts: one made of hide and decorated with cowrie shells, and another made of strings of reed. Beyond these object descriptions, the sources used do not name Bagirmi dances, theatrical forms, dramatic traditions, ceremonial performances, or entertainment contexts.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not document an annual Bagirmi festival calendar, seasonal celebrations, life-cycle rites, wedding customs, funerals, initiation practices, or named rituals. They state that Islam was introduced to the Bagirmi by the start of the 17th century but did not fully replace their traditional beliefs. Sufi orders such as the Tijaniyyah and, to a lesser extent, the Sanusiyya, contributed to further conversions and the consolidation of Islam among the Bagirmi.

## Foodways

The Bagirmi mainly cultivate sorghum and millet and raise cattle, chickens, goats, and sheep. The Bagirmi language source gives *sa* as “eat,” but the supplied sources do not identify particular dishes, cooking methods, drinks, ceremonial foods, dietary rules, or food-related festivals.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not document Bagirmi folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles, or storytelling contexts. They do record efforts to develop written Bagirmi during the 1990s, when texts providing basic literacy instruction were composed through the work of Don and Orpha Raun, Christian missionaries of the Church of the Lutheran Brethren of America. In 2003, Anthony Kimball developed a font for the Bagirmi alphabet and a Keyman input method for Latin keyboards. The source states that published Baguirmi literature continued to expand and was distributed in Chad by David Raun.

## Language & religion

Bagirmi, also called Baguirmi, has the autonym *tàrà ɓármà*. It is the language of the Bagirmi people of Chad and belongs to the Central Sudanic family; it has also been tentatively classified as part of the Nilo-Saharan superfamily. In 1993 it was spoken by 44,761 people, mainly in the Chari-Baguirmi Region and the Mokofi sub-prefecture of Guéra Region. Bagirmi was the language of the Sultanate of Bagirmi from 1522 to 1871 and later of the Wadai Empire before the Scramble for Africa.

The Bagirmi mostly speak Bagirmi as their native language, although some speak Fula or Chadian Arabic. Their main religion is Islam. Islam was introduced by the start of the 17th century but did not fully replace traditional beliefs. The Tijaniyyah and, to a smaller extent, the Sanusiyya are identified as Sufi orders associated with further conversions and the consolidation of Islam.

## Overview

The Buduma are an ethnic group of Chad, Cameroon, and Nigeria who inhabit many of the islands of Lake Chad. They are predominantly fishers and cattle-herders. Their neighbors call them Buduma, meaning “people of the grass (or reeds),” but they prefer to be called Yedina. Their language is known as Yedina; Yedina is a Chadic language of the Biu–Mandara branch spoken around Lake Chad in western Chad and neighbouring Cameroon and Nigeria. The Buduma traditionally claim descent from the peoples of the Sao civilization and Kanem-Bornu Empire. Their material culture is closely connected to water, reeds, fishing, cattle, and movement across the lake.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not describe documented textile or pattern traditions of the Buduma.

**Reed and grass basketry** — The museum records include a sieve or strainer made of reed and grass, a milk vessel with a grass container and conical lid, a basket made from wicker, a coiled dish made in basketry, and an oval mat made from reeds. The records describe materials and techniques but do not name vernacular patterns or distinguish these objects from neighboring cultures.

**Raffia tray** — A museum catalogue records a tray made of raffia. No named pattern, design vocabulary, or local term is supplied.

**Milk vessel and carrying sling** — One catalogue record describes a milk vessel and carrying sling made with grass in basketry technique. Another describes a milk vessel with a sling and conical lid, with the container and lid made of grass and the sling made of twisted and knotted fibre.

**Marea board** — The museum records a Marea board used for pressing cotton seed. The source does not explain the term, its form beyond the catalogue description, or its relation to textile production.

The sources used do not describe everyday or ceremonial clothing, distinctions between men’s and women’s dress, head coverings, belts, or named garments. They record a pair of sandals made of ambatch wood with straps of vegetal fibre. The catalogue also records bracelets made of brass and iron, including a penannular bracelet made of iron whose terminals are coiled and a bracelet made of iron twisted with three loops round the circumference. No source identifies these objects as ceremonial, gender-specific, or associated with a named dress tradition.

### Architecture

The Buduma extensively make use of papyrus reeds. The reeds are used for constructing lightweight huts that can be moved to higher ground if the lake rises. The sources do not provide a vernacular name for the huts, describe their roof types or decoration, or discuss settlement organization, urban traditions, workshops, or other architectural forms. A museum record describes a model passenger canoe made of reed, while another describes a model boat made of two bundles of rushes held together with twisted cotton [?] cord; the rushes were bound and bent up at the tapered end.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records pottery water-pots, a pottery jug or mug with a handle at the side, and a pottery bowl with a flaring foot whose rim is damaged. It also records an iron spear with a bifid point resembling a pitch-fork and a wooden shaft, a socketed iron hoe with a wooden haft, and a fishing implement made of a sickel-shaped bone. Other listed household and working objects include a sieve or strainer made of reed and grass, a wicker basket with no handle and a pointed base, a coiled dish made in basketry, and an oval mat made from reeds. They state that the Buduma are Muslims and that they still incorporate many traditional beliefs and practices into their Islamic practices, but they do not identify those practices individually.

## Foodways

The Buduma are largely fishermen and livestock herders. Some are engaged in commercial fishing, while many fish for personal or familial subsistence. Staples foods include fish, cow milk, water lilly roots that they grind to flour, and other foods native to the region. Although they use or consume many products derived from their cattle, the Buduma do not commonly kill and eat them. The source states that 200 speakers live in Cameroon and that the rest live in Chad. The Buduma prefer the name Yedina, while Buduma is the name used by their neighbors and means “people of the grass (or reeds).” The Buduma are Muslims. ## Overview

The Sara, sometimes referred to as the Kaba, are a Central Sudanic ethnic group native to southern Chad, the northwestern areas of the Central African Republic, and the southern border of South Sudan. In Chad they are concentrated in the Moyen-Chari, the Logone Oriental, the Logone Occidental, and parts of the Tandjile regions; in the Central African Republic they live in the northwest. They comprise roughly 30% of Chad’s population and form the country’s largest ethnic group. The Sara languages are described as belonging to the Central Sudanic languages of the Nilo-Saharan language family. Their social order consists of several patrilineal clans, and their history includes French colonial rule, forced labor, conscription, and political dominance in Chad after 1960.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document Sara textile or pattern traditions.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe everyday or ceremonial clothing, gendered dress, head coverings, belts, footwear, or other Sara garments.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Sara houses, granaries, roofs, settlement forms, architectural decoration, or urban traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum catalogue records include several iron throwing-knives, including examples with leather-bound handles, punched decoration, and a handle wrapped in reptile skin. One record describes five iron throwing knives with an associated hide sheath; another describes four iron throwing knives in a composite leather sheath reinforced with bark, with ornamental stitching and triangular holes. A cane shield has a wooden framework covered with painted cane slats, a leather-wrapped outside edge, and a hide handle tied on the back. The sources used do not document Sara dances, theatrical traditions, mask performances, dramatic forms, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment performance.

The Sara social order was formerly united into a single polity with a national language, national identity, and national religion. Sara subsistence is primarily through hoe farming. Taro, yams, and sweet potatoes are identified as the main staples. Cattle, sheep, goats, chickens, and small horses are also raised. ## Overview

The Zaghawa, also called Beri or Zakhawa, are an ethnic group living in Libya, northeastern Chad, and western Sudan, including Darfur. Their language is spoken especially in east-central Chad, northwestern Sudan, and, by a smaller number of people, Libya. The Zaghawa language is an eastern Saharan language and is also described as Nilo-Saharan; its speakers call it Beria, from Beri and *a*, “Zaghawa” for “mouth.” The Zaghawa have been estimated at 384,150 people, while the language has about 447,400 native speakers. Their folk-culture profile in the supplied sources centres on pastoralism, nomadic clans, camel and livestock keeping, pottery, basketry, caste-based artisan work, Islamic practice, and the material culture recorded around Kebkebiya and Kireyka in Darfur.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The supplied sources do not document named Zaghawa textile or pattern traditions.

**Motif vocabulary.** The supplied sources name no Zaghawa textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The supplied sources do not describe everyday or ceremonial clothing, head coverings, belts, footwear, or named garments. They do record a social distinction between nobles and warriors, traders and merchants, artisan castes, and slaves, but provide no clothing details associated with these groups.

### Architecture

The supplied sources do not describe Zaghawa houses, compounds, tents, roofs, workshops, or other forms of vernacular architecture. The museum records mention a grass enclosure and the bank of a dry river in photographs from Kebkebiya, North Darfur, Sudan, but do not identify a named building type or explain its construction.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Pottery is an inherited occupation of the artisan castes called the *Hadaheed* or *Hadahid*. The supplied museum records show women working with clay vessels in Kebkebiya, North Darfur, Sudan. One woman is described scraping the inside of a clay vessel with a piece of gourd; another is working with a lump of clay; a third is holding a stone beside a round clay vessel. The photographs also show a sieve, containers, and a vegetable-fibre basket called “reika.” The records do not identify particular ceramic forms, decoration, metal objects, or woodworking traditions. Ironwork is listed among the inherited occupations of the artisan castes, whose work was traditionally regarded within Zaghawa society as dirty and of inferior status.

## Jewelry & body adornment

The supplied sources do not document Zaghawa jewelry, silverwork, beadwork, henna, hair practices, tattoos, facial scarification, or body painting. They also do not describe ritual adornment or named ornaments.

## Music & performance

Music is listed among the inherited occupations of the Zaghawa artisan castes, whose musicians included drummers. The supplied sources do not name an instrument, song genre, performance setting, dance accompaniment, or ceremonial repertoire. They also do not describe music at weddings, funerals, courts, markets, or religious gatherings. The sources therefore cover the social position of musicians but not the sound, repertory, or performance practice of Zaghawa music.

## Dance & theatre

## Festivals & rituals

The Zaghawa accepted the Maliki school of Sunni Islam while retaining some pre-Islamic rites. One named practice is *karama*, described as a ritual sacrifice of animals to ward off evil spirits. The sources state that the century of conversion to Islam is debated, with estimates ranging from the 13th to the early 17th century. They also state that Zaghawa leadership converted to Islam as a result of Tijani Muslim missionaries from West Africa travelling through the area to make the Hajj, and that in the 1940s the Zaghawa began turning to Islam from their traditional religion en masse. In contemporary times, the Zaghawa are described as leading a sedentary lifestyle and growing millet, sorghum, sesame, melons, pumpkins, peanuts, and okra. The sources do not name dishes, cooking methods, beverages, ceremonial foods, or dietary rules. They state that the Zaghawa accepted the Maliki school of Sunni Islam, but do not provide further food-related religious practice.

## Oral tradition & literature

The supplied sources do not describe a Zaghawa epic, named folktale cycle, proverb tradition, riddle tradition, or oral-poetry genre. They do identify two published collections, *Contes Zaghawa du Tchad*, containing thirty-seven tales and two legends. A Zaghawa tribesman named Daoud Hari wrote *The Translator*, a memoir about Darfur, and a Zaghawa woman named Halima Bashir co-authored *Tears of the Desert* with Damien Lewis; the sources state that both works spread knowledge about atrocities in Darfur. The language article also lists *Contes Zaghawa du Tchad* among works concerning the Zaghawa language and culture.

## Language & religion

Zaghawa is spoken by the Zaghawa people of east-central Chad and northwestern Sudan, especially Darfur, and by a smaller number of people in Libya. The sources describe it as both an eastern Saharan and a Nilo-Saharan language. Speakers call it Beria, from Beri and *a*, “Zaghawa” for “mouth.” Named clan or dialect groupings include Beria, Tuba, Kobe, and Wegi; the listed Tuba forms include Biria and Brogat, while the Kobe forms include Dirong, Guruf, Kobe, and Kapka. A Zaghawa Latin alphabet was created by Adam Tajir in the 1950s from clan identification marks, sometimes called the camel alphabet. In 2000, Siddick Adam Issa prepared Beria Giray Erfe, and in 2007 the system was turned into a computer font by Seonil Yun in cooperation with SIL International and the Mission Protestante Franco-Suisse au Tchad. An Arabic-script alphabet is also under development. Religiously, the Zaghawa accepted Maliki Sunni Islam while retaining practices such as *karama*.

---
title: "Mende"
subtitle: "Sierra Leone"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]
---

## Overview

The Mende are one of the two largest ethnic groups in Sierra Leone, constituting 31.2% of the total population. They are predominantly found in the Southern Province and the Eastern Province, with significant populations in Bo, Kenema, Kailahun, and Moyamba. The Mende are mostly farmers and hunters. Their language, Mende, belongs to the Mande language family and is also used as a regional lingua franca in southern Sierra Leone; speakers are found in neighboring Liberia and Guinea. Mende cultural life includes rice cultivation, village-based labor, secret societies, masked performances, wood carving, woven fabrics, body adornment, oral literature, and the Kikakui syllabary. The sources describe both male Poro and female Sande institutions as central to socialization, leadership, ritual knowledge, and community life.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Mende woven fabrics** — The Mende produce woven fabrics that are popular throughout western Africa. Museum records include cotton cloth, display cloth, blankets, and hammocks made from hand-spun or machine-spun cotton, sometimes combined with synthetic fibres. Designs include indigo, white, red, brown, blue, green, cream, and buff areas, supplementary weft patterns, geometric bands, diamonds, lozenges, and fringes.

**Kpoikpoi** — *Kpoikpoi* is a hammock made from hand-spun cotton strips that are hand-woven and hand-sewn together. Museum examples use coloured cotton, including red and two shades of indigo, with supplementary weft patterns and tapestry-weave areas. Other examples have wooden poles carved with birds’ heads.

**Country cloth** — A woven cotton “country cloth” is made from panels stitched together. One museum example has nested borders in natural undyed cotton, dark brown, and sand-coloured dyed cotton, with a repeated hair-comb motif and geometric designs framing a central panel.

**Display cloth** — A *kpoikpoi* display cloth may be composed of ten strips of hand-woven and hand-spun cotton sewn together along the selvedges. Museum records describe white cotton crossed by indigo stripes and supplementary weft floats forming a diamond pattern.

**Mende loom weaving** — Museum records identify looms made from wood, reed, cotton, coarse string, cane, and cardboard, with partially woven or unwoven cotton fibre present. Shuttle forms include boat-shaped wooden shuttles with carved designs or cross-hatching on the bow and stern.

**Motif vocabulary.** Hair-comb motif, geometric design, nested borders, lozenges, diamonds, concentric diamonds, wine-glass shape, birds’ heads.

### Clothing & dress

The sources describe Mende clothing mainly through museum records and photographs. A shirt made of vegetable fibre is formed from knotted openwork and dyed with yellow-orange ochre, with ruffs at the neck, waist, and wrists. The records also show cloth garments, tunics, trousers, loincloths, and traditional fabrics. In photographs, women are described as draped in plain cloth and wearing wrapped head-dresses, while men wear tunics and trousers or are draped in cloth. Some people wear European clothing alongside traditional clothing and personal adornments.

Ceremonial clothing is associated with Sande performances. Women wearing masks cover their bodies with masses of raffia or black cloth and must not expose any part of the body. The museum catalogue records fibre head-dresses, woven basketry domes, painted cotton coverings, feather coronas, coral beads, clay-painted surfaces, and fibre fringes. The sources do not document Mende footwear, named everyday garments, or specific belts.

### Architecture

The Mende traditionally live in villages of 70 to 250 residents, situated from 1.5 to 5 kilometers apart. Museum photographs show circular thatched-roof buildings, single-storey buildings with thatched roofs and wooden shutters, and buildings with extended thatched roofs held up by wooden supports. One photograph shows a white-washed building with a thatched roof and wooden shutters. The sources do not provide a vernacular name for these buildings, detailed construction methods, or information about urban architectural traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Mende material culture includes wooden tools, weapons, game equipment, spinning and weaving implements, vessels, and musical or ritual objects. Museum records describe a wooden Leopard society axe with a flat metal blade and curved spikes, an iron spear with a central geometric design, and an iron sword with a curved blade and wooden hilt. Other objects include wooden staffs, combs, palettes, fans, spindles, spindle-whorls, looms, shuttles, mancala boards, and a composite palm-wine vessel made from a calabash with a wooden neck. One mancala board contains 49 white bean counters. The sources do not document Mende ceramics.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Mende jewelry includes gold and silver necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and earrings. Women often wear multiple bells, while Mende hunters often wear a single bell that can be silenced when stealth is necessary. Museum records include a pair of chief’s armlets made of elephant hide inlaid with wire, cowrie-shell rattles, glass beads, coral beads, and a charm wrapped in cloth and vegetable fibre string.

Hair is an important sign of femininity. Thickness and length are admired, and a woman’s hair should be clean, oiled, controlled, and arranged in intricate styles. Loose hair is associated with mourning, while dirty or disheveled hair is associated with insanity and neglect of community standards. Mende masks represent hairstyles, scarification, and neck rings. The neck rings signify health, prosperity, wholesome living, and the concentric ripples associated with the Sowo spirit.

## Music & performance

The sources describe music through songs, drums, rattles, bells, and performance within Poro and Sande institutions. In the 1930s, Lorenzo Dow Turner found a Gullah family in coastal Georgia that had preserved an ancient song in the Mende language, “A waka,” passing it down for 200 years. In the 1990s, Joseph Opala, Cynthia Schmidt, and Tazieff Koroma located a Mende village in Sierra Leone where the same song was still sung. The story is documented in the film *The Language You Cry In*.

Museum records include circumcision drums carved from wood, with skin or hide stretched over the opening or openings and held with rope, leather, or hide strings. They also include rattles made from gourds, cotton string, cowrie shells, seeds, bone, nut-shells, and colored glass beads. Women’s rattles are specifically identified in several records. Necklaces with bells are associated with communication between the worlds of ancestors and the living; women’s multiple bells are linked to community because they ring harmoniously together.

Poro and Sande performances use masks, dancing, and ritual knowledge. The sources do not identify named instrumental ensembles, song genres, wedding music, or court music.

## Dance & theatre

Mende masked performance is closely associated with Sande and Poro. Sande groups conduct masked performances embodying the Sande guardian spirit, associated with water and rivers. The masks represent the collective mind and spirit of the Mende community and express ideals of female morality and physical beauty. They are worn by women, who cover their bodies with raffia or black cloth.

The principal Sande spirit for celebration is *Ndoli jowei*. During initiation, she appears publicly at several events. One event, *yaya gbegbi*, occurs 1–3 days after initiates have been taken into the bush. At this time she comes into town with Sande women, but does not dance because it is not yet a celebration. At the minor feast called *Kpete gbula yombo le* or *Sowo mba yili gbi*, an announcement is made about the date of the *gani* celebration. The new initiates then return to town accompanied by *Ndoli jowei*, and dances are performed by maskers and initiates.

Girls undergo demanding dance training under the direction of *Ndoli jowei*, the dance instructor. *Gonde* is also a dance instructor and provides comic relief, friendship, and encouragement.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not describe an annual festival calendar. They do document initiation rituals associated with Sande and Poro. All Mende women begin initiation into Sande when they reach puberty. Sande teaches responsibilities of adulthood, hardworking behavior, modesty, and proper relations with elders. The society is also described as a guardian, protector, and guide through life.

A key element of Sande initiation is clitoridectomy, or female genital mutilation. The sources state that the procedure is intended to transform children considered to be of neutral sex into heterosexual, gendered adults and to remove the female’s residue of maleness. Initiates are marked with white *Hojo* clay, showing that they are under the protection and control of Sande. Sande law and punishment apply to objects and people marked with the clay.

Poro is the male equivalent of Sande. Boys are initiated into manhood and trained in knowledge considered essential to community survival. The initiation period lasts seven years. Young men aged 20 are called into the society and trained by the group above them and by elders. Poro prepares men for leadership, responsibility, wisdom, and power. Its rituals include masked dancing, secret language, passwords, work, training, and service.

The sources also mention masks at funerals, arbitrations, and the installation of chiefs. The sources do not document marriage ceremonies, birth rites, annual harvest festivals, or religious calendar dates.

## Foodways

Rice is the principal crop named in the sources. Mende farmers are generally known as growers of rice and several other crops, practicing crop rotation to protect soil productivity. Coffee, cocoa, and ginger are grown as cash crops, while rice, pepper, groundnuts, beniseed, also known as sesame seeds, and palm oil are grown for local consumption. Rice cooperatives have been formed in some rural areas.

Traditional farming is organized through labor groups that move from farm to farm. Men clear land for planting rice, while women clean and pound rice, fish, and weed planted crops. This routine continues during ten months of every year, with a couple of months around the New Year allowing more time in the village for domestic pursuits such as house building.

The museum records include a palm-wine vessel made from a calabash with a wooden neck. The sources do not provide named dishes, recipes, cooking methods, dietary rules, tea or coffee rituals, or ceremonial foods.

## Oral tradition & literature

Mende oral tradition describes the people as a mixture of two groups. The original members were hunters and fishers living in small peaceful settlements, while later leaders brought the arts of war and built larger, more permanent villages. These leaders were almost certainly Mane people who descended into the coastal lowlands from the area near Moussadou, Guinea, in the 16th century. They conquered and mixed with the native Bullom people to form the Mende.

Mende oral literature includes stories, songs, and proverbs. F.W.H. Migeod’s 1908 publication *The Mende Language* contains 17 Mende stories with facing-text English translations and 13 Mende songs. Ralph Eberl-Elber published two Mende tales with English translations in 1935. Marion Dusser de Barenne Kilson collected Mende stories in Sierra Leone and published *Royal Antelope and Spider: West African Mende Tales* in 1976, containing 100 Mende folktales in Mende and English. M. Mary Senior published “Some Mεnde Proverbs” in 1947.

## Language & religion

Mende is a major language of Sierra Leone, with speakers in neighboring Liberia and Guinea. It belongs to the Mande language family and is a tonal language commonly described as having five tones: high, low, rising, falling, and rising-falling. It is also spoken by other ethnic groups as a regional lingua franca in southern Sierra Leone.

Kisimi Kamara invented the Kikakui syllabary in 1921. The script achieved widespread use for a time but has largely been replaced by an alphabet based on the Latin script. The Mende Bible was translated and published in 1959 in Latin script. A different account in the Mende people article dates the invention of the script to 1917 and identifies Muhamad Turay as its inventor and Kisimi Kamara as the person who popularized it.

The sources describe Sande and Poro as secret societies with moral, social, ritual, and political functions. Sande is associated with women, water, rivers, white clay, spiritual protection, justice, love, and harmony. Poro is associated with men, initiation, leadership, responsibility, and secret knowledge. The sources do not describe a broader religious affiliation or denomination.

## Sources & further reading

- Lorenzo Dow Turner, documentation of the Mende song “A waka,” as described in the source material.
- F.W.H. Migeod, *The Mende Language* (1908).
- Marion Dusser de Barenne Kilson, *Royal Antelope and Spider: West African Mende Tales* (1976).
- M. Mary Senior, “Some Mεnde Proverbs” (1947).
- [Mende people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mende_people)
- [Mende language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mende_language)
- UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage: the sources used contain no UNESCO inscriptions for Sierra Leone.
- British Museum catalogue records for the objects described in the source material.

---
title: "Temne"
subtitle: "Sierra Leone"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]

## Overview

The Temne, also called Atemne, Témené, Temné, Téminè, Temeni, Thaimne, Themne, Thimni, Timené, Timné, Timmani, or Timni, are a West African ethnic group found predominantly in the Northern Province of Sierra Leone, with communities also in Guinea and other West African countries. Their largest concentrations are in northwestern and central Sierra Leone and the coastal capital city of Freetown. The Temne constitute 31.4% of Sierra Leone’s total population and are the country’s second largest ethnic group. They speak Temne, a language of the Mel branch of the Niger–Congo language family, related to the Baga language of Guinea. Temne society, farming, secret societies, masks, beadwork, weaving, oral literature, and religious practices are documented in the supplied sources.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

*Batik* — A museum catalogue records a brown and green cloth with three figures: two women playing drums and a dancing woman. The design was reserved with liquid wax on white cotton before the cloth was dyed brown with kola; areas covered with wax resisted the dye. The catalogue identifies the maker as John, a son of Mrs. Kamara.

**Beadwork apron** — A British Museum object is a rectangular apron made of glass beads. It shows alternating black and beige triangles separated by bands of blue beads, with a twisted fibre cord across the top for fastening.

**Woven textile equipment** — Museum records from Sinkunia describe a wooden boat-shaped shuttle through which the weft thread passes, and a weaving comb used to beat the weft into the woven section. The comb consists of narrow sticks fixed into a frame and held together with braided basket bands.

The supplied sources do not document the indexed terms *kpokpo*, *Temne country cloth*, *ronko*, *hu ronko*, *gara*, *tika*, *kakunutu*, *Ojei*, *Gbandbani*, *kola-dyed cloth*, or *Temne twin figures* as Temne textile traditions.

**Motif vocabulary.** The documented textile and object descriptions name alternating triangles, geometric patterns, two women playing drums, and a dancing woman.

### Clothing & dress

The sources give limited information about everyday and ceremonial clothing. A Museum of Ethnography catalogue records a *hatt*, or hat, from Sierra Leone. It is top-shaped and made of natural-coloured bast, with the outside completely covered in yellow and black bast. The catalogue states that such hats are worn more rarely by Mendi and more often by Temne. A British Museum apron is made of glass beads and fastened with a twisted fibre cord. The sources do not identify separate men’s and women’s clothing systems, footwear, belts, or a complete ceremonial dress ensemble.

Historical records describe chief’s regalia and taboos associated with the chief’s role. The chief and the Sanko, the masquerader representing the chiefdom spirit, appeared publicly together and carried the same regalia. The sources do not specify the garments or ornaments composing that regalia.

### Architecture

The sources do not provide a general description of Temne house forms, roofing, settlement plans, or decorative architecture. They do record historical villages, courts of justice, and the burial of the dead within the house with gold ornaments. Freetown, a city founded in 1792 as a settlement for freed slaves, is described as having houses with stone foundations and wooden superstructures by 1798, but the supplied sources do not identify this as a specifically Temne architectural tradition.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum records document wooden figures, masks, a wooden shuttle, a weaving comb, and medical or ritual objects. A bowl used as a medicine man’s equipment is made from a round calabash shell, with cowrie shells attached around the edge, cotton lining, metal bells, glass bottles, and string-wrapped charms. A cane switch associated with medicine man’s equipment consists of cane sticks wrapped with cotton and decorated with rows of cowrie shells.

Other records describe a buffalo or bush cow mask carved from wood, painted with blue pigment, fitted with a wire framework, and decorated with raffia. A Sowei mask is carved of wood, stained black, shaped as a human face with a helmet, and pierced for attaching a grass fringe. The sources do not describe Temne ceramics or a broader metalworking tradition.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum records document adornment through cowrie shells, beads, cotton, raffia, and metal. One wooden female figure has red and orange glass beads attached to each earlobe with green thread. Another has metal nails inserted for eyes, while a further figure has a string wrapped in metal around the waist. A separate female figure has six carved rings around the neck and a blue-striped cotton rectangle tied around the waist.

The sources do not document Temne tattooing, henna, hair practices, or named jewelry types. Gold ornaments are mentioned in a historical description of funerary burial, but no specific form is identified.

## Music & performance

The sources do not provide a named Temne musical instrument repertoire or named song genres. A museum catalogue records a batik depicting two women playing drums and a dancing woman, while a historical description mentions marriage dances. The sources also describe secret societies and initiation ceremonies, but do not provide their musical forms.

Temne oral literature includes stories and proverbs in the Temne language. Many recorded stories concern *panis*, the trickster spider, a character also found in the storytelling traditions of the Vai, Mende, and Limba of Sierra Leone. The sources do not explain whether these stories were accompanied by instruments, song, or dance.

## Dance & theatre

The sources mention marriage dances and a museum-recorded batik image of two women playing drums beside a dancing woman. They also document masks and masquerading. The chiefdom spirit, or *kärfi*, is represented by a distinct mask, and an individual called the Sanko performs as its masquerader. The Sanko and the chief appear publicly together, carrying the same regalia and observing the same role-specific taboos.

Secret societies include the men’s Poro and the women’s Bondo, as well as Ragbenle or Ramena. Their practices include secret initiation ceremonies as rites of passage for young boys and girls. The sources do not describe choreographies, theatre plots, named dances, or the performance contexts of the masks in further detail.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not describe an annual Temne festival calendar or named seasonal festivals. They do document initiation ceremonies connected with secret societies. Chiefdoms participate in the men’s Poro, Ragbenle or Ramena, and the women’s Bondo. These societies conduct secret initiation ceremonies understood as rites of passage for young boys and girls.

Temne traditional religion includes sacrifices to patrilineal ancestral spirits and to other spirits, some regarded as good and others as mischievous or vicious. The chief possesses a sacred force distinguishing the office from ordinary community membership, and the chiefdom spirit is represented through a mask and masquerader.

Historical descriptions mention rituals of chief succession involving goat blood and rice flour, marriage dances, and funerary burial within the house with gold ornaments. The supplied sources do not establish a standard calendar date or season for these ceremonies.

## Foodways

The Temne are traditionally farmers who grow rice, cassava, millet, and kola nut. Cash crops include peanuts, tobacco, cotton, palm, and kola nuts. Some Temne are fishermen, artisans, and traders. The supplied sources do not name a Temne dish, recipe, cooking method, beverage tradition, or dietary rule.

Rice flour appears in a historical description of chief succession rituals involving goat blood and rice flour. Portuguese records from the early sixteenth century mention a Temne word for rice, “nack maloo,” borrowed from Mandinka. The sources also describe trade in agricultural products and other goods, including groundnuts, palm kernels, palm oil, rubber, timber, gold, ivory, wood, pepper, and slaves, but they do not identify these as prepared foods or ceremonial dishes.

The museum record for the batik states that kola was used to dye the cloth brown. This is evidence of kola in a material process, not a documented food preparation.

## Oral tradition & literature

Temne oral literature is documented through collections of fables, proverbs, stories, and language materials. In 1861, C. F. Schlenker published Temne fables and proverbs with facing English translations. His source was a Temne man living in Port Loko in the late 1840s. The collection also included translations from the Bible into Temne.

In 1916, Northcote Thomas published an anthropological report whose second part contained a Temne-English dictionary and whose third part contained a grammar and 27 stories told in Temne with interlinear English translation. Many stories feature *panis*, the trickster spider. Thomas’s work also compared Temne vocabulary with Kissi and other related languages.

The sources list Temne names and proverbs, stories and songs from Sierra Leone, and Temne stories as later publications. They do not describe an epic cycle, contemporary literary movement, or formal preservation project beyond these written collections.

## Language & religion

Temne belongs to the Mel branch of the Niger–Congo language family. It is spoken mainly in Sierra Leone’s Northern Province and Western Area, and is related to the Baga language of Guinea. Temne is tonal, with high and low tones. Its alphabet uses specified letters and digraphs, and the sources record grammatical, dictionary, and oral-literature publications in Temne.

The Temne originally practiced a traditional polytheistic religion involving a Supreme Being and Creator called *Kuru Masaba*, followed by lesser deities. Patrilineal ancestral spirits act as intermediaries, and sacrifices may be offered to ancestral and other spirits. Secret societies include Poro, Bondo, and Ragbenle or Ramena.

Most Temne are Muslim, while some retain traditional religious beliefs or combine them with Islam. Christianity expanded from Freetown and missionary activity, with Methodist and Baptist missions among the institutions mentioned in the sources. The supplied material does not provide a more precise current religious distribution.

## Sources & further reading

- Walter Rodney, *A History of the Upper Guinea Coast, 1545–1800*, Clarendon Press, 1970.
- Kenneth C. Wylie, *The Political Kingdoms of the Temne: Temne Government in Sierra Leone, 1825–1910*, Africana, 1977.
- Abou Bai-Sharka, *Temne Names and Proverbs. Stories and Songs from Sierra Leone*, People’s Educational Association of Sierra Leone, 1986.

- Northcote Thomas, *Anthropological Report on Sierra Leone*, 1916.
- [Temne people — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temne_people)
- [Temne language — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temne_language)
