---
title: "Tsonga"
subtitle: "Mozambique"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]
---

## Overview

The Tsonga people, also called *Vatsonga*, are a Bantu ethnic group primarily native to Southern Mozambique, especially Inhambane, Gaza and Maputo, and to South Africa, particularly Limpopo and Mpumalanga. Smaller numbers are found in Zimbabwe and Northern Eswatini. They speak Xitsonga, a Southern Bantu language. In 2011, there were 7.3 million Shangaan speakers, including 4 million speakers in Mozambique and 3.3 million in South Africa; smaller populations were recorded in Eswatini and Zimbabwe. Tsonga communities have been connected through language, cultural integration, trade, traditional leadership and related clan histories. Their folk culture includes initiation practices, traditional healing, dances, music, oral literature, agriculture, pastoralism and objects made from wood, fibre, reeds, pottery, metal and gourds.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources do not document named Tsonga textile traditions or distinctive pattern systems beyond the catalogue descriptions of fibre, bead and textile objects.

**Fibre-cord skirts** — Museum records describe a girl’s skirt made of fibre cords, a skirt made of fibre cords with blue and white bead ornaments below the girdle, and a skirt made of grass or palm leaf strung on a fibre cord.

**Waist-cloth** — A museum record describes a male wooden figure together with a length of cotton textile used as a waist-cloth.

**Reed mats** — A catalogue record identifies a mat made of reeds.

**Beaded drinking vessel** — A gourd drinking vessel is decorated with burnt figures and white glass beads.

**Gourd decoration** — Two vessel records describe gourds inlaid with white beads and decorated with incised geometric motifs in black; one also depicts various animals and has a suspension loop of vegetable fibre tied around the neck.

**Motif vocabulary.** Incised geometric line patterns; burnt figures; depictions of various animals; pokerwork motif.

### Clothing & dress

The sources provide limited information about clothing and dress. A girl’s skirt made of fibre cords is recorded, as is a skirt made of fibre cords with blue and white bead ornaments below the girdle and a leather thong at one end. Another skirt is made of grass or palm leaf and strung on a fibre cord. A museum record also describes a male wooden figure accompanied by cotton textile used as a waist-cloth. The sources do not describe everyday dress, head coverings, belts, footwear or a broader ceremonial clothing system.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Tsonga house forms, settlement layouts, building materials, roof types or architectural decoration.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Museum records document pottery vessels, including a vessel with an everted rim, a red burnished body and additional graphite burnished decoration, and another with a red burnished body, black burnished neck and projecting lip. Metal and wooden tools include daggers, knives and a ceremonial battleaxe with a wooden shaft. One iron knife has a corrugated blade, wooden handle and sheath; another lacks a sheath. Other objects include wooden head-rests, snuff-boxes, a wooden bowl with handles and a carved wooden chain, a wooden receptacle with an incised pattern, a reed and palm-leaf food basket, and gourds decorated with beads, burnt figures and incised motifs.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The catalogue records include a wooden necklace with alternately orientated carved, bi-conical beads resembling vertebrae and six small antelope horns imitating lions’ claws. Metal bangles are decorated on their outer and inner rims with incised linear motifs. Bracelets are made of fibre and beads. A Cleveland Museum of Art staff from the 1800s–1900s bears carved male heads with an ornament signifying maturity and marriage; the associated hairdo is called *isicoco* and uses a fibre or sinew ring into which the wearer’s hair was woven. Other records include snuff-boxes, snuff-bottles and a bone divination-tablet. The sources do not describe tattooing, henna or further adornment practices.

## Music & performance

The sources describe several forms of Tsonga music. More traditional dance music was associated with General MD Shirinda, Fanny Mpfumo, Matshwa Bemuda and Thomas Chauke. Tsonga disco and Tsonga ndzhumbha were popularized by Joe Shirimani, Penny Penny, Peta Teanet and Benny Mayengani. A more westernized sound using English words, sampled vocals and heavy synthesizers is called Shangaan electro in Europe and was pioneered by Nozinja, the Tshetsha Boys and DJ Khwaya.

The museum catalogue includes a marimba from Inhambane, Mozambique, described as a musical instrument with two wooden sticks. It also records a stringed trough zither made from a rectangular tray with seven strings of vegetable fibre, decorated with copper and brass wire ornament and a string loop beneath. The sources do not describe the performance contexts, tuning, repertoire or social roles of these instruments. They also do not document named song genres, wedding music, funeral music or court performance.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name the **Makhwaya**, **Xighubu**, **Mchongolo** and **Xibelani** dances as traditional dances of the Tsonga people. They also describe Tsonga disco and Tsonga ndzhumbha as experimental or popularized musical genres connected with Tsonga communities. The sources do not explain the choreography, costumes, occasions, ceremonial meanings or distinctions between entertainment and ritual performance. They do not document a Tsonga theatrical or dramatic tradition.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not identify an annual Tsonga festival calendar or provide names and dates for seasonal festivals. They do describe life-cycle initiation practices. Tsonga men traditionally attend an initiation school for circumcision called *Ngoma*, also known as *Hogo*, after which they are regarded as men. Young teenage girls attend an initiation school led by older Vatsonga women called *Khomba*; participants are called *tikhomba*. The sources state that only virgins may attend and that the instruction concerns womanhood, conduct as *tikhomba* in the community and preparation for marriage.

Traditional healing also involves ritual initiation. A legend names Nkomo We Lwandle and Dunga Manzi as early Tsonga diviners. A powerful water serpent, Nzunzu, allegedly captured them and submerged them in deep waters. The legend is re-enacted during a diviner’s initiation by ceremoniously submerging initiates in water, from which they emerge as diviners. The sources do not cover weddings, funerals, births or annual religious celebrations.

## Foodways

The Tsonga traditional economy is based on mixed agriculture and pastoralism. Cassava is the staple, while corn, millet, sorghum and other crops are also grown. Women perform much of the agricultural work, while men and teenage boys care for domestic animals, including cows, sheep and goats. Some men grow cash crops. Most Tsongas now have jobs in South Africa and Mozambique.

A British Museum catalogue records a food basket made of reed and palm leaf, but the sources do not identify named dishes, cooking methods, drinks, ceremonial foods, tea or coffee traditions, dietary rules or the preparation of food and beverages. A gourd drinking vessel is recorded, decorated with burnt figures and white glass beads, but its contents are not specified.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources document Tsonga folktales, songs, riddles and proverbs. E. Dora Earthy published Tsonga folktales from the Lenge dialect with facing-text English translations in the 1937 volume of *Folklore*. Henri-Alexandre Junod included Tsonga song lyrics with English translations in his 1913 study *The Life of a South African Tribe*, and also recorded Tsonga riddles and proverbs.

One riddle asks what a mother dearly loves but cannot run to meet on her return home; the answer is the unborn babe in the womb. Another asks what can be beaten without leaving a scar; the answer is water. Recorded proverbs include one about swallowing a large stone and having confidence in the size of one’s throat, one about tattooing marks on the back being known by the tattooer, and one stating that the strength of the crocodile is water. Junod later published *Quelques Proverbes Thonga* in 1931. The sources do not describe an epic tradition or contemporary literary revival beyond the recorded publications.

## Language & religion

Tsonga, or Xitsonga, is a Bantu language spoken by Tsonga people in South Africa and Mozambique. It is mutually intelligible with Tswa and Ronga, and the name Tsonga is sometimes used as a cover term for all three, also called Tswa-Ronga. Xitsonga is an official language of the Republic of South Africa and was officially recognized in the Constitution of South Africa in 1996. It is standardized as a written language and uses the Latin alphabet. The sources name dialects including xiRonga, xiHlanganu, xiBila, xiDjonga, xiN’walungu and xiHlengwe.

Tsonga people acknowledge ancestors, who are believed to affect the lives of their descendants. Traditional healers are called *n’anga*. Spirits identified in the sources include the Ngoni, Ndau and Malopo. The sources do not provide a general account of Tsonga religious affiliation beyond ancestral practice, divination and healing.

## Sources & further reading

- Henri-Alexandre Junod, *The Life of a South African Tribe*, 1913; the sources do not provide publisher information.
- Henri Philipe Junod, *Matimu ya Vatsonga 1498-1650*, 1977; the sources do not provide publisher information.

---
title: "Tsonga"
subtitle: "Mozambique"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]

## At a glance
| | |
|---|---|
| Who | The Tsonga, also called Vatsonga, are a Bantu people. |
| Where | Southern Mozambique, especially Inhambane, Gaza and Maputo, and parts of South Africa, Zimbabwe and Eswatini. |
| How many | 7.3 million Shangaan speakers in 2011, including 4 million in Mozambique and 3.3 million in South Africa. |
| Language | XiTsonga, a Southern Bantu language. |
| Religion | Ancestor belief, divination and traditional healing. |
| Known for | Initiation schools · Traditional dances · Music and oral literature · Mixed farming and pastoralism · Decorated gourds and fibre objects |

## Overview

The Tsonga are linked by language, trade, traditional leadership and shared clan histories. Their culture includes initiation, healing, dance, music, stories and farming. They make useful and decorative objects from wood, fibre, reeds, pottery, metal and gourds. Many Tsonga people now work in Mozambique and South Africa.

## Material culture

Tsonga material culture includes fibre skirts, reed mats, pottery, metal tools, carved wood, beadwork and decorated gourds.

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources show fibre, bead and textile objects, but no named Tsonga textile tradition or pattern system.

- **Fibre-cord skirts** — These skirts are made from fibre cords, sometimes with blue and white beads below the girdle.
- **Waist-cloth** — A length of cotton textile was used as a male figure’s waist-cloth.
- **Reed mats** — A catalogue record identifies a mat made from reeds.
- **Beaded drinking vessel** — A gourd drinking vessel is decorated with burnt figures and white glass beads.
- **Incised gourd decoration** — Some gourds have white bead inlay and black geometric lines, animal figures or a pokerwork motif.

### Clothing & dress

The sources record a few skirts and a waist-cloth but do not describe everyday Tsonga dress.

- **Girl’s fibre skirt** — A girl’s skirt is made of fibre cords.
- **Beaded fibre skirt** — One skirt has blue and white beads below the girdle and a leather thong at one end.
- **Grass or palm-leaf skirt** — Another skirt is made of grass or palm leaf strung on a fibre cord.
- **Cotton waist-cloth** — A male wooden figure is accompanied by cotton textile used as a waist-cloth.

### Architecture

The sources do not describe Tsonga houses, settlements or building styles.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Tsonga everyday objects include pottery, tools, carved wood, baskets and decorated gourds.

- **Burnished pottery vessel** — One vessel has an everted rim, a red burnished body and graphite burnished decoration.
- **Black-necked pottery vessel** — Another vessel has a red burnished body, a black burnished neck and a projecting lip.
- **Ceremonial battleaxe** — A ceremonial battleaxe has a wooden shaft.
- **Corrugated-blade knife** — An iron knife has a corrugated blade, wooden handle and sheath.
- **Reed and palm-leaf basket** — A food basket is made from reed and palm leaf.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Adornment includes carved necklaces, metal bangles, bead bracelets, hair ornaments and snuff objects.

- **Carved wooden necklace** — A wooden necklace has carved bi-conical beads and six small antelope horns.
- **Metal bangles** — Metal bangles have incised linear designs on their inner and outer rims.
- **Fibre and bead bracelets** — Some bracelets are made of fibre and beads.
- **Maturity and marriage staff** (*isicoco*) — A Cleveland Museum staff has carved male heads and an ornament linked with maturity and marriage, while isicoco is the associated hairdo made with a fibre or sinew ring.
- **Bone divination tablet** — A bone tablet was used for divination.

## Music & performance

Tsonga music ranges from traditional dance music to disco, ndzhumbha and Shangaan electro.

- **Traditional dance music** — Traditional dance music was associated with General MD Shirinda, Fanny Mpfumo, Matshwa Bemuda and Thomas Chauke.
- **Tsonga disco** — Tsonga disco was popularized by Joe Shirimani, Penny Penny, Peta Teanet and Benny Mayengani.
- **Tsonga ndzhumbha** (*ndzhumbha*) — Tsonga ndzhumbha was also popularized by Joe Shirimani, Penny Penny, Peta Teanet and Benny Mayengani.
- **Shangaan electro** — This European style uses English words, sampled vocals and heavy synthesizers.
- **Trough zither** — A seven-string zither is made from a rectangular tray and vegetable fibre strings, with copper and brass wire decoration.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name four traditional Tsonga dances but do not describe a Tsonga theatre tradition.

- **Makhwaya** — Makhwaya is named as a traditional Tsonga dance.
- **Xighubu** — Xighubu is named as a traditional Tsonga dance.
- **Mchongolo** — Mchongolo is named as a traditional Tsonga dance.
- **Xibelani** — Xibelani is named as a traditional Tsonga dance.

## Festivals & rituals

Tsonga ritual life includes male and female initiation schools and initiation into divination.

- **Men’s circumcision school** (*Ngoma; Hogo*) — Tsonga men attend Ngoma, also called Hogo, for circumcision and are then regarded as men.
- **Girls’ initiation school** (*Khomba; tikhomba*) — Older Vatsonga women lead Khomba for teenage girls called tikhomba, who learn about womanhood, conduct and marriage.
- **Diviner’s water initiation** (*Nzunzu*) — During diviner initiation, initiates are ceremoniously submerged in water in a re-enactment of the story of the water serpent Nzunzu.

## Foodways

Tsonga foodways center on mixed agriculture and pastoralism, with cassava as the staple.

- **Cassava farming** — Cassava is the main staple crop.
- **Mixed crop farming** — People also grow corn, millet, sorghum and other crops.
- **Pastoral care** — Men and teenage boys care for cows, sheep and goats.
- **Food basket** — A British Museum record describes a food basket made from reed and palm leaf.
- **Gourd drinking vessel** — A decorated gourd vessel is recorded, but its contents are not specified.

## Oral tradition & literature

Tsonga oral tradition includes folktales, songs, riddles and proverbs recorded in published works.

- **Lenge folktales** — E. Dora Earthy published Tsonga folktales from the Lenge dialect with English translations in 1937.
- **Tsonga song lyrics** — Henri-Alexandre Junod published Tsonga song lyrics with English translations in 1913.
- **Unborn-babe riddle** — One riddle asks what a mother loves but cannot run to meet when she returns home, with the answer being the unborn babe in the womb.
- **Water riddle** — Another riddle asks what can be beaten without leaving a scar, with the answer being water.
- **Crocodile proverb** — One proverb says that the crocodile’s strength is water.

## Language & religion

XiTsonga is a standardized Bantu language, and Tsonga religious practice centers on ancestors, spirits, divination and healing.

- **XiTsonga** — XiTsonga is spoken in Mozambique and South Africa, uses the Latin alphabet and is an official language of South Africa.
- **Tswa-Ronga** — Tsonga can be used as a cover term for Tswa, Ronga and related speech forms.
- **Tsonga dialects** (*xiRonga; xiHlanganu; xiBila; xiDjonga; xiN’walungu; xiHlengwe*) — Named dialects include xiRonga, xiHlanganu, xiBila, xiDjonga, xiN’walungu and xiHlengwe.
- **Traditional healer** (*n’anga*) — Traditional healers are called n’anga.
- **Ancestor belief** — Tsonga people believe ancestors can affect the lives of their descendants.

## Glossary

- *Vatsonga* — Tsonga people
- *XiTsonga* — Tsonga language
- *Ngoma* — Men’s circumcision initiation school
- *Hogo* — Another name for Ngoma
- *Khomba* — Girls’ initiation school
- *tikhomba* — Girls attending Khomba
- *n’anga* — Traditional healer
- *Nzunzu* — Powerful water serpent
- *isicoco* — Maturity and marriage hairdo
- *Makhwaya* — Traditional Tsonga dance
- *Xighubu* — Traditional Tsonga dance
- *Mchongolo* — Traditional Tsonga dance
- *Xibelani* — Traditional Tsonga dance
- *ndzhumbha* — Tsonga music genre
- *Shangaan electro* — Westernized Tsonga-associated music style
- *xiRonga* — Named Tsonga dialect
- *xiHlanganu* — Named Tsonga dialect
- *xiBila* — Named Tsonga dialect

- *xiN’walungu* — Named Tsonga dialect

---
title: "Makua"
subtitle: "Mozambique"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]
---

## Overview

The Makuwa people, also known as Makuwa or Wamakuwa, are a Bantu ethnic group found in northern Mozambique and in southern border provinces of Tanzania, including the Mtwara Region. They are the largest ethnic group in Mozambique and are concentrated mainly north of the Zambezi River. Sociologists distinguish four geographical and linguistic subdivisions: lower or Lolo Makua, upper or Lomwe Makua, Maua, and Niassa Makua or Medo. The total Makua population is estimated at about 3.5 million. They speak variants of the Makua language, also called Emakua, a Bantu-group language. Their documented cultural history includes agriculture, hunting, metal ore processing, tool manufacture, trade, oral tradition, traditional religion, and material objects made from iron, wood, bamboo, pottery, fibre, gourds, and seed pods.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document Makua textile traditions, named textile patterns, or distinctive woven techniques.

**Motif vocabulary.** The museum records describe incised lines, circular bands, punctures, zig-zag compartments, straight vertical lines, horizontal bands, and carved ornament on objects, but do not identify these as named Makua motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe everyday or ceremonial Makua dress, garments, head coverings, belts, footwear, or named clothing traditions. The sources mention that, before the 18th century, Makua people exchanged food, ivory tusks, and metal products for textiles, salt, and other products. They also state that the Makua language is spoken alongside Afrikaans and Zulu in South Africa, Portuguese in Mozambique, Swahili by some elders and by many people on the Tanzania-Mozambican border, and English in South Africa and Tanzania.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Makua houses, settlements, roofs, building materials, workshops, or named architectural forms. They state that the Makua people were concentrated in a large region north of the Zambezi River and that their legendary original home was Namuli.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Makua people have a documented history of processing metal ore and manufacturing tools. Iron was extracted from ore in a wood-burning hearth as a community activity and was worked into axes, knives, spears, rings, and other items. Museum records include an axe with a wooden handle and an iron blade, handmade pottery pipe-bowls, a black pottery bowl shaped like an hour glass, bamboo objects, wooden boxes for gun caps, a wooden head-rest, a day reckoner made from short lengths of bamboo threaded on fibre, and a carved ebony figure of a kneeling woman grinding corn.

The museum records also describe an earthenware lime box, a bamboo snuff tube, a double-gourd smoking pipe, a rattle made from thirteen seed pods, and a bamboo flute with three side holes and simple incised decoration.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not describe named Makua jewelry traditions, tattooing, henna, hair practices, or ritual body adornment. Museum records identify seven small circular wooden ear ornaments with incised linear patterns. They also record charms made from teeth, including two *ngiri* (?) teeth suspended on a cord, four leopard's teeth threaded on soft brown cord, and two *ngiri* (?) teeth suspended on two shreds of cotton cloth.

The Wikipedia source states that Makua metalworkers made rings. It does not explain their form, use, gender association, or ritual meaning.

## Music & performance

The museum catalogue records a bamboo flute, described as having one end open, one end closed, three holes at the side, and simple incised decoration. It also records a rattle made from thirteen seed pods threaded onto fibre string and attached to a wooden stick; the seed pods contain dried seeds and have small slits or decorative cuts. These records identify objects but do not describe their musical scales, performance settings, repertories, or names in Makua.

The sources used do not document Makua song genres, named musical traditions, professional performers, wedding or funeral music, court performance, or other musical contexts. The Wikipedia sources describe Makua language varieties and dialects but do not connect them to specific musical forms.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document named Makua dances, theatre traditions, masquerades, dramatic forms, or ceremonial and entertainment distinctions. The museum records include a rattle and a flute, but provide no information about performances in which they were used.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not provide an annual Makua festival calendar or identify named seasonal festivals. They also do not describe Makua birth, initiation, wedding, funeral, or coming-of-age ceremonies.

The traditional religion of the Makua people includes the principal deity Muluku and an evil spirit named Minepa. A legend states that Muluku created the first man and woman from two holes in the ground and gave them the art of using tools. After the humans disobeyed, Muluku summoned two monkeys and gave them the same tools and instruction. The legend explains that Muluku cut off the monkeys' tails and fastened them to the man and woman, telling the monkeys to be human and the humans to be monkeys.

## Foodways

The sources used do not identify Makua staple grains, named dishes, cooking methods, ceremonial foods, beverages, or dietary rules. They state that the Makua people have traditionally been dedicated to agriculture and hunting. Before the 18th century, they exchanged food, ivory tusks, and metal products for textiles, salt, and other products.

A museum record depicts an ebony carved figure of a kneeling woman grinding corn, with a basin in front of her. The record does not identify the corn, the grinding process, the food produced, or the social context of the activity.

## Oral tradition & literature

A mythical legend in Makua oral tradition says that the Makua ancestor was the first man and woman born of Namuli, their original home, while other living creatures came from nearby mountains. Scholars are described as uncertain whether Makua origins were in the mountains, west of Lake Malawi, or northern lands such as Tanzania or the south. They agree that the Makua were likely an established ethnic group in northern Mozambique by the 1st millennium CE.

Another Makua religious legend concerns Muluku, Minepa, the creation of the first man and woman, and the transformation of humans and monkeys. The sources do not document named epics, proverbs, riddles, literary works, or contemporary literary preservation projects. An ethnography of the Makua people was published in 1847 by Eugene de Froberville after he interviewed and learned Makua traditions and culture from over three hundred Makua people in Mauritius plantations.

## Language & religion

Makhuwa, also called Emakhuwa, Makua, Macua, or Mozambican, is the primary Bantu language of northern Mozambique. It is spoken by roughly 5.8 million Makua people, especially north of the Zambezi River and in Nampula Province. The Makua language is the most widely spoken indigenous language of Mozambique.

The sources distinguish dialects and varieties including Central Makhuwa, Meetto, Chirima, Marrevone, eNahara, eSaka, and Ruvuma Makhuwa. Mutual intelligibility among these varieties is limited, and Central Makhuwa, or Makhuwa-Makhuwana, is the basis of the standard language. In Makhuwa, tone is distinctive; the eNahara dialect has low and high tones, with high tone indicated by an acute accent.

Traditional Makua religion reveres ancestors and nature spirits. It is held by 66 to 70 percent of the Makua people according to the Wikipedia source. Coastal Makua traders converted to the Shafi'i school of Sunni Islam under the influence of Swahili-Arab customers. The coastal Muslim people are called the *Maka* in Makua; the term may derive from Mecca or from Makua words meaning “salt” or “coast.”

## Sources & further reading

- “Makua language,” Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makua_language
- Eugene de Froberville, ethnography of the Makua people, published in 1847, as described in the Wikipedia source.
- British Museum catalogue records for the axe, boxes, snuff-box, head-rest, smoking-pipes, calendar, rattle, flute, ear-ornaments, charms, and carved ebony figure supplied in the source material.

title: "Kissi"
subtitle: "Guinea"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]
---

## Overview

The Kissi are a West African ethnolinguistic group found in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. They are the fourth largest ethnic group in Guinea, making up 6.2% of the population. They speak Kissi, a Mel language of the Niger–Congo language family. The Kissi are associated with basket-making, weaving on vertical looms, ironworking and the production of the “Kissi penny.” Their material culture includes iron tools and weapons, pottery, spinning and weaving implements, musical instruments, masks, head coverings and objects connected with the *Bundu* or *Bandu* societies. Kissi traditional religion includes ancestor worship and prayer to deceased relatives.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Vertical-loom weaving** — The Kissi are well known for weaving on vertical looms. Museum records also document a *kpaba*, a weaving implement made of vegetable material, wood, rotang and plant-fibre cords.

**Kondoyila** — A *Kondoyila* is a grey cotton net shirt with large knotted meshes and cauris around the neck opening and sleeves. The catalogue identifies it as part of the dance costume of the *Bandu* society.

**Jo** — The *Jo* is a dance skirt made from plant fibre. Its waistband is made of twisted *Urèna* fibre, while the hanging section is probably pisang bast or similar material, braided at the top and loose below. Brown and black material alternate to produce stripes.

**Spinning implements** — The *temuo* is a round wooden stick that branches into four parts and holds cotton. The accompanying spindle, called *kbendeleng*, has a long heavy shaft with a conical soapstone weight, identified in the catalogue as *dindo*. Spinning yarn is described as women’s work for men’s looms.

**Fujó** — The *Fujó* is a head covering made from pisang fibre or *Urèna* fibre and decorated with cauris. Museum records associate it with girls of the *Bundu* or *Bandu* society after ceremonies.

**Kpaba** — The *Kpaba*, plural *kpabalang*, is a weaving implement. Its wooden frame holds parallel heddles, and its remaining sides and heddles are made of rotang.

**Material fibres** — Catalogue records name pisang fibre, *Urèna*, raffia and *Raphia* materials in clothing, head coverings, spinning and other objects.

### Clothing & dress

The sources document clothing connected with the *Bundu* or *Bandu* societies. Girls wore the *Jo* dance skirt over imported cotton cloth. The *Kondoyila* net shirt belonged to the dance costume and was decorated around the neck and sleeves with cauris. The *Fujó* was braided into a girl’s hair by an older woman after she left the *Bundu* bush following a ceremony; it was later removed. Other museum records describe a hunter’s or warrior’s tunic made from hand-spun and hand-woven cotton strips, with amulets wrapped in cotton and small horns sewn to the back of the neck. The sources do not describe ordinary everyday clothing, footwear or separate men’s and women’s dress beyond these records.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Kissi houses, settlements, roofs, workshops or other architectural traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Kissi smiths were known for ironworking, and museum records identify knives, a fighting dagger, an offering knife, an axe and a razor for circumcision. One knife was forged from a *Kissi penny* and was chiefly intended for harvesting palm fruits. A curved iron dagger from Liberia was used in fighting. Pottery records describe a round black earthen vessel with an incised and fired pattern, and a small black earthen vessel. Other everyday objects include a raffia basket, a sieve for producing palm oil, a stool of white wood with incised decoration, and a sling called *fanda*, used to drive rice birds away from platforms in rice fields.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources document cauris as decoration on *Fujó* head coverings and on the *Kondoyila* net shirt. The *Fujó* is worn by girls after *Bundu* or *Bandu* ceremonies and is braided into the hair by an older woman. The sources do not describe tattoos, henna, permanent body modification or other jewelry traditions.

## Music & performance

Museum records document several Kissi musical instruments. The *sangbaa* is a goblet-shaped drum with a drumskin, a wooden drumstick and a network of cords used to tension the skin. Its foot is tubular and ends in a tripod. The *sansa* has seven metal tongues fastened to a wooden board with a characteristic plaited design. A *tjekó* is a rattle made from a rattan vine with a base formed from part of a calabash fruit and containing seeds of *Canna indica*. A *seláng* is a calabash rattle with an attached bead rattle; the catalogue places it in an ensemble including the *sangbáa*. Another instrument is a scraping stick made from *Raphia vinifera*, with fifty-one grooves over an area of thirty centimetres; a stick or palm-nut is drawn across the grooves in time with dance or song rhythm. A British Museum record also describes an ivory musical horn carved with a lizard, snake and crosshatched decoration. The sources do not name song genres or describe complete performance occasions beyond dance, song rhythm and musical ensembles.

## Dance & theatre

The sources document dance objects associated with the *Bundu* or *Bandu* societies. The *Jo* skirt and *Kondoyila* net shirt formed part of a dance costume, while the *Jajei* ankle rattle was made for girls of the *Bundu* society. A dance rattle made from a hollow bottle-like fruit and covered with seed beads was used by women at *Bundu* parties in connection with the appearance of a masked *Bundu* “devil.” The same catalogue record says that a similar rattle was seen among Kissi men at one of their special dances. A wooden mask with two horns, four teeth probably from chimpanzee and animal-fur decoration is also recorded. The sources do not describe named dances, theatrical plots or shadow-puppet traditions.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not describe an annual festival calendar or provide dates for Kissi festivals. They do document *Bundu* or *Bandu* ceremonies for girls. After returning from the *Bundu* bush, girls wore *Fujó* head coverings braided into their hair, and the coverings were removed after some time. The *Jajei* ankle rattle and the *Jo* and *Kondoyila* dance garments are associated with this society. A razor is identified as an instrument for circumcision, but the sources do not provide a broader account of the rite, its participants or its timing. The sources also do not describe weddings, funerals, birth ceremonies or annual agricultural festivals.

## Foodways

The sources identify rice fields and rice birds in the description of the *fanda*, a sling used from a platform to drive away birds. They also record a sieve used for producing palm oil and a knife chiefly intended for harvesting palm fruits. The sources do not describe named dishes, drinks, cooking methods, dietary rules or ceremonial foods.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not describe Kissi folktales, epics, proverbs, riddles, oral performers or literary preservation projects.

## Language & religion

Kissi, also called Kisi or Kisiei, is a Mel language of West Africa within the Niger–Congo language family. It has northern and southern dialects, and both are tonal. The northern dialect, *kisiduei*, is spoken in Guinea and Sierra Leone; the southern dialect, *kpekeduei*, is spoken in Liberia and Sierra Leone. Kissi is spoken in Guinea in Kissidougou and Guéckédou and their préfectures. The Kissi also use the names Assi, Bakoa, Den, Gihi, Gisi, Gissi, Gizi, Kisi, Kisia, Kisie, Kisiye, Kizi and Kalen. Many Kissi have converted to Christianity, while most continue practicing their traditional ethnic religion. Ancestor worship and prayer to deceased relatives are common. Carved soapstone figures and heads were produced before colonial contact; their purpose is uncertain, with interpretations connecting them either to ancestor worship or to gods associated with agricultural yields.

## Sources & further reading

- George Tucker Childs, *A grammar of Kisi: a southern Atlantic language*, Mouton de Gruyter, 1995.
- G. Tucker Childs, *A Dictionary of the Kisi Language. With an English-Kisi Index*.
- Denise Paulme, *Les Gens du Riz: Les Kissi de Haute-Guinée*, Librairie Plon, 1954 and 1970.

- British Museum catalogue records cited in the object catalogue supplied for this atlas.

The Kissi live in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. Their material culture includes weaving, basket-making, iron tools, pottery, musical instruments, masks and society objects. Kissi women spin yarn for men’s looms. Traditional religion includes ancestor worship and prayer to deceased relatives.

## Material culture

Kissi material culture is known for woven goods, plant fibres, ironwork, pottery, instruments and objects linked to Bundu or Bandu societies.

### Textile & pattern traditions

Kissi weaving uses vertical looms, plant fibres and hand-spun cotton.

- **Vertical loom** — Kissi weavers are well known for using vertical looms.
- **Weaving implement** (*kpaba*) — The kpaba has a wooden frame with parallel heddles, while its other sides and heddles are made of rotang.
- **Cotton holder** (*temuo*) — The temuo is a round wooden stick that branches into four parts and holds cotton.
- **Spindle** (*kbendeleng*) — The kbendeleng is a spindle with a long heavy shaft and a conical soapstone weight called dindo.
- **Head covering** (*Fujó*) — The Fujó is made from pisang or Urèna fibre and decorated with cauris.

### Clothing & dress

The documented clothing is linked mainly to Bundu or Bandu societies, ceremonies and hunting.

- **Dance skirt** (*Jo*) — The Jo is a plant-fibre dance skirt worn over imported cotton cloth.
- **Net shirt** (*Kondoyila*) — The Kondoyila is a grey cotton net shirt with large knotted meshes and cauris around the neck and sleeves.
- **Hunter’s tunic** — A hunter’s or warrior’s tunic was made from hand-spun and hand-woven cotton strips, with cotton-wrapped amulets and small horns sewn to the back of the neck.
- **Girl’s head covering** (*Fujó*) — After a Bundu ceremony, an older woman braided the Fujó into a girl’s hair, and it was later removed.

### Architecture

The sources do not describe Kissi buildings or settlements.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Kissi smiths made iron tools and weapons, while households used pottery, baskets and farm objects.

- **Palm-fruit knife** (*Kissi penny*) — One knife was forged from a Kissi penny and was mainly used to harvest palm fruits.
- **Fighting dagger** — A curved iron dagger from Liberia was used in fighting.
- **Black earthen vessel** — Pottery records include a round black earthen vessel with an incised and fired pattern.
- **Palm-oil sieve** — A sieve was used to produce palm oil.
- **Bird sling** (*fanda*) — The fanda is a sling used from rice-field platforms to drive rice birds away.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Cauris decorate Bundu or Bandu clothing and head coverings.

- **Cauris on a head covering** (*Fujó*) — Cauris decorate the Fujó head covering worn by girls after Bundu or Bandu ceremonies.
- **Cauris on a net shirt** (*Kondoyila*) — Cauris decorate the neck opening and sleeves of the Kondoyila net shirt.

## Music & performance

Kissi instruments include drums, rattles, a lamellophone, a scraper and an ivory horn.

- **Goblet drum** (*sangbaa*) — The sangbaa is a goblet-shaped drum with a skin, a wooden stick, tension cords and a tubular foot ending in a tripod.
- **Seven-tongue instrument** (*sansa*) — The sansa has seven metal tongues attached to a wooden board with a plaited design.
- **Seed rattle** (*tjekó*) — The tjekó is a rattan-vine rattle with a calabash base filled with Canna indica seeds.
- **Calabash rattle** (*seláng*) — The seláng is a calabash rattle with an attached bead rattle and belongs to an ensemble including the sangbáa.
- **Grooved scraper** — A scraper made from Raphia vinifera has fifty-one grooves that are rubbed with a stick or palm-nut in time with dance or song.

## Dance & theatre

Dance objects are especially connected with Bundu or Bandu society events.

- **Ankle rattle** (*Jajei*) — The Jajei is an ankle rattle made for girls of the Bundu society.

- **Horned mask** — A wooden mask is recorded with two horns, four probable chimpanzee teeth and animal fur.
- **Dance skirt** (*Jo*) — The Jo formed part of a Bundu or Bandu dance costume.
- **Net shirt** (*Kondoyila*) — The Kondoyila formed part of a Bundu or Bandu dance costume.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources describe Bundu or Bandu ceremonies for girls but no annual festival calendar.

- **Bundu bush ceremony** (*Bundu*) — After returning from the Bundu bush, girls wore Fujó head coverings braided into their hair, which were later removed.
- **Bandu society ceremony** (*Bandu*) — The Bandu society is linked to the Fujó, Jajei, Jo and Kondoyila.
- **Circumcision razor** — A razor is recorded as an instrument for circumcision, but the sources give no wider details about the rite.

## Foodways

The documented food-related objects concern rice fields, palm oil and palm fruits.

- **Rice-field sling** (*fanda*) — The fanda was used to drive rice birds away from platforms in rice fields.
- **Palm-oil sieve** — A sieve was used for producing palm oil.
- **Palm-fruit knife** (*Kissi penny*) — A knife made from a Kissi penny was chiefly used for harvesting palm fruits.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do not describe Kissi stories, proverbs, performers or literary traditions.

## Language & religion

Kissi is a tonal Mel language, and traditional religion centers on ancestors and deceased relatives.

- **Kissi language** (*Kisi, Kisiei*) — Kissi, also called Kisi or Kisiei, is a Mel language in the Niger–Congo family.
- **Northern dialect** (*kisiduei*) — The northern dialect, kisiduei, is spoken in Guinea and Sierra Leone.
- **Southern dialect** (*kpekeduei*) — The southern dialect, kpekeduei, is spoken in Liberia and Sierra Leone.

title: "Baga"
subtitle: "Guinea"
region: "Sub Saharan Africa"
tags: [ethnography, sub-saharan-africa]

## Overview

The Baga are a West African ethnic group living in the swampy mangrove lands along Guinea’s Atlantic coastline. Their communities extend along the coast north and south of the mouths of the Nunez and Pongo rivers, around the Îles de Los and the Conakry area, and toward the Konkouré River. The sources give no population total. The Baga include Mandori, Sitemu, Pukur, Bulunits, Kakissa or Sobané, Koba, and Kalum communities, and are related to the Landuma, Nalu, and Temne. Their languages belong to the Atlantic branch of the Niger-Congo family. Baga material culture is especially represented by wood and metal carving, agricultural symbolism, ritual masks, figures, drums, combs, and other objects held in international museums.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document a Baga textile tradition or a named pattern-bearing textile comparable to the traditions requested.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name chequerboard, leaf, diamond, chevron, geometric, and linear designs in descriptions of Baga objects, but do not identify them as a formal textile motif vocabulary.

### Clothing & dress

The sources provide little information about everyday Baga clothing. They state that men are typically fishermen and that most families live in rural villages, but do not describe ordinary garments, head coverings, belts, footwear, or women’s daily dress. Ceremonial masking involves a male dancer wearing a wooden Nimba or D’mba mask on his shoulders. The mask is secured with a rope tied onto the torso, while the dancer is concealed in European cloth and a cover called raffia. Museum records describe a large Nimba mask with a raffia leaf fringe and another with raffia tassels attached to the ears and chin. A British Museum photographic print records a carved wooden figure wearing a loin-cloth, but the catalogue does not identify this as a general Baga garment. The sources do not document a named Baga dress system.

### Architecture

Most Baga families live in clusters of cylindrical mud structures. These houses are roofed with thatch made from rice straw, and groups of structures may form small villages. The sources do not provide a named architectural type, detailed floor plans, decoration schemes, or urban building traditions. They state that guinea’s nationalization of land and property through socialist legislation following independence ended the effective power of Baga elders, whose authority had traditionally operated through village councils.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Baga artistic production includes wood and metalwork, while agriculture, fishing, and the tending of palm and kola trees structure everyday life. The British Museum records a globular earthenware divination vessel encased in hide and encircled by tree bark, with two double-pronged wooden objects attached to its mouth. Other catalogued objects include wooden combs, drums, carved figures, a wooden bird figure with metal nails, and a helmet mask. One comb has a woman’s bust with crested hair and elaborate facial markings; another has a chequerboard and leaf-patterned handle. The sources do not describe named pottery wares, metalworking techniques, or specialized household forms beyond these records.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources document facial markings, scarification, hair styling, and ornamented carved representations, but do not identify named Baga jewelry types. Nimba or D’mba masks can include painted wooden ornaments attached to the ears or pendants attached to the nasal septum. Museum records describe figures wearing armlets, bracelets, necklaces, and belts, and a seated figure with a glass-beaded bracelet and glass-beaded skirt. Baga and zoomorphic museum masks are described with scar-like or tattoo-like markings. The Nimba’s elaborate coiffure may be defined by incised designs, including a raised median crest and chevron marks. The sources do not document tattooing, henna, or a specific personal adornment system.

## Music & performance

The sources do not name Baga musical instruments, song genres, or musical forms. They do, however, describe performance contexts for ritual objects. The D’mba or Nimba is danced by a male masquerader during harvest, planting, baby showers, weddings, and ritual ceremonies. Earlier uses included dancing the mask at least twice a year before the arrival of the rainy seasons. The performance was associated with fertility, pregnancy, agricultural continuity, and support for women. Paint and noise embellishments could be added before ceremonies.

The Baga also traditionally made the Bansonyi mask, consisting of a painted pole that could be 20 feet long, decorated with color, a calico flag, and a triangular icon. It was used in male initiation ceremonies. A British Museum record describes a composite drum in two parts, made of carved wood with a skin membrane, with a kneeling woman and child supporting a ring of six masks; a separate drum takes the form of a crown. Another drum has a kneeling female figure with an elaborate headdress, a skin stretched over its top, carved wooden pegs, red and black paint, and a green-painted band of diamonds. The sources do not specify how these drums were played or name their musical repertory.

## Dance & theatre

Baga performance centers on masquerade rather than a named theatrical genre. The Nimba, also called D’mba, is a large wooden dance mask in the form of a woman’s head and torso. It is worn on the shoulders of a male dancer, who is concealed by cloth and raffia. The mask can be at least eight feet tall and can weigh eighty pounds or more. Seeing holes are carved into the torso so that the performer can see.

The D’mba is danced in agricultural, life-cycle, and ritual contexts. Its breasts represent a woman who has given birth to and nursed healthy children, while its form is associated with fertility and the strength of Baga women during pregnancy. The sources state that the mask does not represent a particular spirit or goddess, but an idea. Other museum records describe helmet masks, zoomorphic masks, a crocodile-like composite animal mask, and a wooden figure identified as Anok, a protective spirit belonging to the Simo society.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not name an annual Baga festival calendar or provide dates for festivals. They do document seasonal and life-cycle ritual contexts. The Nimba or D’mba is danced for harvest, planting, baby showers, weddings, and ritual ceremonies. Earlier performances occurred at least twice a year before the arrival of the rainy seasons. The Bansonyi was used in male initiation ceremonies.

Baga funerary practice has included ritually exposing the dead for a period in a sacred grove, burning some possessions and the house of the dead person, and then carrying out a Muslim-style burial. A Museum of World Culture catalogue describes an Anok sculpture as a protective spirit of the Simo society: it is brought out when someone has died and follows the dead person to the grave. The sources do not provide a complete account of birth ceremonies, marriage procedure, initiation stages, or annual observances.

## Foodways

Baga women are known in the sources for their skill in rice farming in the swampy lowlands of the southern Guinea coastline. Men are typically fishermen and also tend palm and kola trees. Historically, the Baga were principally involved in rice and kola-nut cultivation and salt production, which supplied traders along the coast. Rice farming is therefore the principal documented Baga food-related activity.

The sources do not name Baga dishes, cooking techniques, beverages, food vessels used in domestic preparation, or dietary rules. They also do not document a distinctive ceremonial food associated with the harvest, planting, weddings, or initiation ceremonies. The available material supports discussion of rice agriculture, fishing, palm, kola, and salt production, but does not describe how these products are prepared or consumed.

## Oral tradition & literature

According to Baga oral tradition, the Baga originated in Guinea’s interior highlands and were driven westward by aggressive neighbors toward the coastal swamplands. They are considered “first-comers” along many parts of the Upper Guinea coast and consequently acquired landlord’s rights in those areas. The sources do not record named epics, folktales, proverbs, riddles, or professional storytelling genres.

The sources do document cultural revival and preservation through material practice. After the death of Sekou Toure in 1984, Baga culture began to reemerge as an affirmation of tribal identity. Since the early 1980s, some communities have revived the creation of ritual pieces such as the Nimba. The sources also identify Frederick Lamp’s *Art of the Baga People* as a work through which knowledge of Baga art progressed in the western world.

## Language & religion

Baga languages form a dialect cluster of the Atlantic branch of the Niger-Congo family. Varieties named in the sources include Baga Koga or Koba, Baga Manduri, Baga Sitemu, Baga Kakissa, Baga Marara, Baga Sobane, and Baga Kaloum. Baga Manduri is spoken at Dobale; Baga Sitemu is spoken in villages on the Campaces River; Baga Marara is spoken on islands in the Rio Pongo; and Baga Kaloum was originally spoken in the Conakry area and the Îles de Los. Many Baga also speak the Mande language Susu, a regional trade language.

The Baga were traditionally animist and converted to Islam during the eighteenth century under the influence of Muslim Mandé missionaries. They are now predominantly Muslim, while some continue to practice animist rituals. The Marxist government that took power after Guinea’s independence in 1958 pursued forced “demystification,” destroying or confiscating traditional religious icons. After 1984, Baga ritual art and identity began to reemerge. The sources do not document a historical script.

## Sources & further reading

- E. H. P. Hair, “The History of Baga in Early Written Sources,” *History in Africa*, 24, 1997.
- F. Lamp, “The Art of Baga: A Preliminary Inquiry,” *African Arts*, 19 (2), 1986.

## Overview

The Nalu, also called Nalo, Nanum, or Nanu, are a West African ethnic group found in Guinea and Guinea-Bissau. They speak Nalu, an Atlantic language traditionally classified within Niger-Congo, Atlantic-Congo, and Mbulugish-Nalu, although Güldemann classifies it as unclassified within Niger-Congo. The Nalu settled in the region before the arrival of the Mandé or Mandinka peoples, a history that has led to their description as “pre-Mandingas.” Nalu speakers live predominantly along the littorals of Guinea and Guinea-Bissau. In Guinea, most live north of the Nuñez River, on the Tristão islands and in the sub-prefecture of Kanfarandé, in the prefecture of Boké. In Guinea-Bissau, most live in the Cacine estuary in the Tombali region. Estimates place the number of Nalu speakers between 10,000 and 25,000, while Wilson reports around 12,000.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources do not document named Nalu textile or pattern traditions. They record a basket and a storage basket made from vegetable fibre, straw, and bamboo, but do not identify vernacular names, weaving patterns, or distinctions from neighboring cultures.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name crocodile imagery on a wooden mask: the mask is carved in the form of a crocodile with two long horns and has white painted decorations along the top of the snout.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe Nalu everyday clothing, ceremonial dress, garments, head coverings, belts, footwear, or distinctions between men’s and women’s dress.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Nalu houses, settlements, building materials, roof forms, architectural decoration, or named building types.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Museum records identify several objects associated with the Nalu material record. These include a basket made of vegetable fibre, straw, bamboo, and cotton cloth; a stool made of wood; a tool for knocking oysters off mangrove roots, made of iron and wood; a fish-trap made of bamboo; and a storage basket made of vegetable fibre, straw, and bamboo. The records do not provide vernacular names, manufacturing techniques, dates, or information about the social contexts in which these objects were used.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not describe Nalu jewelry, body adornment, tattoos, henna, hairstyles, hair ornaments, ritual ornaments, or other forms of bodily decoration.

## Music & performance

The sources identify the Simo as a West African secret society active among the Nalu and related groups. They do not describe its music, instruments, songs, ceremonies, membership, performance settings, or relationship to dance. No Nalu musical instruments, song genres, musical scales, or performance occasions are named in the sources. The sources also do not document weddings, funerals, courts, tea houses, festivals, or other settings for Nalu musical performance.

The available museum records include a mask carved of wood in the form of a crocodile with two long horns. White painted decorations run along the top of the snout, and a fringe of grass is mounted along the bottom edge. The records do not state whether this mask was used in Simo activities, dance, ritual, entertainment, or another performance context.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not name a Nalu dance, theatrical genre, dramatic tradition, shadow-puppet tradition, or mask-dance form. They record a crocodile-shaped wooden mask with two long horns, white painted decorations, and a grass fringe, but do not explain how or when it was performed or displayed.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not describe an annual Nalu festival calendar, seasonal celebrations, harvest ceremonies, life-cycle rites, funerals, weddings, initiation ceremonies, or religious rituals. They identify the Simo as a secret society active among the Nalu and related groups, but provide no account of its rites or calendar.

## Foodways

The sources used do not describe Nalu staple foods, dishes, cooking methods, dietary rules, beverages, ceremonial meals, or food-related customs. A museum record identifies an iron-and-wood tool for knocking oysters off mangrove roots, but the sources do not explain its broader use, the preparation of oysters, or the place of oyster gathering in Nalu foodways.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not record Nalu folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, named literary works, storytelling contexts, or contemporary literary preservation efforts. Walter Rodney’s description places the Nalu alongside the Landuma, the Baga, and the Temne as peoples described as “pre-Mandingas,” but the sources provide no Nalu oral narrative connected with this history.

## Language & religion

Nalu, also spelled Nalou and referred to as nalɛ or nul, is an Atlantic language of Guinea and Guinea-Bissau. It is spoken predominantly by adults and is considered endangered because its speaker population is dwindling. The language has six dialects: three spoken in Guinea-Conakry and three in Guinée-Bissau, although the relationship between the dialects is unknown. Most Nalu speakers in Guinea live north of the Nuñez River, on the Tristão islands and around Kanfarandé; in Guinea-Bissau, most live in the Cacine estuary in the Tombali region. Nalu speakers are shifting toward Susu in Guinea, while the language continues to be passed to the next generation in a few remote villages around Katoufoura. The sources do not describe Nalu religious beliefs or practices beyond identifying the Simo as a secret society active among the Nalu and related groups.

## Overview

The Loma, also called Loghoma, Looma, Lorma or Toma, are a West African ethnic group living primarily in mountainous, sparsely populated regions near the border between Guinea and Liberia. Their population in the two countries was estimated at 330,000 in 2010. They speak Loma, a Southwestern Mande language belonging to the Niger-Congo family, and are closely related to the Mende. Loma cultural life documented in the sources includes shifting rice cultivation, patrilineal and exogamous social organization, traditional religion, Poro secret rites of passage, large wooden masks, and a writing script developed in the 1930s.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document Loma textile or pattern traditions.

**Mask carving** — Loma masks are large wooden forms combining animal and human motifs. The largest are about six feet high, with feather decorations, and are associated with forest spirits and Poro secret rites of passage.

**Blackened wooden masks** — Museum catalogue records describe wooden masks from northern Liberia that were blackened. The records state that women of the Lorma group used them and that they belonged to the Sandisällskapet.

**Wooden mask with leather beard** — A museum record describes a wooden mask from Guinea associated with Toma, or Loma, with a beard made of skin.

**Motif vocabulary.** Animal and human motifs, feather decorations, feather finial, looking-glass eyes, amulets, horns, central spike, claws, black fur, brown mud, twigs, bicycle chain.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not document everyday or ceremonial Loma clothing in sufficient detail. One museum record describes a composite hat consisting of a woven textile cap with cowrie shells around the rim, plaster, a pair of horns, numerous tufts of black fur, and lumps of medicine. The same record identifies it as a hat or head-dress, but the sources do not provide a vernacular name, gender attribution, or context of use.

### Architecture

The sources used do not cover Loma architecture, house forms, roofing, settlement design, or named building types.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The museum records document several wooden and mixed-material objects. One object is an implement or weapon with a wooden handle wrapped in skin and fitted with two iron hooks. A pall from Lofa County, Liberia, is made of wood and has a seat with carved decoration. Other catalogue records describe wooden figures used as religious or ritual equipment. One male figure is thickly encrusted with blood, and another is recorded as its pair.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources used do not document Loma jewelry, tattoos, henna, hair practices, or named forms of body adornment. Museum records do mention cowrie shells, amulets, medicine, animal skin, claws, and black fur as components of particular hats and masks.

## Music & performance

The Loma language article records hymns composed in Loma by Billema Kwillia in the 1960s. The missionary Margaret D. Miller recorded them, and the Lutheran Church later adopted them. They first appeared in print in Loma in 1970. The most widely used hymn is “A va de laa”; it was translated into singable English in 2004 and also translated into German. The sources do not name Loma musical instruments, secular song genres, or performance settings beyond this hymn tradition and its connection with the Lutheran Church.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document named Loma dances, dramatic traditions, or theatrical genres. They do document large wooden masks associated with Poro secret rites of passage and museum masks attributed to women of the Lorma group belonging to the Sandisällskapet.

## Festivals & rituals

The Loma have retained their traditional religion and resisted Islamic incursion. The religious conflict with Mandinka people was called a historic “rolling war.” Large wooden masks formed part of Poro secret rites of passage; the largest masks were believed by Loma to have forest spirits. Museum catalogue records also identify male wooden figures as religious or ritual equipment and describe a composite hat with medicine attached to it. The sources used do not provide an annual festival calendar or detailed accounts of birth, marriage, funeral, or other life-cycle ceremonies.

## Foodways

The Loma farm rice in shifting farms. The sources used do not name Loma dishes, cooking methods, beverages, ceremonial foods, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not document Loma epics, folktales, proverbs, riddles, or a literary canon. The Loma language article records a video by the Yale Linguistics Department about a story concerning jealousy delivered in Loma. It also records a video concerning Loma last names. These references do not provide the texts of the story or the naming tradition.

## Language & religion

Loma is a Mande language spoken by the Loma people of Liberia and Guinea. It belongs to the Southwestern branch of the Mande languages and, more broadly, to the Niger-Congo family. Dialects of Loma proper in Liberia are Gizima, Wubomei, Ziema, Bunde, and Buluyiema. In Guinea, the dialects distinguished as Toma are an official regional language. Loma uses a Latin-based alphabet written from left to right. A syllabary saw limited use in the 1930s and 1940s before falling into disuse. The Loma call their language Löömàgòòi, or Löghömàgòòi in Guinea, and refer to themselves as Löömàgìtì or Löghömagiti. Led by Wido Zobo and assisted by the weaver Moriba, they developed a script containing at least 185 characters. The Loma retained traditional religion and resisted Islamic incursion.

- Wesley Sadler, *Untangled Loma: a course of study of the Looma language of the Western Province, Liberia, West Africa*, Board of Foreign Missions of the United Lutheran Church in America for the Evangelical Lutheran Church in Liberia, 1951.

region: "Sub Saharan Africa"

## Overview

The Baoulé, also called Baule, are an Akan people and one of the largest ethnicities in Ivory Coast. They traditionally farm in the centre of the country, in the French braid-shaped Baoule “V” between the rivers Bandama and N'Zi, around Bouaké and Yamoussoukro. The Baoulé language, whose native name is *Wawle*, is a Kwa language of the Akan branch and is spoken in central and southern Ivory Coast, including the regions of Lacs, Lagunes, Gôh-Djiboua, Sassandra-Marahoué, Vallée du Bandama, Woroba, and Yamoussoukro. The language article gives an approximate population of 5.3 million speakers. Baoulé folk culture includes farming, hand-woven textiles, carved wood, masks, figures, goldwork, music, dance, naming practices, and a religious system connecting human, earthly, and spiritual worlds.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Pagne** — The sources identify traditional *pagne* as also known as Kente cloth, but do not describe its specific structure or patterns.

**Hand-woven textiles** — The Baoulé are described as well known for unique hand-woven textiles. The village of Sakiaré is described as having 95% skilled hand-weavers.

**Woman’s wrapper or shawl** — Museum records describe wrappers or shawls made from twelve or eighteen narrow strips hand sewn together. Their materials include hand-spun or machine-spun cotton, indigo-dyed cotton, white cotton ikat, plain white cotton, orange- or red-dyed stripes, supplementary weft float patterns, twined white cotton threads, tassels, and short warp-thread fringes.

**Ikat** — The museum records specifically describe white cotton ikat and ikat in white and orange on indigo. The records do not give a Baoulé vernacular name for the textiles.

**Loom weaving** — The shuttle places the weft yarn between the warp yarns, while the beater pulls the inserted weft forward to secure the fabric. Museum records also identify heddle-pulleys as working elements of a narrow-band loom.

**Heddle-pulley** — Heddle-pulleys are carved wooden loom objects. Recorded examples bear opposing faces, bearded heads, an antelope head, or a top-knot; one Cleveland record identifies a miniature face mask on a pulley.

**Supplementary weft float patterns** — This technique is recorded on the wrappers and shawls, where coloured cotton produces additional surface decoration.

**Motif vocabulary.** Lizard, tortoise, geometric decoration, triangles with angled lines, plant motif, concentric semi-circles, antelope head, bearded head, human head.

### Clothing & dress

The sources describe women’s wrappers or shawls made from sewn strips of cotton decorated with ikat, supplementary weft float patterns, twined threads, tassels, and fringes. A museum record describes a hunter’s cap made of coarse dark brown cotton with a light brown cotton edge, rounded top, triangular flaps, geometric chain-stitch decoration, twisted leather thong decoration, and appliqué. The cap carries 41 pairs of leopard (?) claw charms and five sealed leather pouches described as charms. Museum records also describe a masquerade costume consisting of a polychrome wooden mask, raffia [?] skirt, wrist and ankle bands, and rattles around the ankles. The sources do not describe ordinary footwear, belts, or a separate everyday-versus-ceremonial clothing system.

### Architecture

The sources do not cover Baoulé house forms, village architecture, roofing, building materials, courtyards, or named architectural traditions. They mention a carved wooden door with two panels, the upper panel showing a lizard and the lower panel a tortoise, but provide no architectural context for it.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

The sources do not describe Baoulé ceramics. Wooden everyday and status objects in the museum records include carved doors, stools, cosmetic boxes, fly-whisks, heddle-pulleys, drums, bells, musical instruments, masks, figures, and a hunter’s cap. A stool is carved from one block of wood, with a rectangular curved seat, rectangular base, four circles, and a central pillar. Gold objects include a lost-wax cast pendant and beads; bronze objects include women’s anklets. The sources also mention the machete, used for clearing vegetation and making paddles or canoes from logs, and the snail shell, used for grounding and pounding tobacco and making snuffs.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Museum records describe gold beads, a gold-plated hair-pin, gold-plated spectacles, bronze women’s anklets, and a lost-wax cast gold pendant called *srala/boloa atre*. The pendant is a bi-facial rectangle decorated with alternating triangles, angled lines, and openwork circles. One bead is shaped like a musical horn or leopard tooth; another is elongated and clove-shaped. Recorded figures wear bead necklaces, white bead anklets, bone bead necklaces, and anklets of small bone beads. The sources do not describe tattooing, henna, or hair practices as general customs, although one figure has hair carved into side plaits and another has hair dressed with horns.

## Music & performance

The sources identify drums, a bell, and wooden musical instruments among Baoulé museum objects. One bell is an iron instrument with a separate striker linked by string and a wooden end carved as an antelope’s head. Another wooden musical instrument is shaped as a woman’s head with an elongated neck. A Museum of World Culture record identifies a drum from Toumodi, Côte d’Ivoire, associated with the Baoulé; the record gives a diameter of 21 centimetres and a height of 42 centimetres.

The sources do not provide names for Baoulé song genres, instrumental repertoires, or musical scales. They connect masks with dance types including *goli glin*, *kple kple*, *gbagba* or *mblo*, and *bo nu amuin*. The *gbagba* or *mblo* mask is used in entertainment-based performances consisting of a dance sequence. The *bo nun amuin* mask is danced in times of trouble to protect the village and at important men’s funerals.

## Dance & theatre

Baoulé masks are associated with several named dances. The *goli glin* mask belongs to the goli performance. Its appearance resembles an animal, with horns and a boxy, downward-facing muzzle; vertical bars of varying colours appear around the eyes. At night, women are barred from witnessing the dance and take shelter in their homes, while during the day anyone may watch.

The *kple kple*, also called *kouassi gbe*, is related to the goli masks but is described as mundane. These masks are often worn by children for entertainment and are used in playful and frivolous dancing. They are generally circular or elliptical, with a solid red or black colour, rounding horns, eyes, and a rectangular opening.

The men’s sacred *bo nun amuin* mask is a boxy helmet mask representing a menacing animal with bared teeth. Viewing it is restricted to men; a woman or child who sees it risks serious injury or death. The *gbagba* or *mblo* mask is worn with cloth drapery covering the dancer and is used in entertainment-based performances.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources do not provide an annual Baoulé festival calendar or named seasonal festivals. They describe several ritual contexts. The *bo nun amuin* mask is danced in times of trouble to protect the village and at important men’s funerals. Its dance assists the recent passing of the dead in becoming spirits capable of protecting following generations.

Baoulé religious belief is described through three realities: the Domain of God, *Niamien*; the earthly world of human beings, animals, plants, and supernatural beings living in mountains, rocks, rivers, and forests; and the beyond, *blolo*, where ancestral spirits reside. *Blolo bla*, meaning blolo woman, and *blolo bian*, also called *blolo yasua*, meaning blolo man, are private sculptures representing an individual’s spirit spouse. People make offerings of food and money to these figures because the spirit spouse can influence earthly relationships and personal endeavours.

The sources also describe naming practices. Names can reflect the day of the week or circumstances of birth. The third child in a row is named *I'nsan*, the ninth *N'Goran*, the tenth *Brou*, the eleventh from the same mother *Loukou*, and the twelfth *N'Gbin*.

## Foodways

The staple food of the Ivorian diet is yam. It is boiled, cooled, and mashed. Cassava is also integral to Baoulé cuisine. Yams and maize are stored until needed. Other foods are obtained from local markets, where fish is described as especially important and is wrapped in palm leaves.

The sources state that Ivorians typically eat goat meat, sheep meat, lamb, and chicken, shared by the entire community. Goats are milked and chickens provide eggs. Firewood and yams are transported to local markets, where they are sold with other goods. The sources do not give names for particular Baoulé dishes, cooking vessels, ceremonial foods, tea or coffee traditions, or dietary rules.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources do not describe Baoulé folktales, epic poetry, proverbs, riddles, named storytellers, or contemporary literary preservation projects. They do record the transmission of religious concepts through sculpture, dance, naming, and the interpretation of spiritual beings.

The Baoulé language article records that portions of the Bible translated into Baoulé were first published in 1946, that the full New Testament followed in 1953, and that the complete Bible was first published in 1998 by the Bible Society in Abidjan.

## Language & religion

Baoulé, whose native name is *Wawle*, is an Akan language of the Kwa family and Akan branch. It forms a dialect continuum with Anyin and is closely related to Nzema and Sehwi. The language is spoken in central and southern Ivory Coast, including Lacs, Lagunes, Gôh-Djiboua, Sassandra-Marahoué, Vallée du Bandama, Woroba, and Yamoussoukro. Baoulé has five tones: high, low, mid, rising, and falling. Five vowels may be nasalized.

In school, Baoulé children speak French, while at home they speak Baoulé; French study begins in grade one. The religious world includes *Niamien*, the earthly world, and *blolo*, the realm where ancestral spirits reside. Sculptures can house *zulu*, protective spirits. *Waka sran*, meaning “wooden beings,” provide *zulu* with a bridge between the physical and spirit worlds. *Bo usu* refers to forest spirits and supernatural beings with magical powers; their statues assist hunters in attracting prey.

## Sources & further reading

- The sources mention Alain-Michel Boyer in connection with the meaning of *bo usu*, but provide no full bibliographic record.

- [Baoulé cuisine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baoul%C3%A9_cuisine)

## At a glance
| | |
|---|---|
| Who | The Baoulé, also called Baule, are an Akan people. |
| Where | Central Côte d'Ivoire, between the Bandama and N'Zi rivers, around Bouaké and Yamoussoukro. |
| How many | About 5.3 million Baoulé speakers. |
| Language | Baoulé, or Wawle, an Akan language of the Kwa family. |
| Religion | A three-part spiritual world links God, the earthly world, and ancestral spirits in blolo. |
