## Overview

The Bubi, also known as Bobe, Voove, Ewota and Bantu Bubi, are a Bantu ethnic group indigenous to Bioko Island in Equatorial Guinea. Bubi communities also exist in the diaspora and among Bubi native to Gabon and Cameroon. The group once formed the majority population in the region but now numbers around 100,000 worldwide. The Bubi speak the Bube language, a Bantu language with North, South and Central-East variants. Their cultural history includes regional forms of self-designation, a distinctive language and belief system, Bubi royal dynasties, and material objects recorded from Fernando Po, Gabun or Ogove, and Equatorial Guinea.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources used do not document Bubi textile or pattern traditions.

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no Bubi motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The sources used do not describe everyday or ceremonial clothing, garments, footwear, belts, head coverings, or other dress distinctions. One museum record identifies an armlet formed from plaited strings of small pieces of white shell, and another records a head ornament and necklace made from small pieces of white shell, strong bast and two feathers.

### Architecture

The sources used do not describe Bubi houses, villages, roofs, building materials, architectural decoration, or urban traditions.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Museum records include a bowl made of reddish earthenware with a loop handle. Other recorded household objects are two round baskets with lids. One is identified as a small round basket with a lid, associated with Bubi, Bube and Bubi People, and described by its original label as carrying palm-oil berries. Another is a round basket with a lid from Fernando Po, described as a container for belongings. The catalogue records do not document Bubi metalwork, tools, woodworking traditions, or named vessel forms beyond these objects.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The museum catalogue records several forms of Bubi-associated adornment. An armlet is made from a plait of strings of small pierced white-shell pieces. A head ornament and necklace consist of small pierced white-shell pieces twisted around strong bast, with two feathers attached. The sources do not document tattoos, henna, hair practices, or the ritual meaning of these objects.

## Music & performance

The sources used do not document Bubi musical instruments, song genres, vocal forms, performance settings, or named musical traditions. The Bubi articles describe the Bubi as having developed a distinctive society, language and belief system on Bioko Island, but they provide no specific information about music.

## Dance & theatre

The sources used do not document named Bubi dances, theatrical forms, masked performances, dramatic traditions, or distinctions between ceremonial and entertainment performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The sources used do not provide an annual Bubi festival calendar or describe named seasonal celebrations. They also do not document Bubi birth, coming-of-age, wedding, or funeral rites. Traditional pre-Christian beliefs are described in the religion section of the Bubi article. The Bubi spiritual world was said to include Labako-ppua, heaven and the angels; Ommo ich'ori, hell and the bad angels; and Ommo boeboe, limbo. The head god was called Rupe, or Eri in the southern region of the island. Natural landmarks, including rivers, lakes and mountains, were associated with spirits, while sinister spirits were blamed for illness, accidents and misfortune.

## Foodways

The sources used do not document Bubi staple foods, cooking methods, named dishes, ceremonial foods, beverages, dietary rules, or agricultural practices. One museum catalogue record describes a small round basket with a lid as having been used for carrying palm-oil berries, but it gives no broader account of food production or consumption.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources used do not record Bubi epics, folktales, proverbs, riddles, named storytelling genres, or literary revival projects. Indigenous Bubi folklore is mentioned in connection with migration history: it indicates that the tribe immigrated to Bioko Island some 3,000 years ago as a means of escaping servitude. The sources do not provide the texts, themes or performance contexts of this folklore.

## Language & religion

Bube, also called Bubi, Bohobé, Bube–Benga or Etyö, is a Bantu language spoken predominantly by the Bubi. It was brought to Bioko from continental Africa more than three thousand years ago. The language has around 50,000 speakers and three variants: North, South and Central-East. It is tonal and distinguishes words by gender. The Bube language is divided into six dialects, including Rebola and its variations—Basile, Banapa and Basupa—in the North, and Bakake in the North-East. Bube is also spoken in Gabon and Cameroon and in a small mainland area where speakers are shifting to Wumboko.

The Bubi are mainly Catholics, a religious orientation associated in the source with Spanish influence during the colonial age. Traditional pre-Christian beliefs remain prevalent in Bubi spirituality. Rupe, or Eri in the southern region, was the head god who created and cared for the world. The spiritual and material worlds were understood to overlap.
